0.title: 2 Corinthians: Strength in Weakness
0.overview:
The message. Romans sets out the gospel in order, and Galatians fights for it; Second Corinthians lets us see inside an apostle under attack: opposed by rivals, misunderstood by the church he founded, worn out by suffering, and yet kept going by a grace he cannot fully explain. It is the most autobiographical of Paul’s letters, and its theme is the surprise at the heart of the gospel: God’s strength is shown in our weakness, his treasure is carried in jars of clay (4:7), and life comes through death. The whole letter is gathered up in the word Christ spoke to Paul: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (12:9).

Background: the writer. No one seriously doubts that Paul wrote it, with Timothy named beside him (1:1), from Macedonia in northern Greece, probably in AD 55–56, on the journey that would bring him to Corinth for the winter (Acts 20:1–3). He had come through an affliction in Asia so heavy that he “despaired of life itself” (1:8), and had found no rest at Troas or in Macedonia until Titus arrived (2:12–13; 7:5–7).

Corinth. Corinth stood on the narrow isthmus joining mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a port on each sea, so that trade and travellers poured through it. Destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, it was refounded by Julius Caesar in 44 BC as a Roman colony, settled largely with freedmen, and became the capital of the province of Achaia. It was rich, proud and new, a city where people rose by their own effort and wanted to be seen to have risen, and where status, polished speaking and success counted for a great deal. Teachers of standing were paid or kept by wealthy patrons, and manual work was looked down on. All this shaped how the church judged Paul.

Paul and the church there. Paul founded the church on his second journey, about AD 50–52, staying a year and a half and working at his trade beside Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18:1–11). At least four letters followed. The first, now lost, warned against associating with the sexually immoral (1 Corinthians 5:9); then came 1 Corinthians, from Ephesus; then a short “painful visit” (2:1), in which, most likely, a member of the church openly opposed and humiliated Paul and the church failed to stand with him (2:5; 7:12); then a letter written “with many tears” (2:4; 7:8); and then this one. Titus brought news that it had done its work: most of the church had repented and disciplined the offender, whom Paul now urges them to forgive and restore (2:6–8; 7:6–11). But not all were won. Visiting preachers had arrived with “letters of recommendation” (3:1), proud of their Jewish pedigree (11:22), eloquence and visions, and taking the church’s money (11:20). They called Paul weak in person and unimpressive in speech (10:10), fickle (1:17), and suspect for refusing payment (11:7). Paul calls them “super-apostles” (11:5) and “false apostles” (11:13), preaching “another Jesus” (11:4). Behind it all lay the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, which Corinth had begun eagerly a year before (8:10; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4) and then let stall.

One letter or several? Many scholars think 2 Corinthians was stitched together from several letters, especially that chapters 10–13, where the tone changes so sharply, were part of the tearful letter or a later one; some also take 6:14–7:1, or chapters 8 and 9, as separate pieces. But no manuscript ever divides the letter or lacks any part of it. The tearful letter was written to grieve them over an offence (2:4–5), which chapters 10–13 never mention. And the change of tone is explained by Paul turning from the repentant majority to the minority still listening to the false apostles. This commentary reads 2 Corinthians as one letter, and takes the tearful letter to be lost. What followed shows the outcome: Paul spent that winter in Corinth, probably wrote Romans there, and could report that Achaia had given to the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26).

How the letter makes its case. It falls into three movements. Chapters 1–7: ministry, suffering and reconciliation. Paul blesses the God of all comfort and explains his changed plans (1:1–2:13), then breaks off his travel story to describe the ministry itself (2:14–7:4): a captive in Christ’s triumphal procession; a minister of the new covenant, whose glory outshines the fading glory on the face of Moses (chapter 3); a clay jar carrying a treasure, outwardly wasting away, inwardly renewed (chapter 4); an ambassador of reconciliation, walking by faith toward the judgment seat of Christ and the resurrection body (chapter 5); a servant commended by hardship and calling the church to holiness (6:1–7:1). The story resumes at 7:5 with Titus’s good news. Chapters 8–9: the collection. The poor Macedonians gave beyond their means; Christians give because Christ, though rich, became poor for them (8:9), and “God loves a cheerful giver” (9:7). Chapters 10–13: Paul’s defence against the false apostles. He fights with weapons that “destroy strongholds” (10:4), plays the fool to expose his rivals’ boasting, boasts instead of his sufferings, his escape over the Damascus wall and his thorn in the flesh (chapters 11–12), and warns that on his third visit he will not spare those who persist (chapter 13).

Where it leads: to Christ. “All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (1:20). The new covenant written by the Spirit “on tablets of human hearts” (3:3) is the one promised through Jeremiah and Ezekiel; the veil that lay over Moses’ face, and still lies over hearts, is removed when one turns to the Lord (3:16). The God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” at creation has shone in our hearts “in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6), and “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (5:17). At the centre stands the great exchange: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (5:21). And the shape of Paul’s ministry is the shape of his Lord’s: Christ “was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (13:4). Paul’s rivals measured an apostle by eloquence, presence and spectacular experiences. Paul measures him by the cross, “always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies” (4:10). This is not just Paul’s way of coping. It is how the kingdom of God advances: through servants whose lives take the shape of the cross.

For us. The church still admires what Corinth admired: polish, platform and visible power. This letter frees us from measuring ourselves or our leaders that way. Suffering is not a sign that God has left you; he promises not health and wealth but comfort in affliction (1:3–4) and a grace that is sufficient. Paul asked three times for the thorn to be taken away, and the answer was not removal but a greater gift (12:8–9). So you can be “afflicted in every way, but not crushed” (4:8), because “this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (4:17). You have a message to carry, “be reconciled to God” (5:20), and a reason to give freely. And in your own weakness, the very thing you are tempted to hide, Christ’s power is pleased to rest: “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (12:10).

1.title: The God of All Comfort and the Yes of Christ
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens Paul’s most personal letter. After the greeting he begins the account of his recent troubles and travels (1:1–2:13), which he will interrupt at 2:14 to describe the ministry itself.

The message. God’s power shows up in weakness, and his word never wavers. The Father of mercies meets his people inside their afflictions and comforts them so that they can comfort others; he takes them past the end of their own strength to teach them to rely on the God who raises the dead. And because every promise of God has found its Yes in Christ, his people are held firm by God himself.

Why it was said. After a painful visit, a tearful letter and a crushing affliction in Asia, Paul’s rivals in Corinth were calling him weak and unreliable: he had changed his plans, so why trust his word, or his gospel? (See the introduction.)

How the chapter makes its case. The greeting lays the foundation: Paul is an apostle “by the will of God”, and the troubled congregation is still “the church of God” (vv. 1–2). Instead of complaining, Paul blesses the God of all comfort, whose consolation overflows through Christ and is passed from hand to hand (vv. 3–7). He tells of Asia, where he despaired of life itself and learned to rely on God who raises the dead (vv. 8–11). Then he answers the charge of fickleness: his conscience is clear (vv. 12–14); his plans did change (vv. 15–17); but his word rests on God’s faithfulness, whose promises are all Yes in Christ and who has sealed his people with the Spirit (vv. 18–22). He stayed away to spare them, as a helper of their joy, not a master of their faith (vv. 23–24).

Where it leads. Everything runs through Christ. The comfort overflows “through Christ” (v. 5); the God Paul trusts at the edge of death is the God who raised Jesus; and the answer to a quarrel over a travel diary is the Son of God himself, God’s unwavering Yes, in whom every promise to Abraham, to David and through the prophets has been kept.

For us. Suffering is not proof that God has left you, and weakness is not proof that a servant of Christ is a fraud. Bring your afflictions to the God of all comfort, pass on what he gives you, and rest your assurance not on your own grip but on the God who has sealed you with his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God of All Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God comforts his people in their afflictions, so that they can comfort others and learn to rely on him alone. Paul names himself an apostle by God’s will, the very point his critics dispute, and greets a troubled church as still God’s church (vv. 1–2). Then, instead of complaining about a terrible year, he blesses the Father of mercies, whose comfort overflows through Christ as fully as the suffering and is handed on from one believer to another (vv. 3–7). His near-death in Asia shows what the suffering was for: to make him rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead, who has delivered and will deliver, helped by the prayers of the church (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The title “Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (v. 3) is carefully built (see the note on v. 3).

In vv. 4–7 suffering and comfort are bound together in ministry: those comforted in their own trouble have something to give that ease cannot supply (see the notes on vv. 4 and 6).
verseByVerse.examples:
A pastor who has come through a severe depression returns to ministry and finds that his care for depressed people has changed. He is not applying techniques; he is giving what he has received, and his people sense it.

Verse 11 shows the same thing the other way round: the church helping its apostle. A member who has never taught or led prays through the week for a missionary she has met once; what her praying does, and why she should hear how God answered, is the subject of the note on v. 11.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes as an apostle sent by God’s will to a church that, for all its faults, still belongs to God. Each phrase of the greeting quietly answers the doubts some in Corinth had about him, and it ends by wishing grace and peace on people who had hurt him.

An apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God. Every letter Paul wrote begins by naming himself, but here “by the will of God” holds the whole letter’s argument in brief. It was read aloud to people some of whom had been told, by teachers with better credentials and a better manner, that he was unimpressive, inconsistent, possibly a fraud (see the introduction). The first thing they hear is where his commission came from: not from a committee, not from Jerusalem, not from the Corinthians, who might therefore withdraw it, but from God. That is not vanity: if his standing came from their approval, their disapproval would end it. So he puts his authority where his critics cannot reach it (Galatians 1:1).

And Timothy our brother. Not “my assistant”. Timothy had helped to found the church in Corinth (Acts 18:5) and been sent back to it (1 Corinthians 4:17). The man defending his own apostolic authority does not use it to raise himself above the young man beside him.

The church of God. The words “of God” are startling. This congregation had split into factions, tolerated incest, sued one another in pagan courts, got drunk at the Lord’s Supper and quarrelled over spiritual gifts, and it is still the church of God. It is at Corinth the way a ship is at anchor: located there, not owned there. Whatever it is like on a bad Sunday, its title deed is not in the hands of the people who spoil it; God does not wait for a church to deserve his name before he writes it on the door.

The whole of Achaia. The Roman province of southern Greece: Athens, Cenchreae (Romans 16:1), and the scattered believers in between. Paul’s most wounded words would be read well beyond Corinth.

Grace to you and peace. Grace is God giving what was not earned; peace is what grace produces when it lands: the war over, the relationship restored. They come “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”, as from one source. Only God can give grace, yet Paul names the Son beside the Father as its giver and feels no need to explain: the Son is God. A letter soaked in tears opens by wishing on his critics the two things Paul most needs himself.

Sent by the Sent One. Apostle means one sent, and the sender matters more than the messenger. Paul was sent by the risen Christ himself (Acts 26:16–18), and Christ was the Sent One before him, “the apostle and high priest of our confession” (Hebrews 3:1), sent not in splendour but in weakness. Paul’s authority is borrowed from a Lord who “was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (13:4), and a messenger of that Lord should not be surprised to look unimpressive.

When the ground moves. Anyone who has served in a church for long has felt it: the elder quietly criticised, the pastor who learns that a group has been meeting to discuss him. The temptation is to build a case and reclaim the room. But if God put you where you are, the room’s good opinion was never what was holding you up.

Should I leave a church that has hurt me, or that is in a mess? Not simply because it is a mess. Every church is made of sinners, and Paul did not abandon Corinth when it divided, misjudged him and listened to his rivals; he wrote, prayed, wept and waited. Ordinary failures, poor leadership, hurt feelings and secondary disagreements call for work and prayer, not departure. But there are real reasons to leave: where the gospel itself is denied, where open sin is defended and never disciplined, or where abuse is covered up and victims are silenced. Abuse must never be tolerated, and no one is bound to sit under it. If you go, go honestly, without slander, and join another faithful church rather than none.

In everyday life. Think of the person in your congregation with whom things are strained. Before you rehearse your case against them, say to God: they belong to you, not to me. Then wish them, in prayer and if possible in person, grace and peace.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, after a painful visit to Corinth and a severe letter written “with many tears.” Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins his account of a terrible year not with complaint but with praise, blessing God as the Father of all compassion and the source of every comfort.

In the flow. In most letters Paul follows the greeting by thanking God for his readers (1 Corinthians 1:4). Here he blesses God for what God has done for him in affliction, and lays down the theme the whole letter will defend: God’s comfort comes through suffering, not around it, and his power shows itself in weakness (4:7–12; 12:9–10).

Blessed be the God. Blessed (eulogētos) is the opening of Jewish prayer, barukh attah Adonai, blessed are you, Lord (Ephesians 1:3; 1 Peter 1:3). Paul has just come through a burden beyond his strength, and the first thing out of his mouth is a blessing. He fills the old Jewish form with the name of Jesus: every comfort in this chapter is the Father’s, reaching us through his Son.

The Father of mercies. Mercies, or compassions (oiktirmoi). Behind it stands the Hebrew rahamim, from the word for a womb: what a mother feels when her child is hurt, the movement toward the pain before any decision has been made. “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13). Compassion is not something God occasionally does. He is its Father.

And God of all comfort. Comfort (paraklēsis), as noun or verb, appears ten times in five verses, and English has weakened it into a warm drink and a soft chair. The Greek means to be summoned to someone’s side: what a defence counsel does in court, what a friend does on the edge of your bed at two in the morning, strengthening as well as consoling. Its cousin is paraklētos, the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit (John 14:16). Such comfort does not remove the trouble. It puts someone beside you in it, and the someone is God (Isaiah 40:1).

All. Not the God of some comfort. Every real consolation you have received, the friend who said the right thing, the sleep that finally came, the verse that surfaced in a sleepless hour, the hand on your shoulder outside the ward, came out of his treasury. Those were not distractions from God while you waited for him to act. They were God acting.

Of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Father of mercies is the Father of Jesus, and in Jesus the mercies were seen. Meeting a widow following her only son’s body out of Nain, “he had compassion on her and said to her, ‘Do not weep’” (Luke 7:13): the womb-deep pity of God, walking in human flesh to a funeral. And the God of all comfort proved his name finally not by sparing his Son but by giving him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Paul is not thanking God for suffering but blessing the God he found inside it, because the Son had gone into suffering first. When the strength ran out, there was Someone already alongside, whose compassion is not a decision but a nature, and whose consolation has no bottom. He has never once been found to be less than his names.

What it does not mean. Not that God removes all suffering; he comforts us in it. Nor that every comfortable feeling is from God: the comfort of a lie, of a drink, of a sin that numbs the pain for an evening, is counterfeit. God’s comfort always leaves you nearer to him and more truthful about your life.

What if I do not feel comforted? You have not been passed over. Comfort here is not first a feeling but a presence: God summoned to your side. Feelings of consolation often come late, and Paul is writing from the far side. Meanwhile, go where God has promised to meet you: his word read and heard, the prayers of others, the Lord’s Supper, the friend who will sit with you without fixing anything. Tell God plainly that you do not feel him; the Psalms do it constantly (Psalm 13:1; 88). The God of all comfort is not offended by the honesty. He is the one who prompted it.

parallels.desc: I, I am he who comforts you

verseByVerse.quote: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God comforts us in every trouble so that we can pass his comfort on to others in theirs. The key words are “so that”: comfort received is comfort to be given.

Who comforts us in all our affliction. Affliction is thlipsis, from a verb meaning to press or crush: the pressure of a weight. God comforts us in affliction, not only by taking us out of it.

So that we may be able. What we give away is “the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God”, the same substance, handed on, like water in a bucket line, and the God at the head of the line has more. He could have consoled each of his children privately. Instead he has built his family so that his comfort travels from hand to hand, and the weakest believer who has been held by him becomes a carrier of his consolation to another.

All and any. God comforts us in all our affliction so that we can comfort those in any affliction. The woman who was carried through a bereavement is not disqualified from sitting with the man losing his business, because what she has to give is not a technique specific to grief. It is God. So “I have never been through what she is going through” is no objection: the qualification is not that you have suffered the same thing, but that you have been comforted by God, and the currency you hand over is his. You are not being asked to be wise. You are being asked to be there, with what you were given.

The first link in the chain. The chain begins not with Paul but with the one old Simeon was waiting for when he looked for “the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25), and Luke’s word there is Paul’s, paraklēsis. Christ is the comfort of God in person, and he walked the road this verse describes: “because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18). Every comfort handed along a line of believers was first drawn from him, which is why Paul says next that comfort overflows through Christ (v. 5).

Nothing wasted. God comforted you through your hardest stretch not merely so that you would feel better but so that you would be able, and somebody two rows behind you on Sunday may be going through it now. If you are still too bruised to give anything, that is no failure: a bucket is filled before it is passed, and God is not in a hurry with you. There is a harder implication too: some of what God allows into your life is allowed for someone else’s sake, as verse 6 says outright. That does not make you a training exercise, for God loves you for your own sake. It means nothing in it will be wasted: not the sleepless nights, not the questions you could not answer, not even the months you handled it badly. Paul’s opponents looked at a beaten, imprisoned, shipwrecked man and concluded that God was plainly not blessing his ministry. Paul looks at the same evidence and sees not the damage to his ministry but the making of it (12:9).

What do I actually say to someone who is suffering? Often less than you think. Go, and stay; presence is most of it. Say that you are sorry and that you are praying, and then pray, with them if they welcome it. Listen more than you speak, and do not rush to explain why it happened or to promise it will be all right; Job’s friends did best in the week they said nothing (Job 2:13). Offer specific help rather than a general “let me know”: a meal on Thursday, a lift to the hospital, an hour with the children. In time, share briefly what God was to you in your own dark place, and point them to his promises rather than your story. Then keep coming back after everyone else has stopped.

parallels.desc: as one whom his mother comforts

verseByVerse.quote: For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The more believers suffer for Christ, the more comfort flows to them through Christ. Suffering and comfort overflow together, and the comfort never falls behind.

We share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings. Literally, the sufferings of Christ overflow to us. Did the cross leave something outstanding? No. His atoning work is finished and unrepeatable: “a single sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12, 14); “It is finished” (John 19:30). Nothing you suffer adds a gram to the payment for your sin. Paul’s “filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions” (Colossians 1:24) does not top up the atonement; it means that the Messiah’s sufferings spill over into the age of the church through the people who carry his message (1 Peter 4:13). The cross was a payment once for all, but it is also a pattern: its Lord shapes the life of his people to match it, so that being brought low and raised up again is not an interruption of the Christian life but its normal rhythm.

Why are you persecuting me? The risen Christ did not say to Saul, “Why are you persecuting my followers?” He said “me” (Acts 9:4): the Head feels what happens to the body. Our pain does not complete his; our pain is drawn inside his.

Through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too. Two things follow for a suffering believer in the middle of the night. First, the measure is exact: “share abundantly” is used of both, so the comfort overflows at the same rate as the sufferings. That is not a promise that the pain will be small, but that it will never outrun the supply. If the flood rises, so does the boat. Second, the channel is named: through Christ. It is not sent from a distance by a God who has only heard about suffering, but comes through the one whose friends fell asleep while he prayed, who was misrepresented at his trial, deserted by those closest to him, and cried out that God had forsaken him. There is no experience of yours that he learned about second-hand. He goes first into every dark place his people are asked to enter, and he comes out. His suffering for sin is finished, and nothing can be added to it; his sympathy is not finished, and nothing can wear it out.

Which sufferings count? Paul means chiefly what comes upon a person for the sake of Christ and his gospel. But do not draw that line too tightly. He is not building a hierarchy of holy pain; he is telling a church that despises weakness that their apostle’s sufferings are not evidence against him but the family likeness. And every trouble borne in faith by someone joined to Christ is borne in fellowship with him, who sympathises with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

Should a Christian go looking for suffering? No. Paul used lawful means to escape danger: he was lowered over a wall in a basket (11:33) and appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25). Suffering is not a merit badge, and inflicting it on yourself has no value before God (Colossians 2:23). What Paul refused was to avoid suffering at the cost of faithfulness. Do not court it; do not dodge it by denying Christ. When it comes because you belong to him, receive it as fellowship with him, and expect his comfort to overflow in proportion.

verseByVerse.quote: If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever happens to Paul, affliction or comfort, God turns it to the good of the church. His sufferings and his consolations both become theirs, as they endure the same pressures.

For your comfort and salvation. While the Corinthians compared their apostle unfavourably with more impressive teachers, he was being crushed in Asia, and his reading of it is that the crushing was on their account, in two ways. First, as in v. 4, what he receives in affliction he hands on, which is why the sentence works just as well the other way round: “and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort”. His bad years are their supply. Second, a watching church learns how much weight the gospel can bear by seeing what it carries a man through. Doctrine held under no pressure teaches nothing. When the Corinthians heard that Paul had been beyond his strength and had not let go of Christ, they were handed evidence about the strength of the one he was holding. His sufferings had also brought them the gospel in the first place (Acts 18:6–10; 1 Corinthians 2:3).

When you patiently endure. The comfort is not received by studying Paul’s hardships from a safe distance, but where the same pressure bears on you. The word is hypomonē, steadfast endurance: not gritted teeth and not resignation, but staying put under a weight instead of crawling out from under it. God’s comfort is not found by the man who has arranged his life to avoid all pressure. It is found by the one who stayed.

The same sufferings. Most believers will never be flogged for the gospel. They will be passed over at work for being honest, lose a friendship over what they believe, or carry a chronic illness for thirty years. Paul does not put his trials in one category and their smaller griefs in another: whatever is borne under the pressure of belonging to Christ draws on the same comfort.

The shape of the Servant. The shape of this sentence belongs first to Christ, afflicted for the comfort and salvation of others in a sense no apostle shares: “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (Isaiah 53:5). Paul’s sufferings save no one. But his life has been bent into the same shape on a smaller scale: “death is at work in us, but life in you” (4:12). A servant of the Crucified ends up living for others because his Master died for them.

In everyday life. Somebody is watching how you carry the illness, the loss, the long wait. You do not have to perform cheerfulness. But let them see where you go with it: that you still pray, still come to worship, still say that God is good while the tears are real.

Is it wrong to pray for my suffering to end? No. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed (12:8), and Jesus prayed, “if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). Asking for relief is a child speaking to his Father, not a failure of faith. What Paul adds is that while the answer is not yet, the suffering is not empty. Pray for the trouble to lift, and pray too that while it lasts it will do its work, in you and in those who are watching.

Textual note. Manuscripts arrange the clauses of verses 6–7 a little differently, so the King James Version’s order differs from modern Bibles; the meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s hope for this troubled church stands firm, because God never takes his people into suffering without bringing them to comfort.

Our hope for you is unshaken. The word is bebaia: firm, secured, used of a legally binding contract. His hope is not a wish but a settled expectation, and it is for the congregation of 1 Corinthians: lawsuits, incest, drunkenness at the Lord’s table, factions, and since then a visit too painful to repeat and a letter written in anguish. If any pastor ever had grounds for giving up on a church, it was this one.

You will also share in our comfort. His confidence is not in their record but in how God deals with his people: he never takes anyone into the affliction without taking them through to the consolation. Paul is sure of them because he is sure of God. “Share” is koinōnoi, partners: apostle and church are in this together, with no line between the man in the pulpit and the people in the seats.

Into the fellowship of his Son. In his first letter, before a word about their scandals, Paul told them that God “will sustain you to the end”, for “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” (1 Corinthians 1:8–9). Apostle and church are both joined to Christ, and his sufferings and consolation run through all of them. Paul’s hope rests not on Corinth but on the Son into whose life Corinth has been called. Jesus has gone ahead as a forerunner behind the curtain (Hebrews 6:19–20), where none of us can reach to loosen the anchor. He has never yet brought a child of his into affliction and left him there, and his word is not “may” but “will”.

Who have you written off? Hope that rests on a person’s performance is worn out by the second or third disappointment. Hope that rests on God’s character survives the failures, because it was never resting on the record. The question is not whether they deserve better, but whether the God who has not finished with you has finished with them.

What if the comfort has not come and it has been a long time? Then hold to the tense Paul uses: “you will also share”. It is a certainty about the future, not a description of how you feel tonight. Some comfort comes quickly; some in small portions that only add up in hindsight; and some is kept for the morning of the resurrection, when God will wipe away every tear. Meanwhile do not suffer in secret. Tell a pastor or a trusted friend, let the church carry you, and keep putting yourself where God speaks. “Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning” (Psalm 30:5).

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul tells the church plainly that in Asia he was crushed beyond his strength, until he despaired of life itself. An apostle is not ashamed to say that he reached the end of himself.

The affliction we experienced in Asia. The apostle who sang hymns at midnight with his back opened by rods (Acts 16:22–25) says plainly that he came to the end. Asia is the Roman province around Ephesus (on what happened there, see below), and “brothers” includes the sisters of the church.

Burdened beyond our strength. Burdened is bareō, weighed down; utterly is kath’ hyperbolēn, beyond all proportion; beyond our strength is hyper dynamin, past the limit of what he could carry. And despaired is exaporeomai, utterly at a loss: no exit visible in any direction. He could see no way he was coming out of it alive, and he stopped expecting to.

Oxygen for the despairing. Some Christians have come to a place where they no longer wanted to be alive, and have carried on top of that darkness the conviction, often learned from those who call despair unbelief, that a real believer could never get there. This verse takes that conclusion away. The man who despaired of life itself wrote Romans 8. He was not backslidden when it happened; he was in the middle of one of the most fruitful ministries the church has known. And he was not ashamed of it afterwards: he wrote it down, to a church that already thought him too weak, knowing they would read it aloud.

The saints have been here. Elijah asked to die (1 Kings 19:4). Jeremiah cursed the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14). The psalmist ended a psalm with darkness as his closest friend (Psalm 88:18), and God put it in the hymnbook. The Bible does not hand us a faith that floats above the water, but one that has been to the bottom, so that no believer who goes down there would ever think he was the first.

Loud cries and tears. The deepest place in this company belongs to Christ. In Gethsemane his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Mark 14:34), and he “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7). He was not spared death; the answer came on the third day, when God raised him. A believer crushed beyond his strength is on a road the Saviour has already walked, prayed on and come out of alive.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul lost his faith; he lost hope in himself. Nor does it contradict 1 Corinthians 10:13. That verse is about temptation to sin: God will never put you where obedience is impossible and sinning is your only option. It is not a promise that you will never be given more suffering than you can carry. Paul says here that he was, and the next verse says what that weight was for.

In everyday life. If you are the one who is well, look around. Someone in your church may be carrying a weight like this behind a smile. Ask them how they actually are, and wait for the answer.

Is depression a sign of weak faith, and should a Christian get help? Darkness of mind is not in itself a sign of weak faith; Paul, Elijah and the psalmists knew it. Sometimes it has spiritual causes, such as unconfessed sin or bitterness, but often causes in the body, in grief, in exhaustion or in trauma. Seek help, as you would for any illness. Tell your pastor and a trusted friend, and seek out a biblical counsellor, through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation (for example ACBC or CCEF in the US, Biblical Counselling UK in Britain). A good biblical counsellor will ask you to have a medical check-up, so that any bodily cause is found and treated, and will then help you work through the struggle itself from God’s Word, which is sufficient for what you face. If the doctor recommends treatment, do not be ashamed of it; using means is not distrusting God, any more than Paul’s advice to Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach was (1 Timothy 5:23). And if you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today and contact emergency help now. You are not a burden to God’s people. You are one of them.

Uncertain wording. Paul does not say what “the affliction we experienced in Asia” was. The riot in Ephesus recorded in Acts 19:23–41 is the usual guess; some think of a near-fatal illness, others of an imprisonment or a plot we have no record of. What is clear is that it brought him close to death. The silence may be a mercy: a named crisis would let the reader file it under somebody else’s category, but as it stands, whatever is crushing you fits the gap.
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not say what the danger in Asia was; it may have been the riot at Ephesus, severe illness or another threat.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God let Paul come to the point of death so that he would stop relying on himself and rely on the God who raises the dead. The crushing was not random; it was aimed at his self-reliance.

The sentence of death. The sentence (apokrima) was used in official documents for a ruling given in answer to a petition. This is not a mood. It is a man who has heard the judgment read out and knows the appeal has failed.

But that was to make us rely not on ourselves. Here everything turns. Paul is not saying that every affliction comes with an explanation attached, nor handing us a sentence to say breezily at a funeral. He is saying, looking back, that the crushing had a target. Paul had training, languages, stamina and intellect, and a man with resources never discovers what God can do where they run out until he is taken past the end of himself.

But on God who raises the dead. At the moment of extremity he names God not as the one who prevents death or explains it, but as God who raises the dead: a God whose power still works after the sentence has been carried out. Abraham trusted him when his own body was as good as dead, believing in the God “who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17), and he reasoned that God could raise Isaac from the dead (Hebrews 11:19). Paul is not comforting himself that he will probably survive. Either way, the God he serves has already emptied one tomb and has committed himself to emptying the rest (1 Corinthians 15:20). Death is not where his power stops. It is where it was displayed.

The sentence carried out. Paul felt that he had received the sentence of death. Christ received it in fact: he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and the stone was rolled across a grave with the case closed. Then the God who raises the dead raised him. For those in Christ the worst verdict has already been executed on their Substitute, so the death they still face is no longer a sentence but a doorway.

Why resilience is not enough. Our culture’s gospel for hard times is resilience: build your inner resources, reframe the setback, bounce back. Some of it is common sense, and some very old: the Stoic Epictetus taught that peace comes from attending only to what lies within our own power. But every version assumes that the resources for surviving the worst are somewhere inside you. Paul found no hidden reserves at the bottom; he found there were none, and that this was the point. No amount of inner strength bounces back from the grave. Paul’s God does not wait until our strength runs low and then top it up. He raises the dead. You do not need to be strong enough. You need only to be held by someone who is.

Where does your confidence rest? Not the answer you would give in a Bible study, but the one your body gives at three in the morning. When bad news arrives, what do you reach for first: the savings, the contacts, the plan? God gave them, and they are good. But if you have never once been past the end of them, you do not yet know from experience whether the God you profess actually holds. Paul knows. It cost him everything he had to find out.

How do I learn to rely on God and not on myself? It is usually taught in places we did not choose. Timothy Keller often pointed out, in Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, that suffering tends to show us what we have really been resting our weight on, by taking it away. A few things help. Name what you were leaning on. Tell God honestly: I was counting on my health, my savings, my plan. Go to him first, before the phone calls and the spreadsheet, not instead of them. Measure the trouble by the resurrection. The power at work for those who believe is the power God worked in Christ “when he raised him from the dead” (Ephesians 1:20); set your trouble beside that. Take the next step, not the whole road. Ask for today’s bread (Matthew 6:11) and do today’s duty. This is not a test you pass by trusting hard enough. Christ has already gone past the end of every human resource, into death itself, and come out the other side, and he holds you there.

Does God send my suffering, or only allow it? God is truly sovereign over our troubles, not a bystander who reacts to them. Nothing reaches his child by accident; even what others mean for evil, God means for good (Genesis 50:20), and he works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Yet he is never the author of sin, and the cruelty of people or of Satan remains theirs. Scripture holds both together without explaining every case. For the sufferer, what is happening is not meaningless and not out of control. It is in the hands of a Father whose purpose is to bring you to rely on him, and finally to raise you from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who rescued Paul from death will rescue him again, so Paul has fixed his hope on him. Past deliverance is evidence for future deliverance.

He delivered us … and he will deliver us. The same verb three times: he delivered, he will deliver, he will deliver again. The word is rhyomai: to drag someone clear, as a man pulls a child out from under a falling wall. Because God did it, God will do it. We have astonishingly short memories for mercy: we can be delivered in March and be certain by August that God has abandoned us, because we never wrote March down (Psalm 78:11).

On him we have set our hope. The Greek tense describes a decision that still stands, a stake driven into the ground. Between verse 8 and verse 10 nothing in Paul’s circumstances has changed. What has changed is what he is looking at.

The deliverance behind every deliverance. The deepest memory a Christian has is not his own: it is of “Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come” (1 Thessalonians 1:10), the same verb. If God has pulled you out from under the greatest weight of all, his judgment against your sin, he will not leave you under the smaller ones; the God who did not spare his own Son will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32). Every deliverance in a believer’s life is a small rehearsal of the final one, when the God who raised Jesus will raise us also (4:14).

What about the times he does not deliver? This must not be dodged. Perhaps a decade after writing this, Paul was beheaded under Nero, as the early church remembered it. The answer is in the title of verse 9: a God “who raises the dead” has a wider definition of rescue than we do. Paul wrote to Timothy at the end, from prison: “The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom” (2 Timothy 4:18). He did not expect to be released. He meant that the sword would be the last thing that ever happened to him, and that on the far side of it he would be safe. God does not always deliver us from death; sometimes he delivers us through it. Not one child of God has ever failed to arrive.

How do I build this kind of memory? Keep a record. Write down, in a notebook or at the back of your Bible, the specific things God has carried you through and the prayers he has answered, with dates. Tell them to your children and to younger believers, as Israel was commanded to do (Psalm 78:4). Sing the hymns and psalms that rehearse his faithfulness. And when a new trouble comes, read the record before you decide what God is like. The facts on that page are part of the evidence.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, put the middle verb in the present (“and doth deliver”); the earliest have the future, as most modern Bibles do.

verseByVerse.quote: You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church’s prayers really share in the work of Paul’s rescue, and God’s answer will fill many mouths with thanks.

You also must help us by prayer. To join in helping (synypourgeō): several people getting their shoulders under the same load. Paul treats the prayers of ordinary Corinthians as genuine labour applied to his survival. Somewhere in Corinth a believer with no gift anyone could name, no money and no standing was putting a shoulder under an apostle’s survival in Asia. The work of the church is done by people whose names are not recorded, and the God who keeps the record has never once mislaid one of them.

So that many will give thanks. Not “so that I will be delivered” but “so that many will give thanks”. Paul wants the prayer list long because he wants the choir large. The blessing is charisma, a gift of grace: even the answer to prayer is a gift, not wages, and it gives the church something to praise God for.

Behind the prayers of many. These prayers rise to the Father through a Son who always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Before Peter fell, Jesus told him that he had prayed for him, that his faith might not fail (Luke 22:32), and the same Lord carries Paul’s name before the Father now. The Corinthians’ prayers are joined to his, which is why they bear weight at all, and even the thanksgiving Paul longs for will rise through him (1:20).

In everyday life. Tell people what to pray for, and then tell them what happened; a congregation that never hears the outcomes is being robbed of the best half. Pray today for a missionary or pastor in difficulty, by name; then find out how God answers, and give thanks aloud.

If God has decided, what does prayer change? If God had already decided to deliver Paul, did the praying change anything, and if so, is God being steered by us? Scripture’s answer is not that God is persuadable but that he is generous. He ordains the end and the means to it, and he has chosen to make the prayers of his people one of the means. A father who could carry the box himself asks the four-year-old to take the other end, and the child really is carrying it. Nothing is pretended: the father wants the child in the work, not merely watching. So the deliverance was God’s from first to last, and it came through the prayers of many, and both halves of that sentence are true.

Does it matter how many people pray? Yes, but not because God is out-voted. God hears the single prayer of a lonely believer as surely as the prayer of a thousand (James 5:16–18). But he has made us a body, and he loves to answer in a way that draws many into the asking and many into the praise. So do ask others to pray for you; it is not weakness or self-importance. And when you are asked, pray, and later ask how it turned out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–24 — The Yes of God in Christ and Paul’s Changed Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s word can be trusted because the God he preaches is faithful, and his changed plans came from love, not fickleness. He appeals first to a clear conscience and to letters that mean exactly what they say (vv. 12–14), then admits the changed travel plan and denies that he says Yes and No at once (vv. 15–17). His real answer lifts the quarrel to God himself: the Son of God is God’s unwavering Yes, every promise is kept in him, and God establishes, anoints and seals his people with the Spirit (vv. 18–22). And he stayed away to spare them, because he works for their joy and does not lord it over their faith (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
“All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (v. 20) is a key to reading the Old Testament (see the note on vv. 18–20). Not every Old Testament text is directly about Jesus, but the whole line of God’s promise reaches its destination in him.

Verses 21–22 show the Trinity at work in assurance: the Father establishes, the anointing is shared with Christ, and the Spirit is given as seal and down payment (each is treated in the note on vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.examples: A church member accuses her pastor of inconsistency when he changes a plan he had announced. He can do what Paul does: show plainly that the change came from care for those affected (on integrity and changed plans, see the note on vv. 15–17).

verseByVerse.quote: For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand— just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul can face his critics with a clear conscience: he has lived and written among them with transparent sincerity, and he looks to the day of Christ, when each will be the other’s boast.

For our boast is this. The tone changes as Paul turns to what his critics have been saying: that the real Paul was different from the Paul of the letters, that he wrote one thing and meant another. His answer begins with “boast”, a word he will use with open, painful irony in chapters 10 to 12. When a minister’s integrity is publicly dismantled, silence is not humility; it leaves his people with no ground to stand on.

The testimony of our conscience. Not the verdict of the Corinthians, which is divided, nor his self-assessment, which proves nothing (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Conscience watches what we do when nobody is looking, and Paul’s is not accusing him.

Simplicity and godly sincerity. Simplicity (haplotēs) is singleness, being one thing rather than two; its opposite is the man in the pulpit and the different man in the car afterwards. Godly sincerity is eilikrineia, purity of motive, a word the ancients liked to explain as “judged by sunlight”: held up to the sun and found flawless. Hold my ministry to the light, Paul says; it will bear inspection. And it was “not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God”: he is boasting about something he received.

What you read and understand. Some said Paul’s letters had hidden meanings. What the letter says on the surface is what he means underneath, with no code and no second layer for insiders. Plain speech is a form of love, because it refuses to make the other person guess.

On the day of our Lord Jesus. They understand him only partially now; on that day the misunderstanding will be finished on both sides, and each will boast of the other, glad before Christ for what God did through the other (Philippians 2:16; 1 Thessalonians 2:19–20), all of it praise to the Lord who did it.

Treated as impostors. The charge against Paul was first laid against his Lord: “that impostor” (Matthew 27:63), though no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22). He was the one man wholly single-hearted, the same within as without, and he went to the cross misjudged and left the verdict with God, who gave it on the third day. The simplicity Paul claims is the grace of the one sincere man, given to his servant.

When you cannot clear your name. Some people will go to their graves with the wrong idea of you. Paul puts the date of the hearing in the future and leaves it there (1 Corinthians 4:5). Until then the need to be thought well of can rule a heart as surely as money can. The only cure is a verdict that matters more, and in Christ the Judge has already given it: there is now no condemnation for those who are in him (Romans 8:1).

In everyday life. None of us is wholly single-hearted; only Christ was, and his perfect obedience, not ours, is counted to us before God (Philippians 3:9). So think without fear of one place where you have been one person in public and another in private: the email with a barb in it, the reason you gave that was not the real reason. Confess it to the one whose blood cleanses the conscience, and put it right today, plainly.

What is conscience, and can it be wrong? Conscience is the inner sense, given by God, that judges our own actions as right or wrong (Romans 2:15). It is a real witness, and going against it is sin (Romans 14:23). But it is not infallible. It can be too tender, condemning what God allows, or too dull, excusing what God forbids, and it can be seared by repeated sin (1 Timothy 4:2). So it must be taught by Scripture and kept clean by confession. A clear conscience does not prove you right; but a guilty conscience should never be ignored: take it to Christ, whose blood purifies the conscience (Hebrews 9:14), and put right what can be put right.

Textual note. Many early manuscripts read “holiness” instead of “simplicity”, as the ESV notes; the sense is close.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul admits that he changed his travel plans, but denies that he made them lightly or to suit himself. His first plan was meant as a gift to them: a second visit of grace.

I wanted to come to you first. Now the actual grievance, almost too small for so much self-defence: Paul had announced a travel plan (1 Corinthians 16:5–7), changed it to a double visit, Corinth on the way north to Macedonia and again on the way back before taking the collection to Judea, and then changed it again. By the time of this letter the double visit has not happened at all.

A second experience of grace. An apostle’s visit was not an inspection but a gift, and the gift was Christ (Romans 15:29). What was at stake was never his diary but the grace of Christ coming to them through him.

Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Two questions, both expecting the answer no. Vacillating translates elaphria, lightness: the flightiness of a man whose word weighs nothing. His opponents were building a case about his character, and a broken travel plan was the most available brick. A small failure that anyone can check is seized on because it can be made to stand for a large one that nobody can check: he changed his plans, so he is unreliable, so his gospel cannot be trusted either.

According to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time? “According to the flesh” here means deciding as a man does whose only guide is his own convenience. The doubled “Yes, yes” and “No, no” pictures a man saying both at once to different audiences, agreeing with whoever is in the room.

One journey whose plan never changed. The Son “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), and nothing turned him aside. His Yes to the Father, and to us, held all the way to the tomb, and he is patient with servants who must explain themselves, because he is making them people whose word can be trusted.

Explaining to people who have not earned it. An apostle does not owe the Corinthians his itinerary, yet Paul explains himself, at length, to people who have not earned it. That is what pastoral love looks like when it is inconvenient.

Is it a failure of integrity to change your mind? Clearly not, or Paul is condemned by his own defence. Scripture requires not that every announced plan be carried out regardless, but that the reason for changing it be honest. The sin is the changed plan made for self-serving reasons and then dressed up as principle; Paul will tell them in verse 23 exactly why he stayed away. So when a commitment has to be dropped, do not ask, “Can I justify this?”, since almost anything can be justified given a few minutes. Ask instead: if the person affected could see my actual reasoning, would it look like care for them or convenience for me? That is the line between Paul and the man he is accused of being.

What about a promise that has become costly to keep? Then, as far as it is lawful, keep it. Scripture praises the one who “swears to his own hurt and does not change” (Psalm 15:4). A promise may be set aside only if keeping it would mean sinning, if the other person releases you, or if circumstances genuinely make it impossible. Then go to the person, explain honestly and early, apologise for what it costs them, and make it up to them where you can. Do not let them find out by your silence.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had changed his travel plans, and some at Corinth accused him of being unreliable.

verseByVerse.quote: As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s word can be trusted because the God he preaches is faithful: every promise God has made is kept in Christ, and through Christ the church answers “Amen”.

As surely as God is faithful. One of the most audacious turns in Paul’s letters: defending a change of travel plans, within two sentences he is describing the character of the eternal Son of God. That is not evasion: if Paul’s word cannot be trusted, those who heard the gospel from him will soon wonder about the gospel too. So he stakes the answer on something larger, with what amounts to an oath.

Silvanus and Timothy and I. Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth when the church was founded (Acts 18:5). Three named men preached, so this is not one man’s word, and the message they preached was Christ himself. He is God’s definitive Yes, and the Greek tense says that it has become Yes and stays Yes.

All the promises of God. All of them, not only the ones that plainly speak of the Messiah. Set that against the Old Testament. God promised Abraham a land, a seed and a blessing for every nation, and centuries later his descendants were a small, conquered people. He promised David a son whose throne would never end, and the throne of David ended with a blinded king led away in chains to Babylon (2 Kings 25:7). He promised through the prophets a new covenant, a cleansed heart, a shepherd, a servant pierced for transgressions. Anyone who closes the Old Testament sees an enormous amount still owing.

Find their Yes in him. Paul says the whole debt was paid in one Person. Jesus is Abraham’s promised seed, the king on David’s throne, the one whose blood makes the new covenant, the shepherd, and the pierced servant. Every altar, prophecy and unfinished story in the Hebrew Scriptures was reaching toward someone. God has spoken his final Yes, and it has a face and a name. So you do not receive God’s promises one at a time, by earning each or finding the right verse. You receive Christ, and in him you receive them all (Galatians 3:16, 29).

Our Amen to God. Amen is a Hebrew word meaning “it is firm, it is so”, said in worship to affirm what God has said. God says Yes; the church says Amen, adding its signature of trust beneath his promise. Even our Amen is said “through him”, as people joined to Christ, for his glory.

Sealed in the blood of the Yes himself. Every promise God made was costly to keep. To speak his Yes to us, the Father did not let the cup of suffering and judgment pass from his Son in Gethsemane, and the Son drank it to the bottom. That is how firm the Yes is: it was sealed in the blood of the Yes himself, and it will never be withdrawn.

Does this mean I can claim any promise in the Bible, health or wealth, for myself? The promises find their Yes in him: they come to us through union with Christ and on his terms. The great promises of the gospel, forgiveness, the Spirit, adoption, the resurrection, are certain for every believer. Promises given to particular people in particular settings, such as the land to Israel, are not blank cheques for health and prosperity now. The promise that is ours in every case is that all things work together for good for those who love God (Romans 8:28), and he decides what that good is.

What if a promise seems unfulfilled in my life? Read the promise carefully, and read God’s calendar. Some are already fully yours in Christ, such as forgiveness and adoption, whatever you feel; some are being kept slowly now, such as your growth in holiness; and some are kept in full only when Christ returns: no more tears, a resurrection body, the new creation. The saints of Hebrews 11 died not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). An unfinished promise is not a broken one. God’s Yes in Christ has already been spoken; the rest is delivery.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth. “Amen” means “it is true, so be it.”

verseByVerse.quote: And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself makes believers secure in Christ: he establishes, anoints and seals them, and gives his Spirit as the first instalment of all that is to come. This answers the obvious question, how an ordinary believer knows that God’s Yes includes him.

It is God who establishes us with you. Few words in the New Testament give clearer assurance. Every verb has God as its subject and believers as its object, and “with you” puts Paul and his critics inside the same sentence, held by the same hands. Establishes (bebaioō) was used in business papers of confirming a contract so that it would stand up in court, and it shares its root with the unshaken hope of verse 7. It is present tense: God is doing it continually, in Christ, whose standing before the Father is counted as yours. Your place is being actively maintained, today, by someone other than you.

And has anointed us. Oil was poured on a prophet, a priest or a king to mark him out for God’s work. The word is chrisas, the root of Christos, the Anointed One: we share the anointing of the one we are named after. Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38), and from him the Spirit flows to everyone joined to him (1 John 2:20). There is no second-class member of the body of Christ.

Put his seal on us. A seal marked ownership, and guaranteed that the contents had not been tampered with in transit. The Holy Spirit in a believer is God’s stamp saying this one is mine, and his guarantee that what he has sent will arrive intact (Ephesians 1:13–14; 4:30). Here too Christ goes first: on him God the Father has set his seal (John 6:27).

His Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee. The down payment (arrabōn), a commercial term: the first instalment of an agreed price, which binds the payer to hand over the rest (5:5; Ephesians 1:14); in modern Greek it means an engagement. Whatever you have known of God, the moments when Scripture came alive, the peace that arrived from nowhere, the homesickness for a country you have never seen, is the deposit: a first part of heaven itself, paid early. The Father has signed the contract, the Son has paid the price, and the Spirit has been given as the deposit and the ring. He has never lost one he sealed.

The weakest witness in the room. When assurance is thin, we ask, “Do I feel saved?”, which is asking the weakest witness in the room. Ask instead: has God established, anointed, sealed and paid a deposit on someone he intends to abandon? A Christian’s security rests not on the strength of his grip on God but on four actions of God, Father, Son and Spirit, taken while he was still at his worst.

What it does not mean. Not that every believer always feels assured. Assurance can be weakened by sin or trial, and a true believer may wait long and struggle hard before he has it; but God’s seal does not break. Nor may a person who lives in settled, unrepentant sin comfort himself with the seal: the Spirit who seals is the Holy Spirit, and his presence shows itself in a growing hatred of sin.

When are we sealed: at baptism, or in a second experience? The seal is the Holy Spirit himself, given to every believer when he first trusts Christ: “when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13). It is not a later blessing for some Christians, nor conferred by the water of baptism. Baptism, which this commentary holds is for believers because in the New Testament it follows faith (Acts 2:41; 8:12), publicly declares the Spirit’s work already done; many of our paedobaptist brothers (who baptise the infants of believers) call the sacraments seals as well, and we share with them the conviction that the sign does not save without faith. If you trust Christ, you have been sealed.

What about “anointed” leaders and special anointings today? The New Testament never divides Christians into the anointed and the ordinary; every believer has the anointing of the Spirit (1 John 2:20). So be wary of anyone who claims a special anointing that places him beyond question or correction. God does call particular men to preach and lead, and they deserve honour, but their teaching is tested by Scripture like everyone else’s (Acts 17:11).

Where Christians differ: assurance of salvation. Some Christians teach that believers cannot be sure of their final salvation in this life, and many Arminians (who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted and lost) teach that a true believer may finally fall away; they are moved by the Bible’s solemn warnings, which every Christian must heed. This commentary’s view: God himself establishes, anoints, seals and gives the Spirit as a guarantee. These are God’s acts, not ours, and they make the outcome certain. Believers can have a well-founded assurance, resting on God’s promises, the inner witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16), and the evidence of his work in their lives (Westminster Confession 18.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2).
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership. The word for “guarantee” was used in business for a first instalment or deposit, pledging that the full payment will follow.

verseByVerse.quote: But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stayed away from Corinth to spare them, not out of weakness or indifference, because he serves their faith and joy instead of ruling over them.

I call God to witness against me. At last the real reason, introduced with an oath that invites divine scrutiny of his motives. The Corinthians could not see inside him; God could (Hebrews 4:13). Only a man with nothing to hide calls that God as witness against himself.

To spare you. A visit would have meant discipline exercised in person on a church only half repentant, coming with a rod (1 Corinthians 4:21). So he stayed away to give them time to repent, and wrote instead (2:1–4). The man accused of being unreliable had been protecting the very people filing the complaint, and could not say so at the time without making it worse. It is often easier to confront than to wait, for confrontation feels decisive and relieves the tension in the one doing it; Paul chose the slower, more humiliating road.

Not that we lord it over your faith. Talk of sparing them could sound like boasting of a punishment withheld, so he corrects it at once. “Lord it over” is kyrieuō: to rule as master, the word Jesus used of the kings of the Gentiles when he said it would not be so among his disciples (Luke 22:25–26; 1 Peter 5:3). Paul has apostolic authority, and he will use it in chapter 13. But it does not extend to standing between a believer and God.

We work with you for your joy. “Work with” is synergoi, fellow workers: on the same side of the table, and the goal is not compliance but gladness. Any authority in the church that produces fear rather than joy has misunderstood its own job description.

For you stand firm in your faith. This is the church of the factions and the lawsuits, the one that has been listening to men who despise him, and his verdict is generous: they are standing, not because they are impressive, but because they are held. Their faith rests on God, not on Paul: “the Lord is able to make him stand” (Romans 14:4). The one who keeps them upright is Christ, the only Lord of the conscience, who has never yet let a believer fall out of his hand.

The meekness and gentleness of Christ. Paul’s restraint is a likeness of his Lord’s: he appeals “by the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (10:1), the one Lord with every right to rule their faith, who came as one who serves (Luke 22:27) and would not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20). An under-shepherd who domineers is not merely harsh. He misrepresents the Chief Shepherd to his own sheep.

The thing Paul refuses. This needs saying plainly. There are churches where a leader’s approval functions as the measure of a member’s standing with God, where questions are treated as rebellion, where major life decisions require clearance, where people are told that to leave is to leave the Lord. A minister who makes himself the gatekeeper of another Christian’s relationship with God has taken a place that is not his.

What it does not mean. Not that church leaders have no authority; Paul used his. Authority serves; it does not dominate. Believers are still told to obey their leaders and submit to them, so that their work may be a joy and not a groan (Hebrews 13:17).

In everyday life. If you have any authority over others, as a parent, an employer, an elder, ask whether the people under you are more joyful in Christ because of you or more afraid of you. Ask one of them, and listen. And pray for your pastors, that they will lead as helpers of your joy.

But did Jesus not say, Do not take an oath at all (Matthew 5:34)? He was condemning the evasive swearing of his day, which made some promises binding and left others loose; hence “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). He was not forbidding a solemn, truthful appeal to God. Paul makes such appeals (Romans 1:9; Galatians 1:20), God swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), and Jesus answered when put under oath (Matthew 26:63–64). A Christian may take an oath in court or make marriage vows; what he may not do is need an oath to be believed.

How do I tell faithful leadership from lording it? Faithful leaders point you to Scripture and let it bind your conscience, not their preferences. They welcome questions, explain their decisions, and can be corrected. They care about your joy in Christ more than your loyalty to them, and discipline for open sin according to the word, not for disagreement with them. Lording it looks different: control over personal decisions the Bible leaves free, punishment of questions, secrecy, isolation from family and other churches, fear. Where there is abuse of any kind, it must never be tolerated or covered up. Speak to other elders or leaders outside the situation, report crimes to the authorities, and know that leaving such a church is not leaving Christ.

Where Christians differ: church authority over conscience. Some churches claim authority to bind believers’ consciences in matters beyond Scripture. This commentary’s view: Church leaders have real authority to teach Scripture and to discipline, but no authority to rule over faith or bind the conscience beyond what God’s word requires. God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster Confession 20.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2). Leaders serve believers’ joy.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia:<sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,<sup>4</sup>who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.<sup>5</sup>For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.<sup>6</sup>If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.<sup>7</sup>Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.<sup>8</sup>For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.<sup>9</sup>Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.<sup>10</sup>He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.<sup>11</sup>You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.<sup>12</sup>For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you.<sup>13</sup>For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand—<sup>14</sup>just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.<sup>15</sup>Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace.<sup>16</sup>I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea.<sup>17</sup>Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?<sup>18</sup>As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No.<sup>19</sup>For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes.<sup>20</sup>For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.<sup>21</sup>And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us,<sup>22</sup>and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.<sup>23</sup>But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth.<sup>24</sup>Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.

keyVerse.quote: For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.
keyVerse.note: Paul answers a complaint about a changed travel plan with the faithfulness of God in Christ: every promise God ever made, to Abraham, to David and through the prophets, has been kept in one Person, and the church’s Amen rises through him. The same faithfulness holds the first half of the chapter together, for the God who comforts and delivers is the God who keeps his word.

1.reflection:
Paul’s first response to a crushing year is to bless God (v. 3), and he says God comforts us “so that” we can comfort others (v. 4). What comfort has God given you in a hard season, and who around you might need it now?

Paul admits that he “despaired of life itself” (v. 8). Why do you think he told a church that already thought him weak? How does his honesty help Christians who are in the dark, and how can our church make it easier for them to say so?

Verse 9 says the sentence of death came “to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead”. What do you tend to lean on first when trouble comes, and what difference does it make that God is the God of resurrection?

All God’s promises find their Yes in Christ (v. 20), and God himself establishes, anoints and seals believers (vv. 21–22). How should this shape the way we keep our own word, and the way we find assurance when we feel weak?

2.title: Forgiveness, the Aroma of Christ, and the Triumph of God
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 completes Paul’s explanation of his changed travel plans, begun at 1:12. At verse 14 he breaks off the story for the long account of gospel ministry that runs to 7:4; the story of Titus resumes at 7:5.

The message. Love wounds only in order to heal, and the ministry that heals is Christ’s triumph, not ours. Paul wrote with tears because he loved them. Now that the man who wronged him has been disciplined and is sorry, the church must forgive him and welcome him back, or Satan will have the victory. And the anxious apostle who tells them this is no failure: God is leading him in Christ’s victory procession and spreading through him the fragrance of Christ.

Why it was said. Some in Corinth called Paul fickle and harsh for cancelling a visit and sending a severe letter.
