Titus had brought word that the church had disciplined the man who wronged Paul on the painful visit (see the introduction); the danger now was that they would never let him back. Meanwhile polished visiting preachers made him look weak.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul explains the tearful letter, written out of anguish and love (vv. 1–4). He refuses to make the offence a personal quarrel and pleads for the punishment to end in forgiveness, comfort and public love (vv. 5–8), the test of their obedience and the defence against Satan (vv. 9–11). He admits that he left Troas, anxious for Titus (vv. 12–13), then bursts into thanks for Christ’s procession and the fragrance it spreads, which no one is sufficient to carry (vv. 14–16), and sets his sincere, God-commissioned speaking against the peddlers of the word (v. 17).

Where it leads. Paul forgives “in the presence of Christ” (v. 10), before the one who forgave us first, at the cost of his blood. The triumph is Christ’s victory, won at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and those he conquered, Paul the persecutor among them, are the spoils he leads home. And the aroma rising to God from faithful preaching is the aroma of his Son. A chapter that begins in tears ends with the world smelling of Christ’s victory.

For us. Correct with tears, forgive the repentant without delay, bring your anxieties to God, and speak of Christ undiluted. You do not need to be sufficient, only faithful: the fragrance and the victory are his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Severe Letter and Forgiveness of the Offender
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love sometimes has to wound, but it wounds only to heal, and once the wound has done its work, love must heal quickly. Paul explains that he stayed away and wrote in tears, rather than make another painful visit, because his aim was their joy and the proof of his love, not their pain (vv. 1–4). The man who caused the trouble hurt the whole church, and the church has disciplined him; now it must forgive, comfort and publicly reaffirm its love for him before sorrow swallows him (vv. 5–8). That is the real test of their obedience (v. 9), and refusing it would hand Satan a victory (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Church discipline has a defined goal: restoration, not condemnation (Matthew 18:15–20; Galatians 6:1; 1 Corinthians 5). Once it has done its work, withholding forgiveness becomes a sin of its own, one Satan is glad to see (see the note on vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.examples: A church elder removed from office after a moral failure has spent two years in genuine repentance. A vocal minority insists that any restoration betrays those he hurt. This passage does not minimise the hurt (v. 5), but refusing to forgive when repentance is genuine is not faithfulness; it is a gift to the enemy (vv. 10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stayed away rather than make another painful visit, because the people he would have to wound are the very people who make him glad. His change of plan was not fickleness but love.

Another painful visit. “Another” carries a whole episode. Between 1 Corinthians and this letter Paul went to Corinth, and it went so badly that he will not describe it and will not risk repeating it. “Painful” is lypē, grief, sorrow. Acts says nothing of this visit; we know it only from the scar tissue it left in these chapters. From hints (2:5; 7:12; 13:2) it seems that someone in the congregation opposed and humiliated Paul publicly, and the church did not defend him (see the introduction). A second confrontation, before they had had time to respond to his letter, would have done lasting damage.

For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained? A disarming sentence, because it exposes that the apostle needs them. You are my joy, he says; if I come and wound you, I have wounded the only people who can make me glad, and I will go home emptier than I came. A man who did not care could confront them and feel nothing. Paul cannot confront them without paying for it himself.

The joy set before him. In this Paul is a small likeness of his Lord, who has freely bound his own joy to a people. He is the shepherd who lays the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing (Luke 15:5–6), who “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). So Christ’s correction of his people is never cold; it comes from one who sympathises with their weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). A pastor whose happiness depends on his flock is not weak. He is wearing his Master’s heart.

Will this cost me anything? Anyone who must speak hard truth, a parent, an elder, a friend, a manager, should ask not “Am I right?” (usually you are, and being right is the cheapest part of it) but whether it will cost you anything. A rebuke that costs the one who gives it nothing has become an exercise of position rather than an act of love, and the one receiving it can always tell. Real correction is expensive at both ends. That is why so little of it is done well, and why the little that is done well is remembered for a lifetime.

Should a hard conversation be in person or in writing? Usually in person, where tone can be heard and misunderstandings corrected (Matthew 18:15). But Paul shows that writing is sometimes wiser: when a meeting would inflame things, when the other person needs time to think, or when words must be chosen with great care. Never use writing to hide, to fire a parting shot, or to say what you would not say to the person’s face, and reread it the next morning before you send it.
verseByVerse.note: This painful visit is not recorded in Acts; it came between 1 and 2 Corinthians.

verseByVerse.quote: And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wrote the severe letter in tears, not to hurt them but to show how much he loved them. He wrote instead of coming so that the matter would be settled before he arrived, sure that his joy and theirs were one.

And I wrote as I did. Here and in 7:8 Paul refers to a letter written between 1 and 2 Corinthians about the man who had wronged him. It is not chapters 10 to 13, which never mention the offender, nor the long, measured 1 Corinthians, which does not read like a letter written “with many tears”; most likely it is lost (see the introduction). God preserved every word the church would need, not every word Paul wrote.

The joy of you all. He expected the letter to work, because what made him glad and what made them glad were finally the same. They are not a minister and his clients with separate interests, but one body, and the joy belongs to all.

Out of much affliction. Then the cost: affliction, anguish of heart, many tears. Anguish is synochē, a pressing together, the walls closing in. He wrote it the way you write something late at night after four attempts, with your hands shaking.

The abundant love. He says plainly what the aim was, in a sentence that should be printed above every difficult conversation in the church. The letter caused pain, as he admits in chapter 7, but pain was not the purpose. Love was the purpose, and pain the route it had to take. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6).

He wept over it. Paul’s tears have a precedent. When Jesus drew near and saw Jerusalem, “he wept over it” (Luke 19:41), and his sternest words against its leaders ended in a lament: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). The hardest things the Son of God ever said came from a heart breaking for those who heard them. Tears like his are the only ink in which a Christian rebuke should be written.

Anger or love? Rebuke that comes out of anger wants the other person to feel what you feel. Rebuke that comes out of love wants the other person restored, and would gladly skip the whole episode if there were another way. The two can use identical words and still be entirely different acts; the tears are usually where the difference shows. Anyone who has sent such a message and then lain awake knows where Paul was standing, in the silence afterwards.

What if my loving rebuke is rejected? Then you have still done what love required, and the outcome is in God’s hands; Paul too had to wait. Give it time, keep praying, and do not repeat the rebuke louder or recruit others against the person. Keep the door open and treat them kindly meanwhile. If the matter is serious sin in the church, Jesus gives further steps involving others (Matthew 18:16–17). But many rebukes do their work slowly, and the person who angrily rejected your words in March may come back to them in September.
verseByVerse.note: This severe letter is probably lost; some think it is part of 2 Corinthians 10–13.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who wronged Paul hurt the whole church, and Paul, though he is the injured party, refuses to make it a personal quarrel. So the apostle charged with being harsh is seen working to restore the man who wounded him, and tactfully leaves him unnamed.

Who was this man? The older tradition took him to be the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 for living with his father’s wife, pointing to the “punishment by the majority” (v. 6) and to Paul’s hope there that he would be saved (1 Corinthians 5:5). More likely he had publicly opposed or insulted Paul during the painful visit: Paul speaks of the wrong as done against himself (v. 10; 7:12), not as sexual sin, and he is far gentler here than he was over the incest. Either way, discipline aims at restoration.

He has caused it not to me. First, he refuses to make it personal. “Not to me” is not literally true, and everyone knew it. But Paul declines to stand in the centre of the picture. Once it becomes a quarrel between two men, the congregation divides into supporters and the whole thing is lost: the injured leader who insists on his own injury turns one man’s sin into a church of parties.

Not to put it too severely. Second, restraint. He could have said far more, and the man had earned it. With the whole province about to hear the letter read out, he understates: a wounded man refusing to use his platform to settle a score.

No private sins. Yet restraint is not indifference. The pain was caused “to all of you”. There is no such thing as a private sin in the body of Christ. We think of sin as a personal debt; Paul thinks of it as a doctor thinks of an infection in a limb: what is done in one member is felt in all (1 Corinthians 12:26; Joshua 7:1). That is why a congregation can become subtly cold or joyless and nobody can point to a cause.

Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter. Paul’s refusal to stand at the centre of his own injury has a deeper source. The one most wronged in all history “was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). Jesus did not use his trial to settle scores; he let the worst thing ever done against him become the cure for the people who did it. A wounded leader who steps aside so that a church can heal is not weak. He is being like his Lord.

Whom did it touch? Recall the last time you were harsh at home, dishonest at work, or nursed a grudge through a Sunday morning. It never touched only you: a wife who found you difficult that evening, a colleague who learned from you that dishonesty is how things are done, a child who was watching. Sin is never contained where it is committed, which is why church discipline is not the policing of private morals but the care of a shared body. And it is why forgiveness, in the next verses, must be shared too. If the whole body was wounded, the whole body must do the healing.

When someone wrongs me, should I keep it private or tell the church? Begin privately. Most personal wrongs should be covered by love and never mentioned again (1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 19:11). If a wrong is too serious to overlook, go to the person alone first (Matthew 18:15), and only if he will not listen involve one or two others, and then the church. Do not talk about it to everyone else meanwhile; that is gossip, and it turns a sin into a faction, exactly what Paul refuses to do here. The exception is crime and abuse: those must be reported to the proper authorities and the church leaders, and a victim is never required to confront an abuser alone.
verseByVerse.note: The offender is unnamed; he is most likely not the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 but someone who had publicly opposed Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough, so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The discipline has done its work, so the church must stop punishing the man and turn to forgive and comfort him before his sorrow drowns him.

This punishment is enough. “Punishment” is epitimia, a rebuke or penalty: church discipline, carried out by the majority acting together. Paul is not asking whether the man has suffered as much as he deserved; asked honestly, that would never be answered yes about anyone. He is asking whether the discipline has done its work. It has. So it stops.

Hard to start, harder to end. Once a person has been put outside, keeping him there seems the respectable thing: those who want him back look soft on sin, and no one is criticised for being too rigorous. A church that cannot say “enough” has not understood what discipline was for. God himself is the God who says enough. He did not merely permit the prodigal to return; he ran, embraced him and put a ring on his hand (Luke 15:20–22).

Turn to forgive and comfort him. “Rather turn” is a change of direction, required of the same people who carried out the discipline: the majority who excluded him must now go and get him. Forgive is charizomai, to show grace; comfort is parakaleō, the comfort of chapter 1. The man is to be walked back in, not merely permitted to return. Someone has to sit next to him (Galatians 6:1).

Overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. “Overwhelmed” is katapinō, to swallow down, used of the Egyptians drowned in the sea and of death swallowed up in victory (Hebrews 11:29; 1 Corinthians 15:54). Paul pictures a man going under, swallowed not by his sin but by his sorrow. We are alert to the man who repents too little. Paul is alert to the man who has repented and cannot get up, sinking under a guilt already dealt with by the Son, who swallowed up the sorrow that would have swallowed us.

Breakfast on a beach. The Lord himself shows how this is done. Judas was sorry, genuinely and violently, and his sorrow drove him to his death (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, and the risen Jesus did not leave him to sink. He cooked him breakfast by the lake, asked him three times whether he loved him, as if once for each denial, and gave him work to do: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:9–17). A church that restores the repentant does for one sinner what Christ did for Peter, and for every one of us.

If you are the one who is sinking. There is a sorrow God uses and a sorrow Satan uses, and from the inside they can feel identical. The difference is where they end. One drives you to Christ and leaves you lighter; the other drives you in circles round your own failure and leaves you heavier every time (7:10). Paul is so concerned about the second that he writes to an entire province to stop it happening to one man. Tell a pastor or trusted friend that you need help believing you are forgiven; that help is exactly what this verse commands the church to give.

In everyday life. Is there someone who has repented whom you still keep at a distance, still mention in a certain tone, still watch for the next failure? Forgive and comfort them, as Christ has you, with something concrete this week: a call, an invitation, a word of welcome.

What is church discipline, and when is it used? The loving correction of a church member by the church, following Christ’s instructions (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5). Most of it is quiet and private: a brother going to a brother. Formal discipline, up to removal from membership and the Lord’s Table, is for serious, public or persistent sin where the person refuses to repent after patient appeals. Its aims are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church and the honour of Christ, never revenge or the protection of a leader’s reputation.

How can a church tell the repentance is real? By fruit, not a perfect performance: the person owns the sin without blaming others, grieves over the harm done, puts right what can be put right, accepts accountability, and turns from the sin over time (Luke 3:8; 2 Corinthians 7:11). The church should be careful but not suspicious, and never demand a level of grief that would crush. On forgiveness and the slower rebuilding of trust, see vv. 10–11.

verseByVerse.quote: So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul pleads with the church to confirm its love for the forgiven man openly, as publicly as it disciplined him.

I beg you. The urgent sense of parakaleō once more. An apostle with authority to command pleads instead, because some things cannot be commanded into existence. You can order a church to readmit a man, not to love him, and readmission without love would be crueller than exclusion.

Reaffirm. Kyroō, a legal term: to ratify, to make officially and publicly binding, as a will is confirmed or a treaty ratified. Paul asks not only for warmer feelings but for a public act, as public as the discipline was.

Forgiveness made public. We have made forgiveness inward and private; Paul makes it public. Somebody has to stand up, in front of the people who watched him fall, and say that this man is ours and we love him. A restoration never announced is not believed. The man will come back into the room and read every face, carrying his disgrace like a coat he cannot take off, while the whispering moves underground. A public sin healed in private is not healed.

What was done for Paul. Paul is begging for what was done for him. Saul of Tarsus was not quietly tolerated by the church he had hunted: Barnabas brought him to the apostles and vouched for him out loud (Acts 9:27).

Not ashamed to call them brothers. The public love Paul asks for echoes Christ’s. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners in full view of those who despised them (Luke 15:1–2), and he will acknowledge before his Father everyone who acknowledges him before men (Matthew 10:32). He is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11). The sinner Christ restores is not slipped back in through a side door. And our own forgiveness was never a private, unannounced arrangement: God ratified it in public, at the cross, in the empty tomb, in baptism and at the Lord’s Table week by week, so that his children would never have to wonder. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). A church that reaffirms its love out loud only says on earth what its Lord has already said in heaven.

Should a restored person go straight back into leadership? Not necessarily. Forgiveness restores a person to the fellowship and the Lord’s Table at once and completely. Restoration to an office of trust is a separate question, governed by the qualifications God gives for leaders, who must be above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2). After serious sin that may take a long time, or may not be wise at all. And where the sin was abuse of any kind, the person must not be placed again in a position of trust over the vulnerable, however sincere the repentance; protecting the weak is itself an act of love. None of this withdraws forgiveness. It is simply wisdom about trust.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is why I wrote, that I might test you and know whether you are obedient in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The severe letter was written to prove whether the church would obey Christ in everything, and now obedience means forgiving. They passed the first test by disciplining the offender; forgiving him is the second, and the harder.

That I might test you. Not a manufactured loyalty test, which would contradict 1:24, where he disowned lording it over their faith. The word (dokimē) means proving something genuine, as metal is tested to show it is real, not as a student is caught out by a trick question. What is proved is not their loyalty to Paul but whether a church that has received the gospel will act on it when acting is costly: first confronting a man many of them liked, now forgiving a man some are still angry with.

Obedient in everything. “In everything” is the whole issue. Half-obedience is the standing temptation of religious people: we assemble a personal edition of the Christian life from the commands we find agreeable and let the others lapse, one avoided verse at a time. It rarely feels like rebellion; it feels like being busy, or reasonable, or not quite ready.

Obedient to the point of death. One Son has passed this test entirely. Jesus never assembled a personal edition of his Father’s will; he became “obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8), and his obedience included the very command this church now faces: he forgave those who had wronged him. That obedience in everything is counted to everyone who trusts him, so the half-obedient who come to him are not cast off. It is also the source of their growth, because the Spirit of the obedient Son is at work in them, making the commands they had treated as optional their own.

Always working on them. The offender’s sin prompted the letter, but the congregation was what Paul cared about most. God works the same way. A trial is not only something that happens to us but something being worked in us: the tested genuineness of your faith, more precious than gold (1 Peter 1:7). He is proving something in you, and he intends to show it to you on the day Christ is revealed.

Does obeying in everything mean obeying my pastor in everything? No. Paul’s apostolic authority was unique, and his commands are now in Scripture. Pastors and elders are to be respected and followed as they teach and apply God’s word (Hebrews 13:17), and not resisted lightly. But they cannot command what Scripture does not, and you must not obey them if they tell you to sin: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Obedience in everything means obedience to Christ in every area of life, including the costly ones like forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul joins the church in forgiving the man before Christ, because an unforgiving church plays straight into Satan’s hands.

Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Paul binds himself to their decision, though the man had wronged him most. He does not keep a private hold on an injury the church has released.

In the presence of Christ. Paul plays down his own hurt: “if I have forgiven anything”. Then a phrase lifts the matter higher: “in the presence of Christ”, literally in his face, under his gaze. Forgiveness in the church is not a social convenience or an agreement to move on. It is transacted before the Lord, by his authority, in imitation of what he has already done: “as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (Colossians 3:13). It is the same face in which we see the glory of God (4:6).

Not outwitted by Satan. Then the startling reason. The word is pleonekteō: to get the better of someone in a transaction, to cheat a man out of what should have been his. An unforgiving church has been swindled: it thought it was defending righteousness and has been robbed of a brother, of its unity and of its witness. Harsh, unending discipline plays into Satan’s hands as much as none at all.

His designs. Schemes, thought-out plans (noēmata; Ephesians 6:11). Paul names as one of the enemy’s chief instruments not persecution, heresy or immorality, but a congregation that will not forgive a repentant man. The church exists to announce that God forgives sinners; a church that will not practise inside its doors what it preaches at them has made its message unbelievable. And the face in which forgiveness is transacted is the face of the one who forgave us first, at the cost of his own blood. He prayed for those who were driving in the nails.

What it does not mean. Not that Satan is behind every problem. He exploits our sins, including unforgiveness. He is real and clever, but he is a defeated enemy, and his schemes are known to those who read God’s word.

In everyday life. Unforgiveness gives Satan a foothold (Ephesians 4:26–27). Name the person you are still holding something against, and say to God, in the presence of Christ, that you release the debt. You cannot manufacture this, but the Spirit of the Christ who forgave you can do it in you.

Does forgiving mean feeling differently? No. It means deciding, before Christ, not to hold the debt against the person any longer: not to raise it, not to punish with it, not to run it again in your mind at two in the morning. Feelings usually follow, sometimes slowly, sometimes years later; they are the fruit, not the entry fee. If the old anger rises again, forgive again. That is not failure but the ordinary work of a forgiving heart.

Does forgiving mean restoring trust, or pretending nothing happened? Not automatically restoring trust. Forgiveness is released freely, because that is how it was given to us; trust is rebuilt over time and by evidence, and it is not unloving to say so. A forgiven embezzler need not be handed the accounts. But notice which way Paul is pushing this church: they are drifting toward too little restoration, not too much. Nor does forgiving mean pretending. Paul says what happened in this very paragraph. Forgiveness that requires everyone to lie about the past is suppression, and it always leaks.

What if the person has not repented? Then you are still to forgive in your heart, letting go of bitterness and revenge and leaving judgment to God (Mark 11:25; Romans 12:19), and to stand ready to be reconciled the moment he turns. But full reconciliation, the restored relationship, waits on repentance: “If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him” (Luke 17:3). So you need not pretend the wrong is resolved, or put yourself back in harm’s way. You can be free of hatred and still wait, praying, for the person to come home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gospel ministry is Christ’s triumph, not the minister’s, and it does not depend on the minister’s strength. Paul admits that anxiety for Titus and the church drove him from an open door at Troas (vv. 12–13), then breaks into thanks: God leads his weak servants as captives in Christ’s victory procession and spreads the knowledge of Christ through them like incense (v. 14). That fragrance pleases God and divides its hearers, life to some and death to others, so that no one is sufficient for it (vv. 15–16). What Paul can do is refuse to dilute the message and speak sincerely, sent by God and in his sight (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Paul surprisingly pictures himself not as the general in a Roman triumph but as a captive in Christ’s train (see the note on v. 14), the same surprise as in his title “servant of Christ” (doulos Christou, literally Christ’s slave).

The double effect of the gospel, life to some and death to others, echoes Isaiah 8:14 (the stone of stumbling) and Luke 2:34 (see the note on vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.examples: A missionary returns from years in a largely unresponsive field and struggles with a sense of failure: few converts, much opposition. Faithfulness is measured by the fragrance, not by the response (see the note on vv. 15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord, my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul was so anxious for news of Titus and the church that he left an open door for the gospel at Troas and went on to Macedonia. He could have left this out; instead he tells a church that already thinks him weak.

Troas. A port on the Aegean coast near ancient Troy. Paul had sent Titus to Corinth with the severe letter and arranged, it seems, to meet him there. Titus was a Greek believer, uncircumcised, whom Paul had once taken to Jerusalem as living proof that Gentiles are saved without the law (Galatians 2:1–3); he became one of Paul’s most trusted fellow workers, well known in Corinth (8:6, 23). Paul arrives. Titus is not there.

A door was opened. Paul’s phrase for a genuine, God-given opportunity (1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3). Preaching was bearing fruit, exactly what he lives for.

My spirit was not at rest. And he cannot do it. “Rest” is anesis, the relief of a tight strap being loosened, and he had none: he could not concentrate for worrying about a letter, a church and a friend who had not arrived. So he closed an open door to look for Titus, who at last met him in Macedonia with good news (7:5–7).

Who opens and no one will shut. An opportunity is not by definition the will of God. Paul walked away from one without apology, because the door was Christ’s, not his. The risen Christ has the key of David, “who opens and no one will shut” (Revelation 3:7), and the work at Troas did not die: Luke records a church there later, gathering to break bread (Acts 20:6–12). Christ is not so short of workers that his gospel collapses when one exhausted man goes to find his friend. He holds the keys, which leaves his servants free to love particular people.

Is anxiety a sin? The anxiety is in the Bible, unrebuked. Paul wrote “do not be anxious about anything” (Philippians 4:6), and here he is, anxious, and God did not delete it from the record. What Philippians forbids is anxiety left to run: worry that distrusts God and is never turned into prayer. Here distress drove a man across a sea to find out how his people were. His agitation had a direction, and the direction was love; it was not about his reputation, safety or money, but the church, what he elsewhere calls his daily pressure, the anxiety for all the churches (11:28).

What do I do with anxiety for someone I love? Bring it to God, specifically and repeatedly, with thanksgiving, as Philippians 4:6 commands. Then do what love can rightly do: Paul went to find Titus. Write, call, visit, ask. Where nothing can be done, keep praying and entrust the person to the God who loves them more than you do, and talk to a friend who will pray with you. If anxiety becomes constant and disabling, talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; seeking that help is not a lack of faith. Love without news is hard to bear, and God does not despise the sleepless.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast of Asia. Titus was a trusted Gentile co-worker, sent to Corinth with the severe letter.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God always leads his servants in Christ’s victory procession, and through them spreads the knowledge of Christ everywhere like incense. Paul pictures himself not as a conqueror but as one of the conquered, a captive in Christ’s train.

But thanks be to God. Paul has just said he was too distressed to preach, and the sentence bursts into thanks as he remembers how God answered his anxiety (7:6). Before the Titus story resumes in chapter 7 comes his fullest account of Christian ministry, and it begins with a parade.

Triumphal procession. A Roman triumph was the highest honour the state could confer. The general rode in a chariot; his troops followed; the spoils were carried past; and behind them came the prisoners in chains, some to be sold, some to be executed at the procession’s end. Paul has put himself in the chains (see “Uncertain wording” below).

The conquered one. That is not false modesty but the argument of the letter in one image. His critics saw the beatings and imprisonments and called him defeated. Paul says: quite so. I am the conquered one, taken on the Damascus road by a Lord I was fighting. To be Christ’s captive is to have your resistance defeated and to be owned: “you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20). The chains are the grip of a Lord who will not let go of what he has won (John 10:28). The verb appears once more in the New Testament, where Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The victory was won at the cross, Paul is one of its spoils, and there is no higher position open to a human being than to be a trophy of Jesus Christ.

The fragrance of the knowledge of him. Ancient writers describe incense burning along a triumph’s route, so that the city smelled of the victory and the smell clung to everyone in the procession. Through Paul’s preaching the knowledge of Christ spreads like that. A fragrance cannot be argued with; it arrives before the speech does.

Always. Not only when the church is flourishing and the preacher in good voice. Anxious, sleepless and criticised, Paul was still being led in triumph; the parade did not pause while he struggled, though he could not see it. Its outcome was never in doubt. Christ went into death, the one territory nobody had ever come back from, and came out of it on Easter morning with the keys, and he has been leading his captives home ever since: through prisons, through hospital wards, through the years when nothing seemed to be happening. Not one of the chained is ashamed of the chains.

How do I spread the fragrance of Christ in an ordinary week? Mostly by being near him in his word and in prayer, because a fragrance is caught before it is given. Live in a way that smells of him: honesty when a lie would be easier, kindness to people who cannot repay you, joy that does not depend on circumstances, patience in suffering. And speak of him. The fragrance is the knowledge of him, and that needs words: what he has done, who he is, why you trust him. Life without words is a scent with no name; words without life are a label on an empty bottle.

Uncertain wording. The verb thriambeuō is rare. When it names the people led, it normally means leading them in a triumph as defeated captives, its sense in Colossians 2:15. The King James Version’s “causeth us to triumph” makes believers sharers in the victory, but there is no clear example of the verb meaning that; others take it loosely as “display”. The likely meaning is the first: Paul is led as Christ’s captive, a trophy of his victory, which fits a letter that glories in weakness.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman triumph was a victory parade through the city; captives were led in chains, and incense was burned along the route.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Preaching Christ pleases God whatever the response, yet it divides those who hear it: to some it is the smell of death, to others the fragrance of life. No one is equal to a task with such stakes, as Paul’s question admits.

The aroma of Christ to God. Aroma (euōdia) is the word used of sacrifices pleasing to God (Genesis 8:21; Ephesians 5:2). Before gospel ministry is anything to the world, it is an offering to God, and it pleases him whatever the results. When a Christian speaks of Christ to an empty room or a hostile face, the Father receives it first, and to him it smells of his Son, in whom he delights (Matthew 3:17). Faithful witness is first an act of worship.

From death to death, from life to life. The same smell means opposite things depending on who breathes it (compare 1 Corinthians 1:18). In a triumph the incense was, to the soldiers, the smell of home and reward; to the prisoners walking toward execution, the smell of their last hour. So with the gospel. The same word about the same Christ produces life in one hearer and hardening in another, and the message has not failed. Those who are perishing hear only of a crucified man and of their own judgment; to those being saved it is the scent of life. Simeon said of the infant Jesus that he was “appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34). The sun that softens the wax bakes the clay; the difference is not in the sun.

Who is sufficient for these things? A real question, not a flourish. “Sufficient” is hikanos: adequate, equal to the task. When Paul opens his mouth about Jesus, eternal outcomes are in motion. Who is adequate to carry that? Not the man who has just told us that he despaired of life and could not preach for anxiety. The honest answer is: nobody, in himself. Paul leaves the question hanging, then answers it: “our sufficiency is from God” (3:5). That is the only answer there is, and it is enough. The people God uses are not those who feel equal to it, but those who have stopped pretending they are and so draw on somebody else’s adequacy.

A weight lifted. Here is relief for Christians who talk about Jesus and watch nothing happen. If someone you love has gone colder rather than warmer, you have not necessarily done it badly. Your part was the fragrance; the response was never yours to give. And the tenses are a mercy: being saved and perishing are processes under way, not finished verdicts. Saul of Tarsus was as far down the second road as anyone can travel, and was stopped in the middle of it.

Does God want some people to perish? God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but in their turning from their way to live (Ezekiel 33:11), and the gospel is offered sincerely to everyone. Scripture also teaches that God has chosen a people for salvation and is sovereign over who believes (Acts 13:48). Both are true, and Scripture does not ask us to resolve them before we preach. Those who perish are never victims of a God who refused them; they are responsible for rejecting the light they were given (John 3:19). Neither truth is a reason to stop offering Christ to anyone.

Should I keep speaking of Christ to someone who resists? Usually yes, with wisdom: keep praying, loving and keeping the door open. Jesus also told his disciples not to throw pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), so there is a time to stop pressing someone who mocks and let your life and prayers do the speaking for a while. Do not nag or argue to win. But do not conclude from coldness that God has finished with them. Many believers were once hard and scornful hearers, and somebody kept carrying the fragrance into their lives.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unlike the many who hawk God’s word for gain, Paul speaks with pure motives, as one sent by God, in God’s sight and united to Christ.

Peddlers of God’s word. A deliberately insulting word. Kapēleuō is what a kapēlos does: a huckster at a market stall, notorious not for selling as such but for cheating, watering the wine and rigging the scales. Plato uses the word for those who hawked teaching the same way. So the charge is not simply that these men made money from the gospel, but that they altered the product to move it. “Like so many” points at the rival teachers in Corinth.

Not only for money. The coin a peddler most wants is often approval: the warmth of the crowd, the invitation back, the dread of being thought narrow. The heart that needs to be liked will water the wine as surely as the heart that needs to be paid, and only someone who already has God’s approval in Christ is free to stop trimming the message (Galatians 1:10).

Men of sincerity, as commissioned by God. Sincerity is eilikrineia, purity of motive, nothing mixed in. “Commissioned by God” means sent, not self-appointed: the message is not his to adjust, because it is not his.

In the sight of God we speak in Christ. Everyone who speaks about God speaks with God listening to every sentence, including the ones shaped to be liked (Proverbs 16:2; 1 Corinthians 4:5). And to speak in Christ is to speak as someone joined to him by faith (Galatians 2:20). Paul is not a salesman standing apart from his product, but a man united to the one he proclaims.

In the flow. The question of verse 16 gets its quiet answer: only the man whose message and commission both come from God is sufficient (3:5). Claiming this raises at once the charge Paul meets in 3:1, that he is commending himself, and from there to 7:4 he describes what true gospel ministry is.

Do you want to go away as well? The Lord himself refused to peddle. When he taught that he was the bread of life and that his flesh must be eaten, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:66). He did not chase them with a softer version. He asked the Twelve whether they wanted to go away as well, and Peter’s answer is the reason no faithful preacher may water the wine: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:67–68). To speak in Christ is to speak as he spoke, without trimming the hard sayings to keep the crowd.

Undiluted, at his own expense. The peddler waters his wine. God calls everyone who thirsts to come and buy wine and milk without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1), and in his Son he gives the thing itself, undiluted, at his own expense. Every faithful word about Christ he hears with delight, and it will not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

What it does not mean. Not that preachers should go unpaid. Those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and the labourer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:18). But they must never preach for money, or change the message to please people.

How to recognise a peddled gospel. Watch what happens to the hard parts: wrath, judgment, repentance and the cost of following evaporate, until what is left is a message about your best life, with Jesus attached. Watch where the money flows; promises of health and wealth in return for giving are the oldest version of the stall. Paul refused support from Corinth so that nobody could say this of him (chapters 11–12).

Is it wrong to make the message attractive? No, provided you change the manner and never the message. Paul became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22) and spoke differently in a synagogue and in Athens (Acts 17); clarity, illustration, warmth, even humour can serve the truth. The line is crossed when the content is altered to make it sell: when sin is renamed, judgment dropped, the cross softened, or Christ offered as a means to something else. A good cook may serve the bread warm. He may not put sawdust in it.

In everyday life. Before your next conversation about faith, ask which part of the truth you are most tempted to leave out with this person, and why. Then ask God for the courage and the kindness to say it.
verseByVerse.note: A peddler was a street trader known for watering down his wine to increase profits.

Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ,<sup>11</sup>so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.<sup>12</sup>When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord,<sup>13</sup>my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.<sup>14</sup>But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.<sup>15</sup>For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing,<sup>16</sup>to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?<sup>17</sup>For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.

keyVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.
keyVerse.note: Paul has just admitted he was too anxious to stay at an open door, and he answers his own weakness with thanks: the procession is Christ’s, and it never stops. The verse turns the chapter, and the letter, on its hinge. The weak, criticised apostle is not a defeated man but a captive of the risen Lord, and through such people God spreads the knowledge of Christ everywhere.

2.reflection:
Paul wrote “out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears” (v. 4). When you have had to say something hard to someone, what did it cost you? How can we tell whether a rebuke comes from anger or from love?

Paul tells the church that the punishment is “enough” and urges them to forgive, comfort and reaffirm their love for the man (vv. 6–8). Why do churches and families find it so hard to end discipline and restore someone? What would reaffirming love openly look like among us?

Paul admits that anxiety for Titus made him leave an open door at Troas (vv. 12–13). How does his honesty help you with your own anxieties, and what does it tell you about who holds the doors of the gospel?

The same message is a fragrance “from death to death” to some and “from life to life” to others (v. 16). How does this free us when people do not respond to Christ, and how does verse 17 warn us against changing the message to make it more welcome?

3.title: Letters of Recommendation, the New Covenant, and the Unveiled Face
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 stands inside Paul’s long description of his ministry (2:14–7:4). He has just asked, “Who is sufficient for these things?” (2:16); this chapter answers that question without boasting, and opens out into the glory of the new covenant, which chapter 4 continues.

The message. The true credential of a minister of Christ is not a document but a changed people, and the change is God’s work. Under the old covenant God’s law stood outside his people, written on stone; it could only condemn them, and its glory, though real, was passing. In the new covenant the Spirit writes God’s law on hearts, the guilty are declared righteous, and the veil is lifted, so that every believer, looking at the glory of the Lord, is slowly being made like Christ.

Why it was said. Visiting preachers had arrived in Corinth with letters of recommendation and, it seems, traded on their Jewish pedigree and the prestige of Moses (11:22; see the introduction). Measured by their paperwork, Paul looked unqualified.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul refuses to wave paper: the Corinthians are his letter, written by Christ’s Spirit on human hearts, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel promised (vv. 1–3). God has made him adequate as a minister of a new covenant, in which the Spirit gives the life the letter could not (vv. 4–6). Then, through the story of Moses’ shining face (Exodus 34), he argues three times from lesser to greater: if the ministry of death and condemnation, which was passing, came with such glory, the ministry of the Spirit, of righteousness and of what lasts must far surpass it (vv. 7–11). So Paul speaks boldly, not veiled like Moses (vv. 12–13). The veil now lies over hearts that read Moses without Christ, and is removed whenever anyone turns to the Lord (vv. 14–16), who is met in the Spirit (v. 17); and all believers, unveiled, are being changed into his image (v. 18).

Where it leads. Everything Moses’ shining face pointed to stands in Christ. The new covenant is written in his blood, its verdict of righteousness rests on him, and the glory we behold is “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6). On the mountain only Moses saw, and he shone for a while. Now the whole people of God look at Christ and are changed, from one degree of glory to another, until we see him as he is.

For us. Stop measuring yourself and your leaders by credentials, and stop trying to change yourself by effort alone. Drop the veils you keep up, and give your eyes to Christ; the Lord who is the Spirit will do the changing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Ministers of the New Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God, not paper, makes a minister of Christ, and the proof is a people changed by the Spirit. Paul’s rivals came with letters of recommendation, but his letter is the Corinthian church itself, written by Christ’s Spirit on human hearts, as the prophets promised (vv. 1–3). He claims no adequacy of his own: his sufficiency is from God (vv. 4–5), who has made him a minister of the new covenant, in which the Spirit gives the life the law written on stone could never give (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (v. 6) is often misunderstood. In context, “the letter” is the law of Moses written on stone, and the Spirit gives life by writing the law on the heart, as Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 promised (see the notes on vv. 2–3 and 6).
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation prides itself on doctrinal correctness. Its members can explain every article of their confession, but their life together is cold. The letter and Spirit contrast is not a criticism of doctrine or of Scripture (see the note on v. 6). The new covenant minister aims not only to fill heads but to be the one through whom the Spirit writes on hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will not prove his ministry with paper; its proof is what God has done in the people he serves. He sees the charge of self-promotion coming, and refuses to join his rivals in trading credentials.

Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Paul has just claimed to speak as one commissioned by God (2:17), and he hears how that could be taken. “Again” shows the charge was already in circulation: that his letters were self-promotion, and a man with real authority from God would not need to keep asserting it.

Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you? Behind the question lies a real practice. Travel was dangerous and a stranger claiming to teach in Christ’s name could be anyone, so churches wrote letters for those they sent. When Apollos crossed to Achaia, the brothers wrote ahead to welcome him (Acts 18:27); Paul commends Phoebe in this way (Romans 16:1–2) and planned letters for those carrying the collection (1 Corinthians 16:3). He does not attack the practice.

The credential as currency. He attacks what it had become in Corinth. His rivals had arrived with impressive documents, perhaps from Jerusalem, and wanted Corinth’s endorsement too, to carry to the next town (see the introduction). The credential had become a currency of influence, and it still is: the conference platform, the endorsement on a book jacket, the size of a following. None is wrong in itself. The question is whether the credential describes something real or stands in for it.

By what authority? When the chief priests demanded to know by what authority Jesus acted (Matthew 21:23), he produced no document. He pointed to his works: “the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me” (John 5:36). The blind saw, the lame walked, the poor heard good news (Matthew 11:4–5), and at last a tomb stood empty. The Lord of the church carried no letters, because his life was the credential, and his servant can do no better than point to what Christ has done in people.

When is it right to speak about your own ministry? Paul will spend much of the letter defending himself, and calls it foolishness when he gets there (11:1). It is right when the people you serve are being taken from you, and wrong when only your own standing is at stake. Paul is protecting not a career but a church from teachers who will damage it, and his credibility is all that stands between them. A man who defends himself for his own sake is building a reputation; one who defends himself because his people are in danger is doing something else, and the difference usually shows in whether he enjoys it. Paul plainly does not.

Should churches still check references and credentials? Yes. The early church did, and it is simple wisdom and love. Ask for references from a man’s previous church, test his doctrine against Scripture, and carry out proper safeguarding checks for anyone working with children; leaders should be tested before they serve (1 Timothy 3:10). What Paul warns against is letting paper replace life: being impressed by titles, platforms and endorsements without asking whether a man’s teaching is true and his life godly. Check the credentials, and then look for the fruit.
verseByVerse.note: Letters of recommendation were common for travellers; Paul’s rivals at Corinth came with them.

verseByVerse.quote: You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Corinthians themselves are Paul’s letter of recommendation, written by Christ through his Spirit on human hearts, as God promised the new covenant would be. A changed life is the one credential that cannot be forged.

You yourselves are our letter. Asked for his credentials, Paul points at the people asking: former idolaters, swindlers, slaves and freedmen who a few years earlier had never heard the name of Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:9–11; 9:2). Dismissed by them, he says they are written on his heart (7:3); yet the whole city can read them too. A church is a public document, whether it means to be or not.

A letter from Christ delivered by us. In verse 2 they are Paul’s letter; here they are Christ’s, and Paul is only the courier. Every faithful minister discovers that he is the postman, not the author.

Not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. Ink sits on a surface and can be scraped off. The Spirit wrote on their lives, changing what they love, so that the idolater now loves the living God and the thief works so that he has something to give (Ephesians 4:28; Ezekiel 36:27).

Tablets of human hearts. Stone tablets were what Moses carried down Sinai, written with the finger of God (Exodus 24:12; 31:18). Centuries later God promised through Jeremiah, to a nation that had failed to keep what was on them: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Ezekiel put it more bluntly: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26–27; see 11:19).

A promise fulfilled in a Greek port. Paul’s claim is enormous: what the prophets promised has happened, and the evidence is sitting in a difficult church in Corinth, because of Christ. The covenant that writes on hearts is the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20), and the Spirit who writes is the Spirit he poured out from the Father’s right hand (Acts 2:33). Jeremiah foresaw the writing; Paul has met the writer, the risen Christ.

Nothing scrapes away what Christ has written. He paid for the page with his blood and sealed it by his Spirit for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30). The first tablets lay smashed at the foot of the mountain (Exodus 32:19); the letter written on a heart of flesh will be finished on the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

What has been written on you? Stone can be inscribed and remain stone; the law could be recited perfectly by people it never changed. The test is whether anything has moved inward: whether you have come to want what you once merely complied with. No one does that to himself. It is the Spirit’s work, and the only credential any church has ever really had.

What if my life does not look much like a letter from Christ? The letter is still being written, and the Spirit writes slowly; Paul calls the Corinthians Christ’s letter while they are still full of faults. Ask what has changed since you came to Christ, not whether you are finished: a sin you now hate, a person you now love, a hunger for God’s word you once lacked. Those are his handwriting. If you honestly find nothing at all, do not despair or pretend: go to Christ now, ask him for the new heart he promised, and keep coming to him in his word and among his people. He has never refused anyone who asked.

Textual note. In verse 2 some manuscripts read “your hearts”, but “our” is well supported and fits the warmth of the letter (7:3).

parallels.desc: tablets of stone, written with the finger of God
a heart of flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s confidence rests not on his own ability but on God, who alone makes anyone adequate for the work of the gospel. He can be sure of his calling precisely because he does not trust himself.

Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. The confidence (pepoithēsis, settled trust) is real, but it is not self-assurance measured against rivals. It is anchored through Christ and faces toward God, so it holds even under God’s scrutiny.

Not that we are sufficient in ourselves. Not merely for the big things, but for claiming anything at all as coming from himself. This answers 2:16: “Who is sufficient for these things?” Nobody, in himself.

But our sufficiency is from God. The word runs through both verses (hikanos, hikanotēs: adequate, up to the job), and it has a history. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament it renders one of God’s names: Shaddai, the Almighty (Ruth 1:20–21), becomes “the Sufficient One”. God does not merely have sufficiency; he is it. And it recalls a line of men who knew they lacked it. Moses said, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?” (Exodus 3:11). Jeremiah said, “I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth” (Jeremiah 1:6). Isaiah said, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). Every one of them was right. God never argued the point; he supplied what was missing. He has never called a servant and then left him to supply his own strength.

Through Christ. The confidence runs through Christ, the one man who ever stood before God with nothing to hide. He lived the very dependence Paul describes: the Son, himself God, took a true human nature and in it said that “the Son can do nothing of his own accord” (John 5:19), living on the Father’s word and the Spirit’s power (Luke 4:14). Then he went to the cross so that sinners could have confidence to enter the holy places by his blood (Hebrews 10:19).

Which sentence do you live in? “I can do this”, or “I cannot do this, and God is going to do it anyway”? The first sounds like faith and is usually self-reliance in good clothes. The second sounds like defeat and is where God does most of his work. Here is comfort for anyone who has backed away because they did not feel up to it: the class they were asked to teach, the parent they must care for, the marriage they no longer know how to mend. The feeling of inadequacy does not disqualify you; it is simply accurate, and Paul said so in writing. Adequacy was never the entry requirement, because it was never going to come from inside.

So do I still need to prepare, study and train? Yes. God’s sufficiency works through means, not instead of them. Paul asked for his books and parchments in prison (2 Timothy 4:13) and told Timothy to do his best to rightly handle the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). Prepare, learn, take advice, practise, but lean on God rather than on the preparation: pray as you study, and when you have done all you can, go in knowing that any change in people’s hearts will be his gift, not your achievement. Hard work and dependence are not rivals; they are the two hands of faithful service.

verseByVerse.quote: who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has made Paul a minister of the new covenant, in which the Spirit gives the life that the law written on stone could never give. “The letter” here is not the plain words of Scripture but the law standing outside a person, able only to condemn him.

Ministers of a new covenant. Not a better teacher of the old covenant, but a servant of what the prophets promised and never saw (Jeremiah 31:31–34). A covenant is a binding relationship God establishes by his word and seals by sacrifice, in which he is their God and they are his people. This one was inaugurated not with tablets on a mountain but with a body given and blood poured out: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20).

Not of the letter but of the Spirit. The next verse defines the letter: the ministry of death “carved in letters on stone”. It is the law of Moses, standing outside a person and telling him what to do. The Spirit is the life-giver who writes God’s law on hearts.

For the letter kills. Not because it is bad: the law is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). It kills because it states the standard perfectly, gives no power to meet it, and pronounces death on those who fail (Galatians 3:10). It describes the disease with total precision and hands you no medicine, and a diagnosis with no cure is a death sentence read aloud.

But the Spirit gives life. He does what the stone never could: he regenerates a dead heart and writes the command inside it, so that obedience comes from within instead of being demanded from outside (John 6:63; Romans 8:2, 11).

The death of the Lawgiver’s Son. The letter could kill; it took the death of the Lawgiver’s Son to make anything alive. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation now breathes on dead hearts, and they live.

The popular reading has it backwards. This verse is often taken to mean that close attention to the words of Scripture is deadening, and a spiritual impression is where the life is. But the Spirit inspired the words. The warning is aimed at the person who knows the Bible thoroughly, keeps the rules scrupulously, and has never been changed by any of it. A person can live under the letter with a well-marked Bible in his hand.

In everyday life. When you obey God this week, is it a wall you keep running into, or a direction you want to go? If it feels like the wall, do not throw away the commandments; ask the Spirit to write them on your heart, and look again at the Christ who kept them all for you.

Then how should I read the Bible? For its plain, intended meaning, which is what the Reformers meant by reading it literally. Ask what the human author meant his first readers to understand, reading history as history, poetry as poetry, parable as parable. Read each passage in context, let clearer passages explain harder ones, and follow it to Christ, as the apostles did (Luke 24:27), without hunting for secret meanings no ordinary reader could find. And read prayerfully, asking the Spirit who wrote it for understanding and a heart to obey; he works through the words, never around them.

Where Christians differ: the letter and the spirit. Since Origen, the third-century teacher, some have read this verse as a rule of interpretation: the literal meaning of Scripture kills, but the spiritual or allegorical meaning gives life. This commentary’s view: Paul is speaking not about ways of reading Scripture but about two covenants: the law written on stone, which condemns, and the Spirit’s new covenant work, which gives life. The Reformers rightly insisted on the plain, literal-grammatical meaning of Scripture, read in the light of Christ. The law is not abolished as God’s moral standard for believers, but it cannot justify or give life. Only the Spirit, through the gospel, does that.
verseByVerse.note: The “letter” is the law written on stone, which could condemn but not give life.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–18 — The Fading Glory and the Surpassing Glory; the Unveiled Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The glory of the new covenant so surpasses the old that every believer now sees what only Moses once saw, and is changed by it. Moses’ shining face shows that the law came with real glory, but its ministry brought condemnation and was being brought to an end; the ministry of the Spirit, which brings righteousness and lasts, is far greater (vv. 7–11). So Paul speaks openly, not veiled like Moses (vv. 12–13). The veil now lies over hearts that read Moses without Christ (vv. 14–15), but it is removed whenever anyone turns to the Lord, who is met in the Spirit and gives freedom (vv. 16–17), and all believers, unveiled, are being transformed into Christ’s image (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Paul reads the story of Moses’ veil (v. 13) in the light of its fulfilment in Christ: the whole Mosaic arrangement was temporary and pointed beyond itself.

Verse 18 is a key text for the Reformed teaching that sanctification is the Spirit’s work through the word (see the note on v. 18).
verseByVerse.examples: An older believer meets with a young Christian worn out by the effort of holiness: striving, measuring, failing, striving again. She encourages him to meditate slowly on passages that show the character and glory of Christ, and to rest in what he sees before rushing to apply it. Months later he notices his desires changing, not through more effort but through beholding.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the law, which brought death to sinners, came with a glory so bright that Israel could not look at Moses’ face, the ministry of the Spirit must be far more glorious. Paul honours the old covenant’s glory in order to show how much greater the new one is.

The ministry of death. Paul now argues three times in five verses from lesser to greater. To call the law given at Sinai “the ministry of death” sounds close to blasphemy, but it is named for its result. The commandment is good; what it does to a sinner is fatal, because it can only tell him what he has failed to be. Paul turns to Moses because the “tablets of stone” of verse 3 lead straight back to Sinai, and, it seems, because his rivals were proud Hebrews (11:22) who traded on Moses’ prestige (see the introduction). He does not belittle Moses. He shows what Moses’ ministry was always pointing to.

Such glory. Moses comes down from forty days on the mountain carrying the tablets, not knowing that his face is shining, and Aaron and the people are afraid to come near (Exodus 34:29–35). The light is not his. It is left over from where he has been, as a man who has stood near a fire comes back smelling of smoke, and even that reflected edge of God’s glory was more than they could bear. Such was the glory of the covenant that kills: real glory, because it came from God.

Which was being brought to an end. The glory was passing even while they were too frightened to look at it, a picture of the old covenant itself, which was always meant to give way (Hebrews 8:13).

Will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory? If a passing light on one man’s face was more than a nation could look at, how great must be the glory of a ministry that does not condemn but makes righteous, that is written not on the skin but on the heart, and that does not fade?

A face that shone with its own light. Centuries later three men watched another face on another mountain, and “his face shone like the sun” (Matthew 17:2). That light was not left over from a visit; it was his own, coming out. Moses was there to see it, and this time the glory belonged to the man in the middle. The light Moses carried for a season, Christ is for ever.

The death the stone pronounced. How can a ministry of death give way to one of life without God cancelling his own sentence? Only because the sentence was carried out: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The death the tablets pronounced on every lawbreaker fell on the one man who had kept every word on them. The new ministry is not the old one softened: the law’s demand was met in Christ’s life and its penalty paid in his death, and now the Spirit writes on hearts the law that once could only condemn them.

Short-changed? Reading the Old Testament, a Christian can feel quietly short-changed: they had the fire on the mountain, the sea opening, the shining face; we have an ordinary Tuesday. Paul says the comparison runs the other way. Their glory was on its way out. Yours does not fade, in a covenant that cannot be broken, administered by the Spirit of God living inside ordinary people. It looks less impressive because it has moved inside, where the work needed doing.

Does this mean the Ten Commandments are obsolete? No. What is being brought to an end is the old covenant as a ministry: the law standing outside a person, on stone, condemning him. The law itself is holy, and its moral demands still show believers how to love God and neighbour. Paul says we uphold the law (Romans 3:31) and sums up its second table, the commandments about our neighbour, in the command to love (Romans 13:8–10).

Where Christians differ: the law and the Sabbath. Some Christians hold that the whole law of Moses has given way to the law of Christ, though the moral teaching it contains is repeated and deepened in the New Testament. Most in the Reformed tradition hold that the moral law summarised in the Ten Commandments still binds, now written on the heart by the Spirit (v. 3). On the fourth commandment, the Westminster and 1689 Baptist confessions keep it as the Christian Sabbath, moved to the Lord’s Day; others hold that the Sabbath, like the ceremonial law, is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), while the first day remains the day of worship. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). The confessional view (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8) is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both sides honour the Lord’s Day, and both should do so without judging the other.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s verb for “being brought to an end” (katargeō) normally means to set aside or make ineffective, not to grow dim, and Exodus never says the shining faded; Paul draws the point from the veil (see the note on vv. 12–13). So some think he means the glory physically faded; others that it was being set aside, because its covenant was meant to end. Either way, the glory was real and temporary.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

verseByVerse.quote: For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new covenant outshines the old because it brings a verdict of righteousness instead of condemnation, and because it lasts. Beside it the old glory is like a lamp at sunrise: real, but with nothing left to do.

The ministry of righteousness. The comparison is pressed three ways: what the two ministries do (v. 9), how they compare side by side (v. 10), and how long each lasts (v. 11). Condemnation and righteousness are courtroom words. The law brings a verdict of guilty, accurately. The gospel brings a verdict of righteous to the same defendant: this is justification. The Judge declares the guilty righteous because Christ’s righteousness is put to their account, received by faith alone (5:21; Romans 3:21–22; 4:5). That is the whole distance between Sinai and Calvary in two nouns.

No glory at all. What had glory now has none (v. 10). That is what happens when a lamp left burning meets the sunrise: the lamp was never a fraud, but in the new light there is nothing left for it to do.

What is permanent. Then the decisive difference (v. 11): one was being brought to an end, the other is permanent (menō, abiding). The old arrangement was scaffolding: good, necessary work, put up around a building that was coming.

His glory has no evening. The covenant remains because its Mediator remains. Moses came down shining for a while and then died outside the land. The Son went up to a cross and down into a grave, and rose to a life that cannot end; he holds his priesthood permanently (Hebrews 7:24). He is the Lord our righteousness (Jeremiah 23:6), and his glory has no evening.

What does the ministry of righteousness mean for me? If you trust Christ, the verdict over your life is righteous, a gift, not a wage: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (5:21). You stand before God not on your record, good or bad, but on Christ’s. So you can come to God on your worst day with confidence, and your best days add nothing to your acceptance. The new covenant does not lower God’s standard. It meets it, in Christ, for you.

Everything else fades. Health fades, beauty fades fast, careers end, and twenty years of achievement become one line at a funeral. None of these is worthless; the shine on Moses’ face was real. But they are all being brought to an end, and the question is whether you have anything that is not.

Why still read the Old Testament? It would be easy to conclude that the first three-quarters of the Bible can be quietly shelved. But Paul quotes it constantly, in this very argument too. His point is not that the old covenant was wrong but that it was never meant to be the end. Scaffolding does not become rubbish when the building appears; it shows you how the building went up.

If the old covenant was fading all along, did God change his mind? No. It was never a first plan that failed. God promised a new covenant through Jeremiah while the old one was still in force (Jeremiah 31:31–34), and Paul calls the law a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24): appointed for a season, with the end in view. God’s purpose from the beginning was to bless the nations through Abraham’s offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16). What changed was the stage of the plan, never the God who made it (Malachi 3:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the new covenant’s glory will never fade, Paul can speak with complete openness, unlike Moses, who veiled a glory that was passing away. His hope makes him frank, not cautious.

Since we have such a hope, we are very bold. The boldness comes not from temperament (he was too troubled to stay at Troas, 2:12–13) or from success, but from a glory that does not fade. The word is parrēsia, the citizen’s right to speak openly. With nothing to hide, Paul can say it all.

Not like Moses. When Moses had finished speaking to the people he put a veil over his face, removing it when he went in to speak with the LORD (Exodus 34:33–35). Exodus records the veil without explaining it. Paul, standing on the far side of the cross, sees what it signified: Moses veiled his face so that Israel would not watch the glory passing away, and so would not see the end of a covenant that was never permanent. The veil became a picture of Israel’s inability to see what the covenant pointed to. This is not allegory imposed on the text but the instinct the Lord himself modelled on the Emmaus road, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets” (Luke 24:27).

The end behind the veil. “The outcome” is the telos, and Paul uses the same word in Romans: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). The passing glory on one man’s face pictured a covenant that pointed past itself to a face whose glory would not fade. Paul is not guarding a light that is running down; he is announcing what the old covenant was moving towards: Jesus Christ, crucified and risen.

Exposed, so that we could be uncovered. The one who gave us a glory that cannot fade had nothing to hide either. He spoke openly to the world, and in secret said nothing (John 18:20); and on the cross the whole city saw him, exposed, so that our shame could be covered and our faces uncovered for ever.

Managing an impression. Moses covers something that is fading, and the people deal with a screen rather than a face. So it often is in religious life. The love has cooled, the prayers have dried up, and rather than say so we put on the veil: we answer “fine” and keep the vocabulary, the attendance, the tone of voice. Paul’s alternative is not to shine harder. It is the open face of a man whose glory is not his own and so is not running out, and who has no reason to cover anything, even his weakness.

Does boldness mean I must tell everyone all my struggles? No. Openness is not broadcasting: Paul chose what to tell, to whom and why, and wrote of his weaknesses to help the church. What boldness rules out is the managed mask: pretending to God and to those closest to you that all is well when it is not. Have one or two mature believers to whom you tell the truth about your soul (James 5:16). Be honest with God always; he sees through every veil anyway. And in public, be open about the gospel and your need of it, without performing either strength or weakness.

Uncertain wording. Telos can mean the end of something (its stopping) or its goal (what it aimed at), and both may be in view: Israel saw neither the glory come to an end nor what the covenant was moving towards. Exodus also never says why Moses wore the veil. Paul’s reading, that it hid the passing of the glory, is the likely sense here.

parallels.desc: he put a veil over his face
