verseByVerse.quote: But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The veil that covered Moses’ face now lies over the hearts of those who read the old covenant without Christ, and only Christ can take it away. The problem is not the text but the heart, and Paul writes of it with grief, not contempt.

But their minds were hardened. The veil moves from Moses’ face to the reader’s heart. The Scriptures Paul’s own people revere are read every Sabbath by minds hardened (pōroō, made callous, dulled) to what they are for (Romans 11:7).

Two things to say first. This passage has been terribly misused. First, Paul writes as a Jew, a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), with “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” for his kinsmen (Romans 9:2–3): this is grief, not contempt. Second, the hardening is not final. Within a sentence the veil is removed whenever a person turns, and Paul himself is the proof that it happens to the hardest cases.

That same veil remains unlifted. “The old covenant” means the Scriptures, especially the law, read in the synagogue; this is the only place in the New Testament where the phrase appears. The veil is over the heart, not the text. The words are read accurately and honoured, and what they point to is not seen (John 5:39). The problem was never a lack of Bible.

Only through Christ is it taken away. The veil is not removed by debate. Paul could out-argue any man in a synagogue, yet he does not say the answer is a better argument; if you pray for a relative who knows all the answers and remains cold, you are not up against a shortage of information. On the Damascus road Paul did not lose an argument. He was struck blind, and then something like scales fell from his eyes (Acts 9:18): the veil removed by the one person who can remove it, from a man furiously certain he was reading Moses correctly.

Whenever Moses is read. That is, the books of Moses, read each Sabbath (Acts 15:21); and Moses was writing about Christ: “if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me” (John 5:46). The Passover lamb, the bronze serpent, the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15) all point to him. The veil does not hide a stranger. It hides the one the reader is waiting for.

Closer to home. Christians can do the same: read the Bible through on a plan, know the outline of every book, and miss the person the whole library was assembled to present. It is not a Jewish failing but a human one.

What it does not mean. Not that Jewish people are worse than others: every unbeliever has a veil over the heart (4:3–4). Not that the Old Testament is obscure in itself; it is clear to those who see Christ in it. And it never justifies contempt or hostility toward Jewish people, which the church has too often shown, to its shame.

In everyday life. Pray for all who read the Scriptures without seeing Christ. And when you read the Old Testament, ask before you close it: where is this pointing to Christ?

Will the veil ever be lifted from Israel as a people? Christians who share the gospel read Romans 11 differently. Many believe Paul promises a future large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in and all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). Others understand all Israel to mean the full number of God’s elect, Jews and Gentiles together, gathered throughout this age. Both agree that the hardening is partial, that Jewish people are coming to Christ now, and that there is one way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike: faith in Jesus the Messiah. Both should lead us to pray, with Paul, for our Jewish neighbours, and to share the gospel with them gladly.

Uncertain wording. The end of verse 14 is compressed. It can be read as in the ESV, the veil “remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away”, or as saying that the veil remains because it is not revealed that in Christ the old covenant is being brought to an end. Either way, only Christ ends the blindness; the ESV’s reading is the more natural.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses” here means the books of Moses, read aloud each Sabbath in the synagogue.

verseByVerse.quote: But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. As Moses uncovered his face when he went in before the LORD, so anyone who turns to Christ is given to see.

But when one turns to the Lord. The hinge of the chapter, reaching back into Exodus: “Whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil” (Exodus 34:34). The covering was for the crowd. In the presence of God it came off. Turning (epistrephō) is a change of direction, not only of opinion: repentance and faith together. Not when a person understands enough, or has cleaned himself up first, but when he turns.

The veil is removed. Taken away completely (periaireō). Nobody pulls the covering off his own heart, any more than a blind man cures himself by deciding to see. That is the difference between religion and the gospel: one tells a man to lift the veil, the other tells him that when he turns he will find it has been taken. Even the turning is God’s gift, for God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ (4:6). The turning does not earn the sight; it is the moment the sight is given.

The Lord Moses met. Paul has just said to whom we now turn: “only through Christ is it taken away” (v. 14). The LORD before whom Moses stood unveiled has come near with a human face: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Moses had to go into the tent to take off the veil. Now “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and to turn to Jesus is to stand where Moses stood.

Nobody has ever been told to wait. There is no antechamber, no preliminary examination, no queue. A man turns and the covering is gone. That open way in is what the Son of God died to win: the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom, on the afternoon he died (Matthew 27:51).

Open at both ends. If the Bible has gone flat, if God has become an idea you defend rather than a person you know, the instruction is not to try harder to feel it but to turn: face him, and speak to him. Paul attaches no conditions, not even that you have not wasted the last ten years. Anyone may turn, at any time.

If the Bible feels veiled to me after years as a Christian, am I not saved? Not necessarily. Scripture can feel flat in dry seasons, through tiredness, grief, unconfessed sin, distraction or the way we read. The question is not whether you feel the glory today but whether you are turned toward Christ, trusting him and wanting him. If you are, keep turning. Confess what needs confessing. Read more slowly, and pray before you read: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). Read with others, and sit under faithful preaching. The veil does not return over a believer’s heart, but a believer’s eyes can grow dim, and the Lord delights to brighten them.

What can I do for someone who is still veiled? Pray first, because only the Lord removes the veil. Then do what Philip did for the Ethiopian reading Isaiah: open the Scriptures and show them Jesus (Acts 8:35). Answer honest questions without relying on arguments, invite them to read a Gospel with you, and live in a way that makes Christ attractive. You cannot lift the veil, but you can stand beside the person while the Lord does.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s sentence names no subject: it could be “when he turns” (Moses) or “when it turns” (Israel, or the heart of v. 15), but the ESV’s general “one” fits Paul’s point that this can happen to anyone. The verb could also mean that he removes the veil himself, as Moses did, but most translations rightly take it as passive, because verse 14 has just said that only through Christ is it taken away.
verseByVerse.note: Paul echoes Exodus: whenever Moses went in before the LORD, he removed the veil.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord to whom we turn is now met in the Spirit, and where the Spirit is, there is freedom. Paul is not merging two persons, but explaining how the LORD of the Exodus story is known today.

Now the Lord is the Spirit. “The Lord” of verse 16, in the Exodus passage Paul is explaining, is Yahweh, the LORD. Some take it here to mean Christ, but Paul seems to be interpreting the text he has just echoed: in the new covenant, to turn to the Lord is to meet the Spirit, who applies Christ’s work and removes the veil.

There is freedom. Freedom (eleutheria) from the veil first, but also from the covenant that could only condemn, from bondage to sin and death (Romans 8:2; Galatians 5:1), from the terrible arithmetic of a religion in which everything depends on your performance, and from the exhausting business of keeping up a veil over what is fading (v. 13). Above all, freedom of access: a child coming into his Father’s presence.

The Spirit of his Son. Where did that freedom come from? “God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:4–6). The Son went under the law that bound us and paid what it demanded; then the Spirit came to make his freedom ours. The Spirit of the Lord brings freedom because he is the Spirit of the Son who bought it.

Free on the instrument. This is not freedom to do as you please (Galatians 5:13). The heaviest masters are not laws from outside but appetites, resentments and fears, chosen freely, that now cannot be put down. Christian freedom is like a musician’s: years of practice under rules he did not invent have freed him to play the music he hears. He is not free from the instrument. He is free on it.

In everyday life. If you obey God mainly to keep something bad from happening, his disappointment or withdrawal, part of you is still standing at the foot of Sinai. The commandments have not gone soft; the fear has gone out of them, because the verdict was settled before you began. Obey today as a son, not a hired hand.

Does the freedom of the Spirit mean worship should be unplanned and spontaneous? No. Paul means freedom from condemnation and the veil, not a style of worship. God is a God of peace, not of confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33, 40), and the Spirit is as present in a prepared sermon and a written prayer as in an unplanned one. Nor is freedom measured by dramatic experiences. This commentary holds that the sign gifts which confirmed the apostles’ message (12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4) belonged to that founding generation, though many faithful Christians believe they continue; on either view, the Spirit is known most surely where Christ is exalted, the word is believed and lives are changed. Worship is free when it comes from forgiven hearts that know they are welcome.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord the Spirit? Some (modalists, who hold that Father, Son and Spirit are one person appearing in three ways) take this verse to mean the Son and the Spirit are the same person. This commentary’s view: Paul distinguishes the Spirit and the Lord in the same verse: “the Spirit of the Lord”. He is saying that the Lord of the Exodus passage is now encountered through the Spirit, who is himself the Lord, fully God. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three distinct persons, one God (2 Corinthians 13:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every believer, with nothing between him and God, is being changed into the likeness of Christ by looking at his glory, and the Spirit is the one who does it. We become like the one we behold.

And we all, with unveiled face. Here the chapter arrives. On Sinai only Moses went up into the cloud of glory, while the nation stood below, and he veiled what he brought down. Now the whole congregation is on the mountain. There is no spiritual class in the new covenant who see what ordinary members do not: the tired mother, the apprentice, the man never asked to do anything in church, we all. Nothing stands between the believer and the glory of God, and it is safe for the face to be bare.

Beholding the glory of the Lord. We do not yet see him as he is, but we see him truly, as in a good mirror: in the face of Christ (4:6), shown to us in the gospel and the Scriptures. Our part is to look.

Being transformed into the same image. Transformed (metamorphoō) is the verb used of the Lord’s transfiguration and of the renewing of the mind (Romans 12:2). It is passive, done to us by God, and present: happening now, in ordinary weeks, felt or not. The image is that of Christ (Romans 8:29).

From one degree of glory to another. Literally, from glory to glory, by stages. Moses’ glory faded; ours increases. This is sanctification, God’s slow, sure work of making a pardoned sinner holy in fact, and it ends in glorification, when Christ will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

From the Lord who is the Spirit. The end of the sentence takes the weight off the one doing the looking. The change is not produced by the intensity of your concentration. The Spirit is doing it, and he never abandons a half-finished work (Philippians 1:6).

In the flow. Here is Paul’s real letter of recommendation (vv. 2–3): the Spirit making his converts like Christ. And the verse leads into chapter 4, where the glory is seen in the face of Christ (4:6) and carried in jars of clay (4:7).

Painting the face of Jesus. In people who mostly cannot see it happening, the Spirit is painting the face of Jesus on the faces of sinners. The day is coming when the mirror is taken away, and we shall see him as he is, and being like him will be a fact (1 John 3:2). Moses’ face shone for a season and faded. Ours, in him, will shine for ever.

We become what we look at. Holiness here comes not first by effort or resolutions, useful as those are, but by where we look. That is why John Owen, near the end of his life, wrote that the great means of holiness is the beholding of the glory of Christ, and why a man can grit his teeth through disciplines for a decade and change very little. It cuts both ways: look every evening at people who are richer and you will grow discontented without deciding to; feed on outrage and you will grow angry. Those who make idols become like them (Psalm 115:8). So the question is not “Am I trying hard enough?” but “What am I looking at?”

What it does not mean. Not that transformation is instant, or that we become perfect in this life. Nor that effort is pointless: the same apostle tells us to put sin to death and to train ourselves for godliness. But all our effort is the effort of looking, and of removing what blocks the view.

In everyday life. Add up the hours honestly: what is in front of your eyes most in an ordinary week, and where is Christ put before you long enough for anything to happen? Change one habit that keeps your gaze elsewhere, trusting the Spirit who dwells in you to do the changing (Romans 8:11).

How do I actually behold the glory of the Lord? Through the means God has given. Read the Gospels slowly and often, asking in each scene what it shows you of Jesus: his holiness, his compassion, his authority, his cross. Sit under preaching that sets Christ before you, take the Lord’s Supper as a looking at his body given and blood shed, sing hymns full of him, and carry a single verse about him through the day. And pray that the Spirit would show you his glory as you look; beholding is reading with the eyes of faith, asking to see him.

Why do I not feel that I am changing? Because growth is slow and mostly invisible from the inside, like a child’s height marked on the door frame once a year. It is being done to you, whether you feel it or not. Look back over years, not days, and ask those who know you well. Often the clearest sign is that you see your sin more clearly than before, which feels like going backwards but is the light growing. Keep looking at Christ, and leave the measuring to the one who is doing the work.

Uncertain wording. “Beholding” translates katoptrizomai, a rare verb built on the word for a mirror, which can mean looking at something as in a mirror or reflecting it like one. The contrast with the veiled readers of verses 14–15 favours looking. The closing phrase is compressed too (literally “from Lord Spirit”), and can also be read “from the Lord, the Spirit”; either way the Spirit does the changing.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?<sup>2</sup>You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all.<sup>3</sup>And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.<sup>4</sup>Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God.<sup>5</sup>Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,<sup>6</sup>who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.<sup>7</sup>Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end,<sup>8</sup>will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?<sup>9</sup>For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory.<sup>10</sup>Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it.<sup>11</sup>For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.<sup>12</sup>Since we have such a hope, we are very bold,<sup>13</sup>not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.<sup>14</sup>But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away.<sup>15</sup>Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.<sup>16</sup>But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.<sup>17</sup>Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.<sup>18</sup>And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.

keyVerse.quote: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter climbs to this verse. What Moses alone saw on the mountain, and could not keep, every believer now sees in the face of Christ, and the sight changes us. It also settles the dispute the chapter began with: Paul’s true letter of recommendation is the Spirit making ordinary people like Christ.

3.reflection:
Paul’s rivals relied on letters of recommendation, while Paul pointed to lives changed by the Spirit (vv. 1–3). What are Christians most easily impressed by in leaders and churches today, and how could we learn to look for the Spirit’s handwriting instead?

Paul says he is not sufficient in himself, but his sufficiency is from God (vv. 5–6). Where do you feel most inadequate at the moment, and how would it change things to treat that feeling as accurate rather than disqualifying?

The law is holy, yet Paul calls its ministry one of death and condemnation, and the new one a ministry of righteousness (vv. 7–11). How has Christ dealt with the law’s verdict on us, and what difference should that make to the way we obey God?

Verse 18 says we are changed by beholding the glory of the Lord. What fills your eyes most in an ordinary week, and what practical step would put Christ before you long enough for that change to happen?

4.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 continues Paul’s long account of his ministry (2:14–7:4). Chapter 3 showed the surpassing glory of the new covenant; this chapter shows the man who carries it, and the contrast is startling.

The message. God puts the greatest treasure there is, the light of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ, into cheap and breakable containers, so that everyone can see the power is his. The weakness and suffering of Christ’s servants is therefore no evidence against the gospel: it is where the life of Jesus shows, and it is preparing a glory beyond all comparison. That is why Paul does not lose heart.

Why it was said. Corinth admired polish, presence and success, and the rival teachers offered all three (see the introduction). Beside them Paul looked like a failure: plain in speech, often in trouble, physically battered, and some called his gospel obscure. If the ministry is so glorious, the church was asking, why is the minister so weak?

How the chapter makes its case. First Paul defends his method and message (vv. 1–6): his ministry is a gift of mercy, so he uses no tricks; if some cannot see, Satan has blinded them, and if anyone sees, the God of creation has spoken light into the heart. Then he explains the weakness (vv. 7–15): the treasure is in clay jars, his blows never become defeat, and his daily dying shows the life of Jesus, brings life to others and multiplies thanks to God. Last he says why he does not give up (vv. 16–18): his inner self is renewed daily while his body wastes away, and present affliction is light beside an eternal weight of glory.

Where it leads. The glory of God has a face, the face of Jesus (v. 6). The treasure itself once came in earthenware: the Son of God took our frail flesh and was the jar broken on the cross, “crucified in weakness” yet living “by the power of God” (13:4). Paul carries “the death of Jesus” so that “the life of Jesus” may be seen (v. 10), and his hope rests on the God “who raised the Lord Jesus” (v. 14).

For us. This chapter is for every believer who feels too ordinary, too tired or too battered to be of use, and for every church tempted to look impressive. Your weakness is not a disqualification but the design. Look again at the face of Christ, put your troubles honestly on the scales against the glory to come, and do not lose heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Light Shining in Darkness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul does not give up or cut corners, because his ministry is a gift of mercy and its power lies with God, not in technique. Since the ministry came by mercy, he will not lose heart, use tricks or dilute God’s word, but states the truth openly to the conscience (vv. 1–2). If some do not see, it is because Satan has blinded them to the glory of Christ (vv. 3–4). So Paul preaches Christ as Lord, not himself (v. 5), and wherever anyone does see, it is because the God who first commanded light has shone into the heart (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ is “the image of God” (v. 4), the true visible representation of the invisible God (see the note on vv. 3–4). God’s glory is found not in visions or mystical experiences but in the face of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen (v. 6).

Verse 6 echoes Genesis 1:3: conversion is a creative act of God, like the first creation, and so the new birth comes before faith (this is treated fully at v. 6).
verseByVerse.examples: A campus minister explains the gospel to a sharp philosophy student who has engaged every argument and remains unconvinced. The problem may be a blindness no argument can cure. He should not stop reasoning, for Paul commends the truth to the conscience, but he should add steady prayer that the God who speaks light into darkness will do it here.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because his ministry is a gift of God’s mercy, Paul does not give up, and he will not use tricks or water down God’s word to make it succeed. He states the truth openly and leaves it to work on people’s consciences before God.

By the mercy of God. “Therefore” reaches back to the whole of chapter 3: the covenant that does not fade, the veil removed, the glory that transforms. All Paul says about weakness is said by a man who knows what he has been given: “this ministry”, received “by the mercy of God”. He never speaks of it as an achievement.

We do not lose heart. To grow weary, run out of nerve, quit (enkakeō). He says it again in v. 16, and everything between explains why he has not stopped. Losing heart is one of the commonest and least discussed conditions in the Christian life. It is rarely a crisis of doctrine; it is the slow arrival of a Tuesday on which you cannot see the point of continuing: the class taught for years with nothing to show, the marriage prayed over since the children were small, the neighbour who is politely unmovable. Nobody announces that they have lost heart. They simply do slightly less, and then a little less than that.

Mercy, not willpower. Paul’s guard against it is the sentence he has just written. Had he earned his ministry, he would have to keep proving he deserved it, and one day he would be too tired to. But it was given in mercy, so it rests on the God who gave it, and God’s mercy does not get tired.

Underhanded ways. Then he names what he has refused, perhaps answering a charge of hidden motives. “Disgraceful, underhanded ways” are literally “the hidden things of shame”: whatever a man would not want brought into the light. “Cunning” is panourgia, a readiness to do anything to get one’s way, Paul’s word for the serpent in Eden (11:3). To “tamper with God’s word” is doloō, a term from the trade in wine and precious metals: to water down, or mix in something cheaper, close kin to the peddling of 2:17.

What does tampering actually look like? Rarely a denial; usually a dilution: the doctrine kept but drained of force, the demand quoted but never pressed, the warning read in a tone that says nobody here need worry. It also runs the other way: the verse hardened past what it says, used to control people. Either way the speaker has decided he knows better than the Bible what the Bible should do.

The open statement of the truth. Against all of it Paul sets one method, phanerōsis, a bringing into the light: say it plainly, in public, and let it work on the conscience, before God, who sees all. No technique, no leverage, no managing what people may know. It is a slower way to build, and the only way to build anything that will still stand when the builder is gone.

A display of patience. The mercy behind it all has a name and a face. Paul tells Timothy what happened on the road to Damascus: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost, and I received mercy for this reason, that in me Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience (1 Timothy 1:15–16). The Lord who showed mercy to the man hunting his people will hardly withdraw it now that the enemy has become his servant (Romans 5:10).

If I lose heart, does it mean I am not a real Christian? No. Paul would not need to say “we do not lose heart” unless it were a real danger for real believers. Elijah sat under a broom tree and asked to die (1 Kings 19:4); the psalmist told his own soul to hope in God because it was not doing so on its own (Psalm 42:5). Discouragement is a temptation, not a verdict on your standing. The remedy is not to feel stronger but to look again at who gave you what you have: your calling and your salvation came by mercy, and mercy is not withdrawn because you are tired. Rest, tell a trusted believer, keep coming to the means of grace (God’s word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people), and do the next small faithful thing.

How do I commend the truth to someone’s conscience without pressure? Say what is true, plainly, as one who will stand before God for how you said it. Do not exaggerate to make it appealing, or hide the hard parts (sin, judgment, the cost of following Christ) to make it acceptable. Use no guilt, flattery or social debt (I helped you, so you owe me a hearing). Give people time, invite questions, let them see you live it, and leave the result with God. The conscience is his territory, and he makes the truth land.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When people hear the gospel plainly and still do not see, the fault is not in the message but in a blindness Satan has laid over their minds. What he hides from them is the brightest thing there is: the glory of Christ, the image of God.

If our gospel is veiled. The obvious objection: if Paul states the truth openly, why do intelligent, decent people hear Christ clearly presented and remain unmoved? Some in Corinth evidently called his gospel obscure. The problem, Paul answers, is not the message but the hearers, those on the road to destruction (2:15), and someone besides preacher and hearer is at work. “Veiled” picks up the veil of 3:14–15: the covering that lay over the reading of Moses lies over the hearing of the gospel too.

The god of this world. Not a second god. There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6). Satan is a creature; God limits what he may do and has fixed the day his power ends. The title means he is the god people actually serve, the power this age treats as ultimate, worshipped in a thousand forms that never carry his name. Jesus called him the ruler of this world and said in the same breath that he would be cast out (John 12:31; Ephesians 2:2).

Has blinded the minds. Not persuaded, not argued: blinded, a single decisive act. He need not make people believe something false about Christ; it is enough that they cannot see him at all. A person can understand the words of the gospel, even explain them back to you, and still see nothing glorious in Christ: the facts register, but the beauty does not. That is why the same sermon can move one hearer to tears and bore the one beside him, and why Paul says the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Corinthians 2:14).

The image of God. Look at what the blindfold is meant to hide. Three phrases are stacked, each opening into the next: the light, of the gospel, of the glory of Christ, and they arrive at a person. “Image” is eikōn, the true visible representation, not a rough likeness: he is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). The Lord himself put it beyond argument: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). The invisible God has made himself visible in one place only, a Galilean carpenter executed outside a city wall. Why should the enemy take such trouble to hide one face, unless that face really is the one place where God can be seen? The image of the invisible God has stood in the full glare of hell’s hatred and come out risen, and every blindfold in the world stays in place only until he says otherwise.

What it does not mean. Unbelievers are not innocent victims. Paul calls them unbelievers, and this blindness is never against a person’s will; it confirms a direction already chosen (John 3:19). Nor may we write anyone off. The man writing this was once as blind as anyone, on the road to Damascus with letters authorising him to arrest Christians (Acts 9:1–2), when Christ stopped him.

You are up against a blindfold. If you have explained the gospel to someone you love, patiently and well, and nothing has happened, you have not necessarily failed. Blindfolds are not removed by better reasoning. That is why the Paul who reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath (Acts 18:4) also asked churches to pray for him.

Does calling unbelievers blind make Christians proud? Only if Christians claimed to see because they were cleverer or better, and Paul claims the opposite. He was the blind man, the zealous, learned, religious one who was sure he saw clearly (Philippians 3:4–6), and he sees only because light came from outside him (v. 6). A man led out of a dark cellar is not boasting when he calls back to those still inside that there is a door. The moral man cannot see by his morality any more than the sceptic by his scepticism. Everyone who sees Christ was shown him.

Does “perishing” mean my friend is beyond hope? No. It describes the road a person is on now, not a sentence we can read off his life. You cannot know whom God has chosen, and neither did Paul; he kept preaching, because some who are blind today will see tomorrow. The word should make you urgent, not resigned. No one is beyond hope until he dies in unbelief, and while your friend is breathing, the God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, can still speak.

How should I pray for someone who is blinded? Pray to God, not at the devil: ask the Father to do what v. 6 says he does, to shine into this heart. Pray by name for the thing that matters most, that they would see the glory of Christ, not merely that their circumstances improve or their objections be answered. Ask God to send them other believers and to give you a clear word at the right time. And pray with confidence, because you are not asking for something unusual. Opening blind eyes is what Jesus came to do (Luke 4:18).

Where Christians differ: the god of this world. Some ancient heretics (Marcion and the Gnostics) took this to mean the God of the Old Testament, a lesser, evil god. This commentary’s view: The god of this age is Satan, called god because unbelievers serve him and he holds sway over the present evil age. His power is real but limited and temporary, under God’s sovereign control (Job 1:12), and already defeated at the cross (Colossians 2:15). There is one true God, who made the world and rules it.
verseByVerse.note: “The god of this world” is Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A minister of Christ points away from himself to Jesus as Lord, and serves people for Jesus’ sake.

For what we proclaim is not ourselves. If the light the enemy hides is Christ’s glory (v. 4), the preacher must not stand in front of it. This answers rivals who commended themselves and promoted their experiences, gifts and success (3:1; 10:12): the contest was never about Paul. Nobody sets out to preach himself. It happens by increments: the illustration that makes the speaker look perceptive, the discovery that a certain kind of story gets a certain response. The message stays orthodox. The subject quietly changes.

But Jesus Christ as Lord. The earliest Christian confession (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), two words in Greek, and in time it cost lives, because to say Jesus is Lord was to say Caesar was not. It is a claim about who is actually in charge, of the world and of the hearer.

Your servants. The word is slave (doulos), one with no agenda of his own. The apostle who has spent three chapters defending his authority describes his relationship to the people questioning him as slavery to them, the opposite of lording it over their faith (1:24).

For Jesus’ sake. He is not their slave because the customer is always right; he has just refused to trim the message for them. His Master sends him to serve them, and that keeps his service from becoming flattery. A man who serves people for their sake alone will end up telling them what they want. A man who serves them for Christ’s sake will tell them the truth and stay.

He is Lord of all, and he knelt. The shape of that service was set by a Lord who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45), and who on the last night took a towel and washed the feet of the men who were about to abandon him (John 13:4–5).

I am no preacher, so does verse 5 apply to me? Yes. Every Christian speaks about Christ to someone: a child at bedtime, a friend over coffee, a home group, a post online, and the same drift threatens us all. Testimony can become a story about how interesting my journey has been; helping in church, a way of being needed and noticed; online the temptation is built into the format. When people have listened to you, are they thinking more about Jesus or about you? Tell your story so that he is the one who acts in it.

In everyday life. When you catch yourself back in the centre, as all of us do, turn back without despair to the Servant who never sought his own glory (John 8:50) and stands in your place before God. And look for a menial way to serve someone this week, because your Master would have done it.

verseByVerse.quote: For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Conversion is a new creation: the God who spoke light into the first darkness speaks it into the human heart, and what that heart then sees is his glory in the face of Jesus Christ.

Let light shine out of darkness. Verse 4 said the mind is blinded; this verse says what God does about it, reaching back to the first page of the Bible (with an echo of Isaiah 9:2). Darkness was over the face of the deep, with nothing to strike a light from and nobody to strike it. And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Genesis 1:3). Paul says that is what conversion is.

Has shone in our hearts. Paul surely thinks of the light that flashed around him on the road (Acts 9:3), but he says “our hearts”: every believer has had God shine into him, a new creation (5:17). The darkness in Genesis did not cooperate. It did not reach toward the light, make itself receptive, or take a small first step and get helped the rest of the way. Light arrived because God spoke, and when he spoke there was no darkness left to consult.

What regeneration is. Regeneration means new birth: God raising to life a heart dead towards him, so that it can see and believe. Jesus told Nicodemus that unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God, and that this birth is the Spirit’s work, like the wind, which blows where it wishes (John 3:3–8). Faith is the first breath of the new life, not its cause.

The knowledge of the glory of God. Glory is God’s worth made visible, his holiness, power and love shining out, and here it has been given a location: a human face. Moses asked to see that glory and was told, “You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20); he was shown only the back of God going past. What Moses was refused has been given to ordinary believers.

In the face of Jesus Christ. A face that was spat on, that had a crown of thorns pressed above it, that was set toward Jerusalem and would not turn away. There is the glory of God: not in the fire on Sinai, not in the whirlwind, but in the face of a man dying for his enemies. To see it is to watch Jesus in the Gospels, touching a leper, weeping at a grave, silent before Pilate, and to realise that you are looking not at a good man who points to God but at what God himself is like (John 1:14, 18). Whoever has once seen it never quite recovers, and nothing else in the universe repays looking at in the same way.

No one will ever look away. What faith sees now in the gospel, his people will one day see with their own eyes: they will see his face (Revelation 22:4), and the city’s lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). The face that was spat on will be the light of a whole new creation, and no one will ever look away.

Two anxieties removed. First, your own standing: if God lit the light in you, the flickering you worry about is not evidence against you, because you are not the one keeping it burning. Second, the person you have given up on: nothing in their hardness is a problem for a God whose speciality is speaking into a void.

What it does not mean. Conversion is not always sudden or dramatic, as Paul’s was. The light may dawn gradually, like a morning rather than a lightning flash, and many raised in Christian homes cannot name the day. But it is always God’s work.

If God must shine first, why should I tell anyone the gospel? Because the gospel is the light God shines (v. 4). He does not usually shine into hearts apart from the message but through it, when it is spoken (Romans 10:14–17). So your words are the lamp he uses, and his sovereignty is a reason to speak with hope, not to stay quiet. You cannot open a single eye, but you can hold up the light, and God has promised that his word will not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

How do I know God has shone in my heart? Not chiefly by remembering a moment, but by what you see now. Does Christ look glorious to you, not just true but beautiful and necessary? Do you trust him, not yourself, for your acceptance with God? Do you want to know him more, and hate the sin that dims the view? Blind eyes find Jesus dull or irrelevant. If he is precious to you, even when your sight seems dim, that is light, and you did not make it.

Where Christians differ: how does conversion happen? Many Christians in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions hold that God first gives every person enabling grace, so that they are able to believe, and that new birth follows faith; others believe that God offers light, and people by their own will choose to open their eyes. They point to the many calls to believe and to John 1:12, where receiving Christ comes before becoming God’s children. But the next verse says those children were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:13), and John says that everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God (1 John 5:1). This commentary’s view: The picture is creation. As darkness did not cooperate with God in creating light, the blinded heart does not cooperate in its own illumination. God shines in; the result is sight and faith. This is regeneration, God’s sovereign work, effectual because it never fails of its purpose (Ephesians 2:4–5; Westminster Confession 10.1–2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1–2). It is not theological machinery imposed on the text; it is what this verse says. A blinded mind cannot decide to see. But when God says let light shine into a particular human heart, that heart will believe, as certainly as the deep filled with light on the first day, and it believes freely and gladly, because it now sees. Christians who see it otherwise love the same Saviour and are right that faith is a real human act; the question between us is only which comes first.

parallels.desc: let there be light

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Treasure in Jars of Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God puts his treasure in fragile people so that the power is plainly his. Paul’s weakness is the clay jar (v. 7); his life is a run of real blows that never become defeat (vv. 8–9); and in that daily dying the risen life of Jesus becomes visible and reaches others (vv. 10–12). Like the psalmist who faced death, he keeps speaking because he believes, sure that the God who raised Jesus will raise him and bring him with the Corinthians into his presence (vv. 13–14). All of it spreads grace and multiplies thanks to God (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The four contrasts in vv. 8–9 are the pattern of the cross applied to the messengers of the cross. A share in Jesus’ dying is at work in Paul’s ministry (v. 10), and through it resurrection life reaches the churches.

Verse 13 quotes Psalm 116:10, the psalm of a man who faced death and was delivered: the minister speaks in the face of death because he believes, and the resurrection of Jesus (v. 14) grounds his confidence (see the note on vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor steps down after a serious diagnosis and is replaced by a younger, more energetic man. He feels that his frailty disqualifies him; v. 7 says the opposite. The question is not whether the jar is strong but whether the treasure is still in it, and a cracked jar lets the light out.

verseByVerse.quote: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God puts the priceless treasure of the gospel into fragile, ordinary people, so that its power is plainly seen to be his and not theirs.

Jars of clay. The sentence on which the whole letter turns is built from the most ordinary object in the ancient world. Jars of clay (ostrakina skeuē) were cheap, unglazed containers for oil, grain, water and refuse, chipped, cracked and thrown out without a thought. Valuables were sometimes hidden in them where nobody would look twice; the Dead Sea Scrolls survived in them. The jars are human bodies and lives: weak, mortal, made of dust (Genesis 2:7).

This treasure. Into that Paul puts the light of the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Christ (v. 6): the most valuable thing in existence, in a container you would use once and discard. This answers the charge behind the whole letter, that Paul was too weak to be a real apostle (10:10), and prepares for 12:9: “my power is made perfect in weakness”. The Corinthians wanted a minister who looked like the treasure. God gave them one who looked like the jar, so that they would see the treasure.

The surpassing power belongs to God. The mismatch is the point. Had the apostle been imposing, magnetic, healthy, wealthy and admired, the source of the power would be permanently ambiguous whenever people came to Christ under his preaching. Some would credit God; many would credit Paul; and Paul, being human, would eventually have credited Paul. The cheap jar removes the ambiguity. Nobody looks at a cracked storage pot and concludes that the light is coming from the pottery.

The jar that was broken. The treasure itself once came in earthenware. The Son of God took flesh of our dust, a manger, a working man’s hands, and at last an instrument of execution used on slaves, and he was himself the jar broken on the cross, so that the light would pour out over the world. He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God (13:4), and that power is now at work in his cracked servants.

Your weakness is the design. If you think your weakness disqualifies you, the health that limits you, the shyness that dreads meeting people, the education you did not get, the failure everybody remembers, this verse is aimed at you. Your fragility is not an obstacle God is working around. It is the design.

A warning folded into the comfort. A church or a Christian can work very hard at not looking like a clay pot: the polished presentation, the projected confidence. The trouble is that it succeeds. People are impressed, and being impressed is not the same as seeing God. The gospel travels furthest through people visibly unequal to carrying it.

Should I then make a show of my weaknesses, or stop trying to do things well? Neither. Displaying your weakness can become another way of drawing attention to yourself, a clay pot that wants to be admired for being so honestly cracked. And Scripture commends work done heartily, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23); preparing well is not pride. The question is where your confidence lies and whom you want people to see. Do your best, be honest about your limits when it helps others, never hide behind a polished image, and give God the credit openly for whatever good comes.
verseByVerse.note: Clay jars were cheap, fragile, everyday containers.

verseByVerse.quote: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every blow that falls on Christ’s servant is real, but none is final, because God sets a floor beneath each one.

Afflicted, but not crushed. Four pairs, each a real blow and then a limit. Thlibō is the pressing weight of affliction; stenochōreō means squeezed into a corner. The pressure is real, but there is always still room to move. Not comfort. Room.

Perplexed, but not driven to despair. One verb, then the same verb intensified: aporoumenoi all’ ouk exaporoumenoi, at a loss, but not at an utter loss. Yet he had once been at that utter loss: exaporeomai is the word of 1:8, where he despaired of life itself. So he describes the normal condition, not a guarantee against dark seasons.

Persecuted, but not forsaken. Men hunt him; God does not abandon him: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

Struck down, but not destroyed. A man knocked to the ground, like a wrestler thrown. He goes down; the finishing blow does not come.

The Lord stood by me. Who sees to it that each blow stops short of the end? In Corinth itself, when opposition was fierce, the Lord Jesus spoke to him one night in a vision: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you” (Acts 18:9–10). Years later, abandoned by everyone at his trial in Rome, he wrote: “the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:16–17). Each “but not” is not a law of nature or a quality in Paul but the risen Christ keeping his word: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The jar is struck; the hand that holds it does not let go.

In his case the last blow fell. Paul is describing his life in the pattern of his Lord’s. Christ was afflicted in Gethsemane, persecuted from Bethlehem onwards, struck down at Calvary, and in his case the last blow fell. He was forsaken; he said so out loud in the dark. The one place the sequence ran all the way to the end, it ran to the end for us, and came back out on the third day. Every but not in this list was bought at a cross where there was no but not at all.

What it does not mean. Misreading this list has hurt people. It does not say a Christian will be spared affliction; all four blows land. It does not say he will feel calm, or never feel crushed. It says something narrower and more durable: in every case there is a floor, a point below which he cannot fall, and the floor holds.

But what about Christians who are killed for their faith? Were they not destroyed? No. Paul himself, as the early church remembered, would be executed. The body can be killed, but the believer cannot be destroyed, because the God who raised Jesus will raise him (v. 14); Jesus said not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28). The martyr is struck down in the most final way this world has, and the floor still holds: he goes straight into the presence of the Lord (Philippians 1:23), and his body waits for the resurrection. Destroyed would mean cut off from God, which cannot happen to those who are his (Romans 8:38–39).

In everyday life. Write the four pairs out with your own circumstances in the first half: pressed by this, but not crushed. Do not falsify the first half. Then read the second half aloud as a statement about God, not your strength. When a fellow believer is in the first half, do not hurry them to the second; sit with them in it.

Where Christians differ: suffering and the prosperity gospel. Some teach that faith brings health, wealth and success, and that suffering shows weak faith. This commentary’s view: Paul himself was constantly afflicted, perplexed, persecuted and struck down. Suffering is normal in the Christian life (Acts 14:22; 2 Timothy 3:12). God’s promise is not to remove suffering but to sustain us in it and bring us through. The prosperity gospel contradicts the cross and the apostles’ experience.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: “perplexed” (aporoumenoi) but not “driven to despair” (exaporoumenoi) — at a loss, but not utterly at a loss.

verseByVerse.quote: always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s sufferings for the gospel are a daily share in the dying of Jesus, and through them the risen life of Jesus becomes visible in his weak, mortal body.

Carrying the death of Jesus. The four blows amount to the death of Jesus carried about in a body. The word is nekrōsis, the process rather than the event: death at work. Paul does not re-enact Calvary; his sufferings for the gospel are an ongoing dying, a share in Jesus’ sufferings (Philippians 3:10), and “always”: it is the settled condition of his life.

The life of Jesus. Then the purpose: the risen life of Jesus made visible in Paul’s survival, endurance and joy. Here is the mechanism at the heart of the letter. The dying is not the price paid for the ministry but the channel through which it flows: resurrection life shows exactly where a person is being emptied out.

Given over to death. Handed over (paradidōmi), the verb used of Christ, “delivered up for our trespasses” (Romans 4:25), and the passive means that God is the one who hands him over. That is not a sentence to toss at a person in fresh pain, but it is what Paul lives on: he is not the victim of circumstance but in the hands of a God doing something deliberate, who is not careless with what it costs.

Our mortal flesh. Not in some spiritual compartment, but in the body that gets tired, ill and old: where the dying is most obvious, the life is to be displayed.

Through a Friday nobody could explain. Jesus carried his cross through the streets before any of his people carried anything. The dying at work in them is his dying, and it is going the way his went, through death to resurrection: through a Friday nobody could explain, to a morning nobody expected.

Where people actually see it. So the question is rarely only why God has not removed the difficulty. Watch where people actually see the life of Jesus. Not in the Christian whose life has gone well; the world explains that easily. They see it in the man who lost the job and did not become bitter; in the widow who still sings; in the couple who buried a child and are still in church, still kind, still able to sit with someone else who is grieving. Something is showing through, and it is not personality, because personality does not survive that.

Is every hardship the dying of Jesus, or only persecution? Paul means first suffering that comes because of Jesus, the costs of the gospel, but the principle reaches further. Illness, loss and weariness are part of the outer self wasting away (v. 16), and when a believer carries them in union with Christ, trusting him and refusing bitterness, they become the place where his life is seen. Suffering we bring on ourselves by sin or folly (1 Peter 4:15) God can still use, confessed and borne humbly; but it is not suffering for his sake.

Does God cause my suffering, then? God is sovereign over all of it, and he is never the author of evil. The person who wrongs you is responsible for the wrong; the illness is part of a fallen world. Yet nothing reaches you that your Father has not permitted and does not intend to use for your good and his glory (Romans 8:28; Genesis 50:20). That is why Paul can say he is handed over, not merely knocked about. It is not a philosophy to answer every why. It is a refuge: the hands that hold the situation are the hands that were pierced for you.

verseByVerse.quote: So death is at work in us, but life in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The death at work in Paul is producing life in the Corinthians: he is spent so that they may live.

Death in us, life in you. The apostles absorb death and the church receives life. The beatings that took the skin off his back were part of the price of the gospel reaching Corinth at all. The verb is energeitai, from which we get energy: death is busy in Paul, and so, in Corinth, is life.

No invoice. They had questioned his credentials and compared him unfavourably with better speakers. He answers without self-pity and without presenting a bill; there is no “after all I have done for you”. It is simply how the kingdom moves, and he is glad to be where he is.

He did not invent the arrangement. There was a death at work in one man on one afternoon, and the life it produced runs out to every believer who has ever lived and will not be exhausted when the last of them is raised. Christ went all the way down, into death and the grave, so that a people beyond counting might come up into life.

Ground that was bought. The principle is far wider than apostles. Nearly everything good in your life cost somebody else something: parents who went without, missionaries buried in the country they went to, believers burned so the Bible could be read in English, whoever prayed for you for years and died before the prayer was answered. You are standing on ground that was bought.

Whose life is your death producing? That turns the question round, and it is hard, because most of us have arranged our lives to keep the cost low. If death here produces life there, a life that costs nothing is producing correspondingly little, and no amount of activity disguises that. The people whose ministry outlives them are almost always the ones who were spent. And if illness, age or weakness leaves you little to give, hear this as no accusation: the widow’s two small coins were counted the largest gift (Mark 12:43–44), and a life spent in prayer for others is spent.

Does Paul’s suffering, or my pastor’s, pay for anything? No, not as Christ’s death does. Only Christ’s death atones for sin; his sacrifice was once for all and nothing can be added to it (Hebrews 10:14). Paul’s suffering brought the Corinthians life because it was the cost of bringing them the message about the One whose death saves: he travelled, was beaten, stayed, wrote and wept, and so the gospel reached them. The minister’s sacrifice is the delivery, never the payment. That is why Paul can be content with it: he is not trying to save anyone by his pain, only to get the news of Christ to them at any cost.

How do I spend myself for others without burning out? Paul was spent, but not driven. He drew daily on a renewal not his own (v. 16), and he lived in prayer and in the Scriptures. Being spent for others is not the same as never saying no, never resting, or carrying burdens God has given to others; Jesus himself withdrew to pray (Luke 5:16). Give yourself gladly where God has placed you, accept help, share the load with the church, and remember that the life you are passing on is Christ’s, not yours to manufacture.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul keeps speaking in the face of death because he believes, as the psalmist did before him, and because he knows that the God who raised Jesus will raise him with Jesus.

I believed, and so I spoke. Death is at work in Paul; so why does he keep talking? The quotation is from Psalm 116 (Psalm 115:1 in the Greek numbering), the song of a man who had been at the edge: “The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me” (Psalm 116:3). He called on the Lord and was heard, and in the Greek version Paul used he says, “I believed, and so I spoke.” In mortal danger, he opened his mouth about God anyway.

The same spirit of faith. Not the same opinions but the same disposition, the same inability to keep quiet: the faith of the Old Testament saint and of the Christian are one thing, worked by the same Spirit.

We also speak. Speech is not an extra for the more confident sort of believer; it is faith coming out into the open. Most Christians carry a low-grade guilt about not speaking of Christ more, and the usual remedy is a course on how to do it. But silence is often a sight problem, not a technique problem: we have stopped seeing him clearly enough to have anything pressing to say. Nobody needs to be taught how to talk about something they cannot get over.

He who raised the Lord Jesus. Then the second reason, the ground under everything: not hoping but knowing. Without a resurrection he is simply being consumed; with one, he is being invested. Death did its worst to the Son, and God undid it on the third day; the same power stands under every believer being worn down for his sake.

With Jesus. Not only as he raised Jesus, as though the two were separate events of the same kind, but with Jesus: our resurrection is tied to his. Christ has been raised from the dead, “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first sheaf of a harvest that is already his (see firstfruits). Jesus said it to his disciples with the cross only hours away: because I live, you also will live (John 14:19). The believer’s grave is not a separate problem God must solve later. It was answered on the first Easter morning, because the one who rose there rose as the head of his people.

Into his presence. To present, to stand someone before another (paristēmi). What he looks forward to is not “bring us home”, not even “raise us in glory”, but “with you”. After the humiliating visit, the letters and the men who despised him, he pictures arriving in the presence of God with these very people beside him, and the thought gives him pleasure. That is what resurrection hope does to a quarrel. It puts everyone concerned in the same room, before the same face, and makes the present disagreement look exactly as large as it will look then.

I am shy and tongue-tied. Do I have to speak like Paul? No, but you will want to speak of what you believe, and you can. Speaking of Christ is not only preaching or knocking on doors. It is telling a colleague who asks how you cope that you pray, and why; offering to pray for a friend; telling your children what God has done for you; inviting someone to church. What has Christ been to you this week? Say that, simply, to one person. The Spirit who gave the psalmist his voice is in you.

Will we know one another in the resurrection? Yes. Paul expects to be presented with the Corinthians, so he expects to recognise them and be glad of them. Our Lord spoke of sitting at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11), and Paul comforts the Thessalonians that they will be with their departed loved ones and with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). We will be changed, but not into strangers. Every redeemed relationship will be healed and made what it should have been, and at the centre will be the face of Christ.

In everyday life. Think of the believer you find hardest to love. Picture the two of you standing together, raised, before the face of Christ. Let that picture shape what you say to them, and about them, this week.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are hard to pin down. The Hebrew of Psalm 116:10 is difficult: the ESV of the psalm renders it “I believed, even when I spoke”, while the Greek version Paul quotes has “I believed, and so I spoke”; on either reading the psalmist trusted God and spoke in mortal danger. And “the same spirit of faith” may mean a shared disposition of faith or the Holy Spirit who gives faith (the Greek has no capital letters to decide it). The two meet, since that disposition is the Spirit’s work: either way the psalmist and the apostle share one faith.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “by Jesus”; the earliest read “with Jesus”, as most modern Bibles do.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes the Greek form of the psalm.

parallels.desc: I believed, even when I spoke

verseByVerse.quote: For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Paul suffers is for the Corinthians’ sake, so that grace reaches more and more people and their thanks rise to the glory of God.

For it is all for your sake. The afflictions, the perplexity, the daily dying: all of it is aimed at them. He says it three times in four chapters (1:6; 4:12; and here), so that they are in no doubt whom the suffering is for.

A chain with three links. Each produces the next. Grace extends to more and more people: the suffering of one man is how the gospel gets to the next town. Thanksgiving multiplies with it, because a person given what he could not earn will say so. And it all ends in the glory of God. Ministry serves people, and their thanksgiving serves God’s glory.

For your sake he became poor. Paul’s “all for your sake” follows a pattern Christ set, which he names later in this letter: “you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (8:9). All Paul suffers for the Corinthians is a small echo of what Christ did for them first.

The song has one subject. And the chain ends where Christ’s own humbling ends: because he became obedient to the point of death, every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:8–11). The thanks that began with a handful of Corinthians will end in the sound John heard: every creature in heaven and on earth crying, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:11–13). Every grace that went out from the cross comes back as thanksgiving, and the song has one subject.

A larger question than what God is teaching me. The usual Christian question in hardship is, “What is God teaching me?” It is a good question, but smaller than this verse, which asks how many mouths will end up thanking God. The illness that made you dependent has let others serve, and some are praying for the first time in years. Your children are watching how you bear the redundancy that humiliated you. You may never see the results; Paul never saw most of his.

Is it not selfish of God to want his own glory? It would be selfish in us, because we are not the greatest good and our seeking glory robs others. But God is the greatest good there is, and for him to seek less than his own glory would be to point us away from the only thing that can satisfy us. When he draws out our thanks, he is drawing us into joy in himself, which is what we were made for; that is why the Westminster Shorter Catechism puts glorifying God and enjoying him in the same answer. His glory and our happiness are not rivals. Thanksgiving is the moment they become one thing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — The Outer and Inner; the Seen and Unseen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul does not lose heart, because what is happening within him and ahead of him outweighs what is happening to his body. His outer self is wasting away while his inner self is renewed day by day (v. 16); his affliction, heavy as it is, is light and brief beside the eternal glory it is preparing (v. 17); and he keeps his eyes on the unseen things, because they are the ones that last (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between seen and unseen (v. 18) is not the Greek idea that matter is bad and spirit good, or that the body is a prison the soul escapes. It concerns time (see the note on v. 18).
verseByVerse.examples: An elderly woman in a nursing home, her body failing, tells her pastor that she has never felt closer to God. This verse names it: the outer self is wasting away while the inner self is renewed day by day, and the decline itself loosens the grip of the seen and turns her gaze to the unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul does not give up, because while his body is wearing out, God is making him new within, day by day. The decline is visible to everybody; the renewal is invisible, and it is the one that will last.

So we do not lose heart. The phrase from v. 1 returns as his conclusion, and he says in the same breath that he is falling apart.

Our outer self. The body and visible earthly life, subject to ageing, sickness and suffering. Diaphtheirō means destroyed by degrees, and it is happening now: the eyes worse than they were, the strength that does not come back after a hard week. Christian faith does not require anyone to pretend otherwise. The jar is cracking.

Renewed day by day. Set against it is a second process. The inner self, the heart and spirit united to Christ, is being renewed (anakainoō, passive and continuous), not restored to what it was but made new (Colossians 3:10), day by day, in the same increments as the decline. Anyone who has sat with an elderly believer has seen it: a body plainly failing and something else plainly not. A hymn surfaces from sixty years ago, or the person says simply that they are not afraid, and you leave having received rather than given.

What the renewal runs on. It is not automatic; plenty of people grow old and merely become more themselves. It happens in people who are looking at something: who count the affliction light beside glory and fix their gaze on what is unseen (vv. 17–18).

Renewed after his image. The new self is renewed after the image of its creator (Colossians 3:10), and Christ is the image of God (v. 4): the daily renewal is Christ being formed in his people (Galatians 4:19). The body that is wearing out is not carrying an empty soul towards death but a likeness of the risen Lord that grows a little clearer every day, and that cannot be buried.

The mind too. This belongs to the mind as much as to the body. Depression and long mental illness are part of the outer self that is wasting away, and not losing heart is not a feeling to be produced on demand but a direction to face, even when the feelings will not follow. Jeremiah cursed the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14); the writer of Psalm 88 ended it in darkness (Psalm 88:18); Paul himself despaired of life itself (1:8). None of them was rejected for it. A believer in that darkness should seek help, from the church and from a biblical counsellor, who will also ask for a medical check-up, and should know that the inner renewal goes on even when it cannot be felt.

A culture that cannot bear to grow old. Ours may be the first culture to treat ageing as a problem to be solved rather than a stage of life to be lived. We spend fortunes to look younger, house the old where we need not see them, and praise someone for being “still” active or “still” sharp, as though decline were a failure of effort. The anthropologist Ernest Becker argued in The Denial of Death that much of human culture is an elaborate project for not facing our mortality. If the body is all there is, every wrinkle is a loss with nothing on the other side of the ledger. Paul, neither in denial nor in despair, looks straight at the wasting away and names a second process running alongside it. That frees a Christian from both the frantic clinging to youth and the bitterness of the old who feel discarded. Growing old in Christ is not a life shrinking towards nothing but a life ripening towards a harvest.

What it does not mean. Not that the body does not matter, or that the real you is only a soul trapped in a shell. The body will be raised (v. 14). Its present decay is simply not the whole story.

What exactly is the inner self, and how is it renewed? The inner self is you as God sees you from within: your heart, mind and will, joined to Christ by the Spirit. It is not a separate person, and you cannot see it in a mirror. It is renewed as the Spirit applies Christ to you through the means God has appointed: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of believers, and obedience in ordinary things. None of these is magic, and none is optional for someone who wants to be renewed. They are where God has promised to meet his people, day by day.

verseByVerse.quote: For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weighed against the glory it is producing, even Paul’s heavy suffering is light and brief, for the glory outweighs it beyond all comparison.

Light momentary affliction. Beside the man who wrote it, the sentence is almost outrageous. Paul had been flogged five times with thirty-nine lashes, beaten with rods three times, stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19), shipwrecked three times (11:23–27), and had recently despaired of life itself. He calls it light and momentary, not because it was easy, but because of what it is compared with.

Weighing, not minimising. Both words are comparisons. Put a real weight on a scale with nothing opposite and it is heavy. Put the glory on the other side and the same weight rises. The affliction has not changed; something has been added to the other pan.

Nobody may say this for him. A man may say this sentence about his own troubles; nobody may say it about another’s. Handled carelessly it becomes a cruel verse: cheer up, it is only light and momentary, said to a woman who has buried a child. Paul is not minimising anything. He has spent four chapters refusing to minimise it.

Is preparing for us. To produce as a result (katergazomai). The suffering is not merely followed by glory; it is doing something. Nothing is being wasted.

An eternal weight of glory. Behind “weight” lies the Hebrew kabod, glory, from a root meaning heavy, and Paul may be playing on it: glory is substance, the sheer solidity of God. So he sets light affliction against heavy glory, momentary against eternal. What is coming is heavier than what is happening.

Beyond all comparison. Literally “according to excess unto excess” (compare Romans 8:18): one intensifier piled on another, as though he has run out of Greek. It is the expression behind the “utterly” of 1:8, where he was pushed far past his strength; here he doubles it at the other end of the scale. Not that the glory will be worth it, as though it were a fair exchange narrowly won, but that the two cannot be put on the same scale at all: the heaviest grief a human being can carry will one day be found to have been the lighter object, and we do not yet have the vocabulary to say why.

For the joy set before him. Paul learned this way of weighing from his Lord. Jesus, for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God (Hebrews 12:2). Paul could call his own load light because his Lord had carried the full weight of what we deserved, and found it anything but light. Christ bore the wrath that would have crushed us, so that the only weight left for his people at the end is the weight of glory. And they do not weigh alone: we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). The affliction is light because it is shared with Christ, and the glory is heavy because it is his glory, given to those who are his.

My trouble has lasted decades. How can it be momentary? Measured against your life, it is not, and Paul does not ask you to pretend it is. Many of his own troubles lasted for years, and the thorn of 12:7 was never removed. Momentary is measured against eternity. Thirty years of pain, set beside ten thousand years of glory and then ten thousand more, becomes what Paul calls it, without ceasing to be real. You are not asked to feel it as light today, but to believe that God will one day show you it was, and to let that hope hold you up while it is still heavy.

Will those who suffer more receive more glory? Scripture does speak of reward, and of God’s noticing what was borne for his sake (Matthew 5:11–12; Romans 8:17). But the reward is grace, not wages: no one will stand in glory because he suffered enough to deserve it, and the believer who suffered little is not second class. What the verse promises every believer is that nothing endured in faith is wasted. Leave the measuring to God; he will be generous beyond anything we can imagine, and nobody in heaven will be envious.

In everyday life. Put your present troubles on the scales, every one, in full weight. On the other side write what God has promised: to be with him, the face of Christ, a body that will not fail, no more tears. Do not argue with your feelings; look at both columns, and ask God to let the second grow heavier in your sight.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew the word for “glory” comes from a root meaning “heavy” — glory has weight.

verseByVerse.quote: as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul can call his troubles light because he keeps his eyes fixed on what cannot yet be seen, and the unseen things are the ones that last for ever.

Not to the things that are seen. The “as” states the condition: the renewal and the weighing happen in people whose eyes are pointed somewhere. Skopeō means to fix attention on, to take aim at (the root of our word “scope”): a man sighting down a line, not glancing.

The things that are unseen. God, Christ at his right hand, the resurrection, the world to come (Hebrews 11:1, 27; 12:2). But how do you look at something you cannot see? Not by mysticism or pretending. Paul has already said where the unseen is made visible: the glory of God is in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6), beheld in the gospel (3:18). You look at the unseen by looking at what God has said about it, until it becomes as real to you as the things in the room. That is faith in practice: not a feeling, but attention paid to the invisible on the authority of God’s word.

Transient and eternal. Transient (proskaira) means for a season, on a timer. We call the visible real and the invisible abstract; Paul says the opposite. The mortgage, the diagnosis, the argument at work have an expiry date. The unseen things, which feel thin, are the ones with no end.

Your years will have no end. Behind everything that can be seen is a glory with a face. Of the Son the Father says: they will perish, but you remain; you are the same, and your years will have no end (Hebrews 1:10–12). The jar is cracking; the treasure is not.

What it does not mean. Not ignoring present responsibilities, nor that matter is bad and spirit good: Paul goes straight on to the resurrection of the body (5:1–5). The present arrangement is temporary, and what is now invisible will one day be the most solid thing there is.
