Will fixing my eyes on heaven make me careless about this life? The opposite. Those who have done most good in this world have often been those most sure of the next, because they had nothing to lose and nothing to prove. Abraham looked for a city with foundations, and so could live as a generous stranger (Hebrews 11:10). A believer whose treasure is safe can give money away, forgive debts, serve the unthankful, care for creation and work hard at an ordinary job without anxiety, because none of it has to be his heaven. It is the man who looks only at the seen who must cling to it.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart.<sup>2</sup>But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.<sup>3</sup>And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing.<sup>4</sup>In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.<sup>5</sup>For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.<sup>6</sup>For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.<sup>7</sup>But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.<sup>8</sup>We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair;<sup>9</sup>persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;<sup>10</sup>always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies.<sup>11</sup>For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.<sup>12</sup>So death is at work in us, but life in you.<sup>13</sup>Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak,<sup>14</sup>knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.<sup>15</sup>For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.<sup>16</sup>So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.<sup>17</sup>For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,<sup>18</sup>as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

keyVerse.quote: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.
keyVerse.note: This verse answers the question the whole chapter faces: why is so glorious a ministry carried by so weak a man? The weakness is God’s design, so that no one mistakes where the power comes from. Everything else in the chapter, the blows that never destroy, the dying that shows Jesus’ life, the outer self wasting while the inner is renewed, is this one verse lived out.

4.reflection:
Paul says he does not lose heart because his ministry came “by the mercy of God” (v. 1), and he refuses to tamper with God’s word to make it more effective (v. 2). Where are you most tempted to lose heart, and how does remembering that everything you have was given in mercy change the way you keep going?

Verses 4–6 say that unbelief is a blindness only God can cure, and that he cures it as he made light at creation. How should this shape the way we pray for, and speak to, friends who do not believe?

God put his treasure in jars of clay “to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (v. 7). What weaknesses in yourself or your church are you tempted to hide, and how might God want to show his power through them?

Paul calls his sufferings “light” and “momentary” beside “an eternal weight of glory” (v. 17). Why can only the sufferer himself say this, never someone watching? What would it look like this week to fix your eyes on the unseen things (v. 18)?

5.title: The Heavenly Dwelling, the Judgment Seat, and the Ministry of Reconciliation
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 runs straight on from 4:16–18, where Paul’s outer self is wasting away while he looks to the unseen and eternal. It brings his long defence of his ministry (2:14–7:4) to its summit.

The message. Death cannot undo anyone who belongs to Christ, and the cross has changed everything for those it touches. So live to please the Lord before whom you will stand, and above all be reconciled to the God who has already made peace with you at the cost of his Son. Paul’s battered, unimpressive life is explained by the love that drives it and the message it carries.

Why it was said. Rival teachers in Corinth boasted of presence, polish and spiritual experiences, and found Paul’s wasting body and plain speech embarrassing (see the introduction). A minister always near death looked like a failure. Paul shows what his weakness rests on and where it is heading, and his closing plea is aimed at the Corinthians themselves, some of whom were drifting from him and from the gospel he preached.

How the chapter makes its case. The body is a tent that will be taken down, but God has a permanent building ready, the resurrection body, and his Spirit is the deposit that guarantees it, so the groaning of this life is hope, not despair (vv. 1–5). So Paul is of good courage: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and either way his ambition is to please Christ, before whose judgment seat all must appear (vv. 6–10). The fear of the Lord makes him persuade, and the love of Christ, who died for all, controls him; that, not outward appearance, is how a minister should be judged (vv. 11–15). So he sizes no one up by worldly standards, because anyone in Christ is a new creation (vv. 16–17). God has reconciled the world to himself in Christ and sends ambassadors to plead, “be reconciled to God” (vv. 18–20), and it all rests on the great exchange of verse 21.

Where it leads. The chapter climbs: from a tent coming down, to a Judge on his seat, to a King pleading with rebels, to the sinless Son made sin in their place. Every hope in it rests on Christ. His risen body is the pattern of the building from God; his is the judgment seat; his death is the death of all who are his; and in him we become the righteousness of God. The Judge we must face is the one who was judged for us.

For us. Death, the judgment and our own weakness are the three things we most avoid thinking about, and Paul faces all three with courage because of Christ. Ask what love is controlling your life, and whether you have truly stopped refusing the peace God is pleading with you to receive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Heavenly Dwelling and the Judgment Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Death cannot take from a believer what God has prepared, so live now to please the Lord you will meet. The body is a tent that will come down, but God has a permanent building waiting, and the groaning of this life is the longing to put it on (vv. 1–4). God made us for this and has given his Spirit as the deposit (v. 5). So Paul is of good courage: to leave the body is to be at home with the Lord (vv. 6–8), and whether here or there, his ambition is to please Christ, before whose judgment seat every life will be laid open (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: At the judgment seat of Christ (v. 10) Scripture keeps two things apart: justification, which settles the believer’s standing for ever, and the assessment of his life and works (Revelation 22:12). How the two fit together is treated at vv. 9–10. Holding both protects the gospel of grace and keeps real accountability for how a Christian lives.
verseByVerse.examples: A Christian professional excuses a string of ethical compromises at work by telling himself that grace covers everything. He is right about grace, but he is using it as a licence rather than a motive. Paul knew the judgment seat was coming, and it moved him to persuade others (v. 11). For the justified believer it is a spur to faithful living, not a threat of condemnation.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When this body is taken down like a tent, God has a permanent home waiting for us. Paul does not say “we hope” but “we know”.

A tent. Paul’s outer self is wasting away (4:16); here is what happens when the wasting is finished. He was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) and knew what a tent is worth: it goes up in a morning, comes down in an afternoon, and one season it is not worth mending (compare 2 Peter 1:13–14). That is the body, and he does not despise it. A tent is a good shelter for the journey. It is simply not a house.

Destroyed. Taken down, dismantled (katalyō), as a tent when the camp moves. Death is not gentle, but a dismantling is not the end when a house is already standing.

A building from God. Every phrase is the opposite of a tent: “from God”, “not made with hands” (Hebrews 9:11), “a building” with foundations, “eternal”. It is the resurrection body Paul had described to this church, sown in weakness and raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–54): not an escape from the body but a permanent body in place of a temporary one (on the wording, see below).

Destroyed, and built again in three days. The ground of Paul’s “we know” is Jesus. “Destroyed” and “not made with hands” are the words of the charge brought against Jesus at his trial: that he had said he would destroy the temple made with hands and in three days build another, not made with hands (Mark 14:58). He was speaking of the temple of his body (John 2:19–21), and it came true. His body was taken down on a cross, laid in a tomb and raised on the third day, never to be dismantled again. What God did for his Son’s body he has pledged to do for everyone joined to him: Christ’s risen body is the firstfruits and the pattern of every building from God (1 Corinthians 15:20; Philippians 3:21).

Does it matter what happens to my body after I die? Not to God’s power: he will raise his people whether they were buried, lost at sea or burned, because the resurrection depends on him and not on what is left. But the body matters to God, and Christians have long buried their dead as a sign of that hope, laying the body down like a seed (1 Corinthians 15:36–38) and treating it with honour. Families may differ on practical choices, and none of them can hinder the resurrection. What matters is that we speak of the body as Scripture does: not a shell to discard, but a tent God will replace with a house.

Uncertain wording. Paul does not spell out what the “building from God” is. Most interpreters, and this commentary, take it to be the resurrection body; others think of a body given at the moment of death, or of heaven itself, the Father’s house (John 14:2). The first fits best. Paul places the new body at the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52) and speaks of being “unclothed” in between (vv. 3–4), so “we have” expresses certainty: a body prepared and waiting. Meanwhile the believer’s soul is at home with the Lord (v. 8), without the body but not without Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, a tentmaker by trade, pictures the present body as a tent — temporary — and the resurrection body as a permanent building.

parallels.desc: houses of clay

verseByVerse.quote: For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this body believers groan, not to be rid of it, but longing to be clothed with the heavenly body God has prepared. What Paul wants is more life, not less.

We groan. Much Christian talk about death is bright in a way this verse is not. Stenazō is the deep, wordless sound a person makes under a weight. Paul uses it of believers who groan inwardly as they wait for the redemption of their bodies, alongside a creation groaning as in childbirth (Romans 8:22–23): the sound of something that knows it was made for more than this. So Christian hope does not require pretending to be comfortable. Anyone who has been ill for a long time, or has watched someone they love become someone they have to care for, knows the groan. It is not unbelief. It is the right response to a tent in a storm.

Longing to put on. Paul mixes his pictures: the house has become a garment, and he longs to have it on.

Not found naked. To be naked is to be without a body, a self exposed with no dwelling. In much Greek thought that was the goal; Plato could speak of the body as the soul’s prison. Paul calls bodilessness nakedness and shrinks from it.

A correction we still need. Many Christians say that at death the soul goes to heaven, and stop there. That is real and precious (v. 8), but it is the interval, not the end. The Christian hope is a body: a real one, on a real new earth, standing up out of a grave. God made us embodied and called it very good. The body is not the problem; death is, and the answer to death is not escape from the body but its resurrection. Being with Christ without the body is far better (Philippians 1:23), but incomplete.

Clothed in the likeness of the man of heaven. What will be put on? Paul has told this church: “Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49). The heavenly dwelling is cut to the pattern of the risen Jesus, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The Son did not lay his body aside after Easter; a true man sits on the throne of heaven now, and if the Lord of glory keeps his body for ever, his people will not be left without theirs. Our groan, at bottom, is a longing to look like him.

What will that body be like? Truly you, recognisable, as the risen Jesus was known by his friends and ate with them (Luke 24:39–43); physical, not ghostly; yet imperishable, glorious, powerful and fully suited to the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44): no more decay, disease, disability or death, no tiredness that sleep cannot cure. Scripture does not answer every curious question, such as age or appearance, but it says enough: it is the body God always meant you to have, and it will never be taken down. The groaning is not despair but the ache of someone who has seen the house and is waiting for the keys.

Uncertain wording. Verse 3 is compressed. “If indeed” may state a condition or a confident assumption (“since, when we have put it on, we will not be found naked”). “Naked” is usually taken, as here, to mean without a body, between death and resurrection; a minority read it as moral nakedness, being found without righteousness at the judgment (compare Revelation 3:18). The setting of tents, houses and clothing favours the first.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “putting it off” instead of “putting it on” in verse 3, as the ESV margin notes; the point is not affected.

verseByVerse.quote: For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our longing is not to lose the body but to have all that is mortal in it swallowed up by life. Paul would rather not die at all, but have the new body put on over the old when Christ returns.

Burdened. Weighed down (bareō), the word he used of the affliction in Asia (1:8).

Further clothed. To be “unclothed” would be simply to be rid of the body. To be “further clothed” (ependyomai) is to have a garment drawn on over what is already worn: to be alive at Christ’s return and receive the resurrection body without dying (1 Corinthians 15:51–53). He longs for the mortal thing to be covered by something so much more alive that mortality disappears inside it.

Swallowed up by life. To swallow whole (katapinō), the word of Isaiah’s promise that God will swallow up death forever (Isaiah 25:8; 1 Corinthians 15:54). Every funeral has the shape of death swallowing a person; here life does the swallowing. A candle blown out is unclothed; a candle carried outside at sunrise is swallowed up by life, nothing taken away, simply so much light that the flame is no longer needed.

Life has a name. The life that swallows mortality is a Person. “I am the resurrection and the life,” Jesus said beside the grave of Lazarus (John 11:25), and death could not keep its hold on him (Acts 2:24). Death opened its mouth for him on Friday and found on Sunday that it had swallowed something it could not keep down. What happened to the Head in a garden tomb will happen to his body, his people: thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:57).

Is it wrong to wish I could just stop? No; Paul was carrying that weight when he wrote this, and Elijah and Job carried it too. If you know the tiredness deeper than sleep, the private wish to be finished, this verse does not condemn you; it corrects the desire’s aim. What you actually want is not to be switched off but to be so thoroughly alive that everything now wearing you out is swallowed and gone. But if the wish begins to turn into thoughts of ending your own life, tell someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor. That darkness lies to you, and God has given you people and help for exactly this.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself made us for this future and has given us his Spirit as the first instalment of it. The longing is not wishful thinking, and the deposit guarantees the rest.

Prepared by God. To fashion for a purpose (katergazomai). There is a restlessness no arrangement of circumstances satisfies: get the house, the health, the family, and a thin ache remains. We treat it as a fault to be fixed by one more thing. Paul says God fitted it deliberately, and it corresponds to something real.

The Spirit as a guarantee. Arrabōn again, as at 1:22 (and Ephesians 1:14): the down payment that legally commits the payer to hand over the rest, the same kind of thing as what is still to come. The Spirit is our future life given now, and the Spirit who raised Jesus will raise us (Romans 8:11). So: you were built for the resurrection body; you can tell, because you groan; and to prove the groaning is not a cruel joke, God has put a deposit in your hands, and the deposit is a Person.

Poured out by the risen Christ. Jesus said it was to his disciples’ advantage that he go away, for otherwise the Helper would not come (John 16:7); exalted at God’s right hand, he has poured him out (Acts 2:33). The guarantee is not an IOU from a distant God but the life of the risen Lord at work in us; we hold the deposit because Christ, whose fellow heirs we are, holds the whole inheritance (Romans 8:17). The Father who fashioned us for glory, the Son who rose as the firstfruits, the Spirit who lives in us as the down payment: the whole Trinity is engaged in getting us home. God does not make a down payment on something he means to abandon.

The first instalment. The moments when Scripture came alive, the peace that arrived for no reason, the affection for people you once avoided, the fact that you want God at all: these are the first instalment, given so that you could not settle for less. That is why a Christian who is spiritually alive is often more homesick, not less.

Can that guarantee be lost? No. God does not default on his pledge: the Spirit guarantees our inheritance until we acquire possession of it (Ephesians 1:14). A believer can grieve the Spirit, yet in that same verse he is sealed for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30). And the fear of having lost the Spirit is not evidence that one has; it is usually the evidence of a conscience he is still at work in.

Do I need a special experience to know I have the Spirit? No. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), so every believer has him. Scripture does not tie his presence to a dramatic sign, a feeling or the gift of tongues. Its marks are quieter and surer: you call God Father from the heart (Romans 8:15–16), confess Jesus as Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), love his people, fight your sin, and slowly grow in his fruit (Galatians 5:22–23). Look for those, not for fireworks.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guarantee” was used for a deposit or first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.quote: So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even while they groan, believers are always confident, because they live by trusting the Lord they cannot yet see. This life is real fellowship with Christ, but it is life away from home.

Always of good courage. Paul has been groaning; now, without contradiction, he takes heart (tharreō), always, not only on good days. The courage does not wait for the groaning to stop. It rests on the Spirit’s guarantee.

At home, and away. To live in one’s own country, and to be abroad (endēmeō, ekdēmeō). After the Damascus road and the third heaven, Paul still calls this life away from the Lord: with Christ by the Spirit, but not yet face to face. Every Christian knows prayers that feel like speaking into the next room. That is not a defect in your discipleship; it is the address you are currently living at.

By faith, not by sight. Not acting on impressions without evidence. Sight (eidos) is the visible thing itself: Paul contrasts faith not with thinking but with seeing Christ face to face (v. 8; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Peter 1:8). And the verb is “walk”: daily conduct, one foot in front of the other, moving in the dark on the word of Someone who can see.

Blessed are those who have not seen. Jesus drew this line himself. To Thomas, who would not believe until he had touched the wounds, he said: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29). Yet faith is not blind, because it has an object: a crucified and risen Lord whose resurrection body was seen by hundreds of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). We walk on their testimony toward the day when we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Faith is simply what loving Jesus looks like while he is out of sight.

How do I make decisions by faith, not by sight? Not by waiting for a sign or an inner voice, but by trusting what God has said and acting on it without seeing how it will turn out. Start with Scripture: what does God command, forbid or commend here? Then use the wisdom he gives: pray, think carefully, ask mature believers, weigh your circumstances honestly (Proverbs 15:22; James 1:5). Where Scripture leaves you free, choose what seems wisest and most loving, and trust God with the outcome. Faith is obedience that does not need to see the end of the road first.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For a believer, to leave the body at death is to be at home with the Lord at once. That is why Paul, for all his groaning, would rather go.

At home with the Lord. Verse 6 is swapped round to answer the graveside question, what happens to a believer at death? Away from the body, at home with the Lord: no gap, no waiting room, no unconsciousness. Paul tells the Philippians the same from prison: to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). And the Lord said it to a dying criminal with nothing to offer and no time left: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Today. Theologians call this the intermediate state, between death and resurrection: conscious, with Christ, and better than here. Yet it is not the end (vv. 3–4), so a Christian funeral says two things at once: he is with the Lord today, and a morning is coming when he will be given back his body.

Home is a Person. Home is where a person stops being a stranger, and for Paul that is wherever Jesus is. The promise to the thief was “with me”, and Jesus prayed that those the Father had given him would be with him where he is, to see his glory (John 17:24). He wanted us with him before we ever wanted to come.

The last enemy made into a door. It cost the Lord of glory his own descent into the grave to change what death is for his people, and now the worst thing that can happen to a Christian is that he goes home. “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:15), because he paid for every one of them himself.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should seek death, but that they need not fear it. Paul stays, gladly, as long as his Lord has work for him (Philippians 1:24–25).

Can my loved one who has died see me, or can I speak to them? Scripture does not say that the dead in Christ watch over us, and it firmly forbids trying to contact the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). The “cloud of witnesses” (Hebrews 12:1) testify by their lives of faith; they are not spectators sent to guard us. So speak to God about them, not to them: thank him for them, tell him your grief. You have not lost them; you are separated for a while, and they are where you are going.

What if they died with sins they never confessed? A believer is saved not by having confessed every sin but by Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Every believer dies with sins he never knew about or named; if forgiveness depended on a complete list, no one would be home. If your loved one trusted Christ, the unfinished conversations, the last weak years, the failures you remember, do not keep them out. They are at home.

Where Christians differ: what happens at death? Some teach soul sleep, an unconscious state until the resurrection; Roman Catholics teach purgatory for most believers. This commentary’s view: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, immediately and consciously; there is no purgatory and no soul sleep. Centuries asleep could hardly be called far better, or being at home with the Lord; the New Testament speaks of presence, and of presence now. Nor is there an interval of purging for believers who died imperfect. Paul, who knew what he still was, expects to be at home the moment he is away, not because he had reached a standard but because of verse 21: the exchange has already been made. The souls of believers, made perfect in holiness, are received into heaven, where they behold God’s face in light and glory, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). Those who hold the other views are often earnest believers; the disagreement is over what these texts say, not over whether they love Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whether alive or dead, Paul’s ambition is to please Christ, because every life will be laid open before his judgment seat. Believers will not be condemned there, but what they have done with their lives will be shown and weighed.

Our aim. Philotimeomai is a word of ambition: to make something your driving purpose. Paul was an ambitious man, and this was his ambition, living or dead.

The judgment seat. The raised platform from which a magistrate gave verdicts (bēma); Corinth had one, where Paul had stood before Gallio (Acts 18:12). “Appear” is phaneroō: not merely to show up, but to have a life laid open. And what is laid open is what was “done in the body”, not what was intended: the hands, the diary, the money, the tongue.

The seat belongs to Christ. Paul says not “of God” but “of Christ”, and that changes everything. The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22) and will judge the world by the man he has appointed, giving proof of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The One on the seat has lived in a body and knows from the inside its hunger, tiredness and temptation, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Nothing will stay hidden from him, and he has borne his people’s condemnation himself, so none of it will be laid on them (Romans 8:1, 34). He once stood before Pilate’s bēma and was condemned there in our place. He is not looking for reasons to reject his people; he is looking for every cup of cold water, every unseen act of faithfulness, so that he can praise it.

In everyday life. Take this week as it actually was: the hours, the conversations, what you gave your attention to. That is what will be looked at, by Someone who loves you and died for the failures in it. Make it your ambition today to please Christ in one specific thing you would otherwise have done carelessly.

What does “good or evil” mean for a believer? His sins will not be held against him for condemnation; their penalty was paid at the cross. But his life will be brought into the light, what was done in faith and love and what was not, for the Lord will disclose the purposes of the heart (1 Corinthians 4:5). The verdict is not on his salvation but on his service. Scripture speaks of commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:5) and of work that survives the fire (1 Corinthians 3:14); some will suffer loss, though they themselves are saved. That loss is real, but it never touches the believer’s standing in Christ.

Should that frighten a believer? Paul moves straight from it to ambition, not dread, yet he does not treat it as nothing. A Christian may lose a great deal there, the years spent on things that turned out to be nothing, the gifts unused, the reputation protected instead of spent, and will lose nothing of Christ.

Would a loving God really judge anyone? Yes, and his love is one reason he must. A judge who shrugged at the abuse of a child would not be kind; he would be complicit. Love that does not care about evil is not love, and those who most long for a day of judgment are usually those the world has wronged (Psalm 96:13; Revelation 6:10). What makes this judgment good news is the Judge: he was judged himself in the place of everyone who comes to him, so his people can look forward to the day that puts every wrong right.

Is it selfish to want rewards? No, as long as the reward is what Scripture says it is. Jesus urged us to lay up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:20), and the chief reward is not a prize separate from God but the joy of his approval: “Well done, good and faithful servant. … Enter into the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:21). Wanting that is love wanting to please the one it loves. And the reward is grace on grace: God crowns in us the works he worked in us. No one in heaven will boast in his reward; everyone will cast it at the feet of the Lamb.

Where Christians differ: judgment of believers. How can believers, who are justified and free from condemnation (Romans 8:1), be judged by their works? This commentary’s view: believers will not be condemned; their sins are covered by Christ. But their lives will be revealed and evaluated, and their works rewarded according to God’s grace (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Matthew 25:21). Good works do not earn justification, but they are the evidence of true faith, and God graciously rewards them (the Westminster Confession 33.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 32.1). The judgment will also openly vindicate God’s people and show his justice. Both are true because two different things are in view. The verdict on whether you belong to Christ was settled at the cross and is not reopened. What is assessed at the bēma is what you did with the life you were given after that verdict. Paul told this church a letter earlier: the foundation is Christ and cannot be relaid, but what a man builds on it is tested by fire, and some of it burns, though he himself will be saved (1 Corinthians 3:15).
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat (bema) was the raised platform where a Roman official gave judgment; Paul had stood before one in Corinth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Ministry of Reconciliation and the Great Exchange
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The love of Christ, who died in our place, makes Paul an ambassador pleading with the world to accept the peace God has made. The fear of the Lord sends him out to persuade, and he asks to be judged by the heart, not the face (vv. 11–13). Christ’s love controls him: one died for all, so all who are his died with him and now live for him (vv. 14–15). That changes how he sees everyone, for anyone in Christ is a new creation (vv. 16–17). God did it all, reconciling the world to himself and sending envoys to plead (vv. 18–20), and verse 21 shows the cost: the sinless Son made sin, so that in him we become the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
In verse 19 the one acting is God. Reconciliation is begun, accomplished and offered by him. The obstacle is sin; the removal is the cross, and verse 21 states its cost.

What “made him to be sin” means, and why our standing in him cannot be damaged by a bad week, is treated fully at v. 21.
verseByVerse.examples: An evangelism course teaches that the goal is to persuade people to make a decision for Christ. This passage gives a deeper frame: we implore people, on Christ’s behalf, to receive a peace God has already made. The ambassador does not create the peace; he announces it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Paul must answer to the Lord, he works to persuade people, and he wants the church to judge its ministers by the heart, not by appearances.

The fear of the Lord. The judgment seat does not send Paul into anxious self-examination; it sends him out to talk to people. The fear of the Lord is the awe of a creature who has grasped that the nations are like a drop from a bucket before him (Isaiah 40:15), and that every person will stand before his Son’s seat (v. 10). A man who has felt that does not keep quiet about other people’s eternity merely because raising it is awkward.

We persuade. Winning someone over by argument (peithō): not manipulating, nor merely announcing, but reasoning and pleading (Acts 18:4). Christian silence about Christ is sometimes more than shyness: we have stopped believing much is at stake.

Known to God. God already sees Paul’s heart completely; he hopes the Corinthians’ consciences will recognise it too. Whoever lives now as already laid open before God is best prepared for the day when every life will be.

Cause to boast. Then Paul turns, delicately, to his critics (compare 3:1). The Corinthians had said nothing when he was disparaged in front of them; he is not defending himself for his own sake but giving them an answer to use.

Face and heart. Literally, boasting “in the face” rather than “in the heart”. The rival teachers had presence, polish, credentials, visions and delivery; Paul had a wasting body and a speaking manner his critics thought contemptible. We still assess by the face: the platform manner, the numbers, the production. God said long ago how he assesses, to Samuel, busy admiring the wrong brother: “For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). The awkward implication is that the most impressive Christian you know may not be the one God is most pleased with, and neither of you can currently tell.

No form or majesty. The fault line between face and heart runs straight through the story of Jesus. The Servant had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2). Judged by the face, Jesus was a builder from Nazareth with no schooling in the law and no following among the great, and at the end a body so marred it hardly looked human (Isaiah 52:14). Those who boasted in appearance despised him; the Father called him his beloved Son. Paul’s critics were making about the servant the very mistake the world had made about the Master. A church that boasts in the face will always be embarrassed by a crucified Lord, and by the ministers who look most like him. He is holy enough to be feared by angels and kind enough to be loved by sinners, and in the gospel these are not two moods but one glory.

In everyday life. Bring to mind one person you see regularly who does not know Christ, and who will stand before his judgment seat. Let that, and the love that sought you first, move you to the next honest step: a question, an invitation, a word about what Christ means to you.

Should a Christian fear God or not? Both answers in Scripture are true, because there are two kinds of fear. The fear that expects punishment is cast out by God’s perfect love (1 John 4:18), because Christ bore the condemnation. But the fear of the Lord, reverent awe at his holiness, majesty and power, is the beginning of wisdom and grows as we know him better (Proverbs 9:10; Hebrews 12:28–29). A child who adores his father and would not dream of grieving him has the right kind. It is the fear that makes us take sin seriously, take people’s souls seriously, and take God at his word.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whether Paul seems carried away or calm and sensible, none of it is for himself: his zeal is for God, his sober thinking for the church.

Beside ourselves. Literally to stand outside oneself, to be out of one’s mind (existēmi). Festus would later shout it across a courtroom (Acts 26:24), and Jesus’ own family said, “He is out of his mind” (Mark 3:21). Perhaps the charge came from Paul’s ecstatic experiences (12:1–4), perhaps from the shape of his life: a man of formidable training who crossed provinces on foot, took beatings and refused payment. He does not deny it. Whatever in him goes past what people find reasonable is between him and God.

In our right mind. Sober, sane (sōphroneō). When he is measured and careful, that is for their sake, so that they can be taught.

The right way round. There is a passion that belongs between you and God and needs no audience: hours in prayer nobody knows about, giving so extravagant it would embarrass you if discussed. And there is a sober, patient steadiness that belongs to the people you serve. The failure comes when the two are swapped: intensity performed in public, sobriety kept for private life, where zeal quietly cools (Matthew 6:1–6).

For God and for you, all the way down. Paul’s two halves were the shape of Jesus’ life first. Toward his Father he was extravagant, rising a great while before day to pray (Mark 1:35), consumed by zeal for his Father’s house (John 2:17); toward his disciples he was patient and plain. Both were love, and neither was for himself (Romans 15:3).

The sanest act in history. To the watching world the cross was the maddest thing ever done. Yet the foolishness of God is wiser than men (1 Corinthians 1:25), and that holy extravagance was the sanest act in history. The Lord was counted out of his mind for our sake, and gave himself so completely that nothing is left for us to keep back. Hence Paul’s next sentence: “the love of Christ controls us”.

My family thinks I have gone too far with my faith. What should I do? First, you are in good company: they said it of Paul and of Jesus. Then ask honestly whether their complaint has something you should hear: are you neglecting them, lecturing them, or making your faith a reason to be unkind? If so, put it right; a sober, loving life is itself for them. But if what they object to is simply that Christ comes first, that you worship, give, pray and will not join in sin, do not argue and do not retreat. Love them more visibly than before, keep your private devotion private, and let the steadiness of your life answer the charge over time (1 Peter 3:1–2, 15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What drives Paul is Christ’s love, shown when he died for his people: they died with him, and now they live for him.

The love of Christ. The phrase could mean Paul’s love for Christ or Christ’s love for Paul, and the sentence decides it: what follows “because” is not Paul’s devotion but Christ’s death. A ministry powered by how much you love Christ will run exactly as far as your affections do, which on a bad week is not far. A ministry powered by how much he loved you has a fixed and finished event underneath it.

Controls. To press in from both sides (synechō), as a crowd round a man (Luke 8:45). Not a whip driving him, but like the banks of a river, which do not restrict the water but give it force.

One has died for all. Here is representation, which runs all through Paul: one person standing for many. Christ died as the representative and substitute of his people, and what happens to the one counts as having happened to those he stands for, as Adam’s act counted for the race that came from him (Romans 5:18–19). So when Christ died, those who are in him died with him (Romans 6:3–8; Galatians 2:20): the old self, the old account, the old standing went into the grave with him. That is true in two ways. The penalty your sins deserved was paid in his death and will never be demanded of you (Romans 8:1). And the person you were, owned by sin and living for yourself, has lost its claim on you, as a master loses his claim on a slave who has died (Romans 6:6–7).

No longer for themselves. The whole Christian way of life in one line, stated first as a result of Christ’s death, not as a rule. A man who has died is finished with running his own affairs. The cross ends the old life; the resurrection gives the new one its Master and its power, for the risen Christ lives in his people by his Spirit.

Twelve legions a word away. Before the love of Christ pressed in on Paul, it pressed in on Christ himself: it held him to the road to Jerusalem and kept him on the cross when twelve legions of angels were a word away (Matthew 26:53). The Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and a life bought like that cannot go back to belonging to itself.

Something will control you. Every life is driven by some love: to be admired, to feel safe, a particular career or person. Augustine put it in four Latin words in his Confessions, pondus meum amor meus: my love is my weight, and wherever I am carried, it is love that carries me. The question is never whether you will be controlled, only by what. Most of the loves that drive us are hard masters, because they depend on us: success must be kept up, approval earned again tomorrow, and the moment we falter they accuse. The love that pressed in on Paul rested on something finished: one has died for all. A love you have to sustain will wear you out. A love that has already died for you will carry you.

So what does living for him look like on a Monday? Asking, in ordinary decisions, what would please the one who died for me, and not only what I want. It reaches the diary, the bank account, the tongue, the body, the home, and work done as for him. It is not a life with no rest or enjoyment, but a life whose centre has moved. The test is not dramatic sacrifice but small daily choices where self used to sit on the throne.

Can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for them? You can tell every person, without hesitation, that Christ died for sinners, that he is a full and sufficient Saviour, that he offers himself freely to them, and that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). That is how the apostles preached to unbelievers: they proclaimed Christ crucified and called all to repent and believe (Acts 2:38; 17:30). Many in the Reformed tradition prefer that wording to “Christ died for you”, because the personal assurance belongs to the one who believes. But the offer is utterly sincere, and Christ’s love for his people is infinite. No one who comes will find that Christ did not die for him.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Two words in this sentence have been argued over for centuries: “for all”. Some take “all” to mean every human being equally, Christ’s death making salvation possible for all, applied on believing. Others take it to mean all who are in Christ, all his people. Both sides are protecting something real: one the sufficiency and freeness of the offer, the other the effectiveness of the cross. This commentary’s view: Paul says the all for whom Christ died have died with him, and live for him. That describes those united to Christ, not every human. Christ died effectively for all his people, of every nation, securing their salvation, not merely making it possible (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). This is definite atonement (sometimes called limited or particular redemption): the cross was aimed at, and actually secures, the salvation of a definite people. The gospel is offered sincerely to every person, and Christ’s death is sufficient for all, but it was designed to save his people (the Canons of Dort, a Reformed statement of 1619, 2.3, 8). Many faithful Christians read “all” more widely and preach the same Saviour; on either reading the offer to every sinner is real. What is beyond argument is the verse’s logic: his death was for people, in their place, and it did something to them and not merely for them.

verseByVerse.quote: From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Christ died and rose, Paul no longer sizes anyone up by worldly standards, for anyone joined to Christ belongs to God’s new creation.

No one according to the flesh. If one died for all, everything must be looked at again, beginning with people. “According to the flesh” means by the world’s standards: the reflex that files a person within seconds by accent, clothes, job or usefulness.

Christ according to the flesh. The decisive example is Paul himself. Saul had assessed Jesus by exactly those criteria: an executed provincial, a blasphemer, crucified and therefore cursed. He had been completely confident and completely wrong, and a man who has made that mistake about that person never trusts his own first assessment of anyone again.

A new creation. The Greek has no verb: if anyone in Christ, new creation! And kainē ktisis was not, in Paul’s world, a term for personal improvement but the prophets’ great promise about the world itself: “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17; Galatians 6:15). Paul says it has already begun, and where it has begun is inside people: the coming age already breaking into the present. Conversion is creation, not renovation.

Behold. The words echo Isaiah 43:18–19, where God tells his people to stop dwelling on the former things, because he is doing a new thing. “Behold” is a word for pointing, not at an inward process but at an event: Easter. The new creation began on the first day of the week, when Christ rose as the beginning, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), and everyone in him belongs to that morning, in the middle of an old world that does not yet know it has been replaced.

The misheard part. Read as a description of how you feel, this verse is crushing: the temper is still there, the same failure of thirty years. But it does not say if anyone feels new. It says “if anyone is in Christ”. The newness is first a matter of where you are, not how you feel, and it is true because God put you there.

What it means to be in Christ. The phrase can sound like a pious way of saying “a Christian”, but it says where you stand. In the Bible we rise or fall with the one who represents us, as a nation stands with its king (see on v. 14): “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Through faith the Spirit joins us to Christ, so that what is true of him is counted true of us. Martin Luther pictured it as a marriage, in The Freedom of a Christian: the bridegroom takes the bride’s sin and death as his own, and his grace, life and righteousness become hers (v. 21). Most of us build who we are on a record, a reputation, how the week went; in Christ, who you are rests on someone who does not change. So when you come to pray and feel you have no right to be heard, remember that you do not come in your own name. You come in his, and the Father hears you as one who is in his Son. See In Christ in the Theological Dictionary.

What it does not mean. Not that believers no longer sin and struggle (Galatians 5:17). What has passed away is the old order: the guilt, the condemnation, the dominion of sin; what remains is the lifelong work of putting to death the sin that is left. A man does not stop being a citizen because he still has an accent from the old country.

In everyday life. Look at others as people for whom Christ died: the colleague you find dull, the neighbour you have written off, the believer whose background makes you uneasy. Ask what God may be making of them.

If I am a new creation, do the consequences of my past disappear? The guilt does; not always the consequences. In Christ you are fully forgiven, and God will never hold your past against you. But a debt may still need repaying, a broken trust may take years to rebuild, a prison sentence may still need serving, and a damaged body may not be restored in this life. Zacchaeus, newly saved, repaid what he had taken (Luke 19:8). Face those consequences without despair, because they no longer define you; make right what you can, humbly; and do not let anyone, yourself included, call you by your old name. God does not.

Uncertain wording. “We once regarded Christ according to the flesh” has sometimes been taken to mean that Paul had known Jesus in person, or even that the earthly Jesus no longer matters. But “according to the flesh” goes with “regarded”, as earlier in the verse: it describes how Paul once judged Christ, by worldly standards, not which Christ he knew. Whether Paul ever saw Jesus during his earthly ministry is not known.

parallels.desc: behold, I am doing a new thing

verseByVerse.quote: All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reconciliation is God’s work from start to finish: in Christ he ended our quarrel with him, not counting our sins against us, and then gave us the message to tell. All this, everything from verse 14 onward, is from God.

In the flow. After the ministry of the new covenant (3:6) and of righteousness (3:9), here is its warmest name, the ministry of reconciliation, and it turns at once on the Corinthians: be reconciled to God (5:20), and open your hearts to us (6:13).

Reconciled us to himself. Reconciliation (katallassō) is not a religious term but an ordinary one: the ending of a quarrel, enmity turned to friendship, two people who could not bear to be in the same room sitting down together again. So the human problem, underneath everything else, is not chiefly ignorance or unhappiness but estrangement. We were God’s enemies (Romans 5:10), and every other relationship depends on this one.

In Christ God was reconciling. The world means people from every nation, a world in rebellion. That God did the reconciling does not mean there was nothing to settle; the cost (v. 21) measures how real the estrangement was. What it rules out is a reluctant God softened by a merciful Son. God himself was in Christ doing it.

Not counting trespasses. Counting (logizomai) is an accounting term: entering the item in the ledger. The debts are real, and they are not recorded against the reconciled, because God put them on Christ (v. 21; Romans 4:8). Many carry that ledger inside: words to a parent now dead, a year you would give anything to have back. The entry was not made against you: not excused or overlooked, but charged to the Son, on whose cross God cancelled the record of debt (Colossians 2:14).

Entrusting the message. God did the work and then handed the announcement to the very people who had been on the wrong side of the quarrel. The ordinary Christian talking awkwardly to a colleague is carrying something placed in his hands on purpose.

The offended party crossed the room. In every human quarrel the offender has to approach the offended. Here the offended party crossed the room. The barrier was on both sides, our rebellion and God’s just wrath, and Christ removed both. God did not wait for us to make the first move; he came in the person of his Son, into the middle of the quarrel, and settled it in his own body.

What if I have never felt at war with God? Most estrangement feels like indifference. A grown son who never calls his father, never thinks of him, and lives entirely on what his father gave him may feel no hostility at all, yet the relationship is broken. That is the human condition Paul describes: living in God’s world, on God’s gifts, without honouring him as God or giving him thanks (Romans 1:21). The respectable moralist reaches the same place by another road, keeping God at a distance with good behaviour so as never to come to him empty-handed. Either way the quarrel is real, and either way God has crossed the room.

If God has reconciled me, do I have to be reconciled with people? Yes, and the one leads to the other. A person forgiven an unpayable debt cannot keep a ledger against others (Matthew 18:21–35), and Jesus told his disciples to leave their gift at the altar and be reconciled with a brother first (Matthew 5:23–24). Take the first step, whether you are the offender or the offended, as God did. Reconciliation is not always fully possible: the other person may refuse, and where there has been abuse, safety comes first and trust must be earned. But forgiveness from the heart, and readiness for peace as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18), are always required.

Where Christians differ: is the whole world reconciled? Universalists read this as saying every person is already reconciled. Some other Christians read it as a reconciliation achieved for every person, which each must then accept; Reformed Christians read it as the world of those God actually reconciles in Christ, drawn from every nation. This commentary’s view: if everyone were already reconciled, Paul would not need to plead, “be reconciled to God” (v. 20). God accomplished reconciliation in Christ for the world of his people from every nation, and it is received by faith. The message goes to all, calling all to receive it, and no one is reconciled who does not come.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ’s messengers God himself pleads with people to accept the peace he has made: be reconciled to God. The plea is addressed even to those already in the church.

Ambassadors for Christ. An ambassador (presbeuō, used of the emperor’s own envoys) is a sovereign’s personal representative in foreign territory. He carries the message exactly; his authority is borrowed, and absolute while he carries it.

God making his appeal. Appeal means to beg (parakaleō); implore, to plead (deomai). God does not summon; he appeals. The Almighty, who was in the right throughout, pleads with those who wronged him to accept the peace he made at his own expense, holding out his hands all day long to a rebellious people (Isaiah 65:2; Romans 10:21). No one has ever been more patient with his enemies, or more eager to be friends with them.

Be reconciled to God. This is written to a church: Paul is imploring people already in the pews, perhaps because some were drifting. A person can be inside the congregation, holding the doctrine, doing the duties, and never have made peace. If your faith has been an arrangement you inherited rather than a quarrel that was ended, this verse is addressed to you, and it is not a threat but a plea. “Be reconciled” is passive: something done for you, not something you achieve. It has all been done; the only thing left is to stop refusing it. That is what the King is pleading for, through his own ambassadors, barely a generation after his Son died to make it possible.

As the Father has sent me. The first envoy to this rebel province was the Son, who came and preached peace to those far off and near (Ephesians 2:17). He did not merely carry the terms; he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), and he paid for it. Then, risen, he said: “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). Christ is still the one pleading through his ambassadors.

Three things about an ambassador. First, the message is not yours to adjust; an ambassador who improved on his instructions would be recalled. That guards against making the gospel more agreeable, and it is a relief: you are not responsible for whether it is well received. Second, the authority is not yours either, and that is the encouragement: a shy man with a letter from a king has more standing in that room than a magnificent man without one. Third, the posting is foreign. Christians represent a King the locals do not acknowledge, which accounts for a good deal of the strangeness of the Christian life. You were not meant to feel entirely at home here.

I have been in church all my life. How do I know I have actually been reconciled? Not by your attendance or your family, but by whether you have personally come to Christ. Ask honestly: have I seen my sin as an offence against God, not just a mistake? Have I stopped relying on my record and trusted Christ alone, his death in my place? Do I want to belong to him and follow him? If you are unsure, do not wait until you are sure; respond to the plea now. Tell God plainly that you have been at war with him, that you trust his Son’s death for you, and that you give yourself to him. Then speak to your pastor. Whoever comes to Christ is never turned away. And if you have trusted him and still fear this describes you, take heart: the wish to be truly at peace with God is itself the work of his Spirit in you.
verseByVerse.note: An ambassador spoke with the authority of the king who sent him.

verseByVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the cross God treated his sinless Son as sin in our place, so that all who are joined to Christ are counted righteous with God’s own righteousness.

He made him to be sin. God is the subject, his Son the object, and the verb is deliberate. Not that Christ became sinful; the next clause forbids it. God treated him as sin: laid our sins on him and punished sin in him (Isaiah 53:6, 10; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). For over a thousand years the Old Testament had taught the shape of it: a hand laid on an animal’s head, guilt transferred, the innocent dying for the guilty (Leviticus 4; 16:21, on the Day of Atonement). “The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

In the flow. In the best manuscripts verse 21 arrives with no linking word, like a foundation stone. It answers verse 20 (on what terms can God plead with rebels?) and verse 19 (God does not count their trespasses because he counted them against his Son), and turns at once into an appeal (6:1).

Who knew no sin. Said of no other human being (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22): no divided motive, no private version of himself. His enemies watched him for three years and in the end needed false witnesses who could not agree (Mark 14:55–56). Only a sinless one could bear others’ sin. And it is this one, with nothing owing, who is made sin. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34) is what being made sin sounds like from the inside, in the one relationship that had never had a shadow across it.

The righteousness of God. Luther called it the joyous exchange, and it goes further than we expect. Not only forgiven, not only treated as though we had not sinned: we become the righteousness of God, the right standing God gives, credited to us (Romans 3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). This is justification: not God making us good inside, but God the Judge declaring us righteous on the ground of Christ’s righteousness counted as ours (Romans 4:5). As Christ was treated as a sinner though he was not, we are treated as righteous though we are not. He got what was ours: the guilt, the charge, the abandonment. We get what was his: the standing, the welcome, the Father’s pleasure.

In him. Everything turns on the last two words. Righteousness is not a quality transferred into you that you might mislay on a bad week; it is yours because of where you are, in union with Christ. That is why a Christian at his worst is no less righteous before God than at his best. The righteousness counted is the whole obedience of the One who knew no sin, his perfect life as well as his death (Romans 5:19). Our own obedience is never perfect (James 3:2); for his sake God accepts it anyway. The standing was never generated by the performance, and cannot be damaged by it.

Made what he was not. He was made what he was not, so that we might be made what we could never be. The Holy One went down into the dark of our sin, and the guilty walk out of it clothed in his righteousness. The Father planned it, the Son bore it, the Spirit seals it, and it will be the song of the redeemed: worthy is the Lamb who was slain.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ ever stopped being holy, or that the Father hated the Son. Christ was beloved even as he bore the Father’s wrath against sin; the Son was never more pleasing to the Father than in that act of obedience (Philippians 2:8–9).

In everyday life. When your conscience accuses you today, do not answer it with your recent performance, good or bad. Answer it with this verse: my sin was counted to him, and his righteousness is counted to me. Then, freed from earning, go and do the good works God has prepared for you, gladly, in the strength of his Spirit.

How can it be just for God to punish an innocent person in our place? It would be unjust to seize an unwilling stranger and punish him for someone else, but that is not the cross. The Son came willingly, laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). He came as the head of his people, joined to them, as Adam was joined to the race. And he is God himself: the Judge did not lay the penalty on a third party but bore it in his own person. At the cross God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). Justice is not set aside; it is fully satisfied, by God, for us.

If I am counted righteous, does it matter how I live? More than ever, though not as payment. Paul anticipated the question: shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase? By no means (Romans 6:1–2). The same union with Christ that gives you his righteousness also joins you to his death and resurrection, so that sin no longer rules you; those in him are a new creation (v. 17) and live for him who died for them (v. 15). Holiness is not the price of your standing; it is the shape of your new life. You obey because you are accepted, not in order to be accepted.

Where Christians differ: imputation. Some deny that our sin was legally credited to Christ and his righteousness legally credited to us, saying instead that we are made righteous only by inner transformation. This commentary’s view: the parallel is exact. Christ was made sin, not by becoming sinful inside, but by having our sin counted to him. So we become righteous, not first by inner change, but by having his righteousness counted to us. This is double imputation, the heart of justification by faith alone (the Westminster Confession 11.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1; the Heidelberg Catechism Q. 60). Inner transformation follows in sanctification, but it is not the ground of our acceptance with God. And it shows the cross as penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty of our sin (that is the word penal) in our place (that is the word substitution); the punishment God’s justice required fell on him instead of on us (Isaiah 53:5).

Uncertain wording. In the Greek of Leviticus 4 the word for “sin” sometimes means a sin offering, so some translate “made him a sin offering”. Others take it as it stands: God treated him as sin itself. The repetition of the word in “who knew no sin” favours the plain meaning, but either way he bore our sin in our place.

parallels.desc: he was pierced for our transgressions

5.text: <sup>1</sup>For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.<sup>2</sup>For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling,<sup>3</sup>if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.<sup>4</sup>For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.<sup>5</sup>He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.<sup>6</sup>So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord,<sup>7</sup>for we walk by faith, not by sight.<sup>8</sup>Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.<sup>9</sup>So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him.<sup>10</sup>For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.<sup>11</sup>Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience.<sup>12</sup>We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.<sup>13</sup>For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.<sup>14</sup>For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died;<sup>15</sup>and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.<sup>16</sup>From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer.<sup>17</sup>Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.<sup>18</sup>All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation;<sup>19</sup>that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.<sup>20</sup>Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.<sup>21</sup>For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

keyVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter comes to rest on this sentence. It explains how God can plead with rebels instead of condemning them (vv. 19–20), why death and the judgment seat need not terrify a believer, and what the love of Christ that drives Paul actually did (v. 14). The sinless Son received what was ours, and we receive what is his.

5.reflection:
Paul calls the body a tent and longs not to escape it but to be “further clothed” with a resurrection body (vv. 1–4). How does that hope differ from the common idea that the soul simply goes to heaven? What difference does it make to how you face illness, ageing and death?

Paul’s ambition is to please Christ, before whose judgment seat every life will be laid open (vv. 9–10). How can a believer who is free from condemnation (Romans 8:1) take that seriously without fear? What would pleasing Christ look like in your week?

“The love of Christ controls us” (v. 14). What other loves tend to drive your life, and how is a love that has already died for you a different kind of master?

God “making his appeal through us” pleads, “be reconciled to God” (v. 20), and Paul says this to a church. Why might churchgoers need to hear it? Who in your life needs to hear it, and what would it look like to carry that message as an ambassador?

6.title: The Open Heart, the Catalogue of Hardships, and the Unequal Yoke
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 brings Paul’s long account of his ministry (2:14–7:4) to its climax. God makes his appeal through his ambassadors (5:20), and now Paul makes it to the Corinthians directly.

The message. Do not let the grace of God come to nothing in you, for the day of salvation is today. The servant who brings it is known not by success but by endurance and a Christlike character. His heart is wide open to you, so open yours. And because you are the temple where the living God lives as your Father, your heart must stay closed in one direction: towards idols.

Why it was said. The Corinthians had grown cool towards the apostle who brought them the gospel, drawn to rivals who measured a minister by polish and success (see the introduction), and their city’s social life ran through pagan temples. The heart narrowing towards Paul was the heart in danger of opening to idols.

How the chapter makes its case. Isaiah’s promise of a day of favour makes the appeal urgent (vv. 1–2). Paul commends his ministry as his rivals never would: no obstacle laid in anyone’s way (v. 3), endurance (vv. 4–5), the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 6–7), and a string of paradoxes, dying yet alive, poor yet making many rich (vv. 8–10). Then he drops his voice, calls them by name and asks for room in their hearts (vv. 11–13). Last comes the one exception: believers cannot be yoked with unbelief (vv. 14–16), because God lives among his people, welcomes those who come out, and is their Father (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. Isaiah’s day of salvation was first promised to the Servant, whose cry the Father heard on Easter morning. Every paradox of verses 8–10 was true of Jesus first: called an impostor yet the truth, dead yet alive for evermore, rich yet poor to make many rich (8:9). The church is God’s temple because his Son’s body was the true temple, destroyed and raised in three days. And the promise to David’s son, “I will be to him a father”, now belongs to slaves and former idolaters, because the only Son by right has shared his inheritance.

For us. Do not postpone what God offers today, and ask what grace you are sitting on. Measure ministers, and yourself, by faithfulness rather than results. Open a narrowed heart by one concrete act. Draw the line between God and idols through your own life, not around other people. And whatever your earthly father was, the Lord Almighty calls you his son or daughter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Open Heart and the Catalogue of Hardships
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace must not come to nothing in them, because the day of favour Isaiah promised has come, and the man who brings it has proved himself by a cross-shaped life. Paul appeals to them as God’s fellow worker (vv. 1–2), then shows his credentials: no obstacle laid in anyone’s way (v. 3), great endurance under hardship (vv. 4–5), the character the Spirit produces and the weapons of righteousness (vv. 6–7), and a life of paradoxes in which the world sees only weakness and God sees life and riches (vv. 8–10). Then he speaks as a father: his heart is wide open to them, and he asks them to open theirs (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The list of hardships (vv. 4–5) is one of several in 2 Corinthians (4:8–9; 11:23–29; 12:10). Together they show the cross applied to ministry: in a world that crucified its King, those who carry the message of the cross will bear its pattern in their bodies (see the note on vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.examples: A young minister starts a church in a hard part of a city, hoping for rapid growth. After three years he has a small congregation, many failures, and a life that looks more like Paul’s list than his plans. He questions his calling. Here the hardships are marks of a true ministry, not a failed one, and the question is whether he is serving with the character of verses 6–7.

verseByVerse.quote: Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now that you have been reconciled to God, do not let his grace come to nothing in you, for the day of salvation he promised is today.

Working together with him, then. The word is synergeō, to be a fellow worker on the same job (1 Corinthians 3:9). Having begged them to be reconciled, Paul gives the second half of God’s appeal (5:20).

In vain. Literally “to emptiness” (eis kenon): a gift that arrives and produces nothing. The grace is everything just given them in Christ: reconciliation, forgiveness and a righteousness not their own (5:18–21). Some in Corinth were drifting after false teachers (11:3–4) and back into unholy living (12:21).

In a favorable time. Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8, where God tells his Servant, the light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6), that his cry has been heard and his day of help has come. The New Testament tells us when that cry went up: in the days of his flesh Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard (Hebrews 5:7). The answer came on Easter morning. The promise made to Christ is handed on to everyone who is in him: our day of salvation is the overflow of his.

Now. Twice “behold”, twice “now”. We all know a version of “later”: when work settles, when the children are older. Scripture says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15), because a heart that intends to respond eventually is already hardening while it waits.

That today has never ended. The day of salvation dawned in a synagogue in Nazareth, when Jesus read of the year of the Lord’s favour and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). That today is held open still by the One whose cry was heard. Nobody has been promised the favourable time twice, and nobody who comes within it is turned away.

What does receiving grace in vain look like? Years of hearing about forgiveness without ever forgiving anyone. Singing about Christ’s love while nursing the same resentment. Knowing the gospel well and never speaking of it. Receiving comfort and never comforting. None of these is a dramatic fall; each is grace landing on ground that does not let it grow. Ask: what has God given me that I am sitting on? Then take one step of obedience there today, in the strength of the Spirit he has given you.

Does this passage threaten someone’s salvation? Paul has just told this church that they are a new creation, sealed by the Spirit; he does not suggest that God’s work in them might quietly fail. He warns against a life in which grace makes no difference, treated as a finished deal rather than the start of a life with God. That can describe a believer wasting years he will not get back, or someone with every appearance of faith who has never actually come. Paul does not sort them, and neither should we; the warning is for everyone in the room, to be taken personally. And if it frightens you, take heart: the person anxious that grace should not be wasted on him is not a person on whom grace is lying idle.

If God does the work, why does Paul call himself God’s fellow worker? Because God works through means, and the means are people. Paul does not help God save anyone: new birth is God’s work alone (4:6). But in the preaching, praying, pleading and serving, God gives real work to real people. You cannot open one blind eye, but you can carry the message, and God is pleased to call you his co-worker when you do.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s Greek says only “working together”; “with him” is supplied by the ESV. Most take the partner to be God, since God makes his appeal through Paul (5:20) and Paul calls himself and Apollos “God’s fellow workers” (1 Corinthians 3:9). A few think of Paul working with his fellow ministers, or with the Corinthians. The context favours the ESV.

parallels.desc: in a time of favour I have answered you

verseByVerse.quote: We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul takes care that nothing in his own conduct becomes the reason someone turns away from Christ, so that the message is not discredited by its messenger.

No obstacle. Something you strike your foot against (proskopē).

No fault found. To find fault, to ridicule (mōmaomai). The fault he fears is fault found not with him but with the ministry. Protecting the message is the only reason a Christian’s reputation is worth anything at all.

He was fiercely practical about this. It is why he refused financial support from Corinth and worked at a trade, so that nobody could say he was in it for money (1 Corinthians 9:12–15), why the collection was carried by men the churches themselves had chosen (8:20–21), and why he became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22): not to be liked, but to remove every avoidable barrier between a person and the gospel. He learned it from his Master, who ate with tax collectors, touched lepers and welcomed children, removing every barrier but one.

The one stone God laid on purpose. One obstacle must never be removed: Christ himself, the stone of stumbling laid in Zion, in whom whoever believes will not be put to shame (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:7–8).
