A crucified Messiah is a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23). Paul clears the road so carefully precisely so that this stone, and nothing else, is what a person meets. If people are offended that sin is called sin, or that Christ is the only way, that offence is the gospel doing its work. A gospel adjusted until nobody trips over it has been tampered with (4:2).

Every other stone is ours. And there are more than we like to count: the manner that makes people feel small, the church finances never explained, the political opinion nailed to the pulpit as though it were doctrine, the way we speak about people not in the room, the reputation for being unforgiving or slightly dishonest about small things. None of these is the gospel. Any of them can be the reason somebody stops listening.

What if I already have been an obstacle to someone? Then go and move the stone. Name what you did, without excuses: I was harsh with you, I mocked what you believe, I never paid you back. Apologise plainly, put right what can be put right, and do not make the apology a sermon. Many unbelievers have never heard a Christian say I was wrong, and a humble confession can open a door that years of argument could not. Then leave it with God, and do not lay the stone down again.

verseByVerse.quote: but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s credentials as God’s servant are not results but endurance: he has stayed under every kind of pressure, violence and toil without walking away. His rivals came with letters; Paul offers a life (3:1).

By great endurance. The heading over the fullest list of hardships in the letter so far (compare 4:8–9; 11:23–29). Hypomonē (1:6) is a remaining under, staying put beneath a weight: not the ability to avoid trouble but the refusal to walk out from under it. Three groups of three follow.

In afflictions, hardships, calamities. Three words for pressure: thlipseis, pressures; anankai, constraints you cannot get out of; stenochōriai, literally a narrow place, being wedged where there is no room.

Beatings, imprisonments, riots. Three things done to him by others: someone swung the rod, someone turned the key, a crowd turned on him. Philippi, Lystra and Ephesus all supplied them (Acts 16:22–23; 14:19; 19:29), and in chapter 11 he will give the appalling numbers (11:23–25).

Labors, sleepless nights, hunger. Three things he took on for the work: toil to exhaustion; nights spent travelling, working, praying and sitting up with people (1 Thessalonians 2:9); and going without food, by choice or because there was nothing.

What is missing from the list. Results: no churches counted, no converts numbered, no cities won. No one today would commend a ministry with such a document, and that is Paul’s point, aimed at a church that had begun assessing ministers the way the world assesses anyone (see the introduction). His credential is not what he has achieved but what he has borne without giving up.

Carrying the death of Jesus. Paul has already told them how to read such a list: he carries in his body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may be shown there too (4:10). The Master’s life is pressed into the servant’s. Christ too was handed over, beaten, sleepless in Gethsemane and hungry in the wilderness, and for the joy set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). Paul can endure because he belongs to the One who endured first.

Faithful, not successful. There is a word here for the person whose service has produced very little that can be counted: the years in a small church that never grew, two decades of praying for a family member with nothing to show. On this list, none of that is failure. Endurance is the one credential that cannot be faked, borrowed or produced quickly. Faithfulness is commanded; success never is.

What it does not mean. Not that suffering proves a ministry true; false teachers can suffer too. But true ministry is marked by endurance in suffering, not escape from it.

So how should I judge a pastor or a ministry? Not by size, celebrity, polish or how much you enjoy it, but by Scripture’s questions. Does he preach Christ crucified and risen plainly, without trimming it (4:2, 5)? Is his life consistent with it: honest with money, faithful in marriage, gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of status (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? Does he stay when it is hard, and serve when no one sees? Are people being built up in Christ rather than attached to him? A faithful ministry may be small and unremarkable for years. It will be marked by truth, love and endurance.

verseByVerse.quote: by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s ministry is also commended by what God has formed in him: a Christlike character, the Spirit’s power, plain truth, and nothing to fight with but righteousness. This is the more searching half of the list, because a man can endure a great deal and remain unpleasant.

By purity, knowledge, patience, kindness. Purity, hagnotēs, is moral cleanness and sincerity of motive, nothing to keep out of sight. Knowledge is the true understanding of God and his gospel; warm feeling without true teaching is no credential. Patience is makrothymia, long-temperedness: being wronged by the same person repeatedly and not retaliating. Kindness, chrēstotēs, is love’s practical, unglamorous form. It is possible to be doctrinally impeccable and unkind, and this list forbids it (compare Galatians 5:22).

The Holy Spirit. In the middle of a list of virtues, something that is not a virtue at all. None of the qualities around him comes naturally to a human being; he is named among them because he is the one producing them.

Genuine love. Literally “love without hypocrisy”, anypokritos (Romans 12:9). The hypocrite was a stage actor. It is possible to do all the right things for people while performing, and everybody can eventually tell.

Truthful speech and power. The gospel spoken honestly, and the Spirit working through it, without whom the whole list would be self-improvement and not ministry.

Weapons of righteousness. A Roman soldier carried the sword in the right hand and the shield on the left: attack and defence. Both are made of righteousness: right living, and the right standing with God that Christ gives as a gift, since he was made sin for us (5:21). Paul fights with nothing false or invented (compare Ephesians 6:13–17).

The portrait behind the list. Read the list again and a face appears. Christ was pure, knew the Father as no one else does (Matthew 11:27), was patient with slow disciples and kind to the despised; insulted, he did not answer with insults (1 Peter 2:23). The Spirit stands in the middle because his work is to form Christ in his people (Galatians 4:19).

No shield but his own body. The armour was God’s before it was ours. Isaiah saw the LORD, finding no one to intervene, put on righteousness as a breastplate and come himself to save (Isaiah 59:16–17). In Christ he came, alone, and won with no weapon but righteousness and no shield but his own body. Now he arms the weakest of his people from his own armoury.

Defending yourself with righteousness. When you are misrepresented, the instinct is to fight back with the same means: the counter-story, the quiet word to the right person. Paul’s shield is righteousness: you defend yourself by continuing to live rightly. It is slower and harder, and the only defence that does not have to be maintained, because a life is more difficult to answer than an argument.

Should I never set the record straight when I am falsely accused? You may, and sometimes you should; Paul spends much of this letter doing so. The difference is in the weapons. Speak the truth plainly to those who need to hear it, without exaggeration, without attacking the other person’s character, and without a campaign behind their back. Where wrong needs addressing, use the proper channels: go to the person first (Matthew 18:15), involve church leaders, and where a crime has been committed, the authorities. Then leave your reputation with God. Your job is to tell the truth and keep living rightly; vindication is his.
verseByVerse.note: Weapons “for the right hand and for the left” are weapons for attack (the sword) and defence (the shield).

verseByVerse.quote: through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s life looks like failure to those who judge by appearances, but in every case the truth is the opposite of what they see.

Through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. Admired in one town and vilified in the next, for the same work. We are governed by these two more than we know: we drift towards whatever brings praise and away from whatever brings criticism, and after twenty years of small adjustments a life has been shaped by other people’s opinions. Paul walks through both without changing direction, because he expects to give his account somewhere else (5:10).

Impostors, yet true. Deceivers, frauds (planoi). This was actually being said about him, and his answer is not an argument but a plain statement: “and yet are true”.

Unknown, yet well known. Nobody to the great men of the empire; known to the churches, and known by God, which is the knowing that counts. For anyone whose work no one notices, the question is never whether you are known, only by whom.

Behold, we live. A note of astonishment. By every reasonable assessment he should be dead: the stoning at Lystra (Acts 14:19), the night and day adrift at sea (11:25), the affliction in Asia (1:8). And here he is, writing.

Punished, not killed. Disciplined, chastened (paideuō). Behind it lies a psalm: “The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death” (Psalm 118:18). A Father had been at work in the floggings, and had set the limit himself.

The paradoxes of the Master. Every line was true of Jesus first. He was called “that impostor” (Matthew 27:63), and he is the truth (John 14:6). He was the carpenter’s son nobody in Rome had heard of, and the One through whom all things were made (John 1:3). He was smitten by God and afflicted, and the Father did not give him over to death for ever: he died, and behold, he is alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18). Union with Christ gives a servant his Master’s paradoxes, and his Master’s vindication (Galatians 2:20).

The second half of the sentence. The world reads the visible half of a Christian’s life and stops. The second half is supplied by a God who has never once mistaken one of his servants for a fraud.

How do I stop living for other people’s opinions? Not by ceasing to care about people, but by caring more about God’s verdict. Watch where approval and criticism steer you: what you post, what you avoid saying, which convictions you go quiet on. Bring those to God and ask what pleases him. In Christ you already have the only verdict that finally matters: accepted, beloved, righteous (5:21). Then listen to criticism humbly, because it may be true, without being ruled by it; and receive praise gratefully, without needing it. A person secure in God’s love can afford both.

verseByVerse.quote: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s inner life is as paradoxical as his outward one: real sorrow with unbroken joy, real poverty with riches to give away, nothing in hand and everything in Christ.

Sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. Often flattened, as though one cancels the other. Both are true at once, and to the second Paul attaches “always”. He grieves over sin, suffering and the lost (Romans 9:2), and rejoices in the Lord (Philippians 4:4), in the same hour, about different things.

Two floors in one house. Anyone who has stood at a Christian funeral has seen it. The grief is not reduced; a real person is gone and the loss is as large as it feels. And underneath it, not instead of it, is something that will not go out, because the one being buried is with the Lord, and the God who arranged that has not changed since last week. Christian joy was never built on circumstances, so it is not demolished when they collapse.

Poor, yet making many rich. Near the end of his life Paul’s belongings seem to have been a cloak, some books and the parchments (2 Timothy 4:13), and whole provinces were made rich through him. The pattern is his Lord’s, who though he was rich became poor for our sake (8:9).

Possessing everything. A man with no property, no security and no home says he possesses everything, and he is not being brave. All things belong to believers, because they belong to Christ, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23); the God who did not spare his own Son will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32). That is plain fact, not consolation for people who have missed out. The One who owns everything gave himself to his people, and everything he owns came with him. He had nowhere to lay his head, and he is heir of all things.

Grief is not a failure of faith. Christians are often made to feel that a truly trusting person would be at peace by now. That is not in the Bible. Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty (John 11:35). The gospel promises not the absence of sorrow but a joy that runs at a level sorrow cannot reach. If you are grieving, do not hurry yourself out of it; let the sorrow be real, and look for the floor beneath it: forgiveness, the Father’s love, the Spirit, a future, a family in the church. Then ask whom you might make rich this week.

May a Christian work to improve his circumstances, or should he be content with little? Both, rightly understood. Scripture commends diligent work that provides for your family and lets you give to others (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; Ephesians 4:28; 1 Timothy 5:8); there is nothing unspiritual about a better job or a sound budget. What it forbids is the love of money and the anxious craving for more (1 Timothy 6:6–10), and what it teaches is contentment in plenty and in want (Philippians 4:11–12). Work hard, give generously, hold everything loosely, and never think that what you own is what you are.

verseByVerse.quote: We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has hidden nothing from the Corinthians and has room in his heart for all of them; the narrowness between them is on their side, not his. The defence of his ministry since 2:14 stops, and the father speaks.

We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. Only here in the letter does he address them by name: the sound of a man dropping his voice. Literally, “our mouth is open to you”: nothing withheld, nothing said behind a hand. A man defending his authority has spent five chapters admitting weakness (1:8; 2:12–13).

Our heart is wide open. Widened, made spacious (platynō). There is room in him for all of them; whatever they have done, they have not been shut out.

Restricted in your affections. Then the diagnosis, put with great delicacy. “Restricted”, stenochōreō, means cramped, confined: the opposite of the widened heart. “Affections” is splanchna, the inward parts, where Greek located deep feeling; its verb is used of the Lord’s compassion for the crowds (Matthew 9:36). Paul has not withdrawn; they have narrowed. There is a cramped place in them where he used to be.

In the flow. The plea resumes at 7:2, and between the two requests stands the warning against the unequal yoke (6:14–7:1): the hearts closing to Christ’s servant were the hearts in danger of opening to idols.

The affection of Christ Jesus. Where did a heart this wide come from? Paul tells the Philippians, with the same word, that he yearns for them all with the affection of Christ Jesus (Philippians 1:8). The open heart is borrowed: Christ’s own compassion, living in a man taken into that heart when he deserved nothing from it, whom the love of Christ controls (5:14). Christ stretched out his arms on the cross wide enough to take in the world. If there is a cramped place between us and him, it is never on his side.

A cooled relationship. Nothing is formally wrong; the greetings still happen. But something has closed, and the person outside can feel there is less room for him. Paul neither accuses nor demands an explanation. He describes what is true, his heart open and theirs narrow, and leaves it in front of them. Pretending not to notice and making an accusation both close the door further.

A narrowed heart. A real spiritual condition, not merely a social awkwardness. A narrowed heart cannot receive much, which is why the Corinthians could not take in what Paul was giving them. Suspicion does that; so does long-held resentment; so does the quiet decision to protect yourself after being hurt once. It always feels like prudence, and it always costs the same thing: the ability to be loved. Where has your heart narrowed? There is usually a name attached, and a good reason, and holding on to the reason has never made anybody’s heart freer. Open it this week by one concrete act towards that person.

But what if my heart closed because I was really wronged? Then your hurt is real, and God takes it seriously. Opening your heart does not mean pretending nothing happened, or putting yourself back in harm’s way. Where there has been abuse or ongoing danger, safety comes first, and trust is something the other person must rebuild over time. But even then you can refuse bitterness room: forgive from the heart before God (Ephesians 4:31–32), stop rehearsing the wrong, pray for the person, and remain willing for peace if they repent. A heart can be open towards God and towards reconciliation while still being careful.

verseByVerse.quote: In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks only one thing in return: that they make room for him in their hearts as he has for them. He could have commanded; instead he asks, as a father asks his children for their love.

Widen your hearts also. The same word as verse 11: make room, love me back. He is asking to be loved by people who have not been loving him, and a request for affection can be refused.

I speak as to children. Affectionate: he is their father in the faith (1 Corinthians 4:14–15), and a father may say to his children what a colleague could not. It also spares them a formal negotiation between equals.

What he is not asking for. Not an apology, nor agreement about the past; only room. We tend to make reopening a relationship conditional on settling the history: who was right, who should speak first. Paul, who had the stronger case, sets it aside and asks for the one thing that would change anything. A heart that has opened usually finds the record matters less than it did.

Do you love me? Paul learned this way of asking from his Lord. On a beach in Galilee the risen Jesus met the disciple who had denied him three times. He did not demand an account of the courtyard. He asked Peter one thing, three times: “do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). The Lord of glory, wronged and in the right, asked his friend for room in his heart, and then gave him work to do. No leverage, no case, only love asking for love. Every reconciliation in the church is a small copy of the one at the cross, where the offended party made the first move.

Widening is an act. A heart does not enlarge by waiting to feel differently. It is the visit made, the message sent, the refusal to run the grievance through your mind once more, the choice to assume the kinder explanation. Paul had watched Stephen die and gone looking for more Christians to arrest (Acts 7:58–8:3); the room made for him in the church was made not because he apologised his way in but by the One whose heart was wide enough to take in the man hunting him. Nobody received like that can plead a shortage of room.

What if I widen my heart and they still refuse? Then you have done what God asked, and the rest is theirs and his. Paul could not make the Corinthians love him. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18): sometimes it will not be possible. Keep the door open without forcing it. Do not punish them with coldness or keep score of your efforts. Pray for them. Some relationships are restored years later; some only in heaven. Either way, a heart that stays open is free, and it is like God’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–7:1 — Do Not Be Unequally Yoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the church is the temple where the living God lives, believers must not bind themselves to anything that pulls them away from him. Paul states the command (v. 14a) and backs it with five questions, each expecting the answer “none”: righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness, Christ and Belial, believer and unbeliever, God’s temple and idols (vv. 14b–16a). Then he gives the reason, woven from God’s promises to Israel: God dwells among his people (v. 16b), so they must come out and touch no unclean thing, and he will welcome them (v. 17) and be their Father (v. 18). The call to holiness that follows (7:1) rests on these promises.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage applies in several settings. First, marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, stated directly elsewhere: “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). Second, formal religious partnerships, such as joint worship that treats basic differences about God as unimportant. Third, business partnerships that require ethical compromise. Ordinary friendship, work and life alongside unbelievers are not in view (see the note on v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is invited to co-host a community prayer service with leaders of several faiths, some of whom deny the Trinity and that Christ is the only Saviour. He must decide whether this is civic engagement, speaking to the community, or a spiritual partnership, worshipping together. This passage suggests the difference matters: showing the church’s care for the community is not the same as implying that every faith pulls the same yoke toward the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not bind your life to unbelief in a partnership that pulls you away from Christ, because believers and unbelievers are headed in opposite directions and cannot pull together.

The connection. The change of subject is so abrupt that some think this paragraph was originally somewhere else (see the introduction). But the link is there: having asked them to widen their hearts towards him, Paul names the one place the heart must not open. A church that has room for everything has room for nothing in particular.

Unequally yoked. Yoked with a different kind (heterozygeō). Behind it stands the law: you shall not plough with an ox and a donkey together (Deuteronomy 22:10). Two animals of different height, strength and stride on one beam cannot work; the furrow wanders, and the harness injures both. Not that the donkey is wicked; they simply cannot pull together.

For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? The first of five questions, each expecting the answer “none”. “Partnership” is metochē, sharing; “fellowship” is koinōnia. Light and darkness do not negotiate or blend (John 3:19–21; Ephesians 5:8–11); one simply ends where the other begins.

For the first readers. Much of Corinth’s social and business life ran through the temples: trade associations, family celebrations and patrons’ dinners were held in honour of a god, often in a temple dining room. Paul had already warned that such feasts meant sharing the table of demons (1 Corinthians 8:10; 10:14–22). That is why the passage moves straight to idols in God’s temple (v. 16) and touching no unclean thing (v. 17). Marriage is the clearest modern case, but idolatry was the first in view.

Already in partnership. A believer cannot take this yoke because he is already yoked. God called you into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord (1 Corinthians 1:9), the same word, koinōnia, that light can never have with darkness. A Christian is not a free agent shopping for alliances; he is joined to the Christ who bought him, and every binding commitment pulls with that union or against it.

He offers his own yoke. The Lord who forbids the unequal yoke offers his own: take my yoke upon you, for my yoke is easy and my burden is light (Matthew 11:29–30). He fastens us to himself, the One who walks in step with us, carries the heavier side, and never pulls us off the line.

Precision matters. This verse has been used to justify what Paul explicitly refused. Friendship, employment, neighbourliness, hospitality, business dealings: none is forbidden. Friendship is often how unbelievers come to Christ, and a Christian who withdraws from the world cannot carry the message of chapter 5. What is in view is a yoke: binding your direction to someone whose direction is opposed to Christ, in a way you cannot easily undo.

Does this apply to dating? Yes, where dating means looking for a husband or wife. If a Christian should not marry an unbeliever, he should not begin a romance heading that way; hearts follow where time and affection go.

Is it not narrow-minded to refuse to marry someone because of what he believes? Not when you see what marriage is: the closest yoke there is, two lives pulling towards one future, raising children, spending money, facing death together. If Christ is the deepest thing in your life, to marry someone who does not share him is to be one flesh with someone who cannot go with you where you are most truly going. That is not contempt but honesty about you both, and kinder than a marriage in which the most important thing must stay unspoken.

What it does not mean. If you are already married to someone who does not believe, this verse is not about you, and no one should use it against you. Paul could not be plainer: “If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him” (1 Corinthians 7:13), and his reason is hope: “For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7:16). God has used a great many such marriages to save the other half of them.

I knowingly married an unbeliever after I became a Christian. Am I living in sin? You may need to confess that the choice was disobedient, but the marriage itself is real, binding and honourable before God, and staying in it is obedience, not sin. Do not treat every day of it as a fresh offence. Love your spouse well, pray for them, and let your conduct speak more than your words (1 Peter 3:1–2). If the unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, Paul says the believer is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15; the Westminster Confession 24.6). And if there is abuse, seek safety and help from your church at once; God never asks anyone to remain in danger.

In everyday life. Before any binding commitment, ask early, before your heart is fastened: will this pull me with Christ, or against him? Ask a mature believer to help you answer honestly.

Where Christians differ: what is an unequal yoke? Some apply this only to marriage; others to any contact with unbelievers. This commentary’s view: In context, Paul’s main concern is probably Corinthians joining in pagan temple worship and following false teachers. The principle applies to any binding partnership that pulls a believer away from Christ: most clearly marriage (1 Corinthians 7:39), and also business partnerships or alliances that compromise faith and obedience. It does not forbid friendship, work or ordinary life with unbelievers, which Paul assumes (1 Corinthians 5:10; 10:27).
verseByVerse.note: The picture comes from the law forbidding an ox and a donkey to be yoked together at the plough.

verseByVerse.quote: What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ and Satan have nothing in common, and so, at the deepest level, a believer and an unbeliever share no common portion.

What accord has Christ with Belial? Belial (Paul’s Greek spells it Beliar) is a Hebrew word that began as a description, not a name: worthlessness, a thing that yields nothing. The men of Gibeah who surrounded the house were worthless men, sons of Belial (Judges 19:22). By Paul’s time Jewish writers, including those of the Dead Sea Scrolls, used it as a title for Satan. Only here does the New Testament use it. “Accord” is symphōnēsis, the word behind “symphony”: Christ and Belial make no chord, and anything that tries to hold both will be discordant.

Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever? A portion, meris, is an allotted share, like the land each family received in Israel (see inheritance). At the deepest level, what your life is finally for and where it ends, believers and unbelievers have no common share.

Everything against nothing. Paul could have written Satan; he chose the word that means worthless. Christ, in whom every promise of God is Yes (1:20), against the one whose entire estate is worth nothing: not two comparable powers dividing the world, but everything against a name that means nothing. We have no share with worthlessness because we have been given a share in Christ, who is worth more than the world.

What Paul is not saying. Believers and unbelievers share a world, a workplace, a street, a humanity, and Christians who forget that become insufferable. But two people can share a house and thirty years of affection and still be walking in opposite directions on the one road that finally matters, towards God or away from him.

Does this mean my unbelieving relative has no hope? No. The portion describes where a person stands now, not where God may bring him. Every believer once had no share in Christ; such were some of you, Paul told this church, but you were washed (1 Corinthians 6:11). The difference between you and your relative is not that you are better but that grace reached you. So the verse should make you more prayerful and more tender, not more distant. Keep loving them, keep the gospel in view, and pray that God would give them a share in Christ too.
verseByVerse.note: Belial (“worthlessness”) was a Jewish name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is the temple where the living God himself lives, so it can make no room for idols.

What agreement has the temple of God with idols? The question the other four were climbing towards: the reason a believer cannot be yoked to darkness is not chiefly a rule about company but a fact about what he now is. Agreement is synkatathesis, a joint decision, a vote cast together. Idols in God’s temple were the ultimate sacrilege, what Manasseh did and what Ezekiel saw in his vision of the abominations in the temple (2 Kings 21:4–7; Ezekiel 8).

The temple of the living God. Corinth had temples, to Apollo, to Aphrodite on the height above the city, to half a dozen others, each a temple because the god was thought to live there. Paul says the temple is the congregation (1 Corinthians 3:16): not a building, but a group of former idolaters, labourers and freedmen in a Greek port. And “living” matters. The idols had mouths but did not speak (Psalm 115:5); the God who lives among his people sees, speaks, acts and judges. To bring an idol into his house is to insult a holy God who is present and awake.

As God said. The quotation weaves together Leviticus 26:11–12, Ezekiel 37:27 and the covenant promise, repeated in Jeremiah too, that he will be their God and they shall be his people. All were given to Israel, about a tabernacle, a temple and a land; Paul says they are fulfilled in the church by the Spirit. This is the heart of the covenant: God living among his people. “Make my dwelling” recalls God’s tent in the middle of the camp, the picture John uses when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); “walk among them” recalls God at home in the garden in the cool of the day, before anything went wrong.

A garden, a tent, a temple, a body. The whole Bible is the story of God making a way to live with people who could not survive his presence: a garden lost, a tent with a curtain across it, a temple with a room nobody could enter but the high priest, once a year, with blood. Then a body, the true temple, destroyed and raised again in three days (John 2:19–21). And now an ordinary congregation with the living God at home in the middle of them. He gave his Son to have it, and one day he will make his dwelling with us on a new earth for ever (Revelation 21:3).

Someone already lives there. If you are the place where God lives, what you join yourself to is not a private preference; you are deciding what to bring into his house. The point is not only that idols are foolish, but that Someone already lives there.

What counts as an idol today? Anything you look to for what only God can give: security, identity, worth, comfort, meaning. Often a good thing made into an ultimate thing: money, career, a relationship, children, reputation, health, a political cause, pleasure, even ministry. Ask what you most fear losing, what you daydream about, where your spare money and time go, and what makes you angry when it is threatened. Idols rarely look like statues now, but they still demand sacrifices, and they still cannot save. Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:21). Name the one most likely to compete with God for your heart this week, and decide in advance, leaning on the Spirit who lives in his temple, what you will do when it calls.

Is my own body God’s temple too? Yes, though here the temple is the church together: “we”, plural. Elsewhere Paul applies the same truth to each believer’s body, in the context of sexual immorality: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, so glorify God in your body (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Keep your body from sin because it is his house, and treat your church with the same reverence, for when believers gather, God is in the midst.

parallels.desc: I will walk among you and be your God

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave behind the idolatry and impurity of the world around you, and God will welcome you as his own.

Go out from their midst. The quotation continues from Isaiah 52:11, words spoken to the exiles as they left Babylon carrying the vessels of the temple home. Paul applies them to a church inside a pagan city. This verse has done damage in the hands of people who wanted a reason to withdraw, so first, what it cannot mean.

Not withdrawal. The Lord prayed, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). The Christian is planted in society, as light is planted in a dark room. Any version of the faith that measures holiness by how few outsiders you know has misread this sentence.

Touch no unclean thing. This explains “go out” and “be separate”. The uncleanness is now moral and spiritual rather than ritual: not people to be avoided, but defilement. The exiles leaving Babylon were not told to hate Babylonians; they were told not to carry Babylon home with them.

Then I will welcome you. From Ezekiel 20:34 comes the phrase that turns a command into gospel. The verb is for taking someone in: receiving a guest, gathering someone to yourself.

The Servant leads the way out. Paul’s quotation comes just before Isaiah’s prophecy of the suffering Servant (Isaiah 52:13–53:12). The call to go out and touch no unclean thing (Isaiah 52:11) is followed by the promise that the LORD will go before his people and be their rear guard (52:12), and then by the Servant pierced for our transgressions, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (53:5–6). This new exodus is not a march the people manage by their own purity. Only Christ could come out of Babylon clean, and he makes his people clean by bearing their uncleanness. We separate from idols because he first separated us to himself.

A line through your own life. So the separation is real, but it is not a line between us and them. It runs through the middle of your own life, wherever the surrounding culture would make itself at home in the temple of God: what you watch, what you laugh at, how you get money, what you do with your private hours, the ambitions you have absorbed without examining them. You can live in a Christian bubble and be thoroughly Babylonian inside it, or work in the least Christian place imaginable and touch nothing unclean.

What it does not mean. Not that God welcomes us only after we have cleaned ourselves up. He welcomes sinners, and those he welcomes leave their idols; chapter 5 ended with the righteousness of God given to people who had none. But a life divided between God and idols does not feel welcomed, and the way back into enjoying what you already have is to stop carrying Babylon into the room where he lives.

How do I decide what is unclean in entertainment and daily life? Start with what Scripture plainly calls sin, and do not make it entertainment: sexual immorality, cruelty enjoyed for its own sake, mockery of God, greed held up as glory (Ephesians 5:3–12). Then ask honest questions about the rest. Does this make sin attractive to me? Does it leave me colder towards God and people? Would I be comfortable watching it with Christ in the room, as he is? Does it have a grip on me (1 Corinthians 6:12)? Christians will draw some lines differently in matters of conscience (Romans 14) and should not judge one another for it; but each of us must draw them.

Where Christians differ: separation. Some interpret separation as withdrawing from all association with the world, or even from other Christians who associate with unbelievers. This commentary’s view: Separation here means refusing to take part in idolatry and sin, not physical withdrawal from the world (John 17:15; 1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Christians are to be in the world but not of it. Separating from other true believers over secondary matters is not what Paul teaches; he calls for separation from false worship and from those who teach a false gospel (Galatians 1:8–9; Romans 16:17).

parallels.desc: depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing

verseByVerse.quote: and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord Almighty promises to be a Father to all who belong to him, and to treat them as his own sons and daughters. This is where the argument about yokes has been going: Paul reminds them whom they belong to, and what they would be giving up.

A father to you. The chain of quotations ends with the greatest, from 2 Samuel 7:14. David wanted to build God a house; God turned it round and promised to build David one, and of David’s son he said, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son.” It was the founding promise of David’s royal line, standing behind every king of Judah and finally behind the Messiah himself. Paul hands it to Gentiles in a port city across the Aegean, and to all believers.

Sons and daughters. One deliberate alteration: where 2 Samuel says “a son”, Paul writes “sons and daughters”, echoing Isaiah 43:6. The promise to one royal heir has become a promise to a family, and the family includes women, equal heirs, in a world where inheritance ran through sons. In Christ, a slave woman in Corinth stands in the sentence spoken over the throne of David.

The Lord Almighty. Pantokratōr, ruler of all, often the Greek for “the LORD of hosts”, and the contrast with “father” is deliberate. A father who is not almighty can love you and be unable to help; an almighty God who is not a father can help and have no particular interest in doing so. Here is one Person who is both.

How can that be? The Son to whom the promise properly belonged shared his inheritance. He is the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29), and everyone joined to him shares his standing as a son. They are adopted (Galatians 4:5–7), and in Roman law an adopted child took a new father, a new name and the full rights of an heir. The believer is not a servant allowed in the kitchen but a child at the table: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1).

Called Abba by the weakest. The Lord of hosts has taken the promise he made to a king and given it to fishermen and slaves and idolaters who came in late, and he calls them sons and daughters, and he means it. The Son of David, the only Son by right, stood under the Father’s wrath so that we might stand under the Father’s smile. The Ruler of all, who calls the stars by name, bends down to be called Abba by the weakest of his children. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will never be anything less than a Father to us.

What it does not mean. Adoption is not earned by separation; it is God’s gracious gift, which calls us to holy living. Nor is it undone when our separation falls short, as it always does: the Son who was perfectly holy in our place keeps us in the family (Romans 5:19; Hebrews 2:11).

My earthly father was absent or cruel. How can I relate to God as Father? Slowly, honestly, and by letting God define the word rather than your memories. Your father showed you what a father should not be; God shows you what a father is. He is never absent (Hebrews 13:5), never cruel, never fickle; he disciplines only in love and for your good (Hebrews 12:10); he gave his own Son for you. You may need to tell him plainly that the word is hard for you; he will not be offended. Read how Jesus speaks of the Father (Luke 15:11–32; Matthew 6:25–33). Over time the true Father heals what the false one wounded, and the church can be part of that, as older believers become fathers and mothers in the faith to you.

parallels.desc: I will be to him a father
bring my sons and my daughters

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain.<sup>2</sup>For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.<sup>3</sup>We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,<sup>4</sup>but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities,<sup>5</sup>beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;<sup>6</sup>by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love;<sup>7</sup>by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;<sup>8</sup>through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true;<sup>9</sup>as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;<sup>10</sup>as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.<sup>11</sup>We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open.<sup>12</sup>You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.<sup>13</sup>In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.<sup>14</sup>Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?<sup>15</sup>What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?<sup>16</sup>What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.<sup>17</sup>Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,<sup>18</sup>and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

keyVerse.quote: Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain.
keyVerse.note: Every part of the chapter answers this appeal. Paul’s own life shows grace that has not been received in vain, bearing fruit in endurance, Christlike character and a heart wide open to others; and the Corinthians’ narrowed hearts and flirtation with idols show how grace can lie idle. The urgency comes from the next verse: the day of salvation promised to Christ is now, and it is offered to us.

6.reflection:
Paul warns against receiving the grace of God “in vain” (v. 1). What has God given you, forgiveness, comfort, his word, gifts to use, that you are in danger of sitting on? What would one step of obedience in that place look like this week?

Paul commends his ministry by endurance, character and paradoxes rather than results (vv. 4–10). How does this change the way we judge pastors, churches and our own service? Which of the paradoxes in verses 8–10 do you most need to believe about your own life?

Paul tells the Corinthians, “our heart is wide open”, and “you are restricted in your own affections” (vv. 11–12). Where has your heart narrowed towards another believer, and what would it mean to widen it without pretending the hurt did not happen?

Verses 14–18 call believers to separate from idols, yet Jesus prayed that we would not be taken out of the world (John 17:15). Where does the line between the temple of God and the world run through your own life, and how does the promise “I will be a father to you” make that separation a joy rather than a loss?

7.title: Godly Grief and the Joy of Reconciliation
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 closes Paul’s defence of his ministry (2:14–7:4) with a call to holiness and an appeal for open hearts, then resumes the story broken off at 2:13: his restless wait in Macedonia and the arrival of Titus.

The message. The God who has promised to live among his people is making them clean and comforting the downcast, often through a hard word spoken in love. Grief that turns to God leads to repentance and salvation and is never regretted; grief that stays with the self leads to death. Where it has done its work, God gives comfort, joy and love restored.

Why it was said. After the painful visit Paul had sent a letter written with tears (see the introduction), then waited for weeks not knowing whether it had won the church back or lost it; some still suspected him of using them (v. 2). Titus has brought the answer, and Paul wants the Corinthians to see what God has done in them, so that the matter is closed before he turns to the collection (chapters 8–9) and the rivals still at work (chapters 10–13).

How the chapter makes its case. Verse 1 draws the conclusion from God’s promises in 6:16–18: cleanse yourselves, body and spirit. In verses 2–4 Paul opens his heart: he has wronged no one, accuses no one, and is theirs to die and to live. Verses 5–7 tell the story: fighting outside, fear inside, then God comforting him through Titus and news of the church’s longing and zeal. Verses 8–12 explain the painful letter: Paul’s passing regret, godly and worldly grief, the marks of real repentance, and the letter’s aim of showing them their own hearts before God. Verses 13–16 end in joy and complete confidence.

Where it leads. Every promise behind verse 1 has its Yes in Christ, who came to live among us and made us sons and daughters. The God who comforts the downcast is seen most fully in the Son who was “lowly in heart”, troubled in soul before the cross, and who came to us in person. And the chapter’s deepest contrast, Judas’s remorse and Peter’s tears, is finally a portrait of the Saviour who prayed for Peter, looked at him and went looking for him.

For us. Test your sorrow over sin by where it is going, not how loud it is. Say the hard thing when love requires it, and wait for God to use it. Be a Titus to someone who is downcast. And keep hoping for difficult people and difficult churches, because God finishes what he begins.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has promised to live among his people as their Father, they are to clear out of their lives everything that defiles, in body and in spirit.

Since we have these promises. These are the promises just quoted: God will live among his people and be a father to them (6:16–18). The command is their consequence, not their condition. Read the other way round, holiness becomes a test we can never be sure we have passed; as Paul wrote it, holiness is what a person does because the house is already occupied. God did not wait for the house to be clean before moving in; he moved in and began to clean it, paying for every stain with the blood of his Son.

Beloved. Paul drops the word into the middle of a command, one of only two places in this letter where he uses it (the other is 12:19). From someone who does not love you, a command to holiness is a burden; from a father who does, it is an invitation to become what you already are.

Let us cleanse ourselves. Paul includes himself; an apostle does not instruct from higher ground. And cleansing is something a Christian actively does, though earlier chapters spoke of what God does in us. Both are true: we do the cleansing, by the Spirit who lives in the house (Romans 8:13).

Body and spirit. “Defilement” (molysmos) is a stain that clings. Corinth knew defilement of the body well: sexual sin, idol feasts, drunkenness. Religious people forget defilement of the spirit, the sin that leaves no mark on the body: settled contempt, an appetite for other people’s failures, the private rehearsal of grievances, false worship held in the mind. A man can keep his body clean and be filthy where nobody can see, and Paul will not let the two be separated.

Bringing holiness to completion. “Bringing to completion” (epiteleō) means carrying through to the end. This is sanctification: not the once-for-all verdict that declares a sinner right with God (justification), but the slow change by which God makes a forgiven person actually holy, more like Christ (3:18). Our best cleansing is never spotless; God accepts it for the sake of Christ, whose perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19; 1 Peter 2:5). But a Christian ought to be able to name something he is further on with than five years ago. And it is done in the fear of God: not the terror of a God who might reject you, but the awe of someone who knows who is living in the house.

Every promise is Yes in him. All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ (1:20). God said he would dwell among his people; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and by his Spirit he makes believers his temple (6:16). God said he would have sons and daughters; he sent his Son, so that we might receive adoption as sons (Galatians 4:4–5). The house is occupied because Christ opened the door, at the cost of his own body.

What it does not mean. Not that a Christian who still finds defilement in himself has never been cleansed. The blood of Christ has cleansed his guilt once for all (Hebrews 10:14); what he is doing now is clearing out of the house the things that do not belong in it.

What does cleansing myself actually look like? Specific removals, not general resolutions. Name the defilement plainly before God and confess it (1 John 1:9). Cut off its supply: the website, the habit, the friendship that always ends in gossip, the late evening alone with nothing to do. Put something in its place, because an empty house soon fills again (Matthew 12:43–45): Scripture, prayer, the company of believers, work for others. Tell a trusted Christian friend if the sin is stubborn. And keep at it: the work is still in progress.

Does this verse mean I must cut off my unbelieving friends? No. Being unequally yoked (6:14) means a binding partnership that pulls you from Christ, such as marriage to an unbeliever or a venture that demands compromise. To avoid all contact with unbelievers you would have to leave the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10), and Jesus was called the friend of sinners. Keep your friendships, for Christ’s sake; cut off whatever defiles, including any friendship in which you are being drawn into sin rather than drawing your friend toward the Saviour.

Where Christians differ: who does the cleansing? Some say sanctification is entirely God’s work, with believers passive, waiting to be carried along; others speak as though it is entirely up to our effort. This commentary’s view: Paul calls believers to cleanse themselves, yet it is God who sanctifies by his Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Sanctification is God’s work in which we actively cooperate: we work out what God works in (Philippians 2:12–13; the Westminster Confession 13.1, 3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.1, 3). It is never complete in this life; perfect holiness comes at glorification, when we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–16 — Godly Grief, Worldly Grief, and Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When sin is faced with godly grief, God turns a strained relationship into comfort and joy. Paul asks again for a place in the Corinthians’ hearts, denying the charges against him without accusing them (vv. 2–4). He resumes the story from 2:13: in his fear God comforted him through Titus and the news of the church’s longing and zeal (vv. 5–7). He explains why the painful letter was worth the pain: it produced the grief that leads to repentance, not the worldly grief that leads to death, and he names the marks of the true kind (vv. 8–12). He ends in the joy of Titus, refreshed by them, and in complete confidence (vv. 13–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Worldly grief can look like repentance: tears, distress, self-accusation. What matters is whether the grief turns toward Christ (see the note on vv. 9–10, where Judas and Peter are set side by side).
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is found to have been dishonest with money for years. He weeps and says how devastated he is: by the damage to his reputation, the pain to his family, the end of his ministry. He never speaks of the harm done to those he took from, or of the offence against God. His fellow elders see real grief, pointed in the wrong direction. Genuine repentance asks different questions: not “What have I lost?” but “Against whom have I sinned, and what must I do to put it right?”

verseByVerse.quote: Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks the Corinthians to open their hearts to him again: he has wronged none of them, and he says so not to accuse them but because he is theirs in life and in death.

Make room in your hearts for us. Paul picks up where he left off at 6:13. “Make room” (chōreō) means to give space: their affection had shrunk into a cramped corner, and he asks for the room back.

We have wronged no one. Three denials answer charges actually being made: no one treated unjustly (adikeō); no one ruined (phtheirō), perhaps the charge that his teaching led people astray; no one exploited (pleonekteō), the charge that the collection was a scheme, which he answers again at 12:17–18. He offers no evidence: some accusations deserve only a plain contradiction and a life that goes on being what it is (6:3–10).

I do not say this to condemn you. Forced to deny that he is a fraud, his first concern is that they should not feel accused by the denial. Anyone who has suffered a false rumour knows how rare that is: once you finally get to speak, the natural motion is to make somebody pay. Paul closes that door before it opens.

To die together and to live together. This is why he can be generous. It is covenant language, like Ruth’s pledge to Naomi and the bond David and Jonathan swore before the LORD (Ruth 1:16–17; 1 Samuel 20:42): there is no circumstance in which Paul stops being theirs, not if they believe the rumours, not if they never apologise. Where we would say live and die, he puts dying first, for this fellowship has already been through death: people who died with Christ and now live in him (5:14–15). That rebukes how easily Christian relationships are abandoned, over the music in church, a careless comment, a family inheritance. To people cool toward him for months, Paul offers a commitment with no exit clause.

A heart with no exit clause. Only one man has ever been able to make Paul’s three denials without exception. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22), and he was charged with everything. He who alone had the right to condemn came not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17), and he loved his own to the end (John 13:1), knowing that Peter was about to deny him. Nothing in all creation can shut us out of that heart (Romans 8:38–39).

When I am falsely accused, should I defend myself? Sometimes, briefly and plainly, as Paul does here, especially when the accusation damages the gospel or others rely on your trustworthiness. Say what is true, without heat or counter-accusation, and leave it. Do not chase every rumour; you will never catch them all, and the effort will sour you. Let your conduct over years answer what words cannot (1 Peter 2:12, 15), and hand the matter to the Lord, who judges justly, as Christ did when he was reviled and did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). And watch your heart: aim to win the accuser back, not to defeat him.

verseByVerse.quote: I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul speaks to the Corinthians with complete openness and pride, because the news about them has filled him with comfort and with a joy that overflows in the middle of affliction. So ends the defence of his ministry that began at 2:14.

Great boldness; great pride. Frankness (parrēsia): a guarded heart produces guarded speech, an open one says what it means. And literally, much boasting about you. After the factions, the immorality and the cold year, Paul tells them how he speaks of them when they are not in the room: he brags.

Filled with comfort. Comfort is the theme word of the letter (1:3–7), and here it is an accomplished fact: the man who despaired of life itself (1:8) is filled.

Overflowing with joy. Not after the affliction, and not merely in spite of it: in it. Hyperperisseuomai means to run over the top. His circumstances are no safer; something else has been poured in: news that people he loved had turned the right way. What filled him was not health, safety or reputation, but the spiritual good of others. Joy that hangs on circumstances will be up and down for life; joy fastened to what God is doing in people is tied to a work God has promised to finish.

Overflowing through Christ. As we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (1:5). On the night before the cross Jesus spoke of his own joy and wanted it in his disciples, so that their joy might be full (John 15:11). That is the joy running over in Macedonia: not Paul’s temperament, but the joy of the crucified and risen Lord, poured into a frightened man by news that sinners Christ died for had come home. There is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10), and Paul, in a Macedonian lodging with fighting outside and fear inside, was let in on it. So are we, whenever we rejoice in what God rejoices in.

Is it honest to say I am joyful when life is hard? Yes, if the joy is real and you do not pretend the hardship away. Christian joy is not a feeling that everything is fine; it is gladness in God and his work, underneath the grief and not destroyed by it: sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (6:10). So you can say truthfully: this is very hard, and I am glad of Christ and of what he is doing. If you cannot feel joy at all just now, do not manufacture it. Ask God for it, look for what he is doing in others, and wait; joy is the Spirit’s fruit, not your performance.

In everyday life. Tell someone today that you are proud of them in the Lord, and be specific about what God has done in them.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worn out and afraid in Macedonia, Paul was comforted by God, who lifts up the downcast, through the arrival of Titus. He resumes the story broken off at 2:13, and tells it without hiding his fear.

No rest. At Troas it was his spirit that had no rest (2:13); now his body too, literally his flesh, his frail human self.

Fear within. Fighting without we expect. Fear within is the remarkable one: an apostle admitting, unqualified, to a church that already thinks him weak, that he was frightened. The man who wrote that God gave us a spirit not of fear (2 Timothy 1:7) says here that he had fears within, and the Bible keeps both sentences without apology.

But God, who comforts the downcast. Two words turn the sentence, as they turn the story in Ephesians 2:4: before them, the human situation honestly told; after them, what God does with it. The title echoes Isaiah 49:13. Tapeinos means low, brought down. Of all the titles available, Paul reaches for the one that describes what God does for people on the floor: I was down there, and this is what he is like when you are.

The coming of Titus. Not a vision, not a voice: a friend walked in the door. Most of God’s comfort arrives on two legs, with a face and a name: a visit, a meal on a doorstep, a phone call. God comforts; Titus is his means. Pray for a suffering friend, certainly; but the comfort of the downcast usually requires somebody to make the journey.

A troubled soul without sin. Jesus used the same word, lowly, of himself: “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Facing the cross he said, Now is my soul troubled (John 12:27), and in Gethsemane he was greatly distressed and sorrowful even to death (Mark 14:33–34). So fear within is no proof of unbelief: the sinless Son of God felt the full weight of dread and did not sin. And a downcast believer is never alone at the bottom; our high priest went lower than any of us will go.

He did not send explanations. The God of the Bible has a particular address, and it is the low place: he dwells in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit (Isaiah 57:15). The Son did not send explanations from heaven; he came. Every knock at the door of a downcast believer since is a small echo of that coming.

I struggle with anxiety or depression. Does that mean my faith is weak? Not necessarily. Paul was harassed, sleepless and afraid, and he was not walking in unbelief; Elijah asked to die, and the psalmists were often downcast. Anxiety and low mood have many causes: exhaustion, grief, illness, the chemistry of a body living in a fallen world, as well as sin and unbelief. Bring all of it to the God who comforts the downcast. Tell a trusted friend or your pastor, so that someone can be Titus to you. Use the ordinary means God gives, including rest, food and sleep, and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; if the doctor recommends treatment, including medication, receiving it is not a failure of faith. And do not measure God’s nearness by how you feel. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).
verseByVerse.note: Paul picks up the story he broke off in 2:13: waiting anxiously for Titus.

verseByVerse.quote: and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What comforted Paul was not only Titus’s arrival but the comfort Titus himself had found in Corinth, and his news that the church now longed for Paul, mourned its wrong and was zealous for him.

Comforted by you. Follow the comfort as it moves. God comforted the Corinthians; they comforted Titus; Titus came and comforted Paul. The chain runs as chapter 1 said it would (1:4), with God at its head. He could have comforted Paul directly; he chose not to be the only one who comforts, and so gave every ordinary Christian a share in his own work. What a Father, who will not keep even his consolations to himself, but makes his children carriers of them.

Not merely a messenger. Titus had been changed by his stay in Corinth, and the state of the man, as much as his news, lifted Paul. People rarely encourage others by transmitting facts; they do it by being visibly people to whom something good has happened.

Longing, mourning, zeal. Each is a mark of a church coming right. Longing: after months of distance, they wanted to see Paul again. Mourning: lament, the grief voiced at a death; a church that is only embarrassed moves on, but a church that mourns what it did changes. Zeal: heat, eagerness to put things right. Coldness had given way not to politeness but to warmth, and that is real restoration in a marriage, a family or a friendship too: not merely the end of hostilities, but longing, grief and warmth.

Reconciled first to God. Underneath lies the theme of the whole letter: be reconciled to God (5:20). Turned back to God, the Corinthians found their warmth flooding back toward the man who had brought them the gospel. The two travel together: people brought home to the Father through the cross find that the cold walls between them and his servants cannot stand either.

What it does not mean. Not that every problem was solved. Chapters 10 to 13 show that some opposition remained. Paul rejoices in real progress without pretending it is the finished article.

What if I have no one to comfort me, or no one comforts me well? Begin where the chain begins, with God himself, who comforts the downcast directly through his word and Spirit; the Psalms were written for exactly this. Then make yourself known. Most people are not comforted because nobody knows they need it, so ask plainly, even if it feels awkward, and give people the chance to be Titus to you. And look for someone to comfort yourself: comfort often arrives on the return journey: the person you visit frequently sends you home lighter than you came.

verseByVerse.quote: For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s painful letter hurt the Corinthians, and for a time he wished he had not sent it; now that he sees the hurt was brief and did its work, he does not regret it. This is the letter written “out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears” (2:4), sent between 1 Corinthians and this one and probably carried by Titus (see the introduction).

I do not regret it, though I did regret it. He changes his mind twice inside a single line. The letter went off; Paul spent the waiting weeks wishing he had not sent it; now, knowing the outcome, he is glad he did, and does not tidy the admission away. Anyone who has had to say a hard thing knows the sequence: you agonise, you speak, and then comes the awful silence in which you become certain you were too harsh, or too soft. That stretch is in the Bible. What ended it was not a better argument with himself but the outcome: the letter he wished unwritten was right all along.

Only for a while. The grief was real and severe, but it had an end, because it led somewhere. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6). The friend’s wound hurts and heals; the flattery feels better and leaves the thing that was killing you exactly where it was.

The Lord who writes hard letters. The risen Christ sent seven letters to seven churches, most of them wounding, and gives his reason: those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent (Revelation 3:19). Zeal and repentance are exactly what Paul’s letter produced (7:11). But Paul wished his letter back for a while; Christ has never had to wish back a word, because he sees the end of every wound he gives. And the Lord who reproves his people was pierced for their transgressions (Isaiah 53:5), so that even his hardest word to them is spoken by a Saviour.

If an apostle regretted his letter, was the letter Scripture? We do not have the severe letter, and the church never received it as part of the New Testament. Not everything an apostle wrote was given as Scripture; God preserved what he intended his people to have, and the canon he gave is complete. Paul’s passing regret does not touch what we do have: the inspired letter is the one that tells us about the regret, honestly, which is part of why we can trust it.

How do I know whether I should say the hard thing at all? Ask first: is it a real sin or harm, or only a difference of taste? Is it my place? Have I dealt with my own log first (Matthew 7:5)? Do I want this person’s good more than my own relief or vindication? Have I prayed, and if possible taken counsel? If the answers are yes, speak, gently and clearly, and leave the outcome with God. Your feelings afterwards will not tell you whether you were right; only time and fruit will.

In everyday life. If you still carry the regret of something you had to say, it is usually only evidence that you love the person and cannot yet see the end; Paul could only write this sentence because Titus came back. Pray for the person, keep the door open, and wait for God’s timing.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is glad, not that the Corinthians were hurt, but that their hurt turned them to God; for grief that turns to God leads to repentance and salvation, while grief that stays with the self leads to death.

Grieved into repenting. The grief was never the goal; it was the road. Paul rejoices in its fruit: repentance (metanoia), a turning of the mind that turns the whole life round. Anyone who enjoys the discomfort he causes in the name of correction is not doing what Paul did.

A godly grief. Literally, grief according to God: sorrow that sees sin as he sees it. The letter hurt, but did them no harm, only good. And the chain it set going (grief, repentance, salvation) is “without regret” (see “Uncertain wording” below): nobody who has come to Christ in genuine sorrow has wished he had not.

Worldly grief. The two differ not in intensity (both hurt, both produce tears) but in direction. Godly grief sees the sin as an offence against God first, and moves toward him: “Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight” (Psalm 51:4). David had wrecked several lives, yet he says “you only”, because he had seen that all sin is finally against God. Worldly grief is sorrow about consequences: embarrassment, self-pity, the pain of being caught. Entirely about the self, it leads to despair, bitterness and death. It has a religious form too: the person who punishes himself with misery, as though enough bad feeling could pay for the sin, when the only payment that counts was made at the cross.

Two men, one night. Scripture shows both within a few hours. Judas changed his mind, threw the money back into the temple, and said, I have sinned by betraying innocent blood; and he went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3–5). Remorse, confession, restitution: every visible mark is there, and it ended in death, because it never turned toward anyone. Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, went out and wept bitterly, and was restored over breakfast on a beach (Luke 22:62; John 21:15–19). Judas’s end is a warning about despair that will not turn to Christ; it is not a verdict on every believer who has died by suicide in the darkness of illness, and those who grieve such a loss may leave their loved one with the Lord who knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19).

Repentance unto life. The Westminster Shorter Catechism defines repentance unto life as a saving grace whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, does, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience (Q. 87). “Apprehension” means taking hold: at the centre stands the mercy of God in Christ, seen and grasped. Grief without hope of mercy never turns anyone; it only drives him into hiding.

Looking on the one they pierced. Zechariah foresaw a day when God’s people would look on him whom they have pierced and mourn, and a fountain would be opened to cleanse them from sin (Zechariah 12:10; 13:1), and John saw it fulfilled at the cross (John 19:37). There sin is seen at its worst and mercy at its fullest, for the wounds that show our sin are the wounds that wash it away. Worldly grief looks at itself and its losses. Godly grief looks at him, hates the sin that pierced him, and runs to the blood that washes it.

The sound of a sinner being found. The deepest difference between Judas and Peter is not in Peter at all, but in the Lord who had already prayed that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), who turned and looked at him across the courtyard (Luke 22:61), and who came looking for him on the shore. Godly grief is never a payment we offer to win God back. It is the sound of a sinner being found, and the Saviour who finds him does not stand back to measure whether the sorrow is adequate.

What it does not mean. Not that repentance earns salvation. It is the fruit of grace and the way into salvation’s blessings: God grants repentance (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25), and we do not pay for forgiveness with tears. Nor that a believer who has felt worldly grief has lost his salvation. Every Christian’s sorrow is mixed; the question is where it is taking you.

Why do so many public apologies ring hollow? Someone famous is caught, and within hours a statement appears: regret “if anyone was offended”, a promise to do better, a period of stepping back. Often it is about the one apologising: the reputation, the sponsors, the way back. That is worldly grief in a modern suit, sorrow at being exposed rather than at the wrong. But a culture without God has no other kind of apology to offer. If there is no one against whom every wrong is finally committed, contrition can only be addressed to an audience, and audiences have to be managed; and there is no one who can say at the end, “You are forgiven”. Godly grief can afford to be honest, because it is spoken to the One who already knows everything, and who has already paid for it.

What if I do not feel sorry enough? Then you are in good company, because no one’s sorrow is ever as deep as his sin deserves, and we are forgiven not because of the depth of our grief but because of the death of Christ. Paul’s test is direction, not volume. Listen to the sentences in your head: if they are mostly about how this looks and what it will cost you, that is the sorrow of the world; if they are about God, whom you have grieved and whom you need, it is godly grief, already carrying you to the cross. Are you turning to God and away from the sin? Then go on turning. Ask God to show you your sin as he sees it, read the account of the cross slowly, and let tenderness grow as you walk with him. Some of the most genuine repentance is quiet and dry-eyed, and some of the loudest is only worldly grief. Do not wait to feel enough before you come.

What about the shame I keep feeling after I have confessed? Distinguish conviction from accusation. The Spirit convicts of a specific sin to lead you to Christ, and once it is confessed he points you to the cross: it is finished. The accuser keeps a vague cloud of shame over you after forgiveness, to keep you from God. If the sin is confessed and, as far as possible, put right, the lingering shame is not godly grief. Answer it with the promise: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

Uncertain wording. In Greek, “without regret” could describe either the repentance or the salvation it leads to: a repentance never regretted, or a salvation never regretted. The word (ametamelētos) and its place in the sentence allow both, and translations differ. The sense hardly changes: neither the turning nor what it brings is ever regretted. Paul is also playing on words: he “regretted” his letter for a while (v. 8, metamelomai), but the repentance (metanoia) it produced leads where no one regrets anything.

parallels.desc: Peter’s tears and Judas’s remorse

verseByVerse.quote: For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Godly grief proves itself by what it produces, and in Corinth it produced urgency, a will to put things right, anger at the sin, fear of God, longing, zeal and action, until the church stood clear in the matter.

What earnestness. Earnestness (spoudē) is literally speed, urgency. Real repentance is in a hurry; it does not put the matter down to be dealt with when convenient.

Eagerness to clear yourselves. A defence (apologia), but not self-justification, for they had just admitted they were wrong: the desire to put right what they were rightly blamed for, so that the charge no longer stands, and to show they did not approve of the wrong.

Indignation, fear, longing, zeal. Indignation is anger at the sin and at themselves for tolerating it; repentance without any heat in it is usually just embarrassment. Fear is seriousness about God, whose name had been dishonoured, and perhaps about an apostle who might come with a rod (1 Corinthians 4:21).
