Longing is for the restoration of what was broken: sin isolates, and real repentance wants back into the room. Zeal is energy for what is right, where before there had been indifference.

What punishment! “Punishment” (ekdikēsis) means justice carried out, a wrong put right: probably the discipline by the majority of 2:6. They acted, and without action what looks like repentance changes nothing.

Innocent in the matter. “Innocent” (hagnos) means pure, clear: not that they had never been at fault, but that the fault has been dealt with. The matter is closed, and the church must treat it so: no probation, no lasting mark against their name, but a case fully shut.

A case shut at the cross. Paul can close the file because God closes his. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1); it is God who justifies, and Christ Jesus is the one who died and who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34). A repentant believer is clear because every charge against him was answered when Christ was condemned in his place. A church that keeps a forgiven man on probation in its gossip is keeping open a case the Judge of all the earth has shut, at the price of his Son.

No committee manufactured it. Only God could make a congregation that had shrugged at sin and gone cold on its founder suddenly urgent, angry at evil, reverent, longing and zealous. The Son of God was grieved at sin, burned with zeal for his Father’s house (John 2:17) and longed over Jerusalem. A repentant church is beginning to feel about sin as its Lord feels, and so to look like him.

Lay the list beside our usual repentance. We tend to be satisfied with the first minute: an apology, some distress, a request to move on. In Paul’s list the apology is not even mentioned. Hold it against your own repentance, not to see whether it was thorough enough to pay, for Christ has paid, but where the Spirit still has work to do. And if you are judging whether someone who wronged you has turned, this list is a far better guide than his tone of voice.

If someone has truly repented, must everything go back to how it was? Forgiveness, yes, fully and from the heart; the case is shut and must not be reopened in gossip or held over him. But forgiveness is not the same as restoring every position of trust at once. A treasurer who stole may be forgiven and still not handle the money again for a long while, perhaps never; an elder who fell may be restored to fellowship long before he is restored to office (1 Timothy 3:2). Real repentance accepts those consequences without resentment; eagerness to put things right is one of Paul’s marks. Where there has been abuse, protecting the vulnerable comes first: the matter must be reported to the authorities where the law requires it, and the abuser kept away from those he harmed. Forgiving him never means returning a victim to danger, and the church must never tolerate abuse under the name of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wrote the painful letter not chiefly to deal with the offender or to vindicate the one wronged, but so that the Corinthians would see for themselves, before God, how much they really cared for him.

Not for the sake of the one who did the wrong. Paul did not write mainly to punish the offender, now dealt with and forgiven (2:6–8), nor to vindicate the one who suffered the wrong, very probably himself (see “Uncertain wording” below).

Revealed to you. Not to Paul or the other churches, but to themselves, in the sight of God. Grown cold, they would have said this was simply how things stood. The letter did not create their earnestness; it brought it out where they could see it. Paul never believed they had stopped loving him; he believed the affection was buried, and wrote to dig it up, as a father would. And the One who lays us open in his sight has clothed us in his Son, so that for his people being revealed before God is no longer a terror but the discovery of grace.

How God uses tests. God often uses a situation to show his people what he has already done in them. He led Israel forty years in the wilderness, testing them to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). God already knew; it was Israel who needed to find out.

The Son who was tested for us. Deuteronomy 8 has a sequel. In the wilderness for forty days, the Son of God answered the tempter from that very chapter: man shall not live by bread alone (Matthew 4:4). Israel’s forty years revealed a heart that failed again and again; Christ’s forty days revealed a heart that never failed once, and he passed the test as our representative. For those in him, a trial is no longer a court that might condemn us, but the testing of a genuine faith, which will be found to result in praise and glory and honour at the revelation of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 1:7). What the test reveals, he put there.

How do I know what is really in my heart? Partly by watching what comes out under pressure, which does not create what is in you but reveals it. Notice how you respond when crossed, when you lose something, when standing with an attacked believer would cost you. Ask God to search you, as David did (Psalm 139:23–24), and invite honest friends to tell you what they see. And take comfort as well as warning: tests reveal grace as well as sin. You may find there is more of Christ’s work in you than you dared to think.

Uncertain wording. Paul names neither “the one who did the wrong” nor “the one who suffered the wrong”; his first readers needed no names. Some take the offender to be the man of 1 Corinthians 5, who had his father’s wife, with the father as the one wronged. The more likely reading, as at 2:5, is that during the painful visit a member of the church openly opposed and humiliated Paul, and the church failed to stand with him, so that Paul himself suffered the wrong (2:5–11). Nothing in the application depends on the identification.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is comforted, and gladder still at the joy of Titus, because the Corinthians refreshed him and proved true everything Paul had boasted about them.

Therefore we are comforted. The God of all comfort has done what he promised, and it took months, a painful visit, a letter written in tears and a friend’s long journey. God’s comfort is rarely quick. It is always sure.

The joy of Titus. What lifted Paul higher than his own comfort was watching somebody else be happy, the mark of a man who lives for the one who died and was raised for him (5:15). It can be easier to weep with those who weep than to rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15), because another’s gladness can feel like a comment on our lack; Paul simply delights in his friend.

Refreshed. “Refreshed” (anapauō) is the word Jesus used when he promised rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28). Titus had gone to Corinth expecting trouble and came away rested. Some churches send their workers away refreshed and some send them away hollow, and the difference is almost never about size or resources.

Not put to shame. Paul had bragged about the Corinthians to Titus when the evidence was thin, then had to wait to see whether he had made a fool of himself. They proved him right. His word is reliable whether spoken to them or about them, as he insisted in chapter 1 (1:18–20): telling someone the hard truth to his face and speaking well of him elsewhere are both honesty.

Believing the best goes first. Paul’s confidence went ahead of their performance, and very probably helped produce it. We usually do the reverse: approach the awkward member expecting the worst, communicate it without a word, and are proved right. Somebody has to go first in believing the best (1 Corinthians 13:7), and it had been done for Paul first, when Barnabas vouched for him and nobody else would (Acts 9:26–27).

Named before he was a rock. The first time Jesus met Simon, he gave him a new name, Cephas, a rock (John 1:42), long before Simon had shown anything rocklike, with three denials still ahead. Christ speaks of his people by what his grace will make them, and his word makes it so. Paul had to wait anxiously to see whether he would be put to shame; the Lord never waits that way, because what he says of his people he has already undertaken to do.

What is the difference between encouragement and flattery? Encouragement is true, specific and for the other person’s good, points to what God is doing in him (1 Thessalonians 1:2–3), and is said behind his back as readily as to his face. Flattery is exaggerated, vague and usually for the speaker’s benefit, puffs up the person himself, and is said mostly to his face. Praise freely, but praise what is real, name it concretely, and give God the glory. And do not withhold true praise for fear it will make someone proud; Paul was not afraid to boast of the Corinthians.

In everyday life. Ask whether you send whoever serves your church most visibly home refreshed or drained, and do one thing that refreshes him: a note, a thank you, a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Titus’s love for the Corinthians has grown as he remembers how they all obeyed and received him with reverence, and Paul ends the story with complete confidence in them.

His affection. The inner parts (splanchna), where deep feeling is felt. At 6:12 the Corinthians’ affections had become cramped; Titus’s affection is wide, and growing.

The obedience of you all. Not most of them: all. Whatever divisions ran through that congregation, on this they moved together and obeyed the apostolic instructions they had been given.

Fear and trembling. Not fear of Titus, but Paul’s standard phrase for proper seriousness before God (Philippians 2:12; Ephesians 6:5). They received Titus with reverence, taking his message as from God: what happened in that room was more than a difficult meeting with a visiting delegate. Church conflict is often handled as a matter between people only, to be managed with tact and procedure, good things which leave God out. The Corinthians handled theirs before God, and the outcome was not a settlement but a restored church.

Complete confidence. Literally, I take courage in you in everything. This is the church of the factions, the lawsuits and the drunkenness at the Lord’s table, and the chapter’s last word is confidence, preparing for chapters 8 and 9, where he will ask this same church to give generously. It is not a verdict on how good they were. Chapters 10 to 13 deal with the opposition still active among them; Paul is not naive. His confidence is of the same kind as the unshaken hope of 1:7, resting not on their record but on what God does with people he has begun with: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

Receiving the one he sent. Whoever receives the one I send receives me, Jesus said, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me (John 13:20). In receiving Titus, who carried the word of Christ, the Corinthians were receiving Christ, and their obedience was a church bowing again to its Lord. When Christ is received in his word, he brings what only he can give: a cleansed church and a refreshed servant.

He has not lost his touch. God’s faithfulness to finish is the only ground of hope for a difficult church, a difficult family, or yourself. The God who took a wrecked relationship, a humiliated apostle and a letter written in tears, and produced longing, mourning, zeal and complete confidence, has not lost his touch. He has never yet been handed a situation past mending. The Saviour who bled for the church will present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27). Every church that has broken our hearts is a church he has not stopped washing.

Does this mean I must obey my church leaders without question? No. The Corinthians obeyed the apostolic word Titus brought, the teaching that is now in Scripture, and received it as from God. We should gladly follow church leaders as they lead us in God’s word (Hebrews 13:17), but no pastor or elder may bind your conscience beyond Scripture (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2), and leaders are themselves under the word and accountable. Fear and trembling is directed toward God. If a leader demands obedience to something Scripture does not teach, or uses his position to control or harm, you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and the church must deal with him.

How can I keep hoping for a church, or a person, that keeps letting me down? By resting your hope where Paul rested his: not on their track record but on God’s faithfulness to finish what he started. Pray for them specifically. Name real progress, as Paul does, instead of only cataloguing failures. Keep speaking the truth where it is still needed, as he will in chapters 10 to 13. And remember how long God has been patient with you. Hope is not pretending things are fine; it is trusting that God has not given up, and so you will not.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.<sup>2</sup>Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one.<sup>3</sup>I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.<sup>4</sup>I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.<sup>5</sup>For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within.<sup>6</sup>But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,<sup>7</sup>and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.<sup>8</sup>For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.<sup>9</sup>As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us.<sup>10</sup>For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.<sup>11</sup>For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.<sup>12</sup>So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.<sup>13</sup>Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all.<sup>14</sup>For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.<sup>15</sup>And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling.<sup>16</sup>I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

keyVerse.quote: For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this distinction. The Corinthians’ tears were of the first kind, and everything Paul rejoices over (their longing, zeal and restored love) grew from them. The verse gives every believer a test for his own sorrow over sin: not how deep it feels, but whether it turns him to God in Christ, where a sinner finds a salvation he will never regret.

7.reflection:
Paul says holiness flows from God’s promises rather than earning them (v. 1). How does it change the fight against a particular sin to know that God already lives in you and calls you his child?

Paul admits “fear within”, and God comforted him through a friend who made the journey (vv. 5–7). Who in your life or church is downcast just now, and what would it look like for you to be Titus to them?

Read verses 9–11 alongside the stories of Judas and Peter. What are the signs that sorrow over sin is worldly rather than godly, and which of the marks in verse 11 are most often missing from our repentance?

Paul had confidence in a church that had hurt him badly (v. 16). What makes it hard to believe the best of people who have let us down, and how does God’s faithfulness to finish his work help?

8.title: The Grace of Giving: Christ Became Poor
8.overview:
Where we are. With the quarrel mended and Paul’s confidence in the church restored (7:16), chapters 8 and 9 turn to unfinished business: the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, which Corinth had begun eagerly a year before and then let stall (see the introduction).

The message. Christian giving is grace: the grace of the Lord Jesus, who though he was rich became poor for you, running on through you to others. So finish what you began, gladly and in proportion to what you have, not because an apostle commands it but because love that has received so much will want to show that it is real.

Why it was said. The collection meant more to Paul than relief. The Jerusalem leaders had asked him to remember the poor (Galatians 2:10), and a gift from Gentile churches to the Jewish mother church would show that both were one body (Romans 15:25–27). But Corinth’s zeal had cooled during the troubles, some were ready to suspect Paul of profiting from the money (12:16–18), and a proud, gifted church might easily resent being asked, or being compared with the poorer Macedonians.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul begins not with the need but with what God has done in Macedonia: churches in deep poverty and persecution that begged to give, because they had first given themselves to the Lord (vv. 1–5). He sends Titus to help Corinth finish, and asks them to excel in this grace as they excel in faith, speech and knowledge (vv. 6–7). He will not command it; instead he sets beside them the grace of Christ (vv. 8–9). Then comes practical counsel: complete what you once desired, out of what you have, for God welcomes a willing gift by its means (vv. 10–12), and the aim is a fair balance, as with the manna, where no one had too much or too little (vv. 13–15). Last, he commends the three men who will carry the gift, an arrangement made so that the money is handled honourably before God and before people (vv. 16–24).

Where it leads. Verse 9 is the heart of the chapter and one of the great sentences of the New Testament: the eternal Son, rich in the glory of heaven, became poor all the way to a borrowed grave and a forsaken cross, so that beggars might become heirs. Every other line is that sentence repeating itself in his people: the poor Macedonians making others rich, the manna shared out, and ordinary couriers called “the glory of Christ” (v. 23).

For us. This chapter will not give you a figure, but it will not let you off either. It asks whether you have given yourself to the Lord first, whether your giving matches what you once meant and what you now have, and whether money in your hands is handled in the light. Above all it sends you back to the Saviour who became poor for you. Look long enough at his grace, and the hand begins to open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Macedonian Example and Christ Who Became Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Generosity is the grace of Christ at work in his people, so Corinth should finish what it began. Paul shows that grace overflowing from the poor Macedonians, who gave themselves to the Lord before they gave their money (vv. 1–5), and urges Corinth, rich in other gifts, to excel in this one too (vv. 6–7). He will not command it, but sets beside them Christ, who became poor to make them rich (vv. 8–9). Then the practical counsel: complete it out of what you have, for a willing gift is welcomed by its means (vv. 10–12), so that, as with the manna, no one has too much or too little (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 stands with Philippians 2:5–8 and John 1:1–14 as a key text on the incarnation: the Son, without ceasing to be God, went from the riches of heaven to the poverty of the manger and the cross, so that we might become rich (each phrase is opened in the note on v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples: A church board is setting its budget and the share given to work beyond its own walls. One member argues that the church should make sure its own buildings and staff are well funded before giving generously elsewhere. This passage sets before him poor churches begging to give, and the Son of God, who did not secure his own comfort before giving himself for others. Does this budget reflect the grace of verse 9?

verseByVerse.quote: We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s grace made poor and persecuted churches overflow with joy and generosity.

In the flow. Only now, with the relationship mended (7:16), does Paul raise the collection, which seems to have stalled during the troubles; and these two chapters, the Bible’s fullest teaching on giving, invite a church reconciled to God (5:20) and to its apostle to let that grace reach the poor. Because chapters 10 to 13 answer the charge that Paul took advantage of them (12:16–18), his care here over every coin matters for the whole letter.

The grace of God given. Paul is about to ask for money, and he begins as no fundraiser would: with what God has done in Macedonia, northern Greece, in the churches of Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. The word charis, grace, runs through these two chapters ten times, and Paul never once uses the word money; he calls the gift grace, because it is Christ’s grace received and passed on to others. He is not holding up heroes to shame Corinth, but showing what God does by his Spirit there, and can do here. God is the fountain, and every overflow in his people is his own fullness running over.

A severe test. By every human reckoning they could not be expected to give. The Macedonian churches had suffered from the start: riots, a jailing, a congregation Paul had to leave by night (Acts 16:19–24; 17:5–10; 1 Thessalonians 2:14).

Extreme poverty. Literally, poverty down to the depths, the beggar’s level: nothing to spare, and every excuse in the world.

A wealth of generosity. Yet out came joy and generosity, both the language of overflow, from people with nothing to overflow with. “Generosity” is haplotēs: single-heartedness, the open hand that gives without calculating. Poverty makes people tight, and affliction makes them inward; together they produce a closed hand every time, unless something has got in underneath.

Poor, yet making many rich. What got in underneath is the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who though he was rich became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (v. 9). The Macedonians are a living copy of that sentence: out of the depths of poverty, a wealth of generosity, the very shape of the gospel, in which the one who went down to nothing made multitudes rich. Paul had described his own ministry the same way, “as poor, yet making many rich” (6:10). Wherever Christ’s grace truly lands, people made rich by his poverty begin, even in their poverty, to make others rich.

Waiting for the right season. We often have a threshold in mind before we become generous: when the mortgage is down, when the children are through school. The Macedonians never reached it.

Why does having more make us give less? You might expect generosity to rise with income. It tends to work the other way: in a series of experiments, psychologists at the University of California, Berkeley, found that people with less money often gave away a larger share of what they were given than people with more. Paul would not have been surprised. Money quietly takes over work that belongs to God, promising security, then status, and at last a kind of self, until giving it away feels like losing a piece of yourself, and every rise in income only gives you more to guard (see the note on Luke 12:15–21). Neither scolding nor guilt can loosen that grip; only a greater wealth can. The Macedonians had been made rich by someone else’s poverty, and people secure in that no longer need their money to be their saviour. So they can let it go, and find, to their surprise, that letting go is a joy.

Why were the believers in Jerusalem so poor? Several reasons came together. There had been a severe famine in the reign of Claudius, and the church in Antioch had already sent help (Acts 11:27–30). Many Jewish believers lost work, family support and standing when they confessed Jesus, some had their property seized (Hebrews 10:34), and the church cared for many widows (Acts 6:1). And the collection meant more than relief: a gift from Gentiles to the mother church of the Jews was a visible sign that Jew and Gentile were one body in Christ. As Paul wrote, “if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings” (Romans 15:27).
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 8–9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The Macedonian churches (Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea) were poor and persecuted.

verseByVerse.quote: For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Macedonians gave freely and beyond what they could afford, pleading for the privilege of sharing in the gift.

According to their means, and beyond. Every phrase removes another of the usual explanations. According to their means is proportion, the normal biblical standard; beyond their means is literally beyond power, past what they could afford. And Paul watched it happen: “as I can testify”.

Of their own accord. “Of their own accord” (authairetoi) means self-chosen. There was no appeal, no target, no pressure from an apostle; the pressure ran the other way.

Begging to give. Paul is not begging them to give; they are begging to be allowed to. It seems he had been reluctant to take a collection from destitute people, and they pressed him until he agreed. Their word for what they asked is charis again, which the ESV renders favour: they regarded being permitted to give as a privilege granted to them.

Taking part in the relief. “Taking part” is fellowship (koinōnia), and “relief” is ministry (diakonia). Money given to brothers they would never meet was fellowship with them. In many churches the offering is the awkward part of the service, because we think of giving as money leaving; the Macedonians thought of it as being let in on the work God was doing.

What makes people beg to give. Not guilt, which produces a payment and then resentment, nor obligation, which produces a calculation, but grasping what you have already been given. The Macedonians had seen the Son of God empty himself for them, and koinōnia is the word John uses for fellowship with the Father and with his Son (1 John 1:3). To give to Christ’s poor brothers was to have something in common with the one who became poor for them.

Of his own accord. Before the Macedonians begged to give, Someone far greater had freely given everything. No one would take his life from him; he would lay it down of his own accord (John 10:18), and he went to the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2). Of their own accord, Paul says of the Macedonians; of his own accord, the Saviour says of himself. Every glad giver in the church is a small likeness of him.

Does this mean Christians should give beyond what they can afford, even into debt? No. Paul reports what the Macedonians did; he does not command it (v. 8). The rule he gives is proportion: “acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (v. 12); and “I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened” (v. 13). Their example is meant to stir us, not to shame anyone into borrowing or neglecting his family (1 Timothy 5:8). Sacrifice, yes, gladly: going without some comfort so that others may have bread is what love does. But a gift paid for with a debt you cannot repay, or with your children’s needs, is not what God asks of you.

parallels.desc: the widow gave out of her poverty

verseByVerse.quote: and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The secret of the Macedonians’ giving is that they had first given themselves to the Lord. Before any money moved, they had handed over the people it belonged to.

Not as we expected. Here is the key to everything these chapters say about money. Paul was taken by surprise, and the reason was not their circumstances or temperament.

Themselves first. The real giving had already happened; the money only showed it. Giving begins with consecration, handing yourself over to God to be his and for his use: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). “First” states a sequence, which explains why teaching about money often produces so little: we address the wallet, and the wallet was never the problem. Money is what many of us quietly trust to keep us safe, and the hand will not open until the heart has found a better safety in God. A man who has not given himself to God will find good reasons not to give his money; a man who has given himself has already given everything, and what remains is working out the amounts.

Then to us. A second surrender: to Paul, the mission, the church. There is no giving yourself to God in the abstract; it lands on people, usually the nearest inconvenient ones. And Paul calls even that the will of God.

He gave himself before he gave anything. The Macedonians’ order is their Lord’s order. When Christ set out to make us rich, he did not send gifts from a safe distance; he came himself. The Son of God “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20); he “gave himself for our sins” (Galatians 1:4). His poverty was not a donation from his surplus but the giving of his own person, down to his body on the cross (v. 9). So when people who have received him give themselves first and their money second, they are not inventing a technique but answering him in kind: a self given for a self given.

The order is a comfort. Do not ask first, Am I giving enough? Ask, Have I given myself? The second cannot be answered with money at all, so the person with almost nothing is at no disadvantage. From the Macedonians God had already received what he was after: themselves.

What does it mean to give myself to the Lord? It means acknowledging that you belong to him, body, time, money, gifts and future, because he bought you (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and telling him so. It happens decisively when you first trust Christ, and is renewed again and again, often where something specific is asked of you. It sounds like a prayer: Lord, I am yours, and so is everything I hold; show me what to do with it. Then it shows itself in plain decisions: the budget, the diary, the use of your home, your willingness to serve where you are needed rather than where you are noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sends Titus back to Corinth to help the church finish the gift it had begun. Titus had started the collection there; even with so trusted a colleague, Paul asks (parakaleō) rather than orders.

This act of grace. In the Greek simply “this grace”. God’s grace came down in Christ, and the same word describes it going out again as money to strangers, just as comfort was passed on in chapter 1 (1:4) and reconciliation in chapter 5 (5:18–20).

Complete. “Complete” (epiteleō) is the verb of 7:1, bringing holiness to completion. The Corinthians had started a year earlier, and stopped. It is the ordinary shape of religious enthusiasm: the weeks pass, the sum that seemed straightforward in the meeting looks larger at the kitchen table, and the thing quietly lapses. Nobody decides against it.

A person, not a sharper paragraph. Paul’s remedy is not a rebuke but a person. He sends Titus, because good intentions do not need more motivation; they need somebody to come and help finish them.

It is finished. The God we worship finishes. His Son set his face to go to Jerusalem and on the cross cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30), and the Spirit who began a good work in us “will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6). We are a people of half-built towers, and we belong to a Lord who has never left anything of his undone.

A graveyard of good intentions. What did you begin and not finish? A commitment made at a conference, a monthly amount you meant to set up, a person you said you would visit.

Is it wrong for churches to ask for money or organise giving? No. Paul organised this collection carefully, with weekly setting aside (1 Corinthians 16:2) and men sent to gather it. Asking is right when it is honest about the need, puts Christ’s grace before the appeal, leaves people free to give willingly (9:7), and handles the money openly. What is wrong is manipulation: guilt, pressure, emotional stunts, promises that God will repay a hundredfold, or appeals that hide where the money goes. Paul asks, explains and trusts. He never squeezes.

verseByVerse.quote: But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Generosity is a grace to excel in, as much as faith, speech and knowledge. Paul honours Corinth’s real gifts, then asks it to grow in the one it had neglected.

As you excel in everything. “Excel” (perisseuō) is overflow; they were not lacking in any gift (1 Corinthians 1:5–7). Faith, speech and knowledge were what the Corinthians prized, and Paul adds their recent earnestness (7:11). He does not sneer at any of it.

This act of grace also. Then the sentence turns, and generosity is set alongside them as a grace a Christian is expected to grow in. We rarely call someone immature in giving as we might in patience; Paul does. It is possible to know your Bible, speak well, be warm toward the congregation, and give exactly what you gave ten years ago on a smaller income. “See that you excel” means make sure of it: Paul does not expect it to come by drift, and drift is precisely what had happened to the collection.

A rich church learning from a poor one. Gift, eloquence and knowledge do not produce an open hand; if anything they supply better arguments for keeping it shut.

Enriched in him. Yet the Corinthians’ riches were the fruit of Christ’s poverty: “in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:5). To excel in giving is to let the riches Christ bought for them begin to look like the one who bought them. Every gift they boasted of had been poured out by the same open-handed God “who gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5). He is not a God who excels in power and knowledge and is stingy in mercy.

Is generosity a spiritual gift only some Christians have? Paul does list giving among the gifts in Romans 12:8, and some believers are given an unusual capacity and joy in it. But here it is a grace every Christian should excel in, as every Christian is to show mercy though some have a special gift of it. So do not excuse yourself because you do not feel gifted. Grow in it the way you grow in any grace: by looking at Christ, by asking God for it, and by practising it until it becomes a joy.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read your love for us rather than our love for you; either way the bond between apostle and church is the point.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will not command the gift, but invites the Corinthians to show that their love is real. The Macedonians’ eagerness is set beside them as a touchstone, not a whip.

Not as a command. He is an apostle and could order it. He declines because a commanded gift would prove nothing and change nobody. Christian giving must be willing, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (9:7).

That your love also is genuine. “Prove” (dokimazō) is the assayer’s word: testing metal to see whether it is what it claims to be. Money is one of the most reliable tests of love, because it is hard to fake and costs exactly what it costs. Few things reveal what we value as accurately as where the money goes when nobody is watching; as the Lord put it, “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). The heart follows the treasure: where the money goes both shows and shapes what we love. Paul is confident enough in their love to let the test run.

Love that answers his. Paul’s very next word is “for”, and what follows is the grace of the Lord who became poor (v. 9). The love being tested is love kindled by his: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). His love was proved where it cost most, at the cross. And here is the deepest reason Paul names no figure: the standard beside the Corinthians is the Son of God going from riches to a manger and a cross, and that can never be matched, only answered, gladly and again and again.

What it does not mean. “Not as a command” does not mean giving is optional for Christians. It means the gift must be free if it is to be love.

Should my giving go to my local church first? Usually, yes, a regular and substantial part of it. The local church is where you are fed, shepherded and cared for, and Scripture expects those who are taught to share all good things with the one who teaches (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14); the weekly setting aside Paul taught was gathered through the churches (1 Corinthians 16:1–2). But this very collection shows that Christian giving also reaches beyond the local congregation, to needy believers and gospel work elsewhere. A wise pattern is faithful, planned giving to your church, with freedom and joy in giving beyond it as God opens your eyes.

In everyday life. If someone who did not know you read your bank statement, what would they conclude you love? Do not be crushed by the answer; let it lead you to Christ, and then plan next month’s giving deliberately, in proportion, before anything else is spent.

Where Christians differ: must a Christian give a tenth? It is the question every reader of these chapters has. Some teach that the tithe still binds believers, so that a tenth is owed to God. This commentary’s view: the New Testament nowhere commands the tithe of believers, and Paul is the proof. In two whole chapters on giving, the longest treatment of the subject in the New Testament, written to a stalled church that needed a clear standard, he never names a figure. What he gives instead is harder: proportion (according to their means, v. 3), readiness (v. 12), cheerfulness (9:7) and one supreme example (v. 9). A fixed percentage can be paid and forgotten; a proportion has to be weighed again whenever circumstances change, and it will not let you stop at ten if you could give forty. (When Jesus told the Pharisees they ought to tithe, Matthew 23:23, he was speaking to men still under the law of Moses.) Yet the tenth is a useful benchmark, and those who treat it as a starting point rather than a limit are being sensible: Abraham and Jacob gave a tenth before the law was given (Genesis 14:20; 28:22). But it must never become the number that tells a rich man he has done enough or a poor man that he has failed.

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ, rich beyond all measure, became poor for us so that we might become rich in him. The supreme motive for Christian giving is not a need but a Saviour.

You know the grace. Paul has been arguing about a collection, and in one sentence he goes to the incarnation, the ground both chapters stand on. They were told it the day they believed.

Though he was rich. The riches are real, not a figure of speech. This is the Son before Bethlehem, with “the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5), in the form of God (Philippians 2:6), through whom and for whom all things were created (Colossians 1:16). He had never in eternity known a moment of want.

He became poor. The verb is decisive and voluntary: he impoverished himself. “Became poor” (ptōcheuō) is built on the word for a beggar, one with nothing, dependent on what others put in his hand. Trace the descent. He was laid in a manger, born to a family that could afford only the two birds the law allowed the poor to offer (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8). He worked with his hands, had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), and was supported by the means of women who followed him (Luke 8:3). He rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room, and was buried in a borrowed grave. At the end soldiers divided his clothing and gambled for the seamless tunic they did not want to tear (John 19:23–24). He died stripped, owning nothing at all.

The real poverty. Beneath the material poverty lies the deeper one. On the cross he was stripped of the thing that had never been taken from him in all eternity: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). That is destitution. The one who had always had the Father’s face bore the Father’s judgment on our sin, and went without the light so that we could stand in it.

That you might become rich. Not comfortable: rich. Forgiven; justified, acquitted in God’s court and pronounced righteous on the ground of Christ’s own righteousness (Romans 4:5); adopted, taken into God’s family with the right to call him Father and a share in his inheritance (Galatians 4:4–7); indwelt by the Spirit; blessed “with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3; compare 1:18). “All things are yours,” he had already told this church (1 Corinthians 3:21). The exchange is exact and runs in both directions: his poverty for our wealth, as at 5:21 he was made sin so that we might become the righteousness of God.

He did not go back alone. He was rich, and he is rich again, at the Father’s right hand, still the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6). But he did not go back to his riches alone. He went back carrying the people he made rich, heirs of God and fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17). No language of commerce has a word for an exchange like that. Paul has only one: grace.

Why Paul does not need to command. Look at what was done for you, then at your bank account, and see whether the two can be held in the same mind. The Macedonians’ overflowing poverty is a copy of this verse, and the manna, the fairness and the honest couriers are ways of letting the riches he won move toward the poor.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s poverty promises believers material wealth. The riches are spiritual and eternal, as the prosperity gospel forgets. Paul himself, who wrote this verse, was often hungry, thirsty and poorly clothed (11:27), and called himself “poor, yet making many rich” (6:10).

If Christ became poor, is it wrong for a Christian to be wealthy? Not in itself. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and Scripture never treats having money as sin. But wealth is dangerous: it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom (Matthew 19:23), and the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). So the rich are told not to set their hopes on uncertain riches but on God, and to be generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). The question is not how much you have, but whether you hold it as Christ’s, with an open hand, and whether his poverty has made you rich toward others.

Where Christians differ: what did the Son give up? Some, holding kenotic theories (from the Greek word for emptied in Philippians 2:7), teach that the Son gave up some of his divine attributes, such as omniscience or omnipotence, when he became man. This commentary’s view: The Son did not stop being God or lose any divine attribute. He became poor by taking a human nature and the humble life and death of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine privileges for himself (Philippians 2:6–8). He remained fully God while becoming fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion, change, division or separation (the Chalcedonian Definition of AD 451; the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2). His poverty was not a loss of deity but the addition of humanity and the humiliation he willingly bore in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s counsel is that the Corinthians finish what they once eagerly wanted to do, giving out of what they have. After the summit of verse 9 he returns to practical business, with counsel, not a command (v. 8).

This benefits you. A generous person gains most from his own generosity, freed from greed, and the Lord Jesus said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). A closed hand damages the one it belongs to before it damages anyone else.

A year ago. The Corinthians were the first to begin (1 Corinthians 16:1–2), and had stalled, very probably during the troubles of chapters 1 to 7. The most powerful motive is not somebody else’s expectation but our own earlier and better intention, recalled gently: you wanted this; finish it.

Finish doing it. The whole weight is on completion: the desire and the deed should be the same size. Not great things, but that what you actually do should match what you actually meant. Many of us live with a gap there, the quietest self-deception in the Christian life. We are moved by an appeal and count the feeling itself as our response, though nothing has been given, and after some years a person can have a rich interior life of good desires and very little to show.

The one whose willing became doing. God’s desire and God’s deed have never once been different sizes: he purposed to save a people, and sent his Son; he promised a Spirit, and poured him out. And there has been one human life with no gap in it. My food, Jesus said, is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work (John 4:34), and he made the whole journey through Gethsemane to the cross, until he could say, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). Stalled Christians are mended not by a sharper resolution but by union with the one who finished, whose obedience is counted as ours where our own still falls short (Romans 5:19), and whose Spirit now works in us both to will and to work (Philippians 2:13).

Out of what you have. Here is the relief attached to the demand: not out of what you wish you had, or what the Macedonians managed, but out of what is actually in your hand, which is within reach of everyone.

What if I promised a gift I can no longer afford? Then be honest, with God and with whoever you promised. Paul’s rule is “out of what you have”, and circumstances change: a job is lost, an illness comes. Do not quietly let the promise lapse, the very drift Paul is correcting; say plainly what has changed, give what you now can, and keep the intention alive for when you are able. Where a vow can still be kept at cost, keep it (Psalm 15:4). Where it cannot be kept without neglecting your family, God does not ask it.

Uncertain wording. They began “not only to do this work but also to desire to do it”, which sounds the wrong way round. The words are clear; the reason for the order is not. Paul may mean that Corinth led the way not only in starting but even in wanting it, before others; or “desire” may mean a settled will, the deeper thing, named last as the climax. Either way verse 11 is plain: let the doing now match the wanting.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God welcomes a willing gift measured by what the giver has, not by what he lacks. This is the verse for anyone who feels his giving is too small to matter.

If the readiness is there, it is acceptable. “Readiness” (prothymia) is eagerness, a heart leaning forward: the order of verse 5 again, the heart first, then the gift. Where it is there, the gift is acceptable, well received: not tolerated or graciously overlooked, but welcomed.

According to what a person has. And there is the liberty. The measure is your actual resources: not the giving of the person beside you, whose circumstances you do not know, nor what you could have given had life gone differently. Much Christian unhappiness about money is comparison, and it runs both ways: the person of modest means feels his gift is negligible beside the one that paid for the roof, and the person with more looks at the sacrifice of someone with less and wonders whether he is doing anything at all. This verse dismantles both. Comparison usually has an audience in mind, but the God who sees in secret takes that audience away, and the pressure goes with it.

The widow’s two coins. The Lord watched large sums go into the temple treasury, and then a poor widow put in two small copper coins: out of her poverty she had put in everything she had, all she had to live on (Mark 12:43–44). That is the kindness of a God who sees the heart, who sat opposite the treasury and noticed two copper coins worth less than a penny, and counted them the largest gift of the day. And Mark sets the scene days before the cross, where the one watching would himself give everything he had for people with nothing to offer him.

I have almost no money; what can I give? Give what you have, however small, gladly; this verse says it is welcomed. And money is only one of the things in your hand. Give your time, skills, home, prayers, and presence with the lonely and the sick. Peter had no silver or gold, and gave what he had (Acts 3:6). The widow who prays faithfully for missionaries every night is investing in the same work as the rich man who funds them. God does not ask you for what you do not have; he asks for a willing heart and what is actually in your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The aim is not to burden one church in order to relieve another, but a fair balance in which one church’s plenty meets another’s need. Today Corinth helps Jerusalem; another day it may be the other way round.

Eased and burdened. Paul heads off a suspicion, perhaps one already voiced in Corinth: he is not proposing that Corinth be squeezed so that Jerusalem can relax.

Fairness. Equality, an even balance (isotēs), the word that opens and closes the sentence. The aim is that no believer lacks the necessities while others have plenty, and no more than that: not that all Christians hold the same amount, nor that anyone compel a transfer. Every element of this collection is voluntary.

At the present time. Abundance is surplus, over and above need, and “at the present time” shows that this is a picture of one moment. Corinth had more and Jerusalem less, but neither was guaranteed in five years, and one day others may help Corinth. So the picture is not redistribution but circulation: a body in which resources move to wherever the lack currently is.

What came out of Jerusalem first. The circulation had already begun in the other direction. Gentiles in Corinth were rich in Christ because Jewish believers had first carried him to them (Romans 15:27). A church that has received that much has every reason to send back bread.

The radical assumption. Paul takes it for granted that a Gentile church in Greece is responsible for Jewish believers in Judea whom they have never met, will never meet, and who differ from them in language, diet, culture and temperament. There is no natural bond at all, only Christ, and Paul treats that as sufficient. It is easy to feel that money raised here should stay here, where the needs are visible. But if the church is one body, a need in another part of it is not somebody else’s problem being brought to our attention. It is our need, currently being felt somewhere else.

In everyday life. Look at what is genuinely over and above your need. Ask your church whether any member is quietly going without, or which believers elsewhere, persecuted or poor, you could help. Then share it, this month, not some day.

Should I help unbelievers in need, or only fellow Christians? Both, with a particular care for believers. Paul’s rule is: “as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:10). A church that neglects its own poor while giving elsewhere has its order wrong (1 Timothy 5:8, 16). But Jesus’ Samaritan helped a stranger, and God sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). Christians care for the hungry and vulnerable around them because their Father is kind to all, and such mercy often opens a door for the gospel.

Where Christians differ: Christian sharing and economics. Some use this passage to support enforced redistribution of wealth by the state. Others ignore it. This commentary’s view: Paul is speaking of voluntary giving within the body of Christ, not compulsory state action (v. 8; 9:7). He does not call for absolute equality of possessions, but for generous sharing so that no believer lacks basic needs. Christians remain owners of their goods as stewards, but are called to deep generosity, especially to fellow believers (Acts 4:32–35; Galatians 6:10; 1 John 3:17). Christians may disagree on public policy, but they cannot neglect personal generosity.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As God gave manna so that everyone had enough, so now he provides for his people through their sharing. Paul settles the argument with a sentence about breakfast in a desert.

As it is written. In Exodus 16 God sends bread every morning, with instructions to gather an omer a person and keep none of it till morning (Exodus 16:16, 19): “whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack” (Exodus 16:18).

Picture the camp. Some men were strong and fast; some were old, or ill, or slowed by small children. They came back with different amounts in their jars, and when it was measured, everyone had exactly enough. Nobody starved because he was weak, and nobody got ahead because he was quick, and the church is meant to look like that camp. In Exodus God did it by a miracle; in Corinth, through the offering.

Manna keeps badly. There is a sharper point too: the man who gathered much never owned the surplus. If he tried to keep it, as some did, it bred worms and stank by morning (Exodus 16:20). Manna was given daily, for use, and rotted the moment it was treated as property. We think of surplus as margin, security, a reward for gathering faster. Paul, quoting Moses, says the surplus in your jar this morning may have somebody else’s name on it, and that God arranged the imbalance so that his people would become the means of each other’s supply.

The true bread from heaven. Jesus read the manna story as pointing to him: his Father gives the true bread from heaven, and “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:32–35). In Christ every believer, quick or slow, strong or frail, receives the same portion, the whole of Christ, and no one has anything over to boast of. So the church’s sharing of bread is not a political programme but a family likeness: people who all live on the same bread cannot let one another go hungry.

Not gathered but broken. Bread came down six mornings a week for forty years, and the LORD never once failed them. Then the Bread himself came down, not to be gathered but broken: “This is my body, which is given for you” (Luke 22:19). The manna could not be stored; he cannot be exhausted, and the whole family of God, the quick and the slow, will sit down at last at the marriage supper of the Lamb with no one lacking.

Is saving for the future, or for retirement, hoarding? Not necessarily. Scripture commends the ant (Proverbs 6:6–8), Joseph, who stored grain for the famine, and the person who provides for his household (1 Timothy 5:8); leaving an inheritance is called good (Proverbs 13:22). Hoarding is keeping more and more out of fear or greed, trusting the stockpile rather than God, while needs around you go unmet. Jesus’ rich fool built bigger barns and was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16–21). So save wisely for real responsibilities, give generously as you go, and ask regularly whether your savings serve love or have become your security.

parallels.desc: whoever gathered much had nothing left over

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Titus and the Brothers; Transparency in Giving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The way a church handles money is part of its witness to the gospel. Paul thanks God for Titus, whose eagerness is God’s gift (vv. 16–17), and introduces two brothers to travel with him: one famous for the gospel and chosen by the churches, the other long tested (vv. 18–19, 22). The arrangement is deliberate, so that the gift is honourable in the sight of the Lord and of people (vv. 20–21). Such ordinary messengers are “the glory of Christ” (v. 23), so Corinth should welcome them and prove its love before the churches (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Handling ministry money with open accountability applies to every Christian church and organisation. Why Paul, whose own integrity was not in doubt, insisted on it anyway, and before any accusation was made, is set out in the note on vv. 20–21.
verseByVerse.examples: A mission agency introduces a rule that larger payments need two signatures, with an independent audit each year reported to all its members. Some staff feel this implies distrust (on why it does not, see the note on vv. 20–21).

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God for putting into Titus’s heart the same care for the Corinthians that fills his own, so that Titus goes to them gladly and freely.

Thanks be to God. The argument about money pauses, and Paul thanks God for a person: not that Titus agreed to go, but that God put the care into his heart. It is God who works in us, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

Of his own accord. Paul asked him, and Titus accepted; but he was going anyway, out of his own eagerness. The phrase is the one used of the Macedonians in verse 3: everything God does in this chapter he does through people who chose it freely. God put it in his heart, and he is going of his own accord: Titus was not moved like a piece on a board, and the eagerness was his, not for a preaching tour but for handling other people’s money in a difficult church, where he could easily be accused. Yet Someone was behind it, which is why the paragraph opens with thanks rather than congratulation. God’s work in us does not cancel our willing; it creates it.

The same care, from one heart. Paul yearned for his churches with the affection of Christ Jesus (Philippians 1:8). The same earnest care lived in Paul’s heart and in Titus’s, and both had it from the Lord who gave himself for this very church. Christ’s love for the Corinthians did not stay in heaven; it went to Corinth on his servants’ feet.

A habit worth having. When someone shows us real kindness we rightly thank them. Paul thanks God. Think of the friend who kept turning up, the older believer who prayed for you for years. Have you thanked God that they wanted to? That is accuracy about where affection comes from.

How do I know whether a desire to serve comes from God? Test it by Scripture first: God never moves anyone to do what his word forbids. Then ask whether it fits your gifts and opportunities, aims at others’ good and Christ’s glory rather than your own name, and is confirmed by mature believers who know you. Titus’s desire matched Paul’s appeal: inward desire and outward call agreed. You do not need a voice or a sign; a good desire, tested by the word and confirmed by the church, is very often God’s way of leading. Act on it, and thank him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With Titus goes a well-known preacher, chosen by the churches themselves to travel with the gift, for the Lord’s glory and to show Paul’s good faith.

Famous for the gospel. Paul does not give his name (see the box below). One of the best-known preachers around the Aegean spends months as courier and auditor, because the money must be handled properly. Nobody is too senior for the practical work.

Appointed by the churches. “Appointed” (cheirotoneō) originally meant to elect by show of hands. Several men, chosen by the givers, travel with the gift. Paul, who could honestly have said his own integrity was sufficient, arranges things so that it does not have to be taken on trust.

For the glory of the Lord. A collection carefully audited and honestly delivered is done for the glory of the Lord. That is worth saying to the treasurer, the person who counts the offering, the one who checks the invoices and is never thanked. Paul puts that work and the glory of God in the same sentence, because a church whose money is handled honestly is telling the truth about its God, and one whose money is handled loosely is telling a lie about him with every receipt.

Nobody too great for a towel. The brother learned it from his Master. Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, tied a towel round himself and washed his disciples’ feet, and said, “I have given you an example” (John 13:3–5, 15). A famous preacher carrying a collection bag for the poor is not stepping down from the gospel into administration. He is preaching it with his feet.

Does it matter if my service is never noticed or remembered? Not to God, the only audience that finally counts. This brother was famous in his day and is nameless now, yet his work stands in Scripture, and the Lord who knows the names of all the stars knows his; on the last day he will hear it spoken by the Lord of glory. Your Father sees in secret and will reward you (Matthew 6:4). Many of the most important people in your church are those you never hear about: the woman who prays, the man who fixes the boiler. Serve for Christ’s glory, not for recognition, and trust that nothing done for him is forgotten (Hebrews 6:10).

Uncertain wording. Who the famous brother was is not known. Some early writers guessed Luke; others suggest Barnabas, Silas or Apollos. The same is true of the brother of verse 22. Paul’s first readers knew them; there is no way for us to decide.
verseByVerse.note: The famous brother is unnamed; some early writers guessed Luke.

verseByVerse.quote: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul arranges the handling of the gift so that it is honest not only before God but visibly honest before people.

That no one should blame us. Some did suggest that Paul was crafty and took them in by deceit (12:16–18). So independent, church-appointed men travel with the money. And he takes the precaution before any accusation about this sum, which is the only time to do it: safeguards added after an accusation look like an admission.

In the sight of man. The principle comes from Proverbs 3:4 in the Greek Old Testament: two audiences. The first is the Lord, and it is where Christians usually stop: God sees; my conscience is clear. True, and weightier than we usually feel, for no creature is hidden from his sight, and all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Hebrews 4:13). But Paul says it is not enough. The second audience is the watching world, which cannot see motives and can judge only what it can check. With other people’s money it is not enough to be honest; you must be visibly, checkably honest, in a way that does not depend on anyone believing you.

A God with nothing to hide. Jesus could say at his trial, “I have spoken openly to the world” and “I have said nothing in secret” (John 18:20), and his enemies had to look for false witnesses (Mark 14:55–56). Openness did not spare him accusation, and it will not spare his servants, but it leaves the accuser with nothing true to say. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). In the company of his Son on earth, the thief was Judas, the man who held the moneybag (John 12:6); the Son never took a coin that was not his, and in the end gave away everything that was. A church that handles money in the light shows the world a God with nothing to hide.

When oversight feels like an insult. A man of genuine integrity can find oversight faintly insulting: the second signature, the audit, the receipts, the rule that he may not authorise his own expenses. It feels like being suspected. Paul, whose integrity nobody should have doubted, built the structure himself and volunteered for it, precisely because he was trustworthy. The reputation of a ministry is not the private property of the person carrying it; it belongs to the gospel. Money has done great damage to the church’s credibility: the ministry whose accounts nobody sees, the appeal that funded a lifestyle, the collapse that made the news and gave many a reason never to listen again. Such things often start with someone who did not think the precautions applied to him.

In everyday life. Two people count the offering; nobody handles a fund alone; the person who decides the spending is not the person who signs the payment. None of it implies distrust; all of it removes a stumbling block from the road (6:3). If you hold any money that is not your own, ask today whether someone else can see what you do with it.

How should I choose a ministry or charity to give to? Look for what Paul built here. Is the money handled by more than one person, with independent oversight and open accounts? Is the work faithful to the gospel and doing what it says it does? Are the leaders known, accountable to a church, and living modestly rather than lavishly? Does the appeal tell the truth, without pressure or promises of guaranteed return? Give first to what you know well, your own church and workers it sends, and then to others you have checked. A ministry that bristles at reasonable questions about money has answered them.

verseByVerse.quote: And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul vouches for every man who will carry the gift: a brother long tested, Titus his own partner, and the envoys sent by the churches. Then he says something astonishing about them.

Often tested. A third man, also unnamed, described only as often tested and found earnest: a reputation built slowly, in small situations, over years, in a church culture often impressed by the newly arrived and obviously able. Reliability was shown before responsibility was given. One who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10).

More earnest than ever. Titus’s good report has energised this man too. A church that comes right does not merely settle its own trouble; it energises people who have only heard about it.

Partner and fellow worker. “Partner” (koinōnos) is a colleague with a stake in the enterprise; “fellow worker” (synergos), one who labours alongside. That is what Titus is to Paul, for the Corinthians’ benefit.

Messengers of the churches. Literally apostoloi, sent ones: men formally commissioned as the churches’ delegates. They are not apostles of Christ like the Twelve and Paul, sent by the risen Lord himself, who laid the foundation once for all (Ephesians 2:20); but every church still sends and receives trusted messengers.

The glory of Christ. The last phrase, dropped in without explanation, is the largest thing in the verse. Of these couriers of a charitable fund, one unnamed, one described only as reliable, Paul says that they are the glory of Christ: not only that they bring him glory, but that they are his glory. It is the same astonishing claim as chapter 3, where the Corinthians were a letter from Christ, and chapter 4, where the treasure is in jars of clay. Christ has arranged that his glory in this world should be visible in ordinary, unnamed, tested, faithful people doing unglamorous work for churches. He is not ashamed of the arrangement; he chose it. He does not borrow glory from them; he lends his glory to them.

How can an ordinary Christian be the glory of Christ? Because the glory of Christ is seen wherever his character is reproduced, and most clearly in faithfulness that nobody applauds. When a believer keeps his word, handles money honestly, serves unnoticed and loves a difficult church, people see something of the Lord who did all those things perfectly. We are being transformed into his image from one degree of glory to another (3:18). You do not have to be gifted or famous to display him. You have to be his, and faithful in what he gives you to do.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “messengers” is literally “apostles”: men sent by the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When these men arrive, the Corinthians should show the churches that their love is real and that Paul’s confidence in them was not misplaced. After all the high teaching on grace, Christ’s poverty, readiness, proportion and transparency, it comes down to this: put something in the bag.

Proof of your love. Back to verse 8: love that cannot be demonstrated has not yet been shown to exist. By this we know love, John writes, that he laid down his life for us; and then at once: if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him (1 John 3:16–17)? The road from the cross to the collection bag is one sentence long.

Our boasting. Paul has told the Macedonians that Corinth would come through (9:2), and told Titus they were a good people (7:14). Now he tells them in writing that his reputation is attached to what they do next. I have vouched for you: that is a form of love, and it makes a demand precisely because it was given before it was earned.

Before the churches. The demonstration is public. The chapter began with Macedonia’s example held up to Corinth and ends with Corinth’s response held up to everyone. That is the ordinary way God spreads generosity, one congregation catching it from another (Hebrews 10:24).

He vouches for us still. Every church that has caught generosity from another has caught it, in the end, from a Lord who was rich and became poor for its sake. God gave proof of his love on a cross while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8), before there was anything in us to vouch for. And the Son vouches for us still, confessing as his own before his Father a people who had given him every reason to be ashamed of them (Matthew 10:32), and he is not ashamed.

Doesn’t Jesus tell us to give in secret? Yes, and both teachings stand. Jesus forbids giving in order to be seen and praised by others, sounding a trumpet before you like the hypocrites (Matthew 6:1–4). That is about motive. But the same Lord says, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father (Matthew 5:16). Paul is not asking the Corinthians to parade individual gifts; the collection was a church’s gift, and its proof was to be seen so that God would be thanked (9:12–13). So keep your own giving quiet, and let your church’s love be visible for God’s glory.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia,<sup>2</sup>for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.<sup>3</sup>For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord,<sup>4</sup>begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—<sup>5</sup>and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.<sup>6</sup>Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.<sup>7</sup>But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.<sup>8</sup>I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.<sup>9</sup>For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.<sup>10</sup>And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it.<sup>11</sup>So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.<sup>12</sup>For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.<sup>13</sup>For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness<sup>14</sup>your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.<sup>15</sup>As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”<sup>16</sup>But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you.<sup>17</sup>For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.<sup>18</sup>With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel.<sup>19</sup>And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.<sup>20</sup>We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us,<sup>21</sup>for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.<sup>22</sup>And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you.<sup>23</sup>As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.<sup>24</sup>So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.

keyVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
keyVerse.note: Every other line of the chapter hangs from this sentence. Paul refuses to command a gift (v. 8) because he has a stronger motive to offer: the Son who left the riches of heaven for a beggar’s poverty and a cross, to make us rich. The Macedonians’ joyful giving is simply this grace reproducing itself in people it has reached.

8.reflection:
The Macedonians gave out of extreme poverty because they had first given themselves to the Lord (vv. 1–5). Why must giving yourself come before giving your money, and what might it look like for you to renew that self-giving now?

Paul names no figure and gives no command, but asks for giving that is willing and in proportion to what you have (vv. 8–12). Is that standard easier or harder than a fixed rule? Which good intentions in your own giving have quietly stalled?

Read verse 9 slowly. What riches did Christ give up, and what riches has he given you? How should this verse change the way you think about your money and possessions?

Paul takes great care that the gift is handled honourably “in the sight of man” as well as before the Lord (vv. 20–21). What safeguards help a church, or a household, handle money in the light, and why does that matter for the gospel?

9.title: Sowing Generously: The Cheerful Giver
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 completes the appeal for the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (chapters 8–9), the calm stretch of the letter between Paul’s account of his ministry (chapters 1–7) and his battle with the false apostles (chapters 10–13).
