The message. Give freely and gladly, because God gives that way. A gift squeezed out by pressure is not the gift God wants; he loves a cheerful giver. Nor need anyone fear that an open hand will be left empty, for the God who gives seed to the sower keeps the generous supplied so that they can go on giving. What he grows from their giving is not riches but righteousness, thanksgiving and love between believers who have never met, and behind it all stands his own gift, too great for words.

Why it was said. Corinth had begun the collection eagerly a year before and then let it stall (see the introduction). Paul had boasted of their readiness in Macedonia, and Macedonian believers might travel with him. If nothing was ready, there would be an awkward appeal on the spot and a gift given to save face. Behind the delay may also have lain an old fear: if we give this much, will we have enough?

How the chapter makes its case. First Paul removes the pressure: the brothers go ahead so that the gift is ready and willing, a blessing and not an exaction (vv. 1–5). Then he answers the fear. What is given is sown, not lost (v. 6); the decision belongs to each heart, and God loves a cheerful giver (v. 7); God is able to make all grace abound, supplying the generous for every good work, as Psalm 112 and Isaiah 55 had already said (vv. 8–11). Last he shows what the gift will do: meet needs, overflow in thanksgiving, prove the Gentiles’ confession real, and set Jewish believers praying for Greek ones (vv. 12–14).

Where it leads. Two chapters of timetables, delegates and accounts end in an exclamation: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (v. 15). The gift is the one Paul named in 8:9, the Lord Jesus Christ, who though he was rich became poor for our sake. He is the grain of wheat that fell into the earth and died and bore much fruit (John 12:24), the spring of every cheerful gift, and no one has ever come to the end of describing him.

For us. The chapter frees us from two errors: giving under pressure, and the prosperity teaching that turns sowing into investment. Decide your giving in prayer, give it gladly, trust God to supply, and look at Christ until letting go no longer feels like loss.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Sowing and Reaping; the Cheerful Giver; the Inexpressible Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Give freely and gladly, and trust God to supply, because he has first given his Son. Paul sends the brothers ahead so that Corinth’s promised gift will be ready and willing, a blessing rather than an exaction (vv. 1–5). He then answers the fear that giving leaves us poorer: what is sown is reaped, God loves a cheerful giver, and he supplies the generous for every good work (vv. 6–11). The gift will meet needs, overflow in thanks to God, prove Corinth’s faith genuine and bind Jewish and Gentile believers together (vv. 12–14), and all of it flows from God’s inexpressible gift (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The sowing and reaping of v. 6 is not a promise of wealth, and the passage corrects that reading itself (see the note on v. 6, and on seed and bread, v. 10).

Verse 9 quotes Psalm 112:9, where giving to the poor is among the identifying marks of the man who fears the LORD (see v. 9).

“God loves a cheerful giver” (v. 7): God cares about the heart and manner of the giver, not only the amount (see the note on v. 7).
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation runs a pledge campaign with giving targets, published goals and public recognition of the top givers, all of which put social pressure on people to give. Many give generously, but the pastor wonders whether the giving is cheerful or compelled. This passage questions not the amount raised but the method: “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (v. 7; on how compulsion works in churches, see the note on v. 5). The goal is not only generous giving but cheerful givers, people who give because they have been gripped by the inexpressible gift of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hardly needs to urge Corinth to give: he has been boasting of their eagerness, and their example has already stirred Macedonia. He writes again because he has staked his word on it.

In the flow. The Greek opens with for, tying the chapter to 8:24. Some think it was once a separate note (see the introduction), but as it stands it carries the argument on and ends where chapter 8 began, with the grace of God.

Superfluous. Calling it unnecessary was a recognised courtesy, since fourteen more verses follow. Paul is not addressing a delinquent church; he takes their willingness for granted. “Ministry” is diakonia: the money is a service to the saints.

A circle of encouragement. Macedonia is northern Greece; Achaia the southern province, with Corinth its capital. In chapter 8 the Macedonians’ example was held up to stir Corinth; now we learn that Corinth’s eagerness had stirred Macedonia in the first place, and Paul has carried the news between them.

The least of these my brothers. The saints are not a charity’s clients but poor believers in Jerusalem, made holy in Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2), the Lord’s own brothers and sisters. That is why the money is a ministry. What is done for one of the least of these his brothers is done for him (Matthew 25:40), and a bag of coins for hungry saints in Judea is, in the end, a gift placed in his hands.

Carrying news. Some of Paul’s most effective work here is simply carrying news. A church convinced that serious giving is unrealistic will stay convinced if it never hears what a poorer church has just done.

What it does not mean. Paul was not manipulating them. He told neither church anything untrue: the Corinthians really had begun eagerly, and the Macedonians really had given beyond their means. He simply would not let either stay ignorant of what God was doing in the other.

Is it healthy for churches to compare themselves with one another? It depends on what the comparison is for. Comparing to feel superior or to compete for reputation is pride, and Paul condemns it a chapter later (10:12). Telling one church what God is doing in another, so that both thank God and are stirred to love and good works (Hebrews 10:24), is what Paul is doing here. The test is whether it ends in praise and fresh obedience, or in boasting and envy. Hear of other churches gladly, pray for them, learn from them, and never use them as a weapon.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was southern Greece, including Corinth; Macedonia was to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sends the brothers ahead so that his boast about Corinth proves true, and so that no one is shamed into giving when he arrives. He admits his own stake in it plainly, and the plainness is part of his honesty.

The brothers. The three men of 8:16–24, Titus among them, go because Paul has made a claim in public and does not want it found overstated. Nor were the Macedonian visitors imaginary: Acts names men from Berea and Thessalonica among Paul’s companions in Greece a few months later, very probably their churches’ delegates for this collection (Acts 20:2–4).

To say nothing of you. He names his own embarrassment first and theirs only as an aside; leading with theirs would have applied more pressure.

What he is avoiding. If nothing is gathered when he walks in with visitors, there will be an appeal on the spot, before witnesses, and every coin produced will be given to avoid a humiliation. It would look like generosity and be nothing of the kind. So Paul builds the timetable to remove the very pressure he could most easily have used. He holds every card, and arranges not to play them.

Glorified in them before they had finished. On the night before they all ran away, the Lord Jesus said to his Father, “I am glorified in them” (John 17:10). He spoke of their faithfulness while it was unfinished, and then made sure of it, praying for them, sending his Spirit and keeping them to the end (Philippians 1:6). Paul’s confidence in a church is borrowed from Christ’s confidence in his own.

Belief and structure. Paul believes in the Corinthians and still sends three men and a timetable, because good intentions need practical arrangements. The leader who believes the best about people and gives them nothing to act on has only half believed in them.

Is it wrong to make a pledge or promise to give? No. The Corinthians had promised this gift (v. 5), and Paul expected them to keep their word. A pledge freely made, after prayer and with the figures in front of you, can help you and your church to plan. What is wrong is a pledge squeezed out under pressure, or made on a wave of feeling without thought. Once you have freely promised, keep it if you can, as you would any promise (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5); if circumstances truly change, say so honestly rather than letting it quietly lapse.

verseByVerse.quote: So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul arranges everything in advance so that Corinth’s gift will be a blessing freely given, not money extracted under pressure. The same sum can be either, and the amount does not decide which.

A willing gift, not an exaction. The two words are set against each other. “Willing gift” is eulogia, a blessing: a good word spoken, and so a benefit freely given. “Exaction” is pleonexia, greed, the grasping that takes what is not freely offered (compare 2:11; 7:2). The same sum, in the same bag on the same day, is one or the other, and the difference lies only in whether it was freely given.

How compulsion works. In churches it is rarely crude. Nobody is threatened. But there is the giving made visible, the thermometer on the wall, the appeal placed at the emotional peak of a meeting, the pledge card passed along a row, the quiet awareness that the treasurer knows. All of them work, and all move the reason for giving from the heart to what the room expects. Paul builds the structure that makes freedom possible: notice, time, a decision made at home, and the apostle absent while it is made. He is not making it easier to give; he is making it possible to give freely. Before you give next, know which is true of you: I want to, or I would look bad if I did not.

Shaped like the gift it answers. Paul would risk a smaller collection to have a genuine one, because the God who owns everything does not need money on any terms, and because the collection answers a gift that was never extracted. Nobody forced the Son of God to the cross: “I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). A gift squeezed out of the Corinthians would have contradicted the gospel it was meant to celebrate. Grace given freely can only be answered freely.

Not one had to be wrung from him. The first word God spoke over human beings was a blessing (Genesis 1:28), and the Lord Jesus left the earth with lifted hands, blessing his disciples (Luke 24:50–51). The Father has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3), and not one had to be wrung from him. Blessing is simply what he is like.

How do I actually plan my giving? Sit down, with your husband or wife if you are married, with your income and commitments in front of you, and pray. Decide a proportion of what comes in that you will give regularly, first, before other spending, as the firstfruits rather than the leftovers (Proverbs 3:9), and set it up so that it happens without needing to be remembered. Keep something aside for needs that arise, so you can respond freely when God puts someone in front of you. Review it whenever your income changes, and ask whether the proportion should rise. Then give it gladly, and forget about it.

verseByVerse.quote: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Generous giving is like generous sowing: what you release is not lost but planted, and God brings a harvest from it. The harvest, as the following verses show, is not wealth.

Sowing and reaping. A farming proverb Scripture uses often (Proverbs 11:24–25; Galatians 6:7). Picture the farmer walking out in autumn with a bag of seed. The decision is painful, because the seed is food and his family could eat it. The more he keeps back, the less comes up in spring, and it never stops being hard, because the eating is now and the harvest later. Bountifully is literally with blessings, as in verse 5, and the harvest is described in what follows: grace, the means to keep giving, righteousness, thanksgiving to God, and the prayers of others (vv. 8–14).

The grain that fell into the ground. Jesus applied this same farmer’s law to himself: a grain of wheat kept back remains alone; only if it falls into the earth and dies does it bear much fruit (John 12:24), and whoever loves his life loses it (John 12:25). The Son of God was buried like seed in a garden tomb, and the harvest from that one grain is a multitude no one can number. The sowing proverb was never a money trick. It is the shape of the cross, and every gift a Christian lets go of is a small share in the pattern of the one who let go of everything.

Handle with care. This verse has been made the foundation of a cruel distortion. The prosperity teacher quotes it and stops: sow into this ministry and God will return it multiplied. Money is extracted from poor people by a promise God has not made, from a passage whose whole concern is that giving must not be extracted. Three things in the chapter take that reading apart. First, Paul names the harvest three times: the harvest of your righteousness (v. 10), enrichment in order to be generous (v. 11), and thanksgivings to God (v. 12). Second, the supply in verse 10 is seed to the sower and bread for food: provision for a farmer, not a fortune (see the note on v. 10). Third, and most decisively, the supreme example of generosity Paul has just held up became poor (8:9). If sowing bountifully guaranteed material return, the Lord Jesus himself would disprove it, and so would Paul, who knew hunger and thirst, often without food (11:27).

Will God reward me for giving? Yes, and you are allowed to want the reward. Your Father who sees in secret will reward you, said Jesus (Matthew 6:4), and he told us to lay up treasure in heaven. The rewards are real: joy now, a deeper likeness to Christ, the thanks of those helped, and treasure kept for the age to come (Luke 12:33; 1 Timothy 6:18–19). What you must not do is treat God as an investment fund, giving a hundred so that he owes you a thousand. That is not sowing; it is gambling with God’s name on it.

A friend of mine follows prosperity teaching. What should I say? Begin with what is true in it: God is generous, he does reward giving, and he cares about our needs. Then read this chapter together: what is the harvest in verses 8 to 12, and why, if giving guarantees wealth, were Jesus and Paul poor (8:9)? Read 1 Timothy 6:5–10, where Paul warns against those who imagine godliness is a means of gain. Be gentle; many drawn to this teaching are poor or desperate, and have been exploited. Point them to the riches that cannot be taken away, and help them practically if they have given away what they needed.

Where Christians differ: the prosperity gospel and seed faith. Some teach that if you give money to God, often to a particular ministry, he will return far more money to you, so that giving is an investment for personal wealth. This commentary’s view: Paul does promise that God rewards generosity. But the harvest is mainly spiritual: grace, righteousness, thanksgiving, and the means to be generous again (vv. 8, 10–11). God supplies enough for every good work, not luxury. Giving in order to get is the opposite of the cheerful, self-forgetting generosity Paul describes. Christ became poor to make us rich spiritually (8:9).

parallels.desc: one gives freely, yet grows all the richer

verseByVerse.quote: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God wants gifts decided freely in the heart and given gladly, because he loves a cheerful giver. He is after a person, not the money.

As he has decided. Each one: there is no exemption for the poor (8:2). As he has decided: proaireō, to determine beforehand. It is a personal, prayerful decision made in advance, with no fixed amount imposed, reached in private with the figures in front of you before any appeal is heard, as Paul told this church to do weekly (1 Corinthians 16:2).

Not reluctantly or under compulsion. Reluctantly is literally out of grief, with a pang: the gift made and quietly resented, a resentment that tends to surface later as a complaint about how the money is spent. Most compulsion comes from inside: what others will think, or plain guilt.

A cheerful giver. Paul adapts the Greek version of Proverbs 22:8, which says that God blesses a cheerful giver; Paul says he loves him. The word is hilaros, the source of hilarious, though it means glad rather than comic. That is startling, because it means God is not chiefly after the money; the cattle on a thousand hills are already his (Psalm 50:10). What he loves is a particular kind of person.

No wince anywhere in God’s giving. God does not merely approve of cheerful givers; he is one. He gave light and called it good, gave Adam a garden with every tree pleasant to the sight, and gave his Son, to bring many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10). There is no wince anywhere in God’s giving, and when he makes us cheerful givers he is making us like himself.

Made by contemplation. Such joy cannot be produced by trying. It comes from looking at Christ, who though he was rich, for our sake became poor (8:9): a manger, a borrowed tomb, and on the cross not even his clothes. Whoever has grasped that knows he cannot out-give him. So if giving is a duty done with a small inner wince, the answer is not to give more grimly but to look at him, as the Spirit changes us while we behold the Lord (3:18), until giving stops feeling like loss. Cheerful givers are made by contemplation, not by resolve.

I don’t feel cheerful about giving. Should I wait until I do? No. Give what you have decided, and ask God to change your heart as you do. Feelings often follow obedience, and for many gladness came only after they began giving regularly. But do not settle for grudging. Bring the reluctance to God honestly; it usually points to fear about the future or love of something else. And if you are giving out of pressure or guilt that is not from God, a manipulative appeal or a demand nobody has the right to make, you are free to decline it and give where you can give gladly.

parallels.desc: from every man whose heart moves him
the Greek Old Testament adds a line about God blessing a cheerful giver

verseByVerse.quote: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You can afford to give freely because God is able to supply all you need, and he supplies it so that you can go on doing good. The question of capacity is settled, and it is his, not yours.

All grace. The sentence is crowded with all and every: all grace, all sufficiency, all things, all times, every good work. All grace includes the material, since the subject is money, but means every kind of blessing.

All sufficiency. The word is autarkeia. To the Stoic philosophers it meant self-sufficiency: the wise man trained to need nothing from anyone, an admirable and rather cold ideal resting entirely on his own strength. Paul turns the word inside out. The Christian lacks nothing, but his sufficiency is supplied, not self-made: the freedom the Stoic wanted without the self-reliance he required. Paul wrote from prison, “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11). Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6).

Every good work. Then the purpose clause, left out when this verse is quoted on its own: not so that you may be secure, but so that you may abound in every good work. God gives to us so that he can give through us, as a farmer is kept in seed because there is more sowing to do.

The secret is a person. Paul’s contentment had a name: I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13); my grace is sufficient for you (12:9). The “all grace” of this verse is finally the Lord Jesus himself, giving out of his own fullness, grace upon grace (John 1:16), according to his riches in glory (Philippians 4:19). A man who has him can afford to open his hand.

The margin. Everyone has something beyond what he needs: money, time, a spare room, a skill. The verse says it was supplied for good works; treat it as our security and we have mistaken its purpose.

What if I give generously and then find I do not have enough? God promises sufficiency for every good work he calls you to, not freedom from all hardship; Paul knew both plenty and hunger (Philippians 4:12), and was content in both because Christ strengthened him. God also supplies through other believers; that is the point of 8:14, and you may need to receive as gladly as you once gave. And be wise: giving does not mean ignoring debts or your family’s basic needs (1 Timothy 5:8). Tell him your need plainly, and trust him; many who have given in faith testify that he has not let them down.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Giving to the poor is a mark of the godly life, and what it produces outlasts the money.

As it is written. Psalm 112 portrays the man who fears the LORD and greatly delights in his commandments: gracious, merciful and righteous, unafraid of bad news. In the middle of the portrait stands this line: open-handedness is not an optional extra for generous temperaments but an identifying feature, listed alongside faith and courage. Distributed freely is a scattering word, the farmer’s motion of verse 6: arm out, seed flung wide.

His righteousness endures forever. In the psalm it is the man’s own righteousness, his settled godly character shown in his giving, which does not fade. That is the contrast running through the chapter: the money went out and is gone, but what it produced remains.

The portrait’s original. Psalm 111 says the same words of God: his righteousness endures forever (Psalm 111:3). The righteous man of Psalm 112 reflects the righteous God of Psalm 111, who scatters his kindness over the whole earth, sending rain on fields that never thank him. And the psalm describes perfectly only one man: the one who gave to the poor until he had nothing, who gave himself to beggars like us, and whose righteousness endures for ever because it is the righteousness of God himself. Every generous believer reflects a little of him.

What survives. The savings will be spent by somebody. The house will belong to strangers. The estate will be divided and, within two generations, forgotten. The only portion that survives is the portion given away: lay up treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys (Matthew 6:20).

What it does not mean. Giving does not make us righteous before God. That righteousness is Christ’s alone, received by faith (5:21); generosity is its fruit and mark.

Should I give money to people who beg on the street? There is no single rule, and Christians who love the poor differ. Give with open hands and open eyes. Cash can help, or, where addiction is involved, feed what is destroying someone. Often the best gift is food, a hot drink, your time and your name, treating the person as made in God’s image. Local churches and ministries that know the people can often help most wisely. Whatever you decide, do not walk past with a hard heart. Look the person in the eye, and remember who became poor for you.

Uncertain wording. Who is the “he” of the quotation as Paul uses it? In Psalm 112 it is plainly the man who fears the LORD, and most interpreters take Paul the same way, applying it to the generous believer. Some think Paul means God, since verses 8 and 10 speak of God’s giving and Psalm 111:3 uses the same words of him. The Greek allows either. The context favours the believer, since verse 10 speaks of “the harvest of your righteousness”, and either way the believer’s righteousness reflects God’s own.

parallels.desc: he has distributed freely; he has given to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who gives the farmer seed and bread will keep the generous supplied, enlarge what they have to give, and grow a harvest of righteousness in them. This verse decides how verse 6 must be read.

Seed and bread. The words echo Isaiah 55:10, rain and snow giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater. Seed is for the ground; bread is for eating. Every farmer keeps them in separate sacks: eat the seed and there is no crop next year; sow the bread and the family starves this winter. The distinction is a mercy both ways. You are meant to eat: nothing here requires a Christian to give away everything and call the resulting destitution faith. And some of what you have was never meant for consumption. It is seed, and seed kept in the sack does nothing.

Multiply your seed. Not your bread. The increase is in what you have to sow: God makes a generous person more able to give, which is not what most of us would have chosen.

The harvest of your righteousness. The phrase echoes Hosea 10:12: sow for yourselves righteousness, reap steadfast love. Not the harvest of your prosperity, but righteousness: a godly life and its eternal fruit, more like the man of Psalm 112.

The whole offer. Supply, more to give, and more righteousness: enormously generous, and not what the prosperity teachers advertise (see the note on v. 6).

He fills the bag first. He supplies seed to the sower before the man walks out to the field. The seed you scatter was put in your hand, the bread you eat was put on your table, and the harvest is grown by someone else entirely. Every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights (James 1:17).

A harvest that comes through Jesus Christ. Paul prays that believers will be filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:11). The crop is not grown by willpower; it is Christ’s own life reproduced in his people by the Spirit, as branches bear the fruit of the vine (John 15:5). God is making the giver like his Son, the one man whose whole life was sown for others.

How do I tell my seed from my bread? Bread is what your household genuinely needs to live, work and meet its responsibilities, including care for children and elderly parents and modest provision for the future. Seed is what is over and above that, given you to sow. Godly people draw the line differently, but the danger nearly always runs one way: we keep reclassifying seed as bread. Has your standard of living risen with each increase in income while your giving stayed level? If so, some seed has gone into the bread sack. Decide the line in prayer, with your family, and review it regularly.

parallels.desc: seed to the sower and bread to the eater

verseByVerse.quote: You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God enriches his people so that they can be generous, and their generosity returns to him as thanksgiving.

Enriched to be generous. The sentence turns in the middle. Stop at “enriched in every way” and it sounds like a prosperity verse. But this is the third time in four verses that Paul attaches a purpose to the promise of supply (vv. 8, 10, 11); he will not let it stand alone for a single sentence. God’s blessings are given to flow through us, not to stop with us.

Thanksgiving to God. Follow the chain. God enriches the Corinthians; they give; Paul carries it; Jerusalem receives it and thanks God. The money returns to its source as worship.

Enriched in him. Paul has told this church before that in every way you were enriched in him (1 Corinthians 1:5). Their riches came through Christ, at his cost: redemption through his blood, according to the riches of his grace (Ephesians 1:7). The first wealth in view is what is already theirs in Christ; money is the smallest part of it.

A river, not a marsh. A river enriched by rain in the hills does not become a lake; it becomes a river with more water going through it, and everything downstream is better for rain that fell three counties away. Water that stops moving is not a richer river but a marsh, and it goes bad. So the New Testament is unembarrassed about God giving people more. The question is only whether the increase is passing through. Usually it is quietly absorbed, into a larger house or a better car, without a decision ever being taken, while the giving stays where it was when the income was half. The safeguard is the deliberate decision of verse 7, made again whenever circumstances change.

The river has a spring. From him and through him and to him are all things (Romans 11:36). The river has a spring: the river of the water of life, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb (Revelation 22:1). We are not the fountain, and we are not the sea. We are the riverbed, and it is a glory to be the place where his goodness passes through.

Is it wrong for a Christian to enjoy nice things? No. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and gratitude for a good meal, a holiday or a beautiful home honours the giver. Jesus went to feasts and accepted costly perfume. The danger is not enjoyment but absorption: when every increase is spent on ourselves as a matter of course, when comfort becomes something we cannot give up, or when our hope quietly moves from God to our possessions. Enjoy his gifts with thanks, hold them loosely, and make sure the river is still flowing out as well as in.

verseByVerse.quote: For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gift does more than feed the hungry: it fills Jerusalem with thanks to God, because it proves the Gentiles’ confession of the gospel real. Paul expects a bag of money to help heal the deepest division in the early church.

This service. The word is leitourgia, from which we get liturgy, used in the Greek Old Testament of the priests’ temple service. It makes giving an act of worship. Supplying needs is real, for people in Judea were hungry, and Paul never sneers at the practical. But it is the smaller half: the gift does not stop when the need is met, but overflows in many thanksgivings to God.

Approval. Literally, by the proof (dokimē) of this service: the gift proves the Corinthians’ faith real (see “Uncertain wording” below). To feel the weight of that, remember the division between Jewish believers in Jerusalem and Gentile believers in cities like Corinth. Many Jewish Christians were uneasy about a gospel without circumcision. There had been a council about it (Acts 15) and a confrontation between Peter and Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). The suspicion was mutual and serious.

Your confession of the gospel. Now picture what arrives: money gathered by Greek believers, carried hundreds of miles at real risk, for Jewish Christians they will never meet. Their confession is what every believer says aloud, that Jesus is Lord and God raised him from the dead (Romans 10:9); submission is their lives lining up under what their mouths say. The gift shows they meant it, and the Jerusalem believers, who might have doubted Paul’s converts, will conclude that God is truly at work among the nations, and praise him. Giving is evidence of genuine faith (James 2:15–17).

Contribution. Fellowship, sharing (koinōnia): the gift expresses unity with all believers, not only those in Jerusalem.

Offered through him. Why may a collection be called priestly service? Because there is a priest. Christ gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2), once for all. What believers bring now is never a payment for sin but a thank offering, spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5), acceptable not because the sum is large but because it is brought by people who belong to his Son. Yet the God who receives it is the holy God who refused blind and lame offerings (Malachi 1:8, 10). We come gladly, but never casually.

What argument cannot do. Paul had argued for Gentile inclusion at length, and arguments do not dissolve suspicion. Sacrificial generosity does: it is very hard to go on doubting the faith of people who have gone without so that you could eat. Christ has made Jew and Gentile one, reconciling both to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:16), and the bag of Greek coins carried up to Jerusalem was a small, glittering proof that the wall had really come down. The same holds in every division a church knows, between generations or congregations wary of one another for reasons half real and half inherited. Suspicion is rarely argued away. It is dissolved by someone being unmistakably and expensively kind.

In everyday life. Think of believers you find it hard to trust or understand: another tradition, another generation, another church in your town. Do something unmistakably kind for them this week, at some cost to yourself.

Isn’t the best giving simply the most efficient? Many thoughtful people now think so. The philosopher Peter Singer argued that if you would spoil your clothes to save a child drowning in front of you, distance cannot excuse you from saving a child dying far away, and a whole movement now asks donors to calculate where each pound does most good. Paul would agree in part: he wanted real need met, and arranged the gift’s handling with care (8:20–21). But his collection was hardly efficient. It travelled hundreds of miles, at risk, to one church among many poor ones, because it was doing more than moving money: binding strangers together, proving faith real, and turning need into thanksgiving to God. And if God gave by efficiency alone, he would never have spent his Son on people like us. We were not a sound investment. We were loved, and grace gives like that.

If my giving proves my faith, how do I know I have given enough to be saved? You never give in order to be saved, and no amount could do it. Christ alone saves, and his gift was complete before you gave a penny (Ephesians 2:8–9). The gift is proof as fruit is proof that a tree is alive: the fruit does not make the tree live; it shows that it does. So if your giving looks thin, do not try to buy back your assurance with a larger gift. Go back to Christ, rest in what he has done, and ask him to make his grace overflow in you. Generosity grows best in people who are sure they are loved, not in people trying to earn it.

Is giving really part of worship, and should the offering be part of the service? Yes. Paul calls it leitourgia, and elsewhere calls a gift a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Philippians 4:18); such sacrifices are pleasing to God (Hebrews 13:16). Whether the offering is taken in the service or by other means is a matter of wisdom; what matters is that giving is worship offered to God, not a fee or a slot between the songs. However you give, give as you pray: to him, with thanks.

Uncertain wording. Verse 13 is compressed in Greek, literally: through the proof of this service, glorifying God for the submission of your confession to the gospel of Christ and the generosity of the fellowship towards them and towards all. The ESV takes the proof as the Jerusalem believers’ approving test of the gift (“by their approval”); many translations take it as the proof the gift itself gives of the Corinthians’ faith. The submission of your confession most likely means the obedience that goes with what they confess, and “all others” may mean other churches or believers everywhere. The overall sense is clear either way: the gift shows Corinth’s faith to be genuine, and Jerusalem praises God for it.

verseByVerse.quote: while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last fruit of the gift is love and prayer: believers in Jerusalem will long for the Corinthians and pray for them, because they see God’s grace at work in them.

They long for you. A strong word, yearning, an ache of affection, from Jewish believers in Jerusalem toward Greek strangers in Corinth: the two groups whose relationship was the great unresolved strain in the early church. Paul expects the outcome of a collection to be homesickness for one another.

And pray for you. The people who received the money will spend themselves on the people who sent it. A gift received rightly creates a debt of love, which most naturally repays itself in prayer.

The surpassing grace of God. The reason for their longing is not your generosity but the grace of God upon you. The Jerusalem believers look straight past the Corinthians to God, and grace in these chapters has a face: the Lord who became poor for their sake (8:9). That separates Christian giving from mere philanthropy. Philanthropy leaves people impressed with the giver, which is why the names go on the buildings. Grace leaves people looking at God, and the giver drops out of view, as a jar of clay should, so that the treasure is seen (4:7).

That they may all be one. On the night before he died Christ prayed for all who would believe, “that they may all be one” (John 17:21). When believers who have never met long for one another and pray for one another, that prayer of the Son is being answered.

What a sum of money did. It fed the hungry, produced thanksgiving, proved a doubted gospel, and set one suspicious community praying by name for another. When giving feels like a standing order with nothing visibly happening, remember that most of its effects occur where the giver cannot see them.

How can I build real bonds with believers in another culture or country? Give to them, and then get to know them. Support a missionary or a church abroad, ask for their news, and pray for them by name. Welcome international students and immigrant believers into your home. If you can, visit, to learn rather than to impress. Receive from them too: their prayers, their example, their insight into Scripture. Love grows along the channels where gifts and prayers flow both ways, as Paul hoped it would between Jerusalem and Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends two chapters on money by thanking God for the gift behind every gift, a gift too great for words. He breaks off, as though he has looked up from the ledger and seen something.

In the flow. The section that opened with the grace of God given to the Macedonians (8:1) ends with thanks for God’s gift, so that every instruction about money sits inside grace. It is also the last calm word before the storm of chapters 10 to 13.

His inexpressible gift. Indescribable (anekdiēgētos): a gift that cannot be told to the end. It is not vague; it is so definite and so large that words run out before the gift does.

What the gift is. Paul has already named it, and both chapters stand on it: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (8:9). The gift is Christ himself, God’s Son, given for us. “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16). “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). That makes this the proper end of everything Paul has said about generosity. All the practical counsel of these chapters is useful, and none of it is the engine. The engine is that God gave his Son.

Stop and try. Begin anywhere. The Word who was with God and was God, laid in a manger. The hands that made the world learning a trade. The one who had never been refused anything being refused a bed, a hearing, a friend. Follow it to the garden, the whipping post, the nails, the darkness at noon, and the cry of a Son who had never been out of his Father’s sight. Then the morning, the stone rolled away, and the wounds still in his hands so that they could be touched. Now add what it purchased: a debt cancelled that could never have been paid; enemies made sons and daughters; the Spirit of God living in ordinary people; a righteousness not our own credited to us; a resurrection body; a new heaven and a new earth; and, at the end of it, his face. Nobody has ever finished that sentence. The apostles did not, the church has been trying for two thousand years, and those who see him will spend eternity discovering how much of it they had not yet understood.

Every gift flows from this one. The Father gave the Son. The Son gave himself. The Spirit gives him to us. Every other gift in these chapters, the Macedonians’ coins, Titus’s eagerness, the prayers of Jerusalem, flows from that one as streams from a spring. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing (Revelation 5:12).

How do I thank God for a gift I cannot even describe? Start where Paul does, with plain words: thanks be to God. You do not need eloquence; you need to look at Christ and say thank you, often and specifically. Name one part of the gift each day: his birth, his cross, his rising, your forgiveness, his Spirit in you, the face you will see. Sing it with the church; the hymns exist because one voice is not enough. Let your giving, your forgiving and your patience be thank yous too. And do not be troubled that your thanks always falls short. That is what inexpressible means, and eternity is long enough to go on trying.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints,<sup>2</sup>for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.<sup>3</sup>But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be.<sup>4</sup>Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.<sup>5</sup>So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.<sup>6</sup>The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.<sup>7</sup>Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.<sup>8</sup>And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.<sup>9</sup>As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”<sup>10</sup>He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.<sup>11</sup>You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.<sup>12</sup>For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God.<sup>13</sup>By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,<sup>14</sup>while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.<sup>15</sup>Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

keyVerse.quote: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this promise. It answers the fear that stops people giving, since God, not our reserves, is the source of supply, and it names the purpose of his supply: not our security but every good work. It also guards against the prosperity reading of verse 6, because what God promises is enough to keep giving, and the “all grace” behind it is finally his inexpressible gift (v. 15).

9.reflection:
Paul arranges the collection so that no one gives under pressure (vv. 3–5). Where have you felt pressure to give, in a church or elsewhere, and what would it look like to decide your giving freely, before God, in advance?

Verses 6–11 name the harvest of generous giving three times: righteousness, more generosity and thanksgiving to God. How does this answer both the fear that giving will leave us short and the prosperity teaching that giving will make us rich?

Using the picture of seed and bread (v. 10), what in your life is bread to be eaten with thanks, and what might be seed that has quietly been moved into the bread sack?

Paul ends with thanks for God’s inexpressible gift (v. 15). Take a few minutes as a group to name parts of that gift. How does looking at Christ’s giving make a person a cheerful giver (v. 7)?

10.title: Divine Weapons and Boasting in the Lord
10.overview:
Where we are. With chapter 10 the tone changes sharply. The warm, relieved chapters 1–9 give way to four chapters of fierce defence against the visiting teachers Paul will call “super-apostles” and “false apostles”, aimed at the part of the church still listening to them (see the introduction).

The message. Christ’s work is neither done nor measured the way the world does and measures things. Paul fights with weapons that look weak but carry God’s power, he uses his authority to build people up and not to crush them, and he refuses to rank himself by comparison with others. He works the field God gave him and waits for the only verdict that counts: the Lord’s commendation.

Why it was said. The rivals mocked Paul as bold in his letters and feeble in person, a poor speaker (v. 10), and accused him of acting from merely human motives (v. 2). They commended themselves, measured themselves against one another, and moved into a church someone else had planted. Corinth, which prized polish, presence and status, was half persuaded.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, hoping not to be severe when he comes (vv. 1–2). His warfare is not fleshly: God’s weapons pull down the fortresses of proud argument and take every thought captive to Christ, and he will deal with the defiant once the church has returned to obedience (vv. 3–6). He belongs to Christ as surely as they, his authority is for building up, and he will be the same man present as absent (vv. 7–11). He will not join their circle of comparison, but keeps to the field God assigned him, which reaches Corinth because he brought them the gospel first, and he hopes to go on beyond them (vv. 12–16). Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. The chapter begins with “the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (v. 1) and ends with “the one whom the Lord commends” (v. 18). Between them stands the Lord who could have called twelve legions of angels and went silently to a cross, who conquered by dying and builds his church with all authority in heaven and on earth. He is the pattern of Paul’s weapons, the source of his authority, the measure of every life, and the only boast that will bear the weight.

For us. Ask which weapons you reach for in a conflict, whether your authority leaves people more built up or less, whether you are the same person in a message as face to face, and whose approval you are living for. Christ’s verdict on those who are his is already spoken, and it frees us from the ruler of comparison.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Weapons of Divine Warfare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The battle for the church is fought with God’s weapons, not the world’s. Paul appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, hoping he will not need to be severe when he comes (vv. 1–2). He lives in a weak human body, but he does not fight by human methods: his weapons carry God’s power to pull down the fortresses of proud thought and bring every thought captive to Christ (vv. 3–5). He is ready to discipline the defiant, but only once the church as a whole has returned to obedience (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The “weapons of warfare” in v. 4 are the ordinary means of gospel ministry: the word preached, prayer, transformed lives, the power of the Spirit: unimpressive by worldly standards, and divinely powerful (see the note on vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples: A church in a university town hires a communications consultant to help them “win the argument” with the secular culture. The consultant advises them to lead with culturally acceptable values rather than with gospel claims. This passage questions the strategy: the weapons that take thoughts captive to Christ are not clever messaging but the gospel itself, prayer and transformed lives.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!— I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul appeals to the church in the gentleness of Christ, hoping that those who oppose him will change course so that he need not be severe when he comes. The gentleness his critics mocked as weakness is Christ’s.

A change of tone. For nine chapters Paul has been warm and relieved; from here to the end he is fighting. Some scholars think chapters 10 to 13 were a separate letter, but no manuscript lacks them or places them elsewhere (see the introduction). Most likely he turns from the majority who have come right to the minority who have not, and to the rival teachers working on them.

I, Paul, myself entreat you. The pronouns pile up (some think Paul took the pen himself), and from now on the letter is full of I where before it was largely we.

By the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Before a word of combat Paul names the character he intends to fight in. Meekness (prautēs) is the Lord’s own word, I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29): strength under control. Gentleness (epieikeia) is the forbearance of a ruler who has the right to press a charge and does not insist on its full severity. Set at the head of four chapters of self-defence, it governs how they are read.

Humble face to face. Then Paul quotes their taunt. Humble (tapeinos) is what they meant as timid: brave on paper and small in the room. His answer is not to become fierce in person; the gentleness they mistook for cowardice was deliberate, and he asks them to make the confrontation unnecessary.

According to the flesh. The charge was that Paul acted from merely human motives and methods: self-interest, manipulation, the calculations of a man protecting his position.

Force with a hand on it. Meekness is not the inability to be forceful; it is force with a hand on it. The one who models it had more than twelve legions of angels at his disposal and stood silent before Pilate (Matthew 26:53; 27:14). He had every right to come in judgment, and he came in gentleness. And his gentleness was never weakness: it held back the wrath of heaven while he bore it himself on the cross.

Bolder at a distance. The taunt lands near home, because almost everyone is bolder at a distance: the complaint made in the car is not made in the meeting, and the strong opinion typed at eleven at night would soften with a face across the table.

How can I be gentle without being a pushover? Gentleness is about how you use your strength, not whether you have convictions. Say plainly what is right, as Paul does, but choose the gentlest means that will do the job, give people time to respond, and keep your temper on a lead. Hold your ground on truth and on protecting others, and yield freely on your own preferences and rights. A pushover gives way because he is afraid; a meek man gives way because he chooses to, and stands firm because he must. Ask what the Lord Jesus, who is both lamb and lion, would do here.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 10–13 answer rival teachers at Corinth who belittled Paul.

parallels.desc: Moses was very meek

verseByVerse.quote: For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul lives an ordinary, weak human life, but he does not fight by worldly methods: his weapons carry God’s own power to pull down fortresses.

In the flesh. He picks up their word and turns it over. Yes, he walks in the flesh: he lives an ordinary human life in a weak body, a jar of clay (4:7). But living in a body is not the same as fighting by merely human methods.

Fleshly weapons. Rhetoric, reputation, credentials, charm, political leverage, the ability to out-manoeuvre: precisely the arsenal Paul’s rivals carried, and he refuses to pick it up. His weapons are the open statement of the truth (4:2), a gospel about a crucified man, prayer, righteousness (6:7; Ephesians 6:13–18), and a messenger who is plainly not the source of the power.

Divine power to destroy strongholds. Corinth sat beneath the Acrocorinth, a rock rising well over a thousand feet above the city with a fortress on top; a stronghold was not an idea to Paul’s readers but a fact on the skyline. Verse 5 says what Paul means by them: proud arguments and ideas that resist God (compare Proverbs 21:22). The power is God’s, lent to the weapons he ordained. A stronghold falling often looks like this: a man who has spent years explaining why God cannot exist hears the gospel of Christ crucified, the Spirit opens his eyes, and the wall he built comes down from the inside (4:6; Acts 16:14).

My servants would have been fighting. The Lord Jesus fought this way first. Offered all the kingdoms of the world, he answered with nothing but Scripture (Matthew 4:8–10). Before Pilate he said, If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36). He told Peter to put away the sword and healed the wounded man (Luke 22:51). The King refused every fleshly weapon, conquered by dying, and rose. Paul is fighting the way his Lord fought.

Not by might, nor by power. The fortress on the Acrocorinth is long in ruins; Paul’s weapons are still breaking walls, because their power is in the God who said, Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 4:6). He took the cross, the most shameful weapon of the empire, and by it disarmed the powers and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). The gospel of a crucified Saviour has outlasted every empire that despised it.

Do we actually believe it? It is far easier to reach for the fleshly weapons, because they work in the short term: the campaign, the polish, the political alignment, the personality who can hold a room. None is wicked in itself. But a church that has quietly swapped divinely powerful weapons for humanly impressive ones will find it has won some arguments and pulled down no strongholds. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27): a message about a crucified man from a despised province, carried by unimpressive people. That is not a handicap he works around but the chosen instrument.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should use physical force to spread the faith. That is warfare according to the flesh.

In everyday life. In your next difficulty, ask which weapons you are reaching for. If it is charm, pressure, cleverness or influence, put them down and pick up prayer, the truth spoken in love, and patient holiness.

Should Christians be involved in politics at all? Yes, as citizens, and many faithful believers serve God well in public life; Joseph and Daniel served pagan governments. Christians may vote, campaign for justice and hold office, honestly and with love for their neighbours. What this verse forbids is thinking that the kingdom of God advances by political power, or that the church’s mission is won by getting the right people elected. Laws can restrain evil; only the gospel changes hearts. Believers should not divide over policy, and no party should be confused with Christ.

Does this passage license binding demons or breaking strongholds over cities? No. The strongholds of the next verse are false ideas, not demonic territories (see “Where Christians differ” below). Our part against spiritual evil is to stand, resist and pray (James 4:7). To see a city’s strongholds fall, preach the gospel in it, pray for it, and live holy lives among its people.

Where Christians differ: what are the strongholds? Some popular teaching takes strongholds to mean territorial demons over cities, to be bound by special prayer, or demonic footholds in a believer’s life to be cast out. Those who speak this way rightly take spiritual evil seriously, and many pray with great earnestness; the question is only what this verse means. This commentary’s view: Paul defines the strongholds himself in verse 5: arguments and lofty opinions raised against the knowledge of God. The battle is for minds and hearts, fought with the truth of the gospel. Spiritual forces are real (Ephesians 6:12), but Scripture never teaches us to map or bind territorial spirits. Our weapons are the word, prayer and holy lives.
verseByVerse.note: Strongholds were fortified towers or citadels.

verseByVerse.quote: We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fortresses Paul attacks are proud ideas raised against God, and his aim is to bring every thought, set free from them, into obedience to Christ.

We destroy arguments. Now we learn what the fortress is made of. Arguments (logismoi) are reasonings, the constructions the mind builds: intellectual and moral systems that resist God.

Every lofty opinion. Literally a high thing, probably a rampart or tower: pride lifted up against God, like Babel with its top in the heavens (Genesis 11:4). These are not merely mistaken ideas but structures built to keep God at a distance. So the reasons a person gives for not believing are often genuinely held and still not the real reason: they are the wall, and the wall was built for a purpose.

Every thought captive. Two military verbs: he pulls down, and he takes prisoners. First the wall comes down, then the occupants are led out. Every thought: no area of human thinking is exempt.

The knowledge of God has a face. Why captive to Christ? Because the light of the knowledge of the glory of God is in the face of Jesus Christ (4:6), and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). To bring a thought into obedience to Christ is not to make it smaller but to bring it to the one person who is the truth (John 14:6). To be his prisoner is to be at last at home in the truth.

A programme for the whole mind. The verse is usually quoted about the private thought-life, which is legitimate but secondary. Paul is first describing his public ministry, the demolition of ideas that stand against the knowledge of God, and that makes it a vast programme for the mind, the opposite of despising learning. History, law, medicine, economics, the way you read a novel or run a business: all is territory Christ intends to hold, and the mind he conquers is not made smaller but set in order.

The rampart in your own heart. Most of us have a stronghold, a high wall decorated with reasons: the relationship we will not reconsider, the habit with an argument attached, the part of Scripture we have found a way round. It comes down by the same weapons, to the same Lord.

How do I take a thought captive in practice? Notice the thought rather than letting it run unexamined. Test it: is it what God says about himself, about Christ and about me? Then deliberately replace it with what is true, as Paul says: whatever is true, whatever is honourable, think about these things (Philippians 4:8). Take it to God in prayer, and if it returns, do the same again. An unwanted thought is not itself sin; it becomes sin when it is welcomed and fed. And where anxious or intrusive thoughts will not go, do not be ashamed to seek help from a pastor and a biblical counsellor, who will also ask for a medical check-up.

I have serious doubts about the faith. Is that rebellion against Christ? Not in itself. Doubt is often a question looking for an answer, and Christ is patient with honest questions; he showed Thomas his hands (John 20:27). Bring your doubts into the light: read, ask a mature believer, look at the evidence for the resurrection, and keep praying, even if the prayer is, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). The lofty opinion Paul tears down is different: a mind that has decided in advance that God must not be allowed to speak. Does your doubt want an answer, or an exit?

Is taking every thought captive not simply thought control? No; the difference is who does the capturing, and how. Thought control forces views on people by pressure or fear, and Paul has just renounced every such weapon (v. 4). Christ captures minds by truth: he shows them what is real, and they bow freely because at last they see. And everyone’s thoughts are already held by something, a party, an appetite, the crowd (John 8:34). The only question is which master, and only one of them is himself the truth.

Where Christians differ: how should Christians argue for the faith? Some approaches to apologetics, the reasoned defence of the faith, try to meet unbelievers on neutral ground, reasoning from shared premises toward God; others insist that the Christian must argue from Scripture’s view of the world from the start. This commentary’s view: No thought is neutral; all thinking either submits to Christ or rebels against him. Christians should reason carefully and use evidence (Acts 17:2–3; 1 Peter 3:15), but from a standpoint of submission to God’s revelation, not as if human reason were the final judge. The aim is not merely to win arguments but to bring every thought captive to Christ. Faithful Christians who love Christ equally differ over method here, and the approaches often work together in practice: Paul himself reasoned from shared ground with the Athenians (Acts 17:22–31) without ever treating human reason as the judge of God.

verseByVerse.quote: being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is ready to discipline those who persist in rebellion, but he will wait until the church as a whole has returned to obedience.

Ready to punish. The siege picture reaches its last stage, when those who submitted were distinguished from the resistance that fought on. Most of Corinth has come in; a pocket has not, and Paul is ready to exercise church discipline when he comes (13:2, 10). Why would an apostle of the gentle Christ speak of punishment at all? Because the church belongs to a holy God, who disciplines his children for their good, that they may share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). Sin left alone in a congregation is an offence in his house.

When your obedience is complete. But not before. First the church as a whole must return; then Paul can deal with the troublemakers with the church on his side. Acting too early would drive the undecided into the wrong camp. All through the letter he has given them room and time (1:23; 2:3). That is not avoidance. Avoidance hopes the problem will dissolve; Paul says plainly in advance that he intends to act, which is itself a mercy. Timing is most of the skill: a confrontation that would split a congregation in March can sometimes be handled quietly in September, once it is no longer a contest between factions.

Obedience to whom. Paul frames the whole affair not as loyalty to himself but as obedience to Christ, the Lord he is under too (1:24). That keeps discipline from becoming a power struggle, the first thing lost when a leader feels opposition as a personal injury. The question is never whether they are with me, but whether they are obeying Christ.

I gave her time to repent. The risen Christ deals with his churches the same way. Of a false teacher in Thyatira he says, I gave her time to repent (Revelation 2:20–21): time first, then judgment, a patience that is real and a warning that is meant. He walks among the lampstands now, never hasty and never careless. And the Lord who will punish every disobedience has already borne the punishment for every disobedience of his people on the cross. His justice and his mercy meet, and neither is ever late.

What it does not mean. Paul does not want to punish; he wants obedience, and discipline is a last resort. Nor does patience mean delay where someone is in danger: where there is abuse or a threat to the vulnerable, protection cannot wait for a better season.

In everyday life. If you have authority in a home or a church and trouble is brewing, ask God for wisdom about timing before you act. And ask him to make your own obedience complete. In this life it never will be; Christ’s already is, and it is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and his Spirit is at work in you to bring yours on.

Does church discipline still happen today, and what is it for? It should, though many churches neglect it. Jesus laid down the steps: go privately, then with one or two others, then tell it to the church, and only if the person still refuses to listen, treat him as an outsider (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul applied it in Corinth (1 Corinthians 5). It aims at the sinner’s restoration, the church’s purity, the protection of others and Christ’s honour, never revenge or pride. It is for serious, unrepented sin, handled humbly, with the door always open to return (2:6–8). A church that never disciplines is not kinder; it simply leaves people to their sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Only the Lord’s approval counts, so Paul refuses to measure himself by his rivals’ standards. He belongs to Christ as truly as they do, and his authority was given to build up, not to tear down (vv. 7–8). Whatever they say of his presence, he is the same man in person as in his letters (vv. 9–11). He will not join their circle of mutual comparison, but keeps to the field God assigned him, which includes Corinth, since he brought them the gospel, and he hopes to go beyond them (vv. 12–16). Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord, whose commendation is the only one that matters (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The Lord’s commendation (v. 18) is the basis of all true authority in ministry. The super-apostles rested theirs on letters of recommendation (3:1), an impressive presence, skill in speaking, and visions and revelations (12:1). Paul rested his on God’s call (Galatians 1:1), the fruit of his ministry (the changed Corinthians, 3:2), and finally the Lord’s own assessment. This does not mean Paul simply vouched for himself; it means that whether he is a true apostle is decided by the Lord, not by human opinion.
verseByVerse.examples: A minister with a large platform cultivates an online presence that constantly showcases his ministry’s results: attendance figures, conversion stories, speaking engagements, endorsements from well-known figures. He tells himself he is building credibility for the gospel. This passage asks whether he is building the gospel’s credibility or his own, and whether his confidence rests on the Lord’s assessment or on numbers that compare him with other people.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul belongs to Christ as fully as his rivals do, and the authority the Lord gave him exists to build the church up, not to tear it down.

Look at what is before your eyes. Blunt and slightly weary: the plain facts are in front of them, if they will look (see “Uncertain wording” below).

If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s. The rivals evidently claimed to belong to Christ in some special way, perhaps through links with Jerusalem or through visions. Paul does not deny it; whatever they are, he is too. It is a very controlled answer: the meekness of Christ in operation.

Belonging by purchase. To be Christ’s is not to hold a credential or a vision, but to be owned: you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Every believer belongs to Christ in exactly the same way, bought with the same blood, which is why Paul can answer so calmly. Nobody can be more Christ’s than another, and nobody needs a special experience to prove it (1 Corinthians 3:22–23).

For building you up. A key sentence about authority in the church. It is real, and Paul does not apologise for it. It is given, not seized, so it is held on someone else’s terms. And it has a stated purpose and limit: construction, not demolition (13:10). After four verses of siege warfare the irony is deliberate: the demolition is aimed at the strongholds, never at the people. He tears down arguments to build up the person who was living behind them.

I will not be ashamed. His claim will be shown true, and he is content to let the Lord who gave the authority judge how it was used.

All authority, used to build. All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to the Lord Jesus (Matthew 28:18), and he uses every ounce of it to build: I will build my church (Matthew 16:18). He tore down the dividing wall and broke the bars of death, all to build a house for God out of living stones. The one with all authority came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

A simple test. Any elder, parent, employer or husband can apply it: after you have exercised authority, is the other person more built up or less? You may have been entirely right and still used the truth as a wrecking ball. A man who uses his authority to destroy is no longer exercising the authority Christ gave; he is exercising something else and using Christ’s name for it.

What if a church leader is using his authority to destroy people? Then he has stepped outside the authority Christ gave, and it must not be tolerated. Do not stay silent out of misplaced loyalty. Speak to him if it is safe, then to the other elders or the wider church or denomination, taking a witness (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Where there is abuse of any kind, protect the vulnerable first and report it to the proper authorities; spiritual authority never overrides the law or the safety of the weak. Leaders are to shepherd willingly, not domineering over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:2–3). If a church will not deal with it, you are free to leave and find a faithful one.

Uncertain wording. The Greek verb in “Look at what is before your eyes” can be a command (so the ESV), a statement (you are looking at outward appearances) or a question (are you looking only at the surface?). As a command, it tells them to face the plain facts, including his founding of their church; as a statement or question, it rebukes them for judging by appearance (5:12). Either way, what is in front of them, rightly seen, shows that Paul belongs to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s critics said his letters were strong but his presence weak and his speaking contemptible, and Paul lets the taunt stand, because the power of his ministry never lay in his presence. Nor will he have his letters taken as threats from a safe distance.

Weighty and strong. He quotes his critics in their own cruel words. They praise the letters only to make the insult about his presence land harder. The letters are still read today, in more languages than his enemies ever heard of.

Bodily presence. He was evidently unimpressive to look at: perhaps small, worn, marked by beatings. A second-century writing outside the Bible describes him as short, balding and bow-legged; it cannot be verified. His speech of no account: literally despised, in a Greek city where public speaking was the highest art. Paul had told them himself that he came in weakness and fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:1–4), and the charge stung because it was partly true (11:6).

Crucified in weakness. Paul’s deepest answer comes near the end of the letter: Christ was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God, and we too are weak in him (13:4). The weakness the critics despised was the message, written on his body: the death of Jesus carried about, so that the life of Jesus might also be shown (4:10). The Corinthians wanted a man who looked like power and were shown a man who looked like the cross. Paul’s Lord had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2): the glory of God came in a body nobody would have picked out of a crowd, and finished his work on a cross where they mocked him as weak.

For the unimpressive. Some people are simply not impressive in the way a room rewards. The voice is wrong, the manner awkward, the right sentence comes in the car afterwards. They have concluded that God uses other people. Perhaps the most fruitful missionary in the church’s history was despised as a speaker. God did not correct the assessment. He went on using the man, because the treasure was never the jar (4:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not speak well. Acts shows him as a powerful speaker before crowds, councils and kings. He refused the showy techniques the Corinthians admired.

Should churches not want gifted, attractive speakers? Gifts are good, and a preacher should work hard to speak clearly and well; Apollos was eloquent and a blessing (Acts 18:24–28). The danger is making polish the measure. Choose and judge preachers first by faithfulness to Scripture, godliness of life and love for people (1 Timothy 3:1–7; 2 Timothy 4:2). A plain man who opens the Bible faithfully will feed a church for decades; a brilliant one who does not will starve it while it applauds. And listen to sermons for the word of God in them, not for the performance.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized impressive physical presence and polished oratory.

verseByVerse.quote: Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will be the same man in person as in his letters: as firm in action as in writing, and as gentle.

Let such a person understand. The address is singular and slightly cold: probably the ringleader, addressed without being named, which is both a courtesy and a warning.

The same man. The charge was a gap between the written Paul and the present Paul. He promises not more force but consistency, which is a larger claim. The letters have been gentle as well as firm: he has begged, wept and appealed by the meekness of Christ, and all of that will be true in the room as well. He is not warning them that a harsher man is coming; the same man is coming.

Always Yes in him. Paul met this charge before, over his travel plans, and his answer then shows where his consistency comes from: the Son of God was not Yes and No; in him it is always Yes (1:19–20). A man who preaches a Christ with no double-dealing cannot afford to be two men himself; his integrity is borrowed from the faithfulness of his Lord. What Jesus said to the crowds he said to the Pharisees; what he was on the mountain he was in the boat and on the cross. The Word became flesh, and the flesh was exactly what the Word had said.

Two people. Modern life has multiplied this failure. Almost everyone is now two people, the one who writes and the one who is present, typing what would never be said to a face. The respectable version runs the other way: warm and agreeable in person and quietly devastating about the same person elsewhere, a different man in each room. Integrity means undividedness, being one person. The man who is the same in the letter and in the room can be believed the first time, every time, and no ministry or marriage lasts long without that foundation.

I have already written something I would never say to the person’s face. What now? Go back and put it right. If it was untrue, unkind or exaggerated, delete it where you can and apologise, to the person and to anyone else who read it, without excuses. If it was true but should have been said in person, go and say it in person, gently. If it was about someone rather than to them, stop the conversation it started. Then set a rule for next time: write nothing about anyone that you would not be content for them to read with you sitting beside them. Confession and repair are the way back to being one person.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will not rank himself among those who commend themselves, because people who measure themselves by one another are foolish: their ruler never touches the true standard.

Not that we dare. Heavy irony; everyone reading heard the smile in it. What is wrong with his rivals is not first their doctrine but their measuring system.

Measuring by one another. They are both the ruler and the thing being measured. Nothing outside enters the calculation, so the result is always satisfactory: a closed circle of mutual admiration, and, Paul says, without understanding, because it guarantees you will never learn anything true about yourself.

The measure of the stature of Christ. Paul names the true ruler elsewhere: the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13).
