Beside it every comparison collapses, because nobody comes out ahead of him and everybody comes out needing him. And grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Ephesians 4:7), so to resent another believer’s portion is to quarrel with Christ’s distribution.

Everyone kneels at the same height. The Lord Jesus did not come to rank us but to save us. The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other men, or even like the tax collector, who would not lift his eyes and begged for mercy; and it was the tax collector who went home justified (Luke 18:11–14). Before this Saviour there is no top rung to reach and no bottom rung to fear, only a cross where everyone kneels at the same height.

How comparison works. Comparison is the water most people swim in. You do not compare yourself with everyone; you select, unconsciously, a group near enough to be relevant and arranged so that you come out somewhere acceptable. Either you come out ahead and are pleased at being better than someone rather than at anything real, or you come out behind and something corrosive begins: feeling small, resenting someone who has done you no harm. Neither tells you a single true thing about yourself. A generation ago a person compared himself with the families in his street; now he does it several times a day with the edited lives of the most photogenic people on earth, and feels a failure at something he was never in a contest about.

How do I actually stop comparing myself with others? You cannot simply stop; you have to change the ruler. Measure yourself by Christ, which humbles and frees you at once. Remember that your field is assigned by God (vv. 13–14), so another person’s gifts and results are not a verdict on yours. When comparison starts, turn it into prayer: thank God for the other person’s gifts, and ask for faithfulness in your own task. Limit what feeds it, which for many means less scrolling. And rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15); it is the surest cure for envy.

verseByVerse.quote: But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will measure his work only by the field God assigned him, and Corinth lies within it, since he was the first to bring them the gospel.

The field God assigned. Area of influence (kanōn) is probably the plot marked out with a measuring rod (see “Uncertain wording” below). God gave Paul the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9); he did not pick Corinth from a list. He was given a plot, and intends to be assessed on that plot and nowhere else.

The first to come. Corinth is within that field; Paul is not claiming territory that is not his. He came on from Athens, worked at a bench with Aquila and Priscilla, and stayed eighteen months, founding the church (Acts 18:1–11). The rivals came later, to a church already standing.

The work you gave me to do. The Son of God himself kept to an assigned field: sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24), within a small land, leaving the nations to the apostles he would send. And he could say, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). Faithfulness to the given field is the shape of the Saviour’s own obedience.

The size of your field. If God assigns the field, its size is neither your achievement nor your failure; each will be judged by what he did with what he was given. The small congregation is not a lesser version of the large one. The years given to caring for one dependent relative are not wasted years in which a career failed to happen.

A restraint as well as a comfort. Knowing your boundary markers frees you from needing a view on every controversy or feeling guilty about every good work you are not doing. Many an exhausted Christian is failing at nine things because he was only ever given three.

How do I know what field God has assigned me? Look at what he has already put in your hands: your family, your church, your work, your neighbours, the needs you can actually meet. Ask what you are uniquely placed to do. Listen to mature believers who know you, and pay attention to open doors (1 Corinthians 16:9). Begin there, faithfully, rather than longing for someone else’s field. If God enlarges it later, he will make it plain; for now, the plot you are standing on is the one he gave you.

Uncertain wording. Kanōn can mean a measuring rod, a rule or standard, or the area measured out, and it is not certain whether Paul means the territory God allotted him or the standard by which God measures his work. The ESV’s “area of influence” takes the first, which suits the talk of reaching and going beyond in verses 14–16. Either way the point stands: Paul accepts only the measure God set, and Corinth falls within it.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will not take credit for other men’s work; he hopes that as Corinth’s faith grows, it will release him to preach where Christ has not yet been named.

The labors of others. The rivals had come to a church somebody else planted and taken the credit, like a man moving a boundary stone in the night (Deuteronomy 19:14) and then showing visitors round a field he never cleared. The problem is not only ancient. A man arrives at a work built over thirty years by someone tired and unfashionable, makes some improvements, and lets it be understood that things really began when he came. It is rarely a lie, only a matter of emphasis, and the person who did the clearing cannot say anything.

As your faith increases. Paul does not ask for a larger field. He asks that their faith grow, and expects his scope to be enlarged as a result, because a strong church releases its workers instead of absorbing them. That is the right way round; the usual shape of ambition is a man wanting a bigger platform and hoping his people will supply it.

Lands beyond you. He wants Corinth strong so that he can leave; they are a base, not his destination. He tells the Romans he means to go on to Spain, making it his ambition to preach the gospel not where Christ has already been named (Romans 15:20–24, 28). The rivals travelled to places where the church was already gathered; Paul travelled to places where nobody had heard of Jesus. Both were travelling; only one was taking the gospel further.

Other sheep I must bring. I have other sheep that are not of this fold, Jesus said; I must bring them also (John 10:16). Paul would speak only of what Christ had accomplished through him (Romans 15:18). The pioneer is not clearing a way for Christ but following a Shepherd who is already calling his sheep by name where nobody has yet heard the name of Jesus. The lands beyond are not an afterthought; they are the Father’s gift to his Son.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only pioneer work matters. Others water what pioneers plant (1 Corinthians 3:6), and Paul is glad of Apollos. It means no one should take credit for another man’s planting. Ask of any ambition in ministry: does it want a share of what already exists, or the gospel to reach somewhere it has not been?

How does faith increase? Not by trying harder to feel certain. Faith grows the way it began, by looking at its object: “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). The more clearly you see Christ, the more you trust him. So sit under the Word preached and read it yourself, asking what it shows you of him. Bring him your doubts in prayer, as the father did: “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Come to the Lord’s Supper, where he gives himself to be received again. And step out on his promises in small things, because trust that is used grows stronger. Above all, it is his work before it is yours. Jesus is “the founder and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2), and he has never yet let go of a weak believer.

What are the lands beyond for an ordinary Christian today? Thousands of people groups still have little or no access to the gospel, and many neighbourhoods near you hardly know a believer. Every Christian can help the gospel move outward. Pray for unreached peoples by name, give to those going where Christ is not known, welcome people from other nations, and consider whether God might send you. And begin with the lands beyond your own circle: the colleague, the neighbour, the family member who has never heard the gospel explained.
verseByVerse.note: Paul hoped to go on to Rome and Spain.

verseByVerse.quote: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only boast worth making is in the Lord, and the only approval that counts is his.

Boast in the Lord. The chapter ends where the argument has been going, with a quotation Paul had already used in his first letter (1 Corinthians 1:31). It comes from Jeremiah, and he expects his readers to hear the whole: let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practises steadfast love, justice and righteousness in the earth (Jeremiah 9:23–24). All legitimate boasting is in what the Lord is and has done.

Move the object. Brains, strength and money are still what people boast of. Jeremiah does not tell us to stop boasting, for we are built to admire and to say so, but to change its object to the Lord. The religious heart has a fourth it rarely notices, its own goodness, and that cannot bear the weight either, because our best deeds are like a polluted garment (Isaiah 64:6), and the only righteousness worth boasting of is the one Christ gives (Philippians 3:9).

Approved. Approved (dokimos) is the metal-tester’s word again (8:8): tested and found genuine. A man can commend himself brilliantly and be worthless, or be despised as a speaker and dismissed by the church he founded, and be approved.

Whom the Lord commends. It is the Lord who judges me; then each one will receive his commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:4–5). If your sense of yourself rests on the room’s assessment, this verse takes it away; if it rests on his, every unfair verdict on you is provisional.

Wisdom, might and riches in one Lord. When Paul first quoted this line to Corinth, he had just said that Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:30–31). Jeremiah’s three objects of pride are all found in him: he is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the riches of the poor (8:9). Boasting in the Lord is pointing at Jesus Christ and saying that everything worth mentioning in my life is in him.

The only opinion left standing. The commendation Paul is waiting for has already been secured, and not by him. He is approved because he is in Christ, who was made sin for him (5:21). The Father has said of his Son, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased, and in Christ that pleasure rests on us. When everything now being compared has been forgotten, the only opinion left standing will be his.

In the flow. This explains the strange boasting that follows: in chapter 11 Paul will speak as a fool, and when he boasts at last, it will be of his weaknesses, where Christ’s power rests (11:30; 12:9).

Is it wrong to accept praise, or to list my achievements in a job application? No. Receive praise with a simple thank you and give the glory to God in your heart; refusing all thanks can be its own pride. Stating your experience truthfully on a CV is not boasting in the sinful sense; it is honest information. What Paul condemns is self-commendation as a way of life: inflating your record, needing others to be impressed, measuring your worth by what people say. Tell the truth about what you have done, never exaggerate it, and keep reminding yourself who gave you every gift you have (1 Corinthians 4:7).

But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.<sup>13</sup>But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you.<sup>14</sup>For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you.
