But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged,<sup>16</sup>so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.<sup>17</sup>“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”<sup>18</sup>For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

keyVerse.quote: For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter is a quarrel about how a servant of Christ should be measured. Paul’s rivals measured by presence, eloquence and comparison with one another; Paul hands the measuring rod back to the Lord, whose verdict alone stands. That frees him to fight with weapons the world despises and to wait for a commendation already secured for him in Christ.

10.reflection:
Paul begins his defence by appealing “by the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (v. 1). What is the difference between meekness and weakness, and where do you find it hardest to be gentle without giving way on what matters?

Verses 3–5 contrast fleshly weapons with weapons of divine power. Which worldly weapons are churches and Christians most tempted to rely on today, and what would it look like for you to put them down in a conflict you face?

Paul says his authority was given “for building you up and not for destroying you” (v. 8). Think of the authority you hold at home, at work or in church. How might you tell whether the people under it are being built up?

Verse 12 calls measuring ourselves by one another foolish. Where does comparison most affect you, and how does knowing that the Lord’s commendation is the one that counts (v. 18) set you free from it?

11.title: The Fool's Speech and the Catalogue of Suffering
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 stands in the last movement of the letter (chapters 10–13), where Paul turns from the repentant majority to the rival teachers still courting the church. Having said that the only boast worth making is in the Lord (10:17), he now boasts, as a fool.

The message. The church belongs to Christ alone, like a bride promised to one husband, and a true servant of Christ is known not by pedigree, polish or fees but by the marks of the cross: he gives himself away, suffers for the gospel and carries the churches on his heart. If anything is to be boasted of, it is weakness, because that is where the power of Christ is seen.

Why it was said. Visiting preachers had impressed the Corinthians with their credentials and eloquence, lived on the church’s money and treated it roughly, while sneering at Paul as an amateur speaker, suspect for refusing payment (see the introduction). The church could no longer tell the apostle from the impostors, and was listening to “another Jesus”.

How the chapter makes its case. His motive is godly jealousy for a bride betrothed to Christ, who may be seduced as Eve was by a counterfeit Jesus, Spirit and gospel (vv. 1–4). He concedes his plain speech but not his knowledge (vv. 5–6), defends his free preaching as love rather than contempt (vv. 7–12), and unmasks his rivals as false apostles, disguised as Satan disguises himself (vv. 13–15). In the fool’s speech proper he shames a church that tolerates leaders who enslave and strike it (vv. 16–21), matches the rivals’ pedigree (v. 22), and outdoes them as a servant of Christ, not in achievements but in floggings, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger and the daily weight of care for the churches (vv. 23–29). He ends by boasting of weakness, with a basket let down from the wall of Damascus (vv. 30–33).

Where it leads. Every line points past Paul to his Lord: the Bridegroom who gave himself for his bride, the Son who humbled himself so that others might be exalted, the Servant who gave his face to those who struck him and was betrayed by one who ate his bread. The crucified One is the measure of every ministry, and every counterfeit offers a Jesus without wounds.

For us. We still admire what Corinth admired, and still mistake confidence for authority. This chapter teaches us to test teachers by the Jesus they preach and the shape of their lives, to guard a simple devotion to Christ, and to stop hiding the weakness in which he is pleased to be strong.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Jealousy for the Corinthians and the False Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church belongs to Christ alone, and Paul would rather look foolish than watch her be seduced away. His motive is a godly jealousy for a bride promised to one Husband, and his fear is that clever deceivers will do what the serpent did to Eve, offering another Jesus, another Spirit and another gospel (vv. 1–4). He concedes his plain speech but not his knowledge (vv. 5–6), and shows that preaching free of charge was love, not contempt, and the one thing his rivals could not copy (vv. 7–12). Then he names them: false apostles, disguised as their master disguises himself, whose end will match their deeds (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Calling the false apostles servants of Satan (v. 15) raises the question of how to recognise them, since they come disguised. The letter supplies the tests, and they are set out in the note on v. 4.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation is attracted to a visiting teacher who is eloquent, radiantly confident, and preaches a message of spiritual empowerment, prosperity and supernatural experience, all framed in Christian language. The pastor cannot point to an obviously heretical statement. This passage gives him the test: not whether Jesus is mentioned but which Jesus, which spirit, which gospel (v. 4; on the angel-of-light disguise, see vv. 13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will risk looking foolish because he is guarding the church for Christ, like a friend charged with keeping a bride faithful until her wedding. His jealousy is not wounded pride but God’s own jealousy for a people promised to one Husband.

A little foolishness. Paul is about to do something he finds distasteful, and he apologises before he starts. “Foolishness” (aphrosynē) is his name for boasting about himself, speaking “not as the Lord would” (v. 17). “Do bear with me!” is a father who would rather not raise his voice, asking his children to let him say something hard.

A divine jealousy. In ordinary speech jealousy is a vice, yet Scripture says that God is jealous. The difference lies in what is guarded. Envy wants what belongs to someone else; this jealousy guards what already belongs to you and is being taken. A husband who feels nothing when his wife is being drawn away does not love her more than a jealous man, but less. So the LORD, whose name is Jealous (Exodus 34:14), promised an unfaithful people: I will betroth you to me for ever (Hosea 2:19–20).

Since I betrothed you to one husband. A Jewish betrothal was not a modern engagement. It was legally binding and could be ended only by divorce, though the wedding, and the bride’s move to her husband’s home, came later. Paul promised the Corinthians to Christ when they first believed, and acts as the friend of the bridegroom, who in Jewish custom helped arrange the match, watched over the bride through the betrothal and finally presented her to the husband. John the Baptist described himself the same way: his whole joy was to hear the bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29). Paul is not the husband, but he is answerable for the bride until the day arrives.

A pure virgin. At Christ’s return, the wedding day, the church will be presented to him (Revelation 19:7–9). A pure bride is not a church with no sinners in it, for none exists, but one whose love and trust belong to Christ alone and whose teaching has not been mixed with another gospel (v. 4): a heart kept for one Husband and from every idol (1 John 5:21).

The Husband who paid the bride-price. The wedding is Christ’s idea from first to last; Paul only made the introduction. Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, to make her holy, so that he might present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). The bride-price was his own blood. He chose her while she was still unlovely, and he is coming for her. On the day she is handed over she will be without spot or wrinkle, not because she kept herself so, but because he washed her, and he will look at her and be satisfied. That is why Paul’s jealousy is not fussiness: the bride being courted in Corinth belongs to a Husband who died for her, and Paul cannot bear to see her flirt with another Jesus.

Is jealousy ever right for me? Yes, when it guards something that truly belongs to you and to God, and is aimed at the danger rather than the person: a husband or wife when a third person is drawing one of them away, a parent when a child is pulled toward something destructive, a pastor for his people. But test it. Godly jealousy wants the other person’s good and faithfulness to Christ; sinful jealousy wants control, suspects without cause and resents another’s good gifts. The first speaks openly and prays; the second spies, sulks and punishes, and is not God’s jealousy, whatever it calls itself.

Is the church the bride, or am I? Both, in the right order. The bride in Scripture is the whole church, the one people Christ loved and gave himself for (Ephesians 5:25). You are not a separate bride in a crowd of brides; you belong to her. That guards against two mistakes: thinking only of “Jesus and me” and forgetting the rest of the church, and thinking only of the church and forgetting that Christ knows each of his own by name. The faithfulness Paul is anxious about is yours too.
verseByVerse.note: In a Jewish betrothal the bride was already bound to her husband-to-be, and her purity was guarded until the wedding; Paul pictures himself in that guardian role.

parallels.desc: I will betroth you to me forever

verseByVerse.quote: But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul fears that the church will be talked out of its simple, undivided love for Christ, as the serpent talked Eve out of trusting God’s word. The danger is not an open denial but a heart quietly divided.

But I am afraid. The apostle who has just told this church he has complete confidence in them (7:16) now says he is frightened for them. A father can be sure of a child and lie awake about him in the same week.

As the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning. The serpent, whom Scripture later names as Satan (Revelation 12:9; compare v. 14), deceived Eve with clever words that twisted God’s word. His method was panourgia, craftiness: patient, plausible, working with the grain of what the hearer already half wants to believe.

How the deception worked. Everyone remembers the fruit and forgets the method. The serpent did not arrive denying God; he arrived asking a question: “Did God actually say?” He opened a small gap between what God had said and what God had meant, then offered a better reading of God’s motives, that he was holding something back. By the time he flatly contradicted God, “You will not surely die”, the ground was prepared. Error still rarely begins with a denial. It begins with a question that makes the plain word sound naive.

Sincere and pure devotion. “Led astray” means corrupted, seduced, ruined, and the danger reaches the mind through teaching. Yet what Paul fears their losing is not first their doctrine but their devotion. “Sincere” is haplotēs (as in 1:12): simplicity, being one thing rather than two. “Pure” is the chastity of a betrothed bride. The danger is a divided heart, adding something to Christ or quietly replacing him.

The Husband who did not stand by. The serpent’s strategy was to make God look stingy, and the gospel answers that slander: the God accused of withholding the fruit did not withhold his own Son. And Genesis says her husband was with her (Genesis 3:6). Adam watched his bride being talked out of God’s word and said nothing. Christ is the last Adam (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:45), and here the contrast is at its sharpest. The first husband stood by while the serpent seduced his bride; the second gave himself up for his bride to make her holy (Ephesians 5:25–26). He does not leave her alone with the serpent’s questions; he answers them, and he holds her. That is what makes the devotion Paul wants simple: the plain love of a bride for the Husband who did what Adam would not.

The love you had at first. The danger to a Christian is rarely that he will one day decide Christianity is false. It is that the plain love of Christ gets crowded, by other loyalties and by a sophistication about the faith that leaves less warmth than at the beginning. Nobody renounces anything; the devotion simply stops being single. The Lord said as much to the church at Ephesus, sound, hard-working and patient: “you have abandoned the love you had at first” (Revelation 2:4).

What it does not mean. Simple devotion is not simplistic thinking. Paul, one of the most demanding thinkers in the New Testament, means undivided loyalty: a mind that may grow as deep as it likes, so long as it stays fixed on one Lord.

Is Paul saying women are more easily deceived? Not here. Eve stands for the whole church, men and women alike, and most of its leaders in Corinth were men. The point is the method of deception and the bride’s danger, not the sex of the one deceived. Paul does draw on the order of creation and the fall when he speaks about teaching in the church (1 Timothy 2:13–14), and that passage has its own place, but it is never a licence to treat women as gullible. Adam, standing beside her, was not deceived and sinned anyway, and Scripture lays the fall at his door (Romans 5:12).

How do I keep my devotion simple? By keeping Christ himself at the centre of the means God gives, not merely the activities around him. Read the Gospels regularly, so that you know the Lord’s own face and voice and not only doctrines about him. Pray to him, not only about things. At the Lord’s Table, remember him rather than yourself. Watch what competes for the first and last thoughts of your day. And when the faith has become a complicated arrangement of opinions, projects and causes, go back to the cross. Love is kept simple by looking at the one you love.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit “and pure”, as the ESV’s footnote notes; the meaning is not affected, because both words describe the same undivided heart.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A message can keep the name of Jesus and still offer a different Jesus, a different Spirit and a different gospel, and the Corinthians were accepting it without protest. The danger lay not only in the teachers but in the church’s easy tolerance.

Another Jesus. In every case the counterfeit keeps the word. Nobody arrived in Corinth announcing a new deity; they preached Jesus: same name, different person. The rivals seem to have preached a Jesus without the cross, perhaps a triumphant wonder-worker whose servants should be impressive, or a Jesus who required law-keeping.

A different spirit. Not a second Holy Spirit; there is only one. Paul means the spirit at work in a false gospel, a spirit of pride, power and spectacle, which enslaves rather than frees (Romans 8:15; Galatians 1:6–7). The Holy Spirit produces humility and love, and delights to lift up the crucified Christ, not himself (John 16:14). So John says, “test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).

A different gospel. A message other than grace through Christ crucified; Paul told the Galatians that even an angel preaching such a thing should be accursed (Galatians 1:6–9). A gospel is different not because it uses different words, but because it tells a different story about what is wrong with us and what God has done about it.

You put up with it readily enough. Then the sting, aimed at the Corinthians rather than the teachers. Beneath the irony (you put up with them, so put up with me) lies the heart of the crisis: the tolerance is the danger. A church that would argue for an hour about the seating plan sat quietly while the identity of its Lord was adjusted.

A smaller Christ. Every counterfeit is a smaller Christ: a teacher without a cross, a wonder-worker without wounds, a helper without a throne. The real one is more than all of them together, the eternal Son who took our flesh, bore our curse, broke out of the grave and reigns.

So how would you know? The whole letter has been supplying the tests. Ask what this Jesus did. The real one was made sin for us and bore the wrath our sin deserved (5:21); a Jesus who is chiefly an example, a life-coach or a source of personal power is a different Jesus, however warmly he is spoken of. Ask what he asks. The real one calls people to live no longer for themselves (5:15); a Jesus who asks nothing costly has been substituted. Ask what the message does with sin. The gospel names it and deals with it at the cross; a message that never mentions it is not a gentler gospel but a different one, leaving the hearer’s real problem untouched. And ask what ministers it produces: does the messenger bear the shape of the cross, or has his message made him comfortable, admired and rich?

In everyday life. Test what you hear about Jesus, from a pulpit, a podcast or a song, by Scripture. The best protection is not suspicion but knowing the real one well enough that the substitute sounds wrong, as bank clerks, the saying goes, learned to spot forgeries by handling genuine notes.

How do I tell a secondary disagreement from another gospel? Ask whether the difference changes who Christ is or how a sinner is put right with God. Believers who love the same Lord differ on baptism, the end times, church government and worship; those differences matter, but they do not make another Jesus. Denying that Christ is fully God and fully man, denying his bodily resurrection or that his death paid for sin, or teaching that we are justified partly by our own works: these change the person or the gospel, and there Paul draws the line. A useful test: if the other person is right, would my hope before God be different? If not, it is a family disagreement; if so, it is a different gospel.

What if my church begins preaching another Jesus? Neither drift away in silence nor stay in silence. First make sure you have understood: listen carefully and compare what is taught honestly with Scripture. Then speak to the leaders privately and humbly, asking them to show you from the Bible why they teach it. If the error is real, persistent and touches the person or work of Christ, protect yourself and your family and find a faithful church where the apostolic Jesus is preached. Leave without bitterness, and keep praying for those you leave behind.

How can anyone say that someone else’s Jesus is the wrong one? Not by preference, which would be arrogant. Paul measures every later account against the Jesus the eyewitnesses proclaimed (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Jesus is a real man of history, not a mirror in which each person sees what he likes, and to say that a Jesus who did not die for sins or rise is not the real one is no more arrogant than saying a biography has the wrong man. Humility runs the other way: the proud thing is to remake Jesus to suit ourselves. And the Christian claims no credit for knowing the truth; he was blind until God opened his eyes (4:6).

Where Christians differ: another Jesus. Many groups use the name of Jesus while teaching a different person: a created being, a mere prophet, a spirit brother of Satan, a teacher of self-improvement. This commentary’s view: The true Jesus is the one the apostles proclaimed: eternal Son of God, fully God and fully man, crucified for our sins, risen bodily, Lord of all. Any Jesus who differs from the apostolic Jesus is another Jesus, and any gospel that adds to or subtracts from grace through faith in him is another gospel (Galatians 1:8). Christians must test teachers by Scripture (1 John 4:1–3).

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is in no way inferior to the impressive newcomers: he may lack their polish as a speaker, but not their knowledge of God. And whatever his speech lacked, he had made the gospel plain.

Super-apostles. Literally the extra-super apostles (hyperlian apostoloi): probably Paul’s own coinage, the tone of a man repeating a title others use with a straight face. These are not, on balance, the Jerusalem apostles; Paul has no quarrel with Peter and James here and would not speak of them like this. They are most likely the newcomers he will call false apostles in verse 13, and the title is their own or the impression they had created: men claiming a status above Paul’s.

Unskilled in speaking. A remarkable concession. Idiōtēs means a layman, an amateur without professional training. He grants the charge of 10:10, and in a Greek city, where public speaking was the prestige skill of the age, that was no small thing.

I am not so in knowledge. He moves the contest to different ground: not cleverness in general but knowledge of God and the gospel, the mystery of Christ revealed to him (Ephesians 3:3–4), which he has spent ten chapters unfolding. And whatever he lacked in polish, nobody in Corinth could say they had failed to understand him. That is a better ambition for anyone who teaches, and a harder one: being admired is easier than being understood, and the two are often confused.

The knowledge of Christ crucified. What Paul knows is finally not a subject but a person: “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6). In Corinth he resolved to know nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2), and refused clever rhetoric lest the cross be emptied of its power (1 Corinthians 1:17). A crucified Saviour sold with technique becomes one more product on the market; preached plainly, he does his own persuading. God has never needed the world’s eloquence. He spoke creation into being with a word and saved the world through a Word made flesh, who had no form or majesty that we should look at him.

Two separate gifts. Speaking well and having something worth saying are different gifts. An audience cannot easily tell them apart, which is why an articulate man with a thin message is generally preferred to a plain man with a deep one, and the preference is called good communication.

Should I choose a church for its preaching style? Choose it first for what is preached. Do the sermons say what the passage says? Is Christ crucified and risen at the centre? Are you fed, corrected and comforted by God’s word rather than entertained? Style is not nothing; a preacher should work hard to be clear. But a plain man who handles the Scriptures faithfully will do your soul more good over ten years than a brilliant speaker with little to say. If your pastor is no orator, thank God for his faithfulness, and listen for the substance.
verseByVerse.note: “Super-apostles” is Paul’s ironic name for the rival teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul preached free of charge, lowering himself to manual work so that the Corinthians might be lifted up by the gospel, and he will not apologise for it. Gifts from poorer churches paid for his ministry in the richest one.

Or did I commit a sin? The strangest accusation in the letter: Paul must defend himself for not charging them, and he throws the complaint back at them. “Humbling myself” means his labour as a tentmaker beside Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18:3), a lowly trade in Greek eyes.

God’s gospel free of charge. Was that a crime (1 Corinthians 9:12–18)? “God’s gospel” was not his to sell. The message that cost God his Son was offered in Corinth without a price tag, and the messenger made sure his conduct said the same.

I robbed other churches. A military word: to plunder, to strip a defeated enemy. Yes, he says, I took money: from Macedonia, and spent it on you. He accepted gifts from poorer churches, desperately poor ones (8:2), so that he could serve the richer Corinthians free.

How Corinth read it. Teachers of standing were kept by fees or a wealthy patron, and a man who worked with his hands was a tradesman (see the introduction). So Paul’s refusal was read in two damaging ways: either his teaching was not worth paying for, or, worse in that culture, he was refusing the bond a gift creates between giver and receiver, and holding people at arm’s length.

A right he declined. Paul had a right to be supported (1 Corinthians 9:14). In this city, where money bought influence and created obligation, taking it would have compromised the gospel and let his rivals claim to be his equals, so he removed the stumbling block (6:3) at real personal cost.

Humbling myself so that you might be exalted. The phrase is the gospel in miniature. Christ, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself and humbled himself to death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8); though he was rich, he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (8:9). Paul’s long hours at the workbench, night and day (1 Thessalonians 2:9), were a small, deliberate copy of that descent: he preached the Christ who stooped, and stooped himself, so that his hands preached the same sermon as his lips. A minister who insists on being lifted up has told the church what he thinks of a Lord who went down.

Should my pastor be paid? Yes. Those who labour in preaching and teaching are worthy of their wages (1 Timothy 5:17–18; Galatians 6:6), and a church that underpays its pastor while expecting all his time is not imitating Paul but disobeying him. Some ministers rightly work another job, by necessity or choice, as Paul did and as many church planters and pastors of small congregations do; that is honourable, not second-class. The point here is motive and effect: money must never buy influence over the message, and a minister must be willing to give up his rights when they would hinder the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even when he went short in Corinth, Paul would not lean on the church; gifts from Macedonia met his needs, and he vows to keep it that way.

I did not burden anyone. There were times in Corinth when he did not have enough, and still he did not ask. The rare word means to weigh on someone like a dead weight.

The brothers who came from Macedonia. Most likely from Philippi. Silas and Timothy arrived from there while Paul was in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and the Philippians sent to him repeatedly (Philippians 4:15–16). The poorest churches in the region were funding the apostle’s work in the richest city he served, so that the rich church would not have to pay and could not say it had.

Not silenced in Achaia. Then the vow, under oath: he will go on refusing their money and go on saying so (1 Corinthians 9:15). That sounds stubborn until you see what it protects: the one visible proof that he was not in this for gain (see the note on vv. 11–12).

The truth of Christ is in me. Paul swears not by heaven or the temple but by the truth of Christ living in him. The one who called himself the truth (John 14:6) has taken up residence in this man (Galatians 2:20), and Paul’s honesty rests on the Lord who indwells him, not on his own reputation. That is why his refusal to be a burden is more than policy. Christ came not to be served but to serve, and his life in a man shows itself, as here, in a servant who would sooner go hungry than lean his weight on the people he came to help.

The cost of an unimpeachable position. Paul’s policy made him poorer and more tired, and it was used against him anyway. He kept it because the gospel’s credibility was worth more to him than his comfort or reputation. Most such decisions are invisible and unrewarded: the businessman who loses the contract rather than pay the bribe everyone pays, the minister who will not let a major donor steer a decision.

Was Paul wrong to swear an oath, when Jesus said do not swear? No. The Lord forbade casual oaths that made ordinary words sound weightier, and the games of swearing by lesser things so that the oath did not really bind (Matthew 5:33–37). He did not forbid every solemn appeal to God in a serious matter: God swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13), and Jesus answered under oath at his trial (Matthew 26:63–64). Paul’s honesty is under attack and the gospel’s honour is at stake. Christians may take a lawful oath when the matter is weighty (the Westminster Confession 22.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 23.2), but their everyday yes should be simply yes.

Is it wrong to accept a gift that comes with strings? A gift given freely in love should be received with thanks; refusing it out of pride is no virtue. But some gifts buy access, silence, influence or a favour later. Ask what accepting would imply to the giver and to others, and whether it would make you less free to do right. If so, decline graciously and, where you can, explain why. Paul’s rule was simple: whatever would hinder the gospel, he would rather do without.

verseByVerse.quote: And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing their money was not a lack of love, and Paul will go on refusing it, because it is the one thing that shows his rivals are not his equals.

Because I do not love you? God knows I do! He answers the obvious misreading before it can be spoken (on how Corinth read his refusal, see the note on vv. 7–8), not with an argument but with God as witness. Some things cannot be demonstrated to people who have decided otherwise, so he states it and moves on.

To undermine the claim. The rivals took payment and wanted to be counted Paul’s equals: we work on the same terms as Paul, so judge us as you judge him. The money made the comparison impossible. So long as Paul worked for nothing and they took payment, the difference was visible to everybody, and no rival could answer it except by giving up his fees, and so becoming what he only pretended to be.

Love that refused the easy proof. Christ’s love, too, was read as its opposite. At the cross they mocked him: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42). He could have silenced every doubter in a moment, and he stayed, because he had come to save them, not himself. Paul’s refusal is a small shadow of that: he declines the thing that would make him look loving, because accepting it would hurt the people he loves, and lets God be his witness. Love that copies Christ will sometimes look, for a while, like the absence of love.

What should I do when people I love think the worst of me? Say the truth once, plainly and without heat, as Paul does. Then stop arguing. Commit your reputation to God, who knows, and go on doing good to those who misjudge you, which over time is the only answer that persuades. Examine yourself in case some of the criticism is true, and own that part. Do not withdraw your love to punish them or keep a ledger of the injustice. The Lord who was misread more than anyone entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

Uncertain wording. The Greek of verse 12 is compressed, literally something like that I may cut off the opportunity of those who want an opportunity, that in what they boast they may be found just as we are. Most take it as the ESV does: the rivals wanted an opening to be counted Paul’s equals, and his free preaching denied it. A few read the last clause as Paul’s own aim, that the rivals be forced to work on his terms, without pay. Either way the money showed the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rivals are not misguided brothers but false apostles in disguise, doing what their master Satan does when he poses as an angel of light.

False apostles, deceitful workmen. After twelve verses of irony Paul simply says what these men are. False apostles, pseudapostoloi, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament, perhaps coined for the occasion. Deceitful workmen (dolioi, crafty, treacherous): skilled, busy and productive, and working by trickery.

Disguising themselves. The verb means to change one’s outward form, to masquerade. Paul does not call them sincere men who have gone wrong. They may not know whose servants they finally are (v. 15), but they know they are posing.

An angel of light. No wonder: this is the pattern working as it always has. The popular picture of evil is darkness, something obviously repellent, which is precisely why the real thing gets through. Satan’s most effective form is not the monster but the angel of light: the impressive, the luminous, the manifestly spiritual, the thing that looks better than what you already have. His most dangerous tactic is to imitate truth.

The light he counterfeits. This letter has already said whose light it is. The god of this world blinds unbelievers to keep them from seeing “the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God”, and God has shone in our hearts “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:4–6). So the angel of light is a forger of Christ, and his ministers are forgers of Christ’s apostles. Satan can only borrow light; Christ is the light, and every disguise will be stripped off on the day he appears. The test of any bright thing is simple: does it show me the face of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, or something else that glows?

Discernment cannot run on instinct. If you are waiting to feel uneasy, you will be caught, because the disguise is designed to produce the opposite feeling. So the test is never how it made you feel, but the one Paul gave in verse 4: which Jesus, which Spirit, which gospel. Those are questions of content, which an ordinary Christian with a Bible can answer without any special sensitivity.

Does Satan really appear as an angel? The point here is disguise rather than visions: his usual angel of light is a teacher, a message, a movement that looks holy. But the warning covers the spectacular too. Even an angel from heaven preaching another gospel is to be rejected (Galatians 1:8). A vision, a voice, a dream or a miracle proves nothing by itself. God’s revelation is complete in Scripture, and every claim to a new word from God must be tested by what he has already said, and refused if it adds to it or contradicts it. Christ’s sheep are kept safe not by experiences but by his voice in his word.

Can I call someone a false teacher without being harsh? Yes, and you should be careful to. Be sure of the facts, and judge the teaching by Scripture, not by rumour or a clip out of context. Keep the label for what touches the gospel itself. Speak about the teaching more than the person’s motives, which only God sees fully. Warn those in danger, because love requires it, and pray for the teacher, because he too can be rescued. Paul is severe here because a church is being lost; he is never cruel, and he never enjoys it.

verseByVerse.quote: So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan’s servants pose as champions of righteousness, but the disguise will not survive the judgment, where they will be judged by what they have done.

His servants also. If the master appears as light, his servants appear as righteousness; the disguise runs all the way down. They are diakonoi, the word Paul uses of himself and of true servants of Christ, disguised not as scholars or men of power but as morally serious people, talking of law-keeping, morality or holiness. In a religious community that is the best camouflage, because a man visibly strict about right and wrong is trusted and rarely questioned.

Severity that looks like holiness. The counterfeit is often more demanding than the genuine article. The Judaizers in Galatia, who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, wanted more law, not less; the false teachers of Colossae wanted more self-denial. Some severity is a bid for control: such rules have an appearance of wisdom, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:23).

Their end will correspond to their deeds. There is an end, telos: final judgment. The disguise works now and will not work then (Philippians 3:19; 2 Peter 2:1–3). And they will be judged by their deeds, not their appearance, the exact reverse of Corinth. Behind that one line stands the holiness of God, whose eyes are too pure to look on evil (Habakkuk 1:13); the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). A disguise can fool a congregation for years; it cannot survive a moment in his presence, where everything is naked and exposed (Hebrews 4:13).

The righteousness they counterfeit. Paul’s own work is the ministry of righteousness, which far exceeds in glory the ministry of condemnation (3:9), and he has said what that righteousness is: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (5:21). The true servant hands out a righteousness that is not his own, Christ’s, given to sinners who have none. That is justification: the guilty pardoned and accepted as righteous, on no ground in themselves, because Christ’s obedience and death are reckoned to them and received by faith alone (Romans 4:5; Philippians 3:9). The gift does not make holiness optional, for the grace that acquits a sinner also makes him new (Romans 6:1–4; Titus 2:11–14). The counterfeit hands out demands, and that is the surest way to tell them apart. One leaves you looking at your own performance and wondering whether it is enough; the other leaves you looking at Christ, crucified for you, and knowing that it is.

The restraint. Paul says it in one line and stops, without gloating or threats. The accounts will be settled by a Judge who will do right, and that frees a man to speak plainly and let the matter go. If you have been hurt by a leader who used righteousness as a weapon, take comfort: their end will correspond to their deeds, and you do not have to arrange it.

Can a false teacher repent and be saved? Yes. While a man lives, the door of repentance is open, and Paul himself is the proof: the fiercest enemy of the gospel became its greatest preacher. He tells Timothy to correct opponents with gentleness, in the hope that God may grant them repentance (2 Timothy 2:25–26). So we warn against the teaching firmly and pray for the teacher sincerely. What we may not do is pretend the danger is small, or assume that a man who dies still leading others astray will be excused.

Should I listen to false teachers to understand them? Most Christians do not need to, and many should not. If you are not responsible for answering a teaching, there is little gain in feeding on it, and real danger, because the disguise is designed to work. Pastors and those who must protect others may need to study it, with prayer, good guides and their Bibles open. For everyone else, the best protection is to know the true gospel deeply and stay close to a faithful church. You do not have to taste every dish to know which one is poisoned.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — The Fool’s Boast and the Catalogue of Sufferings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A servant of Christ is proved by what he has suffered for him, not by what he can display, so if Paul must boast, he will boast of weakness. Under protest, playing the fool, he shames a church that tolerates leaders who enslave and strike it (vv. 16–21). He matches the rivals’ pedigree (v. 22), then outstrips them as a servant of Christ with a catalogue of beatings, shipwrecks, dangers and hunger, crowned by his daily care for all the churches (vv. 23–29). The speech ends in an anticlimax that is its point: a basket let down from the wall of Damascus (vv. 30–33).
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of sufferings is Paul’s chief credential. His opponents proved themselves by impressive experiences and social standing; Paul offers a body worn out in service (why the marks of a true servant are the marks of the cross is treated at v. 23).
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor has served for 25 years in a declining neighbourhood with little visible breakthrough. When a search committee from a larger church comes to interview him, they ask about his “greatest ministry successes.” He does not know what to say. This passage suggests a different category: faithfulness in hardship and daily care for the congregation are the apostolic credential. The question “what have you built?” is not the only or even the primary question.

verseByVerse.quote: I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks the church to let him play the fool for a while and boast as his rivals do, while saying plainly that this is not how the Lord would speak.

Accept me as a fool. Three verses of throat-clearing before the fool’s speech proper, and the hesitation is the point. Paul is playing a part, and wants everyone to know it. In ancient drama the fool could say what others could not. If the Corinthians insist on weighing men by their boasts, he will give them a boast to weigh, and they will not like what is in it.

Not as the Lord would. What follows is not how a Christian should ordinarily talk. Boasting about oneself is not Christlike, and Paul does it under protest; his candour says something about Scripture, which records him doing something beneath the gospel and saying so.

I too will boast. “According to the flesh” means about worldly credentials and achievements. The alternative was worse: if Paul stayed silent while impressive men listed theirs, a church would be lost to a different gospel. So he enters a contest he despises, to win people out of it. He takes the conventions of ancient self-praise, ancestry, achievements, hardships nobly borne, and fills them with floggings, shipwrecks, hunger and an undignified escape in a basket. He does not win the contest; he blows it apart from the inside.

The only one with the right to boast. The speech is built to end where Paul has already pointed: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (10:17). The only person who ever had the right to boast never did it for himself. Christ, the Word who was God, the maker of the stars, emptied himself and took the lowest place, and the Father boasted of him instead: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17). So Paul enters the world’s game to steer it to the one place it cannot go, the cross, the foolishness of God that is wiser than men (1 Corinthians 1:25). He will boast of his weakness (v. 30), because that is where the power of Christ shows (12:9).

Answer a fool according to his folly. A genuine pastoral principle, easily misapplied. Sometimes the only way to reach people is to meet them briefly on their own ground: to answer “a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes” (Proverbs 26:5), though the verse before warns against becoming like him. What keeps Paul’s tactic from worldliness is that he says out loud what he is doing and why. It is misused when a church adopts the world’s methods for the world’s reasons, calls it strategy, and enjoys it. Paul plainly does not enjoy it.

Is it ever right for me to talk about my achievements? Yes, when there is a real need and the aim is not your glory: a job application, a reference, a report to those you answer to, a testimony of what God has done. Paul does it to protect a church. The test is motive and manner. Does someone need to know, or do you need to be admired? Do you say it truthfully, without inflation, giving God the credit? Can you stop once the need is met? If you are always steering conversations toward your successes, that is the boasting Paul calls foolish.
verseByVerse.note: Paul adopts the rivals’ style of boasting to expose it, calling it foolishness.

verseByVerse.quote: For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With biting irony Paul shows the “wise” Corinthians what they have been tolerating: leaders who enslave them, prey on them, exploit them, look down on them and strike them.

Being wise yourselves! The irony turns savage, and it is aimed at the congregation. Corinth prided itself on knowledge and wisdom; these fine judges have been sitting contentedly under men Paul has just called servants of Satan.

Makes slaves of you, devours you. Someone had taken control, over consciences, decisions and what could be questioned, as Paul had refused to do (1:24). “Devours” is about money: these teachers were consuming the church’s resources, as the scribes devour widows’ houses (Mark 12:40).

Takes advantage, puts on airs. The first verb simply means “takes”, and here, as in 12:16, it means catching someone as in a trap: exploitation dressed up as ministry. “Puts on airs” is literally “lifts himself up”: the manner of a man who has let it be known that he is a considerable person, and you are fortunate to have him.

Or strikes you in the face. Here the list may stop being metaphorical. Someone may have physically hit a member of the congregation, or it may be a figure for public humiliation; either way, it is abusive leadership.

Why people submit to it. Confidence is easily mistaken for authority: a man who behaves as if he has the right to treat you badly creates the impression that he must have it. Being under a strong figure relieves the burden of thinking. And harshness feels like seriousness, so a hard leader seems more committed to the truth. One man founded the church and refused its money; the others enslaved it, ate it and struck it, and the Corinthians could not tell which was the apostle.

It shall not be so among you. They should have known, because the Lord had settled the question. The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, he said, but it shall not be so among you; whoever would be great must be your servant, for even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:42–45). His authority is absolute, and he used it entirely for the good of those under it. The measure of a leader is not how firmly he holds people but how closely he resembles the King who gave his life for them.

He gave his own face. The Good Shepherd is the opposite of the man in this verse. He does not enslave; he sets free. He does not devour; he feeds. He does not take advantage; he lays down his life. He does not lift himself up; he washed his disciples’ feet. He struck no one in the face; he gave his own face to those who struck him and spat on him. Every bruised sheep can run to him, and he will carry it in his arms.

What does spiritual abuse look like? It is the use of spiritual authority to control, exploit or harm people, and its marks are often the five in this verse. Control: you may not question the leader, and doubting him is treated as doubting God. Exploitation: money, time or bodies are taken for his benefit. Manipulation: guilt, fear and shame are used to get compliance. Self-exaltation: he is beyond correction and surrounded by people who protect him. Humiliation: people are shamed in public, isolated or frightened. Physical harm or sexual misconduct is not spiritual abuse only; it is a crime. A godly leader can be firm, but he welcomes questions, admits his faults, protects the weak, and points you to Christ rather than himself.

What should I do if I am being abused by a church leader? Tell someone you trust, outside his circle of influence, and do not carry it alone. If you are in danger, or a crime has been committed, go to the police; that is not disloyalty to the church but obedience to God, who appointed the authorities to protect the vulnerable (Romans 13:4). Bring it to the other elders, or to the wider body the church belongs to, and put what has happened in writing. You may need to leave, and it is not a sin to do so. Abuse is never to be tolerated or covered up in the name of peace or forgiveness. Forgiveness does not require you to stay within reach of harm, and Christ is never honoured by a church that protects the wolf instead of the sheep.

Doesn’t the Bible tell me to submit to my leaders? Yes, to leaders who keep watch over your souls as those who will have to give an account (Hebrews 13:17). That submission is real, and a healthy church gives it gladly. But it is not unlimited. Elders must not domineer over those in their charge but be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3). No leader may bind your conscience beyond the word of God (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2), command you to sin, or demand obedience that belongs to Christ alone. The more a leader insists on his own authority, the more carefully you should ask whether he is exercising Christ’s.

verseByVerse.quote: To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!
verseByVerse.commentary:
With mock shame Paul confesses that he was too weak to treat them as his rivals did, and in doing so he redefines strength.

Too weak for that! One line, among the sharpest in the letter. Having listed five ways the Corinthians have been mistreated, Paul apologises with mock contrition for never having managed any of them: too weak to enslave you, eat your money or hit anyone. They had called him weak (10:10); if gentleness is weakness, he admits it.

The weakness of the crucified. Underneath the irony is a real definition of strength, learned at the cross. Christ “was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (13:4). By Corinth’s measure the cross was the weakest moment in history; by God’s it was the strongest, for there sin, death and the devil were broken. Real strength is the capacity to be wronged and not retaliate, to hold power and decline to use it for oneself. When Paul says he was too weak to enslave them, he is confessing that he had been made to resemble his Lord, the strongest man who ever lived and the gentlest, who had power to destroy his enemies with a word and used it to heal the ear of a man who came to arrest him.

What makes the sarcasm defensible. Scripture contains sarcasm: Elijah suggested Baal might be asleep (1 Kings 18:27). Paul’s is aimed not at the weak but at people in comfortable error who have stopped listening to plain speech, and it defends others rather than himself. It comes after ten chapters of tenderness, so nobody could mistake it for his settled attitude: sarcasm from a habitually gentle man is a shock; from a habitually sharp one it is just his manner.

May I use sarcasm? Rarely, and with great care. James warns how much damage the tongue can do (James 3:5–10), and our speech should always be gracious (Colossians 4:6). Am I defending someone else, or my pride? Is it aimed at comfortable error, or at someone weak or hurting? Would the person know I love them? Is it a rare exception or my habit? Never use it on your children, your spouse, or anyone who is struggling. If you are known for a sharp tongue, the safest course is to put it away entirely.

Uncertain wording. “To my shame, I must say” renders a terse Greek phrase, literally I speak according to dishonour, which does not say whose dishonour. Most take it as the ESV does, Paul ironically owning his own shame; others read “to your shame”, or Paul echoing the disgrace his critics heap on him. On every reading the irony is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever pedigree the rivals claim, Paul has it too, and he refuses to make a speech about it. Three questions, three identical answers: “So am I.”

Are they Hebrews? The fool’s speech begins in earnest, to a drumbeat. The rivals were Jewish Christians who boasted of their pedigree, and each word carries its own weight. Hebrews is the language and culture claim: Hebrew- or Aramaic-speaking, perhaps from Palestine, raised in the tradition rather than assimilated into the Greek world. Paul was a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), and once addressed a Jerusalem crowd in Aramaic, to their evident surprise (Acts 21:40–22:2).

Israelites, offspring of Abraham. Israelites is the covenant claim: the people God chose, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants and the law (Romans 9:4; 11:1). Offspring of Abraham is the promise claim: heirs of the man to whom God swore that in him all nations would be blessed. Paul matches them three times without elaborating, and the flat repetition makes the point: whatever they have, he has, and there is nothing more to say.

Why he does not dismantle it here. When the same credentials were used to bind Gentile Christians to the law, he listed his pedigree in full and counted it all as loss, as rubbish, for the sake of Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). Here the rivals are not, as far as we can tell, demanding circumcision; they are trading on prestige. So Paul refuses them the advantage and moves on to the ground where the real difference lies.

The offspring of Abraham. Yet the third claim holds more than the rivals meant. The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and the offspring, singular, is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Every Hebrew, Israelite and son of Abraham was a branch of a family tree that existed for one Man, and from that family, according to the flesh, came the Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever (Romans 9:5). Everything Israel was meant to be, he was. So a pedigree has worth only in connection with him. If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29), and if you are not, no ancestry can make you so.

A contest that ends in a tie. Credentials can always be matched. Paul is about to show that the question was never what a man has been given, but what he has been willing to lose. And every heart keeps such a list. The religious one reads: raised in the church, sound in doctrine, faithful in attendance. The irreligious one reads: decent, tolerant, kinder than most. Both are attempts to stand before God on a record, and both fail: no record of ours can stand before a holy God, and the only one that can is Christ’s, given to those who trust him (Philippians 3:9).

Does my Christian upbringing count for anything? As a gift, not as a credential. To be raised in a believing home, to learn the Scriptures early, to be prayed for by name: these are great mercies, like Timothy’s (2 Timothy 3:15). Thank God for them. But they do not make you a Christian, and give you no standing above someone converted last month from a life of open sin. And if you came to faith with no background at all, you have lost nothing that matters: the newest believer is as fully a child of Abraham by faith as the oldest member (Galatians 3:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a servant of Christ Paul goes beyond his rivals, and his proof is not his successes but his sufferings.

Are they servants of Christ? The fourth question breaks the pattern. The first three got “So am I”; this one gets “I am a better one”. On the only ground that matters he will not concede a tie.

Talking like a madman. He interrupts himself. The word means out of one’s mind, stronger than fool: he has moved from foolishness to raving, and he can hear himself. But he does not take it back, because it is true.

Labours, imprisonments, beatings. Everyone in that room expected achievements: churches planted, miracles worked, revelations received. He lists what has been done to him. Imprisonments: at Philippi (Acts 16:23), and others not recorded. Near death: often (1:8–10). Every item is heightened, “far greater”, “far more”, “countless”; the next verses count only the official beatings.

The measure of a servant. A diakonos (servant) waits at table, and Paul’s claim is that such a man is measured not by what he has accomplished but by what he has borne. We measure by output, because output can be counted and photographed; Paul measures by cost.

The shape of the Master. This way of counting comes from the Master himself. Measured by output at the moment it ended, the Lord’s ministry looked like a failure: about three years, a handful of followers, nearly all scattered by Friday morning. What he had was what had been done to him, and it saved the world. So Paul’s scars prove that he serves Christ. They are a share in his Lord’s sufferings: not in their atoning work, which Christ finished alone, but in the hostility the world still aims at him through his people. “For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too” (1:5). Paul’s scars were the marks of his Master, and his Master’s scars are the price of our peace.

In everyday life. On Paul’s accounting, the most useful servant in a congregation may be someone with nothing to show: who has kept turning up, kept forgiving, kept praying for a family member for thirty years, and been quietly worn down by it.

Should I seek out suffering to prove my faithfulness? No. Paul went looking not for beatings but for people to preach to, and the beatings came. Christians are not called to court persecution, make themselves difficult in order to be opposed, or treat hardship as a ladder to holiness, but to follow Christ and accept the cost when it comes rather than trim the message to avoid it. If you are free from persecution, thank God and use the freedom well. The question is not how much you have suffered, but whether you would be willing to.

If my life is fairly easy, am I a lesser Christian? Not because it is easy. God appoints different measures of hardship to different servants, and it is not a competition (John 21:21–22). But every Christian life has a cost somewhere: the sin you refuse, the opinion of others you give up, the time and money you give away, the patience you keep with a difficult person. Ask whether your faith is costing you anything at all. And use your ease for those whose life is not easy: pray for particular persecuted churches, and give to support them.

verseByVerse.quote: Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul gives the count: synagogue floggings, Roman beatings, a stoning and shipwrecks, most of them recorded nowhere else. Each was suffered for the name of Christ.

Forty lashes less one. The synagogue punishment. The law permitted forty strokes and no more (Deuteronomy 25:3); Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could never break the command. The victim was bound, stripped to the waist and struck with a strap; later Jewish law describes a third of the strokes on the chest and two thirds on the back. Men died of it. Five times: 195 strokes. A synagogue gave it to its own, so Paul must have kept placing himself under its authority, walking in again, knowing what had happened the last four times, because his own people were there and he would not stop going to them first.

Beaten with rods, stoned. Beating with rods was the Roman punishment, carried out by officials called lictors, and illegal to inflict on a Roman citizen. Paul was one, and said so at Philippi, after the beating (Acts 16:22–23, 37); the other two occasions are nowhere else in the New Testament. The stoning was at Lystra: the crowd dragged him out of the city, supposing he was dead, and he got up and went back into the town (Acts 14:19–20).

Three times I was shipwrecked. None of these is the famous shipwreck of Acts 27, which had not happened yet, so there were at least four. “A night and a day I was adrift at sea” covers twenty-four hours in the open sea, probably clinging to wreckage, waiting.

Why are you persecuting me? Before his conversion Paul beat believers in the synagogues (Acts 22:19), and the risen Lord counted every blow on his people as a blow on himself (Acts 9:4). Now the same Lord counts these strokes too, for Paul suffers in union with him. And he who held Paul through a night and a day in the deep is the Lord who walked on the sea and commands the wind and waves.

What Acts leaves out. Acts gives one beating with rods out of three and none of the five floggings. The account you have of anyone is partial, and the hardest parts are usually the parts left out. People in your church are carrying things that would appear in no summary of their lives, and the God who keeps the real record has not mislaid a single stroke of it.

Why did God let this happen to his best servant? Because he was making Paul like his Son, and making the gospel visible through him. The Lord had said at the start, “I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name” (Acts 9:16). The beatings were not God’s neglect but his appointment, and every one was limited: Paul was struck down but not destroyed, carried through until his work was done (4:8–10). Through his scars churches were planted, and through his letters written in chains we still read the gospel. God does not waste the suffering of his people. He does not always tell us why, but he always knows, and he never lets go.
verseByVerse.note: The law allowed up to forty lashes; the synagogues gave thirty-nine to be sure of not exceeding it. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment. The shipwrecks were before the one described in Acts 27.

parallels.desc: Paul stoned at Lystra
beaten with rods at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s journeys meant danger from every side, from nature, from strangers and from his own people, and the plain grind of sleeplessness, hunger and cold.

On frequent journeys. Paul travelled perhaps ten thousand miles, much of it on foot, and here says “danger” eight times in a single sentence: the sound of a man reciting a life. First the ordinary hazards of ancient travel: unbridged rivers, deadly in flood, and mountain roads in Asia Minor notorious for bandits. Then the list turns human and covers everybody: Jewish opponents plotted against him (Acts 9:23; 20:3), Gentile mobs attacked him (Acts 16:19–22; 19:23–41). Then city, wilderness and sea, the three places a person can be. Nowhere was safe.

Danger from false brothers. Held to the end because it is the worst. A man knows to watch the river, the road, the mob. What cannot be guarded against is the person inside the fellowship who is not what he appears, who prays with you and works against you (Galatians 2:4). It goes deeper than persecution, because it comes from inside the family. The psalmist knew it: not an enemy, which he could have borne, but his companion, his familiar friend, with whom he walked to the house of God (Psalm 55:12–14).

Toil and hardship. Then the grinding daily conditions, with nothing dramatic in them. “Often without food” may mean voluntary fasting, or simply going without. “Cold and exposure” means lacking clothing and shelter (4:11); years later, in a Roman prison, he would ask Timothy to bring the cloak he had left at Troas (2 Timothy 4:13). Tired, hungry and cold: most Christian faithfulness looks far more like this verse than like the floggings, and it is this sort that wears people out.

He who ate my bread. Here too Paul walks where his Lord walked first. Jesus applied another psalm of betrayal to Judas at the Last Supper: “He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me” (John 13:18; Psalm 41:9). The Son of God chose a false brother into his own circle, washed his feet, handed him the morsel, and was sold by him for silver. So the deepest wound in Paul’s list is one Christ knows from the inside. And the night he was betrayed was the night he gave his body and blood for those who would desert him: the false brother could hand him over; he could not stop him saving his people.

What should I do if someone in my church has hurt me? First, take it to the Lord honestly, as the psalmist did; he knows this wound from the inside. If the person is a believer and the matter is serious, follow the path Jesus gave: go to him privately, then with one or two others, then to the church (Matthew 18:15–17). If it involves abuse or a crime, go to the authorities and to other leaders at once. Forgive from the heart, which means giving up revenge, even if trust takes much longer to rebuild. And do not let one false brother persuade you that the whole family is false. Paul was betrayed, and he never left the church.
verseByVerse.note: Rivers without bridges could be deadly in flood; roads through the mountains were infested with robbers.

verseByVerse.quote: And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heavier than every beating and shipwreck was the burden Paul carried every day: his care for all the churches.

Apart from other things. After the floggings, the stoning and the shipwrecks Paul says: apart from all that, here is what actually weighs on me. “Pressure” is something set upon a person, a crowd pressing in, and it is daily: it does not stop when the ship reaches harbour or the bruises heal.

Anxiety for all the churches. His word is care, concern (merimna), the word of “do not be anxious about your life” (Matthew 6:25; compare Philippians 4:6). Its reach is every congregation he had planted, scattered across four provinces, most out of contact, several in trouble he could do nothing about from where he was.

Is this anxiety sin? Many faithful people are quietly condemned by this question. The anxiety Scripture forbids is the fretting of someone who has forgotten he has a Father: worry about food, clothing and tomorrow. What Paul describes is not about himself at all. It is the weight of caring what becomes of others, what love feels like when the people you love are at risk and out of reach. The test is what the concern is about and where it goes. Is it fear for yourself, or care for someone else? Does it drive you to God, or round in circles? Paul’s went to God in prayer and then into action: he left Troas for Macedonia because he could not bear not knowing how Corinth had responded (2:13; 7:5–7).

The affection of Christ Jesus. Such care is Christ’s own love beating in a servant’s heart: Paul yearns for his people “with the affection of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:8). The churches are not Paul’s but Christ’s, bought with his blood, and the Head shares his care with those who serve them. Paul could be in only one city at a time; Christ walks among all the lampstands, his churches (Revelation 2:1), and always lives to intercede for them. That is why the burden is bearable. Paul carries a share, but the whole rests on the Chief Shepherd, and Paul can cast every anxiety on him, because he cares for his people (1 Peter 5:7) far more than any apostle could.

The hidden half of pastoral work. This burden appears in no report: the elder awake at two in the morning over a family coming apart; the Sunday school teacher who cannot stop thinking about one child; the pastor carrying a dozen private sorrows he may not discuss. Paul lists it as a suffering, alongside the whip and the sea. Pray for your pastor and elders, who carry a daily burden of care you will mostly never see, and tell one of them this week that you are.

Is my constant worry about my children godly care or sinful anxiety? Usually both, tangled together, and the way to untangle it is to pray it. Concern for their souls and safety is good; that is what Paul felt for his churches. But when it becomes a sleepless loop of imagined disasters, a need to control every outcome, or a fear that God will not care for them as you would, it has crossed into the anxiety Jesus forbids. Turn each worry into a specific request, give thanks for what God has already done for them, do the next thing you actually can do, and leave them in his hands, which are far safer than yours. He loves them more than you do.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul feels every believer’s weakness as his own and burns at every fall, and if he must boast, he will boast of weakness.

Who is weak, and I am not weak? This is where Paul’s daily care comes from: he keeps no protective distance from his people. When a believer is struggling, with doubt, with temptation, with a conscience troubled about food offered to idols, Paul does not counsel him from a position of strength but feels his weakness with him (1 Corinthians 9:22). He had told this church he would give up meat permanently rather than trip one weak brother (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? “Indignant” is literally “I burn”. When someone is tripped up into sin, especially by a false teacher, something in Paul catches fire: grief for the one who has fallen, and anger at whoever caused it.

Tenderness and heat. That is what a pastor’s heart is made of: tenderness toward the person who is struggling, heat toward whatever is causing the struggle. Get them the wrong way round and you have Corinth, tolerating men who devoured them and criticising the apostle who would not take their money. Most of us find it easier to be irritated by the struggling person, the one who keeps failing and needing, than by what is doing the damage. Paul’s reflexes ran the other way, trained by his Lord, who had compassion on the crowds because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36), and kept his “woe to you” for the leaders who failed them (Matthew 23).

Boasting of weakness. Then the sentence the whole fool’s speech has been climbing toward. Unlike the rivals, Paul will boast of weakness, and not as a rhetorical trick: weakness is where the power of Christ rests (12:9–10). The world counts what a man can do. God displays his power exactly where a man can do nothing: in a clay pot, in a beaten apostle, in a crucified Messiah. God has never needed anyone’s strength, and there has never been a weakness he could not fill.

What it does not mean. Weakness is not a virtue in itself: laziness, cowardice and sin are weaknesses too, and Paul never boasts of those.

What does boasting in weakness look like in practice? Being honest about your limits instead of hiding them, and pointing to Christ when good comes out of them. Admitting you are struggling when your church rewards looking fine. Saying, when asked how you got through, that you did not, and God carried you. Telling your testimony with the failures left in. Accepting help rather than insisting on managing alone. Letting your children see you pray because you do not know what to do. It is not running yourself down for sympathy, or false modesty; it is refusing to steal the credit for what God has done through a weak instrument.

verseByVerse.quote: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul swears that his catalogue is true, and then ends it not with a triumph but with the night he was lowered from the wall of Damascus in a basket.

I am not lying. The catalogue is so far outside what anyone boasts about that it might be read as rhetoric, so he calls God as witness. And even mid-oath, in one of the most painful passages he ever wrote, praise comes out of him almost by reflex: “he who is blessed forever”.

The governor under King Aretas. Then the story, deliberately, almost comically, anticlimactic: his first escape as a Christian (Acts 9:23–25). Newly converted and preaching in the synagogues of Damascus that Jesus is the Son of God, he provoked a plot, and the gates were watched. Aretas IV, king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus, ruled from about 9 BC to AD 40, so the escape came before then, which helps to date Paul’s early years (Galatians 1:17–18). Acts says the Jews plotted to kill him; here the governor guards the city. The accounts fit naturally: his Jewish opponents could easily have enlisted the governor’s help.

Let down in a basket. The word suggests a large woven hamper for provisions; the disciples lowered him through a window in the wall at night, like a delivery. Roman soldiers had a crowning honour, the wall crown, for the first man up the wall of a besieged city. Paul’s wall story goes the other way: first down the wall, in a basket, fleeing. That is the joke, and it is a serious one.

How much he must suffer for my name. Of all the incidents he could have ended on, he chose the beginning, and Christ had foretold the pattern. In that same city the risen Lord had said of him to Ananias: “I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name” (Acts 9:16). Saul had come to Damascus with letters to arrest the followers of Jesus; he left it in a basket, hunted for preaching Jesus (Acts 9:20). The man who would carry the gospel across the empire left his first city as freight. The basket was the first instalment of that promise, and this chapter’s catalogue is the rest. So the boast is not finally about Paul at all. It is about the Lord who stopped him on the road, turned the hunter into the hunted, and kept him through every danger until his work was done. The glory belongs to the name he suffered for.

In the flow. The basket joins this chapter to the next. Before the story of being caught up to the third heaven (12:1–4), Paul tells the story of being let down, and the order is the argument: whatever he has seen of glory, he boasts of weakness.

When should a Christian flee danger, and when should he stay? Fleeing is often right. Jesus withdrew when his hour had not yet come, Paul left Damascus, Thessalonica and Berea when lives were at risk, and the scattered early church spread the gospel as it went (Acts 8:1–4). Flee when staying would achieve nothing but harm, when others depend on you, or when the door is open elsewhere. Stay when fleeing would mean denying Christ, abandoning those in your care, or running from a duty God has plainly given you; Paul later went to Jerusalem knowing chains awaited him (Acts 20:22–24). Pray, take counsel, and remember that faithfulness, not bravado, pleases the Lord.

Uncertain wording. “The governor” translates ethnarchēs, literally ruler of a people, and what such an official was doing in Damascus is not known; no other source says Aretas controlled the city at this time. He may have governed it for Aretas, or headed the Nabataean community there, or been a desert chief whose men watched the gates from outside. Paul’s point does not depend on it.
verseByVerse.note: Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus; he died around AD 40.
