Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;<sup>26</sup>on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers;<sup>27</sup>in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.<sup>28</sup>And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.<sup>29</sup>Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant?<sup>30</sup>If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.<sup>31</sup>The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.<sup>32</sup>At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me,<sup>33</sup>but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

keyVerse.quote: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
keyVerse.note: This is the sentence the whole fool’s speech has been climbing toward. Paul has matched and outdone his rivals, but his credentials turn out to be scars, dangers, sleepless care and a basket over a wall, because the power of Christ is seen where his servant is weak (12:9). It overturns Corinth’s scale of values, and ours.

11.reflection:
Paul pictures the church as a bride betrothed to Christ and fears she will be led astray from “a sincere and pure devotion to Christ” (vv. 2–3). What tends to crowd or divide your devotion to Christ, and what helps you keep it simple?

Verse 4 warns of “another Jesus” who keeps the name but changes the person. What versions of Jesus are popular today, and how would you test them against the Jesus the apostles proclaimed?

The Corinthians put up with leaders who enslaved, exploited and struck them (v. 20), yet despised a gentle apostle who would not take their money. Why are people drawn to domineering leaders, and what marks a leader who resembles Christ?

Paul boasts of beatings, hunger, anxiety for the churches and a basket over a wall (vv. 23–33). Where are you tempted to hide your weakness, and how might it become a place where Christ’s power is seen?

12.title: The Thorn in the Flesh and Power in Weakness
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 12 completes the “fool’s speech” of chapter 11, in the letter’s last movement, where Paul answers the rival teachers still courting the church, and then turns to his coming third visit.

The message. The power of Christ rests not on the impressive but on the weak who lean on him. Paul will build nothing on his vision of paradise; he boasts of a thorn that would not go, a prayer that was refused, and the risen Lord’s answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” The same self-giving shapes his love for the church: he wants not what is theirs, but them.

Why it was said. The visiting “super-apostles” traded on visions, polish and pedigree, and the Corinthians had begun to measure Paul by them: weak in person, odd about money, perhaps a swindler working through his helpers (see the introduction). Some had also never turned from the sexual sins dealt with in 1 Corinthians.

How the chapter makes its case. He plays the rivals’ highest card, a man caught up to the third heaven, but tells it as if of someone else and refuses to let it count (vv. 1–6). Then he tells what came with it: a thorn, three pleadings, and the word of Christ that turned his weaknesses into his boast (vv. 7–10). The fool’s speech over, he says the church should have defended him; the signs of an apostle were done among them, and his only “wrong” was refusing their money (vv. 11–13). He comes as a father who spends himself for his children (vv. 14–15), answers the charge of trickery with a checkable record (vv. 16–18), and speaks before God for their good (v. 19), fearing he will find quarrels and unrepented sin (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. The voice that spoke belongs to the Lord who “was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (13:4). Before “my power is made perfect in weakness” described Paul’s thorn, it described Christ’s cross, where God did his greatest work in utter weakness. And the father who will “most gladly spend and be spent” for children who love him less is a small copy of the Son who, though rich, became poor for us (8:9).

For us. We still prize experiences and an impressive front, and hide what is weak. This chapter frees us to bring our thorns to Christ honestly, to accept his answer when it is no, and to find that his grace is enough for today. It also asks whether we love people, or only what we can get from them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Thorn in the Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s power is seen not in a servant’s spiritual heights but in the weakness he cannot escape, so that is what Paul will boast of. He matches his rivals’ visions with a journey to paradise, told as if of another man, and refuses to rest his reputation on it (vv. 1–6). What he does boast of is the thorn given to keep him from pride (v. 7), the prayer three times refused (v. 8), and the Lord’s answer that his grace is enough and his power is made perfect in weakness (v. 9). So Paul is glad to be weak for Christ’s sake, because then he is strong (v. 10). This is the heart of the letter.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “power is made perfect in weakness” is the theological summit of the letter (see the note on v. 9).

The threefold prayer (v. 8) and its refusal show as clearly as anything in the New Testament that God’s answer is sometimes no, with something better given instead (see the notes on vv. 8 and 9).
verseByVerse.examples: A woman with a chronic pain condition has prayed for healing for years. She has been told that her lack of healing shows insufficient faith. This passage speaks directly to her (see the note on v. 8). “My grace is sufficient for you” is not a consolation prize; it is a gift that the removal of the thorn would not have given him.

verseByVerse.quote: I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul turns, unwillingly, to visions and revelations, the ground his rivals were proudest of, and says at the outset that they prove nothing. He will tell of one only to refuse to let it count.

I must go on boasting. He feels forced to, and now calls it useless too: not that the vision was worthless to him, but that it is worth nothing as an argument. It did not make him a better servant of Christ; the thorn that came with it did rather more (v. 7). Nobody would guess from the tone that he is about to describe one of the most extraordinary experiences recorded of any Christian, and that reluctance is the point of the passage.

Visions and revelations. “Of the Lord” can mean given by the Lord, or visions in which the Lord himself is seen. His rivals were probably boasting of theirs. In a religious culture fascinated by ecstatic experience, a man who could describe the heavenly world had credentials nobody could check and everybody envied.

Experiences cannot be checked. Our age prizes spiritual experience as much as Corinth did. In any contest of spirituality, whoever describes the most remarkable inner life wins, and the claim cannot be tested. Paul will not compete on that ground. His credentials in this letter are things anybody could verify: a church that exists, a body with scars, an empty purse, a life lived in the open.

The revelation he did lead with. Paul had one revelation he spoke of everywhere, and it was not paradise but the risen Jesus on the Damascus road. He received his gospel through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12); last of all, Christ appeared also to him (1 Corinthians 15:8). That appearing made him an apostle, and he told it to crowds and to kings (Acts 22; 26). The visions of the Lord he hides; the Lord of the visions he proclaims.

Does God still give visions and revelations like these? Not as he gave them to Paul, whose experience belonged to his apostleship. God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the faith has been once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God may still use dreams, impressions and providences, and he draws near to his people in deep experiences of his love. But no claimed vision carries authority over others, adds to Scripture or binds anyone’s conscience; every such claim must be tested by Scripture and set below it. If you have had a vivid experience, thank God for whatever good it did you, and build your life on his written word.

Where Christians differ: does God still speak through dreams or prophecy today? Many brothers and sisters who expect him to do so also hold Scripture as the final authority. This commentary’s view: revelatory gifts belonged to the apostolic foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20). Both sides agree that nothing may be set beside the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul himself was once taken up into the presence of God, but he tells it as if it happened to someone else, because it was a gift and not a credential. Twice he admits that he does not know how it happened: “God knows.”

I know a man in Christ. Verse 7 gives him away: it is Paul. The third person lets him describe the experience without standing next to it and taking the credit. And the first thing he says of the man who went to heaven is not that he was special but that he was in Christ, joined to him by faith (Galatians 2:20), the only thing that would ever get anyone there.

Fourteen years ago. That lands around AD 42, in the silent years after Damascus and before the first missionary journey, the long stretch in Tarsus, Syria and Cilicia that Acts passes over in a sentence (Galatians 1:21; Acts 9:30; 11:25–26). If his authority had rested on it, he would have led with it in every city. Instead it appears once, under duress, in a passage he calls foolish.

Caught up. A strong passive verb: seized, snatched. It happened to him; he did not achieve it by technique, which is worth saying whenever people offer methods for producing such experiences. “The third heaven” is the dwelling place of God, in the simple scheme of Paul’s world: the sky of the birds, the sky of the stars, and beyond them God’s dwelling. Yet the one man in Scripture who could have written an authoritative account of the geography of heaven says twice that he does not know what happened to him.

Paradise. A Persian word for a walled garden or park, used in the Greek Old Testament of Eden, and by the Lord to the dying thief: “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7). It is the presence of God.

Humility that was not his own. Fourteen years of silence is a great deal of humility in a man who had been to paradise, and it was learned from the Lord who had shared the Father’s glory before the world existed, who could have dazzled the crowds with heaven and instead showed them his hands. The garden shut with a flaming sword was opened by the Son of God, who was himself shut out, crucified outside the city, so that a dying thief could hear the words, “today you will be with me”.

Caught up together. Paul was caught up once, briefly and alone. The whole church will be caught up together on the last day to meet the Lord, and so always be with him (1 Thessalonians 4:17). What one apostle glimpsed and could not describe, every child of God will enter and never leave.

Was Paul dead, or did his soul leave his body? He does not know, and so we do not need to. That he allows both tells us that a person can be with God apart from the body, as believers who die are now (5:8; Philippians 1:23), and that God can take a living man into his presence as he pleases. The passage does not teach Christians to seek out-of-body experiences: the ordinary way into paradise is to die in the Lord, and that is enough.

What will heaven be like, if Paul could not describe it? Scripture tells us what matters most: the presence of God and of Christ, whose face we will see (Revelation 22:4), and no more sin, death, mourning or pain (Revelation 21:4). Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, and at his return they will be raised bodily to live in a new heavens and new earth (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; 2 Peter 3:13). Paul’s silence is not a hint that heaven is vague, but that it is greater than words.

Where Christians differ: visits to heaven today. Many popular books claim detailed visits to heaven, and grieving readers have found them comforting; the apostle’s report is short, reluctant and full of admitted ignorance. This commentary’s view: Paul was taken to paradise and forbidden to describe what he heard (v. 4); he waited fourteen years to mention it, and then only to rebuke boasting. Claims today to have toured heaven and brought back detailed descriptions do not match his reticence, add to Scripture, and often contradict it. Scripture is sufficient to tell us what we need to know about heaven (2 Timothy 3:16–17; the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6).

Uncertain wording. Are “the third heaven” (v. 2) and “paradise” (v. 3) one place, or two stages of one journey? Paul’s repeated phrases suggest one experience told twice, and most interpreters take the two names for the same place. Some Jewish writings of the period counted several heavens, so a minority read an ascent through the heavens into paradise beyond. Either way, Paul was brought into the presence of God.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks of himself in the third person. The “third heaven” means the highest heaven, the presence of God; fourteen years before this letter would be in the early 40s AD.

verseByVerse.quote: and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul heard in paradise could not and must not be repeated, and he will boast of it only as God’s gift; of himself he will boast only in his weaknesses.

Things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. The first phrase means unspeakable, too holy for human words; the second, not permitted. Some of it could not be put into words, and some was not allowed to be. That is worth knowing when someone claims a private revelation that must be received on his authority alone. God may give a person something meant for him only, and the mark of a genuine one here is that Paul never traded on it: he built no following on what he could not disclose.

On behalf of this man. Hence “this man”. The man caught up to paradise he will boast about, because everything that happened to him was received, God’s gift and not his achievement. About the man writing the letter, with the scars and the tentmaker’s hands, he will boast only of what shows his weakness; in himself he is a clay jar (4:7). The times when God has plainly been at work in you are worth speaking of, but they are not your credentials, because you did not produce them.

The secret things. The Bible is not a transcript of all God knows; it is what he judged his people needed. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Much unhappiness comes from demanding the first half, and much peace from being content with the second.

The Word who could be told. What Paul heard in paradise he could not repeat; what he was sent to tell he repeated everywhere: Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). That is not second best. No one has ever seen God; the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known (John 1:18; many early manuscripts read the only God, which most modern Bibles follow). The heaven Paul glimpsed in silence came to earth in a person who ate, taught, wept and died in full view, so that what God most wants us to know of himself could be heard, seen and touched (1 John 1:1). The unspeakable things stayed in paradise. The Son did not.

Should I tell others about my experiences of God? Often, yes, with care. Telling what God has done for you can encourage others and give him glory, as the psalmists do: come and hear, and I will tell what he has done for my soul (Psalm 66:16). But ask why you are telling it: to point to God or to yourself? Will it help the hearer trust Christ, or make them feel they are missing something? Never use an experience to win an argument or claim authority over someone else. And some are best kept between you and the Lord, as Mary treasured things in her heart (Luke 2:19).

verseByVerse.quote: though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul could boast of his revelations and tell nothing but the truth, but he holds back so that people will judge him only by what they can see in his life and hear in his teaching.

No more than he sees. He is not retracting the vision; every word would be accurate, unlike the rivals’ exaggerations. But to refrain is to spare, to hold back: Paul deliberately withholds true information about himself to keep people’s opinion of him accurate. All of us manage what people know about us, and we almost always manage it the other way, putting forward what is impressive and leaving out the rest.

Not ourselves but Jesus Christ. Why does Paul care so much that no one think too highly of him? Because an inflated apostle would stand in the light where only Christ belongs. What we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants (4:5), and the light God shone into his heart was the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (4:6), not in the face of Paul. A preacher famous for his visions draws eyes to himself; one known only for what can be seen and heard leaves the hearer looking past him to his Lord. Paul’s reticence is not shyness. It is a window kept clean.

Judge the visible man. “He sees in me or hears from me” is an uncomfortable test in an age built on presentation: is the impression people have of you larger than the reality they could observe? That gap disappoints people later, and is why so many admired people are a grief to those who live with them. There is a mercy in Paul’s policy too. A man who has arranged to be overestimated must keep up the estimate, and the work never ends; Paul can admit that he despaired of life and left Damascus in a basket. Christ is the one person whose reputation never disappoints those who live closest to him. The disciples who saw him tired, hungry and weeping, at table and on the road for three years, came away worshipping.

Is it dishonest to keep good things about myself hidden? No. Honesty forbids deceiving people, not keeping things private, and Jesus told us to give, pray and fast in secret (Matthew 6:1–6). What would be dishonest is creating a false impression, making yourself look better than you are, or worse in order to be praised for humility. Let your reputation be no larger than your life.

verseByVerse.quote: So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Paul a painful, lasting affliction to keep the revelations from making him proud, and he used Satan’s own blows to do it.

To keep me from becoming conceited. Literally, from being lifted up too high. The purpose stands at both ends of the sentence, as though the danger of pride needed saying on both sides of the affliction. The greater the revelation, the greater the danger.

A thorn was given me in the flesh. Skolops means a sharpened stake or a splinter: something driven in. What it was, nobody knows (see the box below), and because it is unnamed, no sufferer is shut out of the passage: whatever is driven into your flesh fits the gap. “Was given” is a reverent way of saying that God gave it. Satan sent it, but Paul knows from whose hand it came.

A messenger of Satan to harass me. The torment is real and comes from the enemy, who meant it for harm. “Harass” (kolaphizō) means to strike with the fist, the very word used when they struck Jesus at his trial (Matthew 26:67), and it is in the present tense: blow after blow. Satan sends it to wreck a man; God appoints it to save him from something worse, and turns the devil’s fist into his own surgeon’s hand.

Satan’s weapon, God’s purpose. This is the shape of Job, where Satan can go only as far as God permits (Job 1–2); of Joseph, who told his brothers, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20); and supremely of the cross, where Satan entered Judas and the rulers did their worst, while God was delivering up his Son by his definite plan for the saving of the world (Luke 22:3; Acts 2:23). On the cross Satan struck the Son of God with everything he had, and by that very blow his head was crushed. So the thorn is not the price of the revelation; it is what God provided so that the revelation would not ruin Paul with pride.

How can both God and Satan be behind the same thing? Because they are doing different things through it. Satan aims to torment and destroy, and he is guilty for it; God aims to humble, protect and strengthen, and he is righteous in it. God does not do evil, tempt anyone to sin, or delight in pain (James 1:13), but nothing happens outside his rule, and he can turn what is meant for evil to good. So a Christian can resist the devil and still say of his suffering, this has come to me from my Father’s hand. You do not have to work out where one purpose ends and the other begins, only which one will win.

What if my thorn is something I brought on myself? Then confess the sin that caused it, and receive God’s forgiveness fully; the guilt is gone in Christ, even if the consequences remain. Paul’s thorn was not the result of his sin, but the promise of verse 9 is not limited to blameless suffering. A recovered addict with a damaged body, a man living with the results of a foolish decision, a woman bearing the scars of a past she regrets: God’s grace is sufficient for them too, and he can use even the consequences of our sin to humble us, keep us close to him, and make us gentle with others who fall.

Uncertain wording. What the thorn was is unknown, and the guessing has gone on for nineteen centuries. “In the flesh” suggests the body, and the main proposals are a chronic illness, perhaps of the eyes (Galatians 4:13–15; 6:11), or the relentless human opposition that dogged him, as Israel’s enemies could be called “thorns in your sides” (Numbers 33:55). The Corinthians probably knew, and Paul did not need to say. What is clear is that it was painful, persistent and humbling.

Textual note. Some manuscripts lack the second “to keep me from becoming conceited”, but most modern Bibles, like the KJV, keep it.
verseByVerse.note: No one knows what the thorn was; suggestions include a chronic illness, poor eyesight, or persistent opposition.

parallels.desc: thorns in your sides

verseByVerse.quote: Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begged the Lord again and again to take the thorn away, and the answer was no. Scripture records the refusal as a mercy, not a failure.

Three times I pleaded with the Lord. This line has helped to keep a great many Christians in the faith. Not a passing mention in his devotions, but repeated, earnest imploring. Paul does not draw the comparison, but the number recalls the Lord himself, who prayed three times in Gethsemane about a cup he wanted removed, and submitted to the Father’s will (Mark 14:32–41; Matthew 26:39–44). The Lord here is almost certainly Jesus, since verse 9 speaks of the power of Christ; Paul usually prays to the Father, and here he prays directly to the Son, which tells you who he understood him to be.

That it should leave me. He asked for exactly what he wanted, and it was right to ask. Every element that is supposed to guarantee an answered prayer is present: an apostle praying, an unselfish request (a healthy Paul could serve more churches), no hint of unconfessed sin, no lack of faith, no failure to persevere. And the thorn stayed. That must be said plainly, because some believers have been told that healing is theirs if they can muster the faith for it, and have concluded, after years, that the fault is in them. Some have stopped praying; some have stopped believing. This verse was written for them.

He stopped at three. Paul did not conclude that persistence was the missing ingredient and press on to three hundred. He received an answer, and it settled the matter. There is a kind of prayer that will not accept a reply, and it is not greater faith; it is a refusal to let God be God. What changed was not the circumstance but the man, and what changed him was one sentence, which he carried for the rest of his life and which the church has been living on ever since.

The cup was not taken from him. The Lord to whom Paul prayed has asked as we ask. In the days of his flesh he offered up prayers with loud cries and tears to the one who was able to save him from death (Hebrews 5:7), and the cup was not taken from him, because if it had passed from him it would have come to us. Now every plea for a thorn to go reaches someone who knows what it is to ask and be refused for a greater good, and when he says no, he does not fall silent.

Should I stop praying for healing after three times? Not necessarily. Paul stopped because he received a clear answer, and we do not receive answers in his apostolic way; Jesus told a parable about praying and not losing heart (Luke 18:1). Keep bringing your need to God as long as it is on your heart, honestly and without guilt. But let your prayer change as Paul’s did: ask also for grace to bear it, for God to be glorified in it, and for the will to accept his answer. Many believers find the prayer moving over time from “take it away” to “be with me in it”, and that is not defeat. It is the Gethsemane prayer: “not my will, but yours, be done”.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus too prayed three times in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ did not remove the thorn; he gave himself instead, with a grace that is always enough and a power that shows itself most fully in weakness. So Paul now boasts gladly of the very weaknesses he begged to lose.

But he said to me. The summit of the letter. The verb is in the perfect tense: he has said, and it stands, not a passing comfort but a permanent word.

My grace is sufficient for you. Not “will be” or “has been”, but “is”, already true while the thorn is still going in. “Sufficient” means enough for the need: not a promise of relief, but a promise that the supply will not run out before the trouble does. And see what was not said. The Lord gives no explanation beyond the clause of verse 7, does not say how long, does not promise eventual removal. He gives himself, and that answer is better than the request.

Made perfect in weakness. To reach a goal, to be completed, fully displayed. Divine power does not merely cope with human weakness; it comes to its full expression there. Weakness is not the obstacle power works around but the place it was always heading for. This is the principle of the whole letter: we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (4:7).

All the more gladly. Not “I will put up with them” but “I will boast all the more gladly”: the thing he begged to lose has become the thing he is pleased to have.

The power of Christ may rest upon me. “Rest upon” (episkēnoō) means to pitch a tent over, to dwell upon. It is built on the word for the tabernacle, where the glory settled in the wilderness, as in the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). Christ’s power settles on the weak by his Spirit, the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead, who dwells in his people (Romans 8:11) and strengthens them with power in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16). The weakness is the ground the tent is pitched on. He did not take the thorn away. He came and lived on it.

A risen man with wounds. The voice that said my grace is sufficient for you belongs to a risen man with wounds. He was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God (13:4), so when he speaks of power made perfect in weakness he is describing his own cross before he describes our trouble. There has never been a thorn deeper than his crown, and there is no weakness he will not pitch his tent on. The grace he promises is his own presence, as new each morning as the need it meets, until weakness is swallowed up in glory.

What it does not mean. Not a call to cultivate weakness, refuse medicine or make a virtue of incapacity; Paul prayed for removal, and was right to. It means that when the weakness does not lift, you have not been shut out of God’s power.

What is grace, in this verse? Not only God’s pardoning favour, though it is that, but his active help moment by moment: the strength to keep going, the comfort that holds you up, the patience you did not have, the faith that does not fail. It is the Lord himself at work in you, which is why it is always sufficient: it is measured not by your need but by his fullness. You will rarely feel it in advance. Most believers find it given for the day, like manna, and see only looking back how much was supplied.

How do I take hold of this grace when I feel nothing? By trusting the word, not waiting for a feeling. Christ said it is sufficient; believe him and act on it. Pray honestly, even if all you can say is help. Keep using the ordinary means: Scripture (especially the psalms of lament), the Lord’s Supper, believers who will pray with you. Do the next small duty and leave tomorrow’s for tomorrow. Get the medical and practical help you need, which is one of the ways God gives grace. And tell another believer, so you are not carrying it alone; grace often arrives through their hands.

Is this not just a pious way of explaining away an unanswered prayer? It would be, if Paul had been left with nothing. But he was given what he had not thought to ask for: a word from the risen Christ and his presence in the trouble. The claim can be checked against a life: the man who heard it went on through beatings, shipwreck and prison (11:23–27) and wrote this letter with more joy than his rivals ever showed. Above all, it is the pattern of the cross, where God did his greatest work through what looked like defeat; a comfort invented to soothe us would hardly look like that.

Where Christians differ: healing and faith. Some teach that it is always God’s will to heal believers who have enough faith, and that remaining sick shows lack of faith. Those who teach it usually want to honour God’s power and compassion, which is right; the question is whether Scripture makes that promise. This commentary’s view: Paul, the great apostle, prayed in faith three times for his thorn to be removed, and the Lord said no. God does heal in answer to prayer, and we should pray for healing (James 5:14–15). But he sometimes chooses not to, for purposes better than healing: humility, dependence, and the display of his power in weakness. Paul left Trophimus sick (2 Timothy 4:20) and advised Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23).

parallels.desc: he gives power to the faint

verseByVerse.quote: For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ’s sake Paul is glad, not merely resigned, to be weak, because his weakness is where Christ’s strength is found.

Content. The Greek word is stronger: to take pleasure in, to be well pleased. Paul names five things. Weaknesses: his own incapacity. Insults: outrages done to him, including the Corinthian talk of him as contemptible. Hardships: the grinding pressure of not enough. Persecutions: being hunted. Calamities: being squeezed into a narrow place with no way out. One phrase governs the sentence: “for the sake of Christ”. He takes pleasure not in suffering but in what it is for and in who meets him inside it. Take Christ out of the sentence and it becomes unhealthy; leave him in and it is one of the freest sentences in the letter.

For when I am weak, then I am strong. Both halves are literal, and “then” matters: not “even though I am weak”, but “when I am weak”, at that very moment. The strength is not his own coming back but Christ’s power resting on him (v. 9). A self-reliant person can do only what he can do; one leaning on Christ can say with Paul, I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13).

Well pleased. Paul’s word is the one the Father used at the baptism: “with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). The Father is pleased with the weak who lean on his Son, because his Son is the one in whom he is well pleased.

A different account of usefulness. Most of us assume God uses us in proportion to what we bring: the more competent and spiritually together, the more useful. This verse says God’s power is shown most where our resources fail. Think of the times you have been most useful to another person. It is rarely when you were flourishing; it is nearly always when you had been through what they are going through, and had nothing to offer but that.

Does this mean I should not try to be competent or strong? No. Paul worked hard, planned carefully, argued brilliantly and used every gift God gave him; laziness is not a spiritual weakness to boast of. The point is where your confidence rests. A skilled surgeon, a gifted teacher, a strong father can all be weak in this sense, if they know that every ability is on loan and that nothing of eternal worth will come from them without Christ. The danger is not strength but self-reliance. Use every gift, and then lean on him as though you had none.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — Signs of Apostleship and Pastoral Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A true servant of Christ seeks people, not what he can get from them, and speaks before God for their good. The fool’s speech over, Paul says the church should have defended him, since the signs of an apostle were done among them and his only “wrong” was to take nothing (vv. 11–13). He is coming a third time, as a father who spends himself for his children even if he is loved less for it (vv. 14–15), and he answers the charge of trickery with a record they could check (vv. 16–18). All of it was said in the sight of God to build them up (v. 19), and he fears finding quarrels and unrepented sin when he comes (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: The “signs of a true apostle” (v. 12) are offered not as Paul’s chief credential but as evidence that the Corinthians had already received from him what a true apostle gives. His chief credential, as the whole letter argues, is a ministry shaped like the cross. Making miracles the main test was the super-apostles’ error.
verseByVerse.examples: A church board judges its pastor entirely by attendance, baptisms and giving. This passage suggests a broader test: has the ministry produced changed lives, gospel truth and pastoral care, and has the minister borne the shape of the cross? The absence of spectacular growth does not disqualify; the absence of gospel integrity does.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church should have defended Paul instead of forcing him to defend himself, for the marks of a true apostle, miracles included, had been done among them.

I have been a fool! You forced me to it. The fool’s speech ends, and Paul steps out of the character with obvious relief.

I ought to have been commended by you. That is the real grievance of all four chapters. He founded the church and was slandered in it by newcomers, and the people who owed him everything sat quietly. Anyone left undefended by people who knew better knows that the attack wounds less than the silence of those who could have spoken.

Even though I am nothing. Both halves are true. Measured against the men impressing Corinth, he is not behind by a step; measured in himself, he is nothing (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). That is not self-hatred but the realism of a man who wrote that our sufficiency is from God (3:5). A Christian can hold a very high view of what God has done through him and a very low view of his own contribution at the same time, and neither is false modesty.

With utmost patience. The signs came wrapped in endurance, staying power under weight. Paul puts it first because anyone can be impressive for an evening, and only a certain kind of man is still there eighteen months later, making tents.

With signs and wonders and mighty works. Signs point beyond themselves, wonders astonish, mighty works display power. This is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament that the apostles worked miracles, in Corinth as elsewhere (Romans 15:19). But see where he places the fact: at the end of four chapters of weakness, in a single line, after the beatings and the basket and the thorn.

What Christ accomplished through me. Whose signs were they? Paul will speak only of what Christ has accomplished through him, by the power of signs and wonders (Romans 15:18–19). The same three words first marked out Jesus himself, a man attested by God with mighty works and wonders and signs (Acts 2:22). So the signs of an apostle were the risen Lord’s own credentials, carried by the men he had sent, bearing witness that the one who healed in Galilee was alive and still at work (Hebrews 2:3–4). They never pointed to Paul but back to the one who sent him, and “one who is sent” is exactly what apostle means. Christ is the great sign and wonder of God, whose greatest mighty work was done in weakness on a cross and in power at an empty tomb.

What it does not mean. Miracles alone do not prove truth: false prophets can do signs (Matthew 24:24).

In everyday life. When a pastor, a missionary or a fellow member is criticised unfairly behind their back, say a word in their defence the next time you hear it. Silence is not neutral.

If the sign gifts have ceased, should I still pray for miracles? Yes. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped acting, but that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gifts of working miracles at will, as signs confirming new revelation. God is as powerful as ever and still answers prayer in ways that leave doctors puzzled. So pray boldly for the sick (James 5:14–15), for conversions, for deliverance from danger, and give him the glory when he answers. What we should not do is treat miracles as the proof of a ministry, or tell sufferers that their lack of healing shows lack of faith.

How should I treat Christians who believe the gifts continue? As brothers and sisters in Christ. This is an in-house difference among people who love the same Lord and gospel, and many charismatic believers shame the rest of us by their zeal in prayer and evangelism. Hold your convictions with charity, and argue from Scripture, not caricatures. Test every claimed word or sign by the Bible, as they themselves should, and reserve your warnings for teaching that adds to Scripture, promises health and wealth, or replaces the gospel with spectacle.

Where Christians differ: the signs of an apostle today. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, brothers and sisters who love the Lord, believe such signs continue, and some argue that miracles should be normal in every church today. This commentary’s view: Paul calls signs and wonders the signs of an apostle, marks that distinguished true apostles from false; if they were common to all believers, they could not mark out apostles. An apostle in Paul’s sense was a witness of the risen Christ appointed by him (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), the last of whom saw him (1 Corinthians 15:8), and the apostles were a foundation laid once (Ephesians 2:20). So the miraculous sign gifts were tied to that foundation (Hebrews 2:3–4) and are not the norm today; the church is now led by elders and taught by the apostles’ words in Scripture. God remains free to do wonders.

verseByVerse.quote: For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only way Corinth was treated worse than other churches was that Paul took no money from them, and he will not start now: he wants them, not what they have.

Forgive me this wrong! The irony has one more turn, bitter and funny, aimed at an accusation so absurd that stating it plainly refutes it. They received everything other churches did: the gospel, the teaching, the miracles. The single respect in which Corinth received less is that he refused their money.

Not what is yours but you. This will be his third visit (13:1), and the policy has not changed. Here is the line between shepherd and hireling. The false teachers wanted what the Corinthians had: their money, allegiance and admiration, and the standing of leading a well-known church. Paul wanted the Corinthians themselves. Run it as a test both ways. Of anyone who ministers to you: does he want you, or something you can supply? And of yourself, wherever you are the stronger party: are you after the person, or the gratitude, loyalty and sense of being needed that they give you?

Parents for their children. He speaks as their spiritual father (1 Corinthians 4:15), and the argument is simply how families work. A father does not present his children with an invoice. Money in a household runs downhill, from those who have it to those who do not, and nobody calls it a transaction. That is the position of the Father who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and who has never once sent anyone a bill.

He became poor. Paul had already told the Corinthians where this way of loving a church came from: “you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (8:9). In God’s family the wealth runs downhill, from the Son who had everything to children who had nothing. When Paul works nights so as not to be a burden, he is preaching 8:9 with his hands.

How do I know whether I want people or what they give me? Watch what happens when they stop giving it. If someone you serve stops thanking you, disagrees with you or no longer needs you, do you still care for them? Do you rejoice when they grow beyond needing you, or feel threatened? Do you pray for them when no one will ever know? A parent who loves a child is glad to see him become independent; a parent who loves being needed resents it. Ask God to purify your love until it seeks people and not what is theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will gladly pour out everything he has, and himself, for their souls, even if the more he loves them, the less they love him.

Spend and be spent. The two verbs share a root, the first active, the second passive. To spend is to lay out what you have: money, time, energy. To be spent is to be laid out yourself, used up in the process, as happens to people who serve others for a long time. The mother of a disabled child knows it, and so does the man caring for his wife through a long decline, and the pastor in his twenty-fifth year.

Most gladly, for your souls. Not willingly or without complaint, but with delight. And the object is their souls, not their approval; he is spending himself on what will still exist in a thousand years. He learned it from a Lord who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

If I love you more, am I to be loved less? Paul lets the question stand, and it is heartbreaking. He has loved them more than any of the newcomers ever will, and it has cost him their affection: the men who exploited them are admired; the man who worked nights so as not to burden them is suspected. Love does not always receive love back, and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But the question does not become a threat or a withdrawal. He asks it, then goes on loving them and announces he is coming again. Love that stops when it is not returned was something else all along. Christ loved most and was loved least. He was spent entirely, and gladly, “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2), for people who at the time were shouting for his death.

When love stops paying. Our culture answers Paul’s question: if a relationship does not give back what you put in, walk away. The sociologist Anthony Giddens described the modern ideal as the “pure relationship”: a bond kept up for what each person gets out of it, lasting only as long as both are satisfied. There is honesty in that, and real abuse must never be called love (see the note on 11:19–20). But the ideal turns love into a trade, and trades end when one side stops paying. Then every friendship is provisional and every marriage a contract under review, and none of us is safe, for all of us will one day have little left to give. The love that saves us is of another kind. Christ set his love on people who gave him nothing back but a cross, and he has not withdrawn it since. Only people loved like that can afford to go on loving those who do not love them back.

Is it wrong to want to be loved back? No. Paul plainly wanted it; he asked them earlier to widen their hearts to him (6:13). Longing for love in return is human and good, and God made us for it. What would be wrong is making your love conditional on it, or punishing people when it does not come. Bring the ache to God honestly, as Paul brings it into the open here, and go on loving, because your love is first a response to his. If you are pouring yourself out for someone who does not love you back, you are standing where your Lord stood, and he sees it.

How do I keep from burning out while being spent for others? Paul was spent for souls, not for every demand people made of him. He refused some things, rested at times, accepted help, and was sustained by the churches’ gifts and the company of friends like Titus. Being spent gladly is not the same as being consumed by guilt or other people’s expectations. Keep a day of rest. Share the load; you are not the only servant God has. Let others care for you, and keep your own soul fed, because you cannot give what you do not receive. The Lord who spent himself also withdrew to lonely places and prayed.

verseByVerse.quote: But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
When some accused Paul of cheating them through his helpers, he answered not with protests but with names they could check.

Crafty, you say. The meanest accusation yet. He had never taken a penny from them, so the charge changed shape: he did not take it himself; that was the clever part. Most likely the suspicion was that the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem was the real scheme, with the money skimmed off through the men he sent. The very safeguards Paul built, delegates chosen by the churches and his refusal to handle funds alone (8:20–21), had been turned into evidence of a cleverer fraud. Such suspicion cannot be disproved: honesty becomes proof of cunning.

Did Titus take advantage of you? Paul’s answer is a series of questions with names attached, the only thing that works against such a charge: check the record, and name one. They knew Titus, and his conduct among them had been spotless. This was probably his earlier visit, when he made a start on this very collection (8:6), so they had already watched him handle their money.

The same steps. The closing questions are quietly conclusive. The word for steps means footprints: Paul and his co-workers walked in the same tracks about money, with the same integrity, and everyone had watched them do it.

In his steps. The charge against Paul was deceit, and the answer was a life that could be watched. That is the pattern Peter saw in Jesus: “Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:21–22). Paul and Titus walked in the same footprints because both were walking in his. The only answer to a slander that cannot be disproved is a character that does not need defending.

How should a church handle money so that no one can suspect it? As Paul did: never let one person handle funds alone. Have at least two unrelated people count every offering and sign for it. Keep clear records and let the members see them, and have the accounts checked by someone independent. Make sure those who decide on spending are accountable, and that no leader can quietly benefit. None of this implies that anyone is dishonest; it protects the honest from suspicion and the church from temptation. We aim at what is honourable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (8:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has not been on trial before the Corinthians; he has spoken before God, as a man in Christ, and every word was meant to build them up.

Defending ourselves to you? Paul stops and reframes all four chapters. He has answered charges, matched credentials, listed sufferings and refuted accusations, and anyone would call that a defence. He says it is not, or at least that they are not the court.

In the sight of God. God is the audience; the Corinthians have merely been in the room (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). A man defending himself before people manages an impression. A man speaking before God says what is true and lets the impression fall where it will, which is why these chapters contain so much no advocate would include: that he despaired of life, could not rest at Troas, is unimpressive in person, and left Damascus in a basket. And for those in Christ the only verdict that counts has already been given: they are not on trial before God, because Christ stood trial for them and was condemned in their place. It is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends (10:18).

Speaking in Christ. Paul speaks as a man joined to Christ and answerable to him, and Jesus lived his whole ministry before that same court. I do not seek my own glory, he said; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge (John 8:50). Before the council and before Pilate he did not plead for his reputation; he entrusted himself to the Father, and the Father vindicated him. In Christ, Paul can do the same: say hard and humiliating things, leave his name with God, and spend his words building up the very people who doubt him.

All for your upbuilding, beloved. Every word, the irony, the catalogue of floggings, the fool’s speech he found so distasteful, was construction work on them, not self-protection, the authority given for building up and not for destroying (10:8; 13:10). And the sentence ends on “beloved”, used only once before in the letter (7:1), saved for people who have doubted him, listened to his enemies and left him to defend himself alone. That is the tone the whole passage was meant to be heard in. It is God’s word before it is Paul’s, the word the Father speaks over all his children for the sake of his Son.

How do I live before God rather than before people? Remember, often, that he is the one you will answer to, and that he already knows everything. Before a difficult conversation, ask what you would say if God were the only listener. When praise comes, give it to him quickly. When criticism comes, ask him whether it is true before asking how it makes you look. And let your words aim at the hearer’s good, not your own defence. The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25).

verseByVerse.quote: For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul dreads arriving to find the church still torn by quarrels and pride, and some still unrepentant of sexual sin, which would bring him not to anger but to grief.

I fear. Twice he says it, and “perhaps” guards it: he dreads a possibility; he does not predict it, nor describe their sin as settled before he has seen it. If they are unrepentant, they will find him “not as you wish”, coming with the rod rather than with love in a spirit of gentleness (1 Corinthians 4:21). He would far rather not.

Eight sins of a church. These are not the sins of a pagan city but of a congregation. Quarrelling: strife. Jealousy: resentment of another’s good. Anger: outbursts of temper. Hostility: selfish ambition and factions. Slander: speaking against people. Gossip: whisperings. Conceit: puffings-up. Disorder: tumult. All are relational, and all can survive for years in a church that would be horrified by anything more obvious. Several appear among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20), the opposite of the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). Where the Spirit is not followed, these are what grow instead.

My God may humble me. Even the humbling would come from the hand of the God he belongs to. And he would mourn, the strong verb for grieving as at a death (1 Corinthians 5:2): not merely discipline them, though he will, nor be angry, though he might be. The apostle who had been caught up into paradise is afraid of arriving in a Greek port and finding people he loves unrepentant.

The old Corinthian sins. Impurity, sexual immorality and sensuality were dealt with in the first letter (1 Corinthians 5–6). The church had come back to Paul, but some may never have turned: a congregation can be genuinely restored in its relationships and still contain people for whom nothing has changed. Repentance is more than regret or a better mood in the church: it is a turning of the mind and life from sin to God, which shows itself in deeds (Acts 26:20).

Humbled by sins not his own. Paul expects to be brought low by other people’s sins, as a father is shamed by his children’s, a faint likeness of something far greater. Christ was humbled not by any sin of his own, for he had none, but by ours: he humbled himself to the point of death on a cross (Philippians 2:8), and the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6). Paul could grieve over the impurity in Corinth and discipline it. Christ carried it, so that people who had lived exactly that way could be washed of it (1 Corinthians 6:11).

He wept over Jerusalem. The Lord of the church mourns before he judges. He wept over Jerusalem, which would not come to him (Luke 19:41), and then went into it to die for sinners. “As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezekiel 33:11). The heart of God toward an unrepentant church is not cold impatience but grief, and a door still open to everyone who turns.

Why does Paul put gossip in the same list as sexual immorality? Because both destroy, and both grieve God. We rank sins by how shocking they look, and gossip and conceit rarely shock anyone. God ranks them differently: Romans 1:29–30 puts gossips and slanderers in the same catalogue as murderers, and a whisperer separates close friends (Proverbs 16:28). Sexual sin defiles the body and breaks covenants; gossip and slander poison a whole church and wreck reputations that took decades to build. Do not excuse the respectable sins because they are common. They are common because we excuse them.

What should I do if I recognise myself in this list? Repent specifically, not generally. Name the sin to God: not “I have not been very loving”, but “I said that about her and it was not true, or not mine to say”. Receive his forgiveness, which is complete in Christ (1 John 1:9). Then put it right where you can: apologise to the person you slandered, correct the story you spread, make peace with the one you quarrelled with (Matthew 5:23–24). Starve the habit: stop listening to gossip as well as spreading it. If sexual sin is involved, tell a mature believer and get help; this is a battle no one wins alone.

In everyday life. Pick the one of these eight most at home in you, very likely the quietest, and ask the Spirit, whose fruit is its opposite, to root it out this week. You will not be free of all eight in this life. Christ never once fell into any of them, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), so you fight them as a forgiven child, not to win his love.

Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.<sup>2</sup>I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows.<sup>3</sup>And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—<sup>4</sup>and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter.<sup>5</sup>On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—<sup>6</sup>though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.<sup>7</sup>So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.<sup>8</sup>Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.<sup>9</sup>But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.<sup>10</sup>For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities.
