keyVerse.quote: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
keyVerse.note: Here the risen Christ himself speaks, and his answer gathers up the whole letter: treasure in jars of clay, life through death, strength through weakness. He does not promise that the thorn will go, but that his grace will always be enough and that his power will settle on the weak. That is why Paul, unlike his rivals, boasts of weakness.

12.reflection:
Paul had an extraordinary vision but would not build his reputation on it, wanting people to think of him only what they could see and hear (vv. 1–6). Why are claims of spiritual experience so persuasive, and how should we weigh them? Where is the impression people have of you larger than the reality?

Paul pleaded three times for the thorn to go, and the Lord said no (vv. 8–9). Where have you seen “My grace is sufficient for you” prove true when a prayer was not answered as hoped? How would you help someone who has been told that their illness shows a lack of faith?

“For when I am weak, then I am strong” (v. 10). What weakness are you most tempted to hide, and what might it look like to let it become a place where Christ’s power rests?

Paul says, “I seek not what is yours but you,” and will spend and be spent for people who love him less (vv. 14–15). In your family, friendships or service, how can you tell whether you love people or what they give you?

13.title: Self-Examination, Final Warnings, and the Grace Benediction
13.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 ends the letter’s last movement (chapters 10–13), Paul’s answer to the false apostles and those still listening to them. Having boasted of his weakness (chapters 11–12) and confessed his fear of what he may find (12:20–21), he gives his final warning before the third visit, and then his blessing.

The message. Do not mistake gentleness for weakness: the crucified Christ lives by the power of God, and he is not weak in dealing with his people. The test that matters is not whether Paul is a true apostle but whether Christ is in them, and all Paul’s warning, praying and waiting aims at their mending, not his vindication. The last word is grace, the triune God pronounced over the whole difficult church.

Why it was said. The Corinthians had demanded proof that Christ spoke through Paul (v. 3), the old charge that he was bold in letters and feeble in person (10:10), and some had not repented of the sins he named (12:21). He writes before he comes so that he need not be severe (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Paul promises a fair hearing and no more sparing (vv. 1–2). Their demand for proof is answered by the crucified and risen Christ, whose weakness and power Paul shares (vv. 3–4). Then he turns the test round: is Christ in you? (v. 5). He prays they will do right even if he looks a failure (vv. 6–7), for his authority works only for the truth and for building up (vv. 8–10). Then come five short appeals and the promise of God’s presence (v. 11), greetings (vv. 12–13), and the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament (v. 14).

Where it leads. Verse 4 gathers the whole letter into one sentence: Christ “was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God.” Paul’s willingness to seem to fail so that others may do right copies, in small, the one numbered with the transgressors so that sinners might be counted righteous. And the letter that began with “the Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (1:3) ends with Son, Father and Spirit pronounced over loyal and disloyal alike, because God’s blessing was never rationed to the deserving.

For us. When you examine yourself, look for Christ, not for enough holiness to feel safe. Receive correction while there is time to act on it. Measure every use of authority, your own included, by what it builds. And go out under the blessing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s power is real, and it works through weakness, so the test that matters is not of Paul but of the church. Paul will come a third time, with a fair hearing and no more sparing (vv. 1–2). Their demand for proof is answered by the crucified and risen Christ, whose weakness and power Paul shares (vv. 3–4). Then he turns the test round: is Christ in you? (v. 5). He prays for their good even if it leaves him looking a failure (vv. 6–7), because his authority works only for the truth and for building up, and he writes now so that he need not be severe when he comes (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Many churches have joined the call to self-examination (v. 5) to the self-examination Paul asks for before the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:28–31). True self-examination is not cultivating doubt but looking for Christ rather than for enough personal righteousness, and how the test is run is set out in the note on v. 5.
verseByVerse.examples: Before communion a pastor gives the congregation a few minutes for self-examination. This passage makes the goal clear: not to find enough holiness to qualify for the table, but to ask whether Christ is there, whether the faith that receives him is real.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is coming a third time, and unrepented sin will be dealt with at last, fairly and on proper evidence. He has warned them twice, and the patience they mistook for weakness is about to end.

This is the third time I am coming. The first visit founded the church (Acts 18:1–11); the second was the short, painful visit not recorded in Acts (2:1–5; 7:12; see the introduction); the third is very probably the three months in Greece of Acts 20:2–3.

Two or three witnesses. Paul quotes the law (Deuteronomy 19:15), one of the oldest protections in Scripture: no one is to be condemned on one person’s word. Jesus built it into church discipline (Matthew 18:16), and Paul applies it to charges against elders (1 Timothy 5:19). Paul is the injured party, and the first thing he establishes is the procedure that protects the accused. A man who wanted revenge would not begin there.

I warned them. Once in person, now again in writing: nobody will be able to say they did not know. That is how God deals with people: warnings come before judgment, in time to be acted on. Through Jonah, Nineveh was given forty days (Jonah 3:4).

I will not spare them. At 1:23 he stayed away to spare them; the sparing is over. They had mistaken patience for inability, the mistake Peter answered about God himself: the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you (2 Peter 3:9). Delay is not weakness but time given to repent. Behind the warning stands God’s holiness: sin in a church is never private, because the church is the temple of the living God (6:16), and he will not leave his temple defiled for ever.

The trial where the witnesses failed. This protection was denied once, to the one person who least deserved condemnation. At Jesus’ trial the false witnesses did not agree (Mark 14:56), and the court condemned him anyway, on his own confession that he was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed (Mark 14:61–64). The injustice was men’s; the purpose was God’s. The innocent was condemned by an unjust court so that a just God could acquit the guilty who believe in him (Romans 3:26). Every fair hearing in a church is held in the light of that unfair one.

The court that needs no witnesses. Our age has built a court Paul would hardly recognise. It sits online, hears one side, often in a single clip, passes sentence within the hour, and offers no appeal and no pardon. Part of what drives it is good: a hunger for justice where the powerful have too often escaped and victims were too often not believed. But justice that drops the rules of evidence soon becomes something else, and a crowd that never checks the charge seldom forgives the guilty either. The gospel holds both together, because it comes from the one courtroom where justice and mercy were satisfied at once: God neither pretended sin was small nor let the guilty off without a price, but bore the sentence himself. People acquitted there can take wrongs seriously and still refuse to join the mob, because they know what it is to be guilty and spared.

What does church discipline actually involve? It is the church’s loving care for its members, including correction of serious, unrepented sin. Most of it is quiet and private: a word between friends, a visit from an elder, an honest conversation (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). Only when someone persistently refuses to repent of plain sin does it become public, and in the last resort the church may remove him from membership and the Lord’s Table (1 Corinthians 5:4–5, 13). The aim at every stage is restoration, not humiliation: to win the brother back. Done with patience, evidence and tears, it is one way Christ protects his flock and calls wandering sheep home.

Why insist on witnesses when someone is accused? Because God hates false accusation and injustice, and because a single report, however sincere, can be mistaken, exaggerated or malicious. Requiring confirmation protects the innocent from rumour and the church from being manipulated. It does not mean that a lone victim of abuse should be ignored. Other evidence can confirm a charge, and patterns of behaviour often come to light when one person speaks. Serious allegations, especially of abuse or crime, must be taken seriously at once and reported to the proper authorities; the requirement of witnesses governs the church’s verdict, not whether it listens.

Uncertain wording. How Paul applies the law’s “two or three witnesses” is not certain. Many take his three visits, or his repeated warnings, as the witnesses themselves; others think he means just what the law says, that charges will be confirmed by witnesses when he comes. Either way, nothing will be done on rumour.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three

verseByVerse.quote: since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They want proof that Christ speaks through Paul, and they will have it, for Christ is not weak in dealing with them. Paul turns the question from himself to his Lord, whose power they have already seen among them.

Proof that Christ is speaking. “Proof” (dokimē) means evidence, the result of a test. They wanted what the super-apostles gave them: presence, force, the manner of a man plainly in charge (11:5–6). Paul, working at his trade and declining their money, did not look the part.

Standing inside the evidence. They asked for proof from a man who had given them everything; the church itself was the proof (3:2), and so were his scars. A wife loved faithfully for thirty years can still ask whether she is loved, because she is looking for a gesture rather than a life. The demand for proof is often a sign that the actual evidence has stopped being looked at.

Not weak but powerful. They asked about Paul; he answers about Christ, who has shown his power among them in their conversion, the gifts and the miracles: the Lord who calmed the sea with a word and now works with the same power through jars of clay.

A domesticated Christ. A church that disregards a gentle minister can slide into disregarding the Lord who sent him: the messenger’s mildness is attributed to the message, then to its Giver, and a congregation ends up with a tame Christ, so endlessly patient that nothing is ever at stake. If your picture of Christ has become someone who never presses, confronts or requires anything, it did not come from the Gospels, where he cleared the temple with a whip and wept over a city that would not come to him (John 2:15; Luke 19:41). He is not weak in dealing with his people. He is patient, which is a different thing entirely.

How does Christ show his power in a church today? Mostly in ways that do not look spectacular. Sinners are converted under ordinary preaching. Broken marriages are mended. Believers persevere through cancer, grief and persecution with a peace nobody can explain. Quarrelling members are reconciled. A small, unimpressive congregation keeps going for a hundred years and sends out missionaries. That is resurrection power, as real as any miracle, at work wherever Christ’s word is faithfully preached. Learn to see it, and thank him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by God’s power, and Paul, weak in him, will come to Corinth with that same risen power. Weakness and power are not rival columns; both belong to Christ, and both are shared by those who are in him.

Crucified in weakness. This is the foundation of the whole letter. To every eye the cross was defeat: he was held by nails driven by men he had made, and died the way the powerless die, publicly, slowly, with nothing to show. Yet the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25).

By the power of God. Then the sentence turns, and the turning is the gospel: the body that hung there is alive, by a power that reached into a sealed tomb (Romans 1:4; Ephesians 1:19–20). Forgiveness, the Spirit, the church and the hope of a body that will not fail all run through that single fact.

He lives. Notice the tense: not that Christ was raised and then left the story, but that he “lives”, now. He “will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him” (Romans 6:9). And his life now is not idle. He lives to do four things for his people.

He reigns. God “raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority” (Ephesians 1:20–21). Every power that frightens you is under his feet, “for he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). He “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3), so nothing in your life slips out of his hands.

He prays for you. “He always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). When the accuser points to your sin, the answer is not your record but a living Saviour, “who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34), on the ground of his finished sacrifice.

He gives his Spirit and builds his church. “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this” (Acts 2:33). Every new birth, answered prayer and bit of growth is the risen Christ at work by his Spirit, keeping his promise, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

He holds the future. “I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). The one who will raise his people is already alive on the other side of death: “Because I live, you also will live” (John 14:19). His life now is the guarantee of yours.

Weak in him, but we will live with him. Paul applies it to himself and to every servant of Christ since. His weakness, in suffering and humility, is not a matter of temperament but a share in the weakness of a crucified Lord. And the power he brings to Corinth is not his own recovered strength but the life of a reigning, praying, Spirit-giving Lord, exercised through a man who has none of his own. They had been sorting people into strong and weak and had put Paul in the wrong column. He is telling them the columns do not work, because the one they worship is in both.

Weakness and power at once. The Christian life is not weakness followed by strength, as though weakness were a phase to get through, but both at once, in the same person, as in Christ himself: the risen Lord still bears the wounds.

What does it mean to be weak in him? Your frailties, limits and sufferings, borne as a believer, are part of your union with Christ, not outside it. Worn out from serving, misunderstood for doing right, sick, grieving or simply ordinary, you share the pattern of his life on earth, and are not further from him but closer. Not every weakness is holy; sin is not weakness in him. But what makes you feel least useful may be exactly where his life is at work in you.

verseByVerse.quote: Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The test that matters is not of Paul but of the Corinthians themselves, and it comes down to one question: is Jesus Christ in you? Paul words it to expect the answer yes.

Examine yourselves. They had been examining Paul for months; he turns the instrument round. In the Greek “yourselves” comes first, for emphasis. “In the faith” means truly believing, united to Christ.

Test yourselves. “Test” is the word for testing metal: is the gold really gold? This verse has often been used to manufacture doubt, so it needs care, for the reader most troubled by it is usually the one who least needs to be.

Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? The test is a single question: is Christ there? Not “are you holy enough?”, not “is your faith strong enough?”, not “have you felt the right things?” The sign of a true believer is that Christ dwells in him by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27). That does not mean Christ is a feeling inside you, but that by his Spirit he has joined you to himself, so that his life is at work in yours: a new heart that trusts him, wants him and turns from sin, however weakly (Ezekiel 36:26–27). And the Greek form of the question expects the answer yes: Paul is confident about them.

Unless indeed you fail to meet the test! A sharp afterthought, not what he expects: adokimos is metal that proves counterfeit. And the argument turns. If they find Christ is in them, then their faith came through Paul, which proves his apostleship (v. 6). If not, they have bigger problems than Paul.

How the test is run. Look for Christ, not for your performance. Do you love him at all? Do you want to be free of sin, even where you keep losing? Does the gospel still move you? Do you love his people, including the difficult ones? Is there anything in you that you did not put there? None of these will find your obedience perfect; the righteousness you stand in is Christ’s, whose perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9). You look inward, find very little to be proud of, and then find Christ there, not because you have kept hold of him but because he has taken up residence and has no intention of leaving.

The dead do not check their pulse. People entirely indifferent to Christ do not usually lie awake worrying whether he is in them. The very fear that you might fail this test, when it comes with a longing for Christ and a hatred of sin, is itself a sign of a heart God has made alive. If this verse troubles you in that way, its warning was aimed at the careless, not at you.

Should I examine myself before the Lord’s Supper? Yes. The church has often linked this verse to the Lord’s Table, where Paul says, “Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat” (1 Corinthians 11:28). The examination is not whether you are worthy enough to come; no one is. It is whether you are trusting Christ and willing to turn from your sin. Confess what you know is wrong, put away any grudge, and come. The examination is meant to bring those who find Christ in them to the table, not to keep them away. The Supper is for sinners who need grace, not for saints who think they have outgrown it.

What if I examine myself and honestly do not find Christ? Do not despair and do not wait: the test is not a final verdict but a summons. Christ invites everyone who is weary and burdened, and promises that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). You do not have to fix yourself first. Confess your sin, trust him as the one who died for sinners, and talk to a pastor or mature Christian who can walk with you. If you are simply unsure, take the uncertainty to Christ rather than further into yourself. Assurance grows by looking at him.

Where Christians differ: self-examination and assurance. Some say believers should never doubt their salvation; others make constant introspection the mark of true faith. This commentary’s view: self-examination is commanded, especially for those whose lives contradict their profession. Assurance rests first on God’s promises in Christ, confirmed by the inner witness of the Spirit and the fruit of a changed life (1 John; the Westminster Confession 18.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2). Self-examination should lead not to endless morbid introspection but to looking at Christ, and to repentance where needed. Those who find Christ in them can rest assured.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wants the Corinthians to do right far more than he wants to be proved right, even if it leaves him looking a failure. If they find Christ in them, they will know he is genuine; but his prayer is for their holiness, not his reputation.

Though we may seem to have failed. If they repent before he arrives, there will be no showdown, and his critics will go on saying he is all letters and no presence. He prays for exactly that outcome. He would rather be permanently misjudged than have them sin so that he can be proved right.

Numbered with the transgressors. Paul’s prayer has the shape of the cross. Jesus was willing to look like the ultimate failure, rejected, condemned as a blasphemer and numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12), counted a sinner so that sinners might be counted righteous (5:21); and the Father vindicated him in his own time, raising him from the dead. Paul, willing to seem to have failed so that the Corinthians may do right, makes a small copy of his Master’s great exchange.

How rare that is. In a dispute most of us want the other person to do right and our position to be publicly established. Paul prays away his own vindication. He can, because the verdict on him is not the Corinthians’ to give: it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends (10:18). A man who believes that can afford to look like a failure.

What if the person who wronged me changes but never admits I was right? Then thank God, and let it go: their change is what matters. You may long for an apology, and sometimes it is right to ask for one, especially where a wrong needs to be acknowledged for the sake of others. But do not make your peace depend on being vindicated. God knows who was right, and his opinion is the one that will stand. Holding out for a public admission often keeps a conflict alive long after the real problem is gone. Paul prayed for the outcome in which nobody would ever know he had been right.

verseByVerse.quote: For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s authority works only for the truth of the gospel, and nothing anyone does can finally work against that truth. He cannot turn it against people who are doing right, and his opponents cannot overthrow it.

Only for the truth. “The truth” means the gospel and God’s will. Paul’s authority is not a possession to use as he likes; it was given for one purpose and does not work for any other. If the Corinthians are doing right, he cannot act against them: not may not, but cannot.

Nobody can do anything against the truth. The wording invites a larger reading too: not the super-apostles, nor anyone else. The truth of God is not fragile. It has outlived better attackers in every century, and does not depend on the reputation of those carrying it, so the worst that can happen to a faithful person is to be misunderstood for a while. Gamaliel, of all people, saw it: if this undertaking is of man it will fail, but if it is of God you will not be able to overthrow it (Acts 5:38–39).

The truth before Pilate. The fullest proof of this verse stood in Pilate’s hall. Jesus said that he had come into the world to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37), and Pilate asked, “What is truth?” Then the world did everything it could against the one who is the truth (John 14:6): it killed him and sealed him in a tomb, and on the third day the stone was rolled away. That is why Paul can say flatly that nothing can be done against the truth: he knows what happened the one time the whole world tried.

The limits of church authority. A minister’s authority is borrowed, and extends exactly as far as the gospel does. Used to defend what the gospel does not teach, or to protect a man rather than serve a people, it has stopped being authority. So the question about a leader is not whether he has authority, but what he is using it for. Authority spent on truth is real however gently it is exercised; authority spent on anything else is only a show of authority.

Is it not arrogant to claim to have the truth? It would be, if Paul claimed to own it. He claims the opposite: he is under the truth and cannot act against it. The proud position is to make yourself the measure of what is true; to say the truth stands over you and judges your own teaching is to make yourself small. And the truth Paul means is not a theory of his own but a person, Jesus Christ, who died for those who opposed him and rose again. To believe in that truth is not to look down on anyone; it is to stand under the same truth as the person you speak to, and point him to the Saviour who has borne with you.

What if my church leaders ask me to do something against Scripture? Then you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), respectfully but firmly. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and no church may bind it to anything contrary to his word (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2). Make sure first that it is really a matter of Scripture, not preference; most disagreements with leaders are about wisdom, where you should be slow to resist and quick to trust. But if you are asked to sin, to keep silent about abuse, to deny what the Bible plainly teaches, or to give a leader the obedience due to Christ, decline graciously, explain why from Scripture, and seek counsel from other mature believers.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is glad to be the weak one if it means the church is strong, and what he prays for is their mending.

Glad when we are weak. Rejoicing, not resignation. After four chapters answering the charge that he is weak, he is delighted to be the weak one, provided they are strong.

Your restoration is what we pray for. “Restoration” (katartisis) is a rich word: being put right, mended, equipped. Its verb is used of mending nets, as James and John were doing when Jesus called them (Mark 1:19), and by Greek medical writers of setting a broken bone. That is what God does with a damaged church or Christian: not replacement or papering over, but mending. A mended net still shows where it tore, and it holds fish.

Prayer and command. In verse 11 the same word becomes a command, “Aim for restoration.” He prays for the mending and then tells them to work at it, which is how Scripture usually holds God’s work and ours together.

Weak so that you may be strong. Paul’s gladness has a source. The whole letter is built on an exchange: death is at work in us, but life in you (4:12); he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (8:9). That is the shape of Christ’s own work. He went down into weakness so that his people might be made strong, and out of the anguish of his soul he sees and is satisfied (Isaiah 53:11). A servant who is glad to be the weak one, so long as the church is strong, is wearing his Master’s likeness.

He mends them himself. Peter knew what it was to be mended. He had torn himself apart with three denials, and the risen Lord met him by the lake, made him breakfast and restored him with three questions (John 21:9–17). Years later Peter wrote that after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you (1 Peter 5:10), using the very word behind Paul’s prayer here. God does not replace his broken people with better ones; he mends them himself.

That is what a father says. A parent who has spent himself raising children is not diminished when they outgrow him; the point was to be surpassed. The opposite instinct is common in Christian work and rarely admitted: the counsellor whose people never quite manage without him, the leader who cannot delegate, the parent who needs to be needed. It looks like devotion and is a subtle self-service; the sign is whether you are glad when they no longer require you.

How do I help someone without making them dependent on me? Aim from the start at their growth, not your role. Point them to Christ and Scripture rather than yourself; teach them to pray and read the Bible for themselves; connect them to the wider church; give them responsibility as soon as they can carry it, and let them make small mistakes. And watch your own heart: if you feel a pang when someone you helped moves on, take it to God and ask him to make you glad. That gladness is the surest sign your help was love.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes his hard words now so that he will not have to use them in person, because the Lord gave him authority to build the church up, not to tear it down. Every severe sentence in this letter was written in the hope of sparing them a harder conversation.

Not severe. “Severe” comes from a verb for cutting off. They said he was bold at a distance and feeble in person (10:10); in fact he was bold at a distance so that he need not be severe in person, which is not cowardice but mercy. Anyone who must confront somebody can learn from it: say it early, and give the other person room to move before you are face to face. A warning that arrives in time is a kindness; the same words, kept until the confrontation, are only a verdict.

For building up. He said it at 10:8 and repeats it at the close, because it sets the purpose of all Christian authority, and the plainest test of power in a church: not whether the person has the right, but what is being built. Discipline that aims at restoration is building; the same discipline aimed at showing who is in charge is tearing down, though the words may be identical.

Not to condemn but to save. The authority is the Lord’s, and so is its purpose. God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). Even Christ’s rebukes serve that end: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19). He spoke his sharpest words to churches he meant to keep, and he warned before he acted, as Paul is doing here.

How should I receive correction? Quickly, humbly and gratefully, even when it hurts. Proverbs says that whoever heeds reproof is honoured, and that a wise man loves the one who reproves him (Proverbs 9:8; 13:18). Listen to the whole of it before defending yourself. Ask whether it is true, even partly, rather than whether it was fairly delivered. Take it to God, thank the person, since it is rarely easy to say, and act on it. Correction received in time is one of God’s great mercies.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Final Greetings and the Trinitarian Benediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter ends where all Paul’s hope for Corinth lies: in the God of love and peace, and in a blessing he does not divide. Five short appeals ask a quarrelling church to rejoice, mend, comfort one another, agree and live at peace, with the promise of God’s presence (v. 11). A holy kiss and greetings from other churches remind them that they are one family, and not the whole of it (vv. 12–13). Then the grace of Christ, the love of the Father and the fellowship of the Spirit are pronounced over them all (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology:
The benediction names the three persons acting distinctly and together, each giving to the believer. Why Christ is named first is taken up in the note on v. 14.

The fellowship of the Holy Spirit can mean the fellowship the Spirit creates among believers, or our sharing in the Spirit himself, or the Spirit as the one who brings us into fellowship with the Father and the Son. These do not compete; the Spirit does all three, and the life he shares with us shows itself in real love among believers.
verseByVerse.examples: A church has closed every service with this benediction for decades, and it has become a familiar ending. One Sunday the pastor pauses before it and asks what the congregation is about to receive: the grace that flows from Christ’s cross, the love of the Father that sent him, the fellowship the Spirit creates with God and among the people in the room. The benediction is not a farewell but a sending out under the blessing of the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends with five short commands that would heal a divided church, and with the promise that the God of love and peace will be with them.

Finally, brothers, rejoice. After a whole letter of defence, irony and warning, he calls them brothers. “Rejoice” was also the ordinary farewell, but here it is a command, said to a quarrelling, suspicious congregation by a man who had been flogged five times (11:24).

What it means to rejoice. The Greek word (chairō) shares its root with the word for grace (charis): joy is the natural response to grace received. It is not a mood worked up or a cheerful face, but turning your heart towards what God is and has done, and being glad in him. So it can be commanded: you cannot order a feeling, but you can choose where to look, and gladness follows the looking. It can live alongside tears. Paul described himself “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (6:10), and the prophet could say, with the fields bare and the stalls empty, “yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation” (Habakkuk 3:18). Christian joy does not deny the trouble. It rests on something the trouble cannot touch.

Aim for restoration. The mending he prayed for in verse 9 he now tells them to work at. Mend the nets. Set the bone.

Comfort one another. The great word of the letter appears one last time (1:3–4): it opened with comfort coming down from God and closes with comfort passing between believers. That comfort did not start with them. Paul told them at the outset where it comes from: as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (1:5). Because he suffered, his people are never comforted by someone who does not understand; and because he lives, the comfort never runs dry.

Agree with one another, live in peace. Literally, think the same thing (Philippians 2:2): not uniformity of opinion, but the shared mind of people pulling in one direction, which a church loses first when it sorts itself into parties. “Live in peace” is the plainest of the five and the hardest: end the quarrels (12:20).

And the God of love and peace will be with you. The promise comes last, but it is not a wage: obedience does not earn God’s presence. Yet a church at peace knows and feels it, and a quarrelling church does not, though he has not left it. The title, found only here in the New Testament, names exactly what that congregation lacked, and love and peace had to come from him, because they were never going to come from the Corinthians. He is not a distant reward for peaceful people; he is the one who made peace by the blood of his Son’s cross, when we were his enemies.

How can I rejoice when my church is a mess? By rejoicing in the Lord rather than in the church’s condition (Philippians 4:4). Paul commands joy to a church that has broken his heart, because the grounds of joy are in Christ, who has not changed, is still building his church, and will present her spotless in the end. Thank him for the faithful people in your church, and do your part in the mending. Joy is not pretending things are fine; it is knowing that the Lord is greater than the mess.

Does agreeing with one another mean I must never disagree? No. Christians will differ on many matters of judgment, and Paul himself disagreed sharply with Barnabas (Acts 15:39). What Paul forbids is factions, rivalry and the refusal to seek common ground. Disagree honestly and kindly, keep the gospel at the centre, do not let disagreement curdle into contempt, and give way on what is not essential for the sake of peace. As far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18).

In everyday life. Most church peace is made in small moments: the chair you take next to someone you clashed with, the kind word after a hard meeting, the decision not to replay an old argument on the drive home. If there is someone you have not spoken to properly since a disagreement, the first move may be yours.

Uncertain wording. Two of the commands can be read more than one way, because the Greek forms may be passive or not. “Aim for restoration” (katartizesthe) may mean “work at mending things” or “let yourselves be mended”, and some translate it “mend your ways”. “Comfort one another” (parakaleisthe) may mean “encourage one another”, “be comforted”, or “listen to my appeal”. The sense is close in every case: let God and one another put right what has gone wrong, and receive what Paul has urged.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to greet one another as family, and to remember that they belong to a church far bigger than their own congregation.

A holy kiss. Paul gives this instruction in four letters (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26). A kiss on the cheek was the ordinary greeting between family and close friends, saying: this person is one of mine. The word “holy” guards it: a genuinely family greeting, pure and without any other intent, a caution evidently needed then and now.

Across every line. What makes it worth a command is who was greeting whom. In a Corinthian gathering the kiss crossed every line the city cared about: a slave greeted his owner, a labourer a householder, a Jew a Greek. And Paul tells this particular church to do it: the one that had sorted itself into factions, taken its members to court and humiliated the poor at the Lord’s Table. It is very hard to greet someone as family in front of the congregation while carrying a grudge against them, which is presumably part of the point.

All the saints greet you. Paul is most likely writing from Macedonia (7:5; 9:2–4), and he sends greetings from believers the Corinthians have never met: probably the Macedonian churches such as Philippi and Thessalonica, poor and afflicted, whose gifts had supported his work in Corinth (11:9). A troubled congregation is not alone, and not the whole story. The church has never been the size of the room you are standing in.

One in Christ Jesus. The dividing lines disappeared in that room because everyone in it had been received by the same Lord on the same terms. There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, no male and female, for all are one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28). He himself is our peace, who has broken down the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). The holy kiss was not a social experiment, but what people do who have been forgiven by the same blood and adopted into the same family: they greet each other as kin, because in him they are.

Kissed before he could confess. A sinful woman wept over Jesus’ feet and would not stop kissing them, and he sent her away forgiven (Luke 7:38, 45–48). And in the story Jesus told of a lost son coming home, the father saw him a long way off, ran, embraced him and kissed him before the boy could say a word of his rehearsed confession (Luke 15:20). That is the welcome behind every holy kiss in Corinth: a Father who runs to meet the returning, and a Son who received sinners at a cost no one else could pay.

What it does not mean. A literal kiss is not required in every culture; the form is not the command. But the substance is not optional, and it is easily lost. A congregation can hold sound doctrine and never make warm, unembarrassed contact across the lines its society draws, and then something the New Testament assumed would be visible every week has quietly disappeared.

What does a holy kiss look like in my church? Whatever warm greeting your culture uses within families, given to fellow believers, especially those you would not naturally greet: a real conversation with the visitor nobody knows, an embrace for the widow who sits alone, a word for the person you clashed with at the last meeting. Respect people’s comfort, and keep every gesture appropriate and above reproach, especially with children and between men and women. The holy kiss is family affection made visible; make sure no one leaves your church on a Sunday feeling like a stranger.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s last word is a blessing: the grace of Christ, the love of the Father and the fellowship of the Spirit, pronounced over the whole church without exception. It is the fullest benediction in the New Testament: three persons, three gifts, one sentence.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul closes every letter with grace; here alone he opens the blessing out into all three persons, and names Christ first, which is unusual for him. Grace has been at the heart of the letter (8:9; 12:9): the free, undeserved favour shown in Christ to people who have earned the opposite. It comes first because it is through Christ’s grace that we come to know the Father’s love.

And the love of God. The Father’s love is the source of everything (John 3:16; Romans 5:8). Christ did not persuade a reluctant Father to love us; the love came first and sent him. John puts it plainly: love does not begin with our loving God but with God loving us and sending his Son as the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). A propitiation is a sacrifice that absorbs the holy anger sin deserves and so removes it, and here the Father himself provided it.

And the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. “Fellowship” (koinōnia) means sharing, communion, having something in common. It means both our fellowship with the Spirit, who gives us a share in God himself, and the fellowship among believers that the Spirit creates, making a collection of unrelated people into a body. The second was precisely what this church needed.

Be with you all. All of them: the ones who had stayed loyal, and the ones who had listened to his enemies; the man who had insulted him publicly; the people who had let it happen and said nothing; those who had not yet repented, whom he expected to have to mourn over. Paul has one blessing and he does not divide it.

The whole letter in one sentence. The letter began with a man who had despaired of life itself and found God to be the Father of mercies; it has gone through tears and floggings, a thorn never removed, a church that broke his heart and mended, and an apostle lowered from a window in a basket. And each of the three gifts has been its subject. Grace was what Paul was told was sufficient. Love was what he was accused of lacking. Fellowship was what had broken down between him and them.

The Trinity. This is one of the clearest witnesses to the Trinity in Scripture. Written about twenty-five years after the resurrection, it shows Christians within a generation naming Father, Son and Spirit together as the one source of blessing, the faith the church later set out as one God in three persons. It does not mean three gods, nor one God wearing three masks in turn; it means one God who eternally exists as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God and each truly distinct, into whose one name believers are baptised (Matthew 28:19).

Never rationed to the deserving. Before there was a world, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit lived in perfect fellowship, needing nothing. This last sentence opens that life to quarrelling, suspicious, half-repentant Corinthians, and it closes on “you all”, because the blessing of God was never rationed to the deserving, and he has not changed.

Why does the Trinity matter for ordinary Christians? Because it is the shape of our salvation and our prayers. The Father planned it and sent the Son; the Son accomplished it, living, dying and rising for us; the Spirit applies it, uniting us to Christ and one another. Without the three persons there would be no Son sent to stand in our place before the Father, and no Spirit to bring us home. We pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. And because God has always been a fellowship of love within himself, love is not something he needed us for; it is what he is, and what he shares with us freely.

What is a benediction, and does it actually do anything? A benediction is a word of blessing spoken over God’s people in his name, as the priests blessed Israel with “The LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24–26). It is not magic, and does not work apart from faith, but it is more than a polite wish: a declaration of what God gives in Christ, spoken by his word, which he is pleased to use. When you hear it, do not reach for your coat. Receive it, believe it, and go out under it.

In everyday life. Pray this blessing slowly, one phrase at a time, over someone you find difficult in your church. Paul did not divide the blessing, and neither should you.
verseByVerse.note: This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is still widely used to close Christian worship.

parallels.desc: the priestly blessing

13.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>2</sup>I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—<sup>3</sup>since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.<sup>4</sup>For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.<sup>5</sup>Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!<sup>6</sup>I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test.<sup>7</sup>But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.<sup>8</sup>For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.<sup>9</sup>For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.<sup>10</sup>For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.<sup>11</sup>Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.<sup>12</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss.<sup>13</sup>All the saints greet you.<sup>14</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

keyVerse.quote: For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers the whole letter into one sentence. The crucified and risen Christ is both weakness and power, and those who are in him share both, so Paul’s frailty is no evidence against his apostleship and gentleness is no evidence that Christ is weak. It is the answer to the Corinthians’ demand for proof, and the pattern of every faithful Christian life.

13.reflection:
Paul insists that every charge be established by two or three witnesses (v. 1), yet he will not leave unrepented sin alone. How can a church, or a family, take wrongs seriously without acting on rumour or joining the online crowd?

Verse 5 tells us to examine ourselves, and the test is whether Jesus Christ is in us. How does looking for Christ differ from looking for enough holiness? When has self-examination helped you, and when has it turned into unhealthy introspection?

Paul prays that the Corinthians will do right even if it leaves him looking a failure (v. 7), and is glad to be weak if they are strong (v. 9). Where do you find it hardest to let go of being proved right, or of being needed?

The letter ends with the grace of Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit pronounced over all the church, the loyal and the difficult alike (v. 14). How might receiving that blessing change the way you treat the people in your church you find hardest?
